api/NanoQL.Experimental.Distribution.htm.summary: Class Distribution Namespace NanoQL.Experimental Assembly NanoQL.dll A discretized probability density and cumulative probability: buckets of a range, each holding a density, an average and the cumulated and excess probabilities. [Experimental("NQL0001")] [WorkingType] public sealed class Distribution Inheritance object Distribution Inherited Members object.GetType() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks A mutable working type (§2.7), QuantLib's API: values or densities are added, then Normalize(), which the reads call, computes the cumulative and excess probabilities. The density is uniform within a bucket, as CumulativeDensity(double)'s interpolation reads it. QuantLib's default constructor leaves the size uninitialized; a distribution here is built of its buckets. Three members depart from QuantLib's, each fixed on that density (Divergences/DistributionMembersTests.cs): CumulativeDensity(double) in the first bucket interpolates from 0, where QuantLib's reads the cumulative at index −1 (distribution.cpp:220-230); ExpectedShortfall(double) integrates the density above the quantile, where QuantLib's sums the left edges from the bucket after the quantile's over a denominator leaving its first term out (5.625 and 9 for a uniform's 5.25 and 9.5, :328-341); and Tranche(double, double) keeps the mass above the detachment in the last bucket, where QuantLib's sets the last cumulative to 1 before computing the last density from it, 0 (a total probability of 0.7, :236-284). A tranched distribution's buckets end at the tranche's width D − A: the bucket spanning it is uniform up to it, and the buckets Tranche(double, double) truncates to it, the mass above the detachment among them, are an atom there, as CumulativeDensity(double) and ExpectedShortfall(double) read them. QuantLib's keeps their widths, which its left-edge shortfall never reads; the uniform shortfall read past the tranche (3.5 for 3 at 0.5 on a uniform's [2, 5] tranche). Each instrument values in the context's base currency and unit, CommoditySettings, QuantLib's CommoditySettings, converting its prices and quantities with the context's UnitOfMeasureConversions and ExchangeRates. A unit conversion factor here is the value of one unit of the first unit in the second, the conversion's own Convert(Quantity) of a unit quantity, whichever way the conversion is stored; a quantity converts to the base unit by the factor from its unit to the base, and a price, money per unit, by the factor from the base to its unit. QuantLib's factor is the stored conversion's whatever its orientation, and its call sites multiply a quantity by the factor from the base to its unit and a price by the factor from its unit to the base, so one of the two is inverted: a payer vanilla swap on 1,000 gallons a month at a 0.5 spread prices 882,000 there, 42² times its value, 500, here; on the base unit every factor is 1 and the prices are QuantLib's (Divergences/EnergyUnitConversionTests.cs). api/NanoQL.Experimental.EnergySwap.html.summary: Class EnergySwap Namespace NanoQL.Experimental Assembly NanoQL.dll The base of energy swaps: a calendar, a pay and a receive currency, and pricing periods. [Experimental("NQL0001")] public abstract class EnergySwap : EnergyCommodity Inheritance object Instrument Commodity EnergyCommodity EnergySwap Derived EnergyBasisSwap EnergyVanillaSwap Inherited Members EnergyCommodity.CalculateFxConversionFactor(Currency, Currency, Date, EvaluationContext) EnergyCommodity.CalculateUomConversionFactor(CommodityType, UnitOfMeasure, UnitOfMeasure, EvaluationContext) EnergyCommodity.CalculateUnitCost(CommodityType, CommodityUnitCost, Date, EvaluationContext) EnergyCommodity.CalculateSecondaryCostAmounts(CommodityType, double, Date, EvaluationContext) Commodity.SecondaryCosts Instrument.SetupExpired() Instrument.Validate() Instrument.FetchResults(InstrumentResults) object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks An extension point: EnergyVanillaSwap and EnergyBasisSwap derive from it. A swap prices each pricing day of each period on its calendar, from the adjusted start, reading its index's stored fixing up to the index's last quote date and its forward price after it. The fixing is read as the index reads it, so a day the index doesn't fix is refused ("… is not a valid fixing date"): a swap's calendar must be its index's on its fixed days, as QuantLib's. Each payment is made in the currency of the leg the net amount goes through, the receive leg's when the discounted amount is positive, at that currency's exchange rate, and discounted on that leg's curve. QuantLib pairs the payment's currency with the other leg's rate in the basis swap and a payer vanilla swap, and a receiver vanilla swap's payment never changes currency, its pay-receive flag 0 where −1 would switch it (Divergences/EnergySwapPaymentTests.cs), so only a receiver's payments to the holder are QuantLib's; the NPV, in the base currency, is the same either way. Quantity sums the periods' amounts under the first period's unit, as QuantLib's, right for periods in one unit. api/NanoQL.Experimental.ExtendedBinomial.summary: Class ExtendedBinomialTree<T> Namespace NanoQL.Experimental Assembly NanoQL.dll The time-dependent binomial tree base: two branches from each node, node index of column i going to nodes index and index + 1, its moves read from the process at each step's time: QuantLib's ExtendedBinomialTree. [Experimental("NQL0001")] public abstract class ExtendedBinomialTree<T> : Tree where T : ExtendedBinomialTree<T> Type Parameters T The derived tree, QuantLib's curiously recurring parameter. Inheritance object Tree ExtendedBinomialTree<T> Derived ExtendedEqualJumpsBinomialTree<T> ExtendedEqualProbabilitiesBinomialTree<T> ExtendedJoshi4 ExtendedLeisenReimer ExtendedTian Inherited Members Tree.Underlying(int, int) Tree.Probability(int, int, int) Tree.Columns object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks Immutable once built, on its process, which it keeps. A node at step i is built from the process's drift and volatility at tᵢ, read as if they held for the whole history to that step, so the tree's spread at step i is that of a constant volatility σ(tᵢ), not the integrated one. On constant parameters the tree is exact, and every QuantLib engine flattens its process to constant parameters before it builds a tree (BinomialVanillaEngine), so through an engine the extended trees equal the standard ones; on a tree built directly on a time-dependent process the per-step reads are an approximation that doesn't converge to the time-dependent price. QuantLib's design, kept (Conventions/ExtendedTreeTimeDependenceTests.cs). An extension point, as in QuantLib: the equal-probabilities and equal-jumps bases and the Tian, Leisen-Reimer and Joshi trees derive from it. api/NanoQL.Experimental.ExtendedBlackSch.summary: Class ExtendedBlackScholesMertonProcess Namespace NanoQL.Experimental Assembly NanoQL.dll A Black-Scholes-Merton process on its Black volatility, stepped by a built-in scheme: QuantLib's ExtendedBlackScholesMertonProcess. [Experimental("NQL0001")] public sealed class ExtendedBlackScholesMertonProcess : GeneralizedBlackScholesProcess Inheritance object StochasticProcess StochasticProcess1D GeneralizedBlackScholesProcess ExtendedBlackScholesMertonProcess Inherited Members GeneralizedBlackScholesProcess.Apply(double, double) GeneralizedBlackScholesProcess.Expectation(double, double, double) GeneralizedBlackScholesProcess.StdDeviation(double, double, double) GeneralizedBlackScholesProcess.Variance(double, double, double) GeneralizedBlackScholesProcess.Time(Date) GeneralizedBlackScholesProcess.X0 GeneralizedBlackScholesProcess.StateVariable GeneralizedBlackScholesProcess.DividendYield GeneralizedBlackScholesProcess.RiskFreeRate GeneralizedBlackScholesProcess.BlackVolatility GeneralizedBlackScholesProcess.LocalVolatility StochasticProcess1D.InitialValues() StochasticProcess1D.Drift(double, Vector) StochasticProcess1D.Diffusion(double, Vector) StochasticProcess1D.Expectation(double, Vector, double) StochasticProcess1D.StdDeviation(double, Vector, double) StochasticProcess1D.Covariance(double, Vector, double) StochasticProcess1D.Evolve(double, Vector, double, Vector) StochasticProcess1D.Apply(Vector, Vector) StochasticProcess1D.Size StochasticProcess.InitialValues(Span<double>) StochasticProcess.Evolve(double, ReadOnlySpan<double>, double, ReadOnlySpan<double>, Span<double>) StochasticProcess.Factors object.GetType() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks The diffusion is the Black volatility at the time and the asset value, extrapolated, and the drift the curves' forward rates over the next 1e-4 of a year less half its square, as QuantLib's. The step is the scheme's, in the log price. Three fixes (Divergences/ExtendedBlackScholesProcessTests.cs). Milstein's correction is the log price's, ½σ·∂σ/∂ln S·(ΔW² − 1)Δt, ∂σ/∂ln S the Black volatility's central difference over a log strike of ±1e-4, 0 on a strike-independent volatility, where the step is the log-Euler one; QuantLib adds the asset's own, ½σ²(ΔW² − 1)Δt, to the log price, its mean 1.25e-3 high a step at Δt 0.25 and σ 0.4. Euler's step, and the predictor-corrector's predictor, are the log-Euler step on the process's drift and diffusion; QuantLib's centre on the asset's mean, x₀e^((r−q)Δt), which lacks the −σ²Δt/2 (2.02e-2 high a step at Δt 0.25 and σ 0.4) and refuses a strike-dependent volatility ("not implemented"). The corrector is QuantLib's on a strike-independent volatility. On one that depends on the strike, QuantLib's corrector, its diffusion the mean of the two ends' on the same increment, is Heun's scheme, which converges to the Stratonovich equation, ½σ·∂σ/∂ln S above the log drift: on a SABR smile its error stops falling with the step, E[S_T] 0.09% low; nanoql's takes each end's drift less ½σ·∂σ/∂ln S, the Itô predictor-corrector, which converges at order 1 there and keeps QuantLib's bits where ∂σ/∂ln S is 0. On flat curves and a flat volatility all three are then the exact step, and on a smile they converge to the process at their orders, Euler's ½ and the others' 1. api/NanoQL.Experimental.FFTEngine.html.title: Class FFTEngine | nanoql
api/NanoQL.Experimental.FFTEngine.html.summary: Class FFTEngine Namespace NanoQL.Experimental Assembly NanoQL.dll The fast-Fourier-transform engine for European options (Carr and Madan, 1998, "Option valuation using the fast Fourier transform", Journal of Computational Finance 2, 61-73): one transform prices every option of an expiry. [Experimental("NQL0001")] public abstract class FFTEngine Inheritance object FFTEngine Derived FFTVanillaEngine FFTVarianceGammaEngine Inherited Members object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks An extension point, as in QuantLib: an engine for another model derives it and returns, for each expiry, the model's state there: its characteristic function, its discount factors and the strip of exponents with a finite moment. Immutable: QuantLib's cache of precalculated prices is the list form's result, so Calculate(IReadOnlyList<VanillaOption>, EvaluationContext) returns each option's results in the list's order, QuantLib's precalculate followed by each option's NPV(), one transform per expiry on the grid QuantLib's map would hold; a single option is a list of one, QuantLib's uncached route. An expired option gets its expired results without joining a transform. QuantLib's update() and clone() aren't ported: there is no state to clear or separate. Documented divergences (Divergences/VarianceGammaFftTests.cs). The grid is sized from the largest |log K| of the expiry's strikes and at least 2^14 points, QuantLib's size wherever its own is at least 2^14 (every QuantLib case), where QuantLib's size is undefined when every strike is below e^(−λ), and below 2^14 points, as for any strike between 1 and about 60, its frequency spacing 2π/(λn) is too coarse for the transform to price. The damping is QuantLib's 1.25, and its grid, wherever E[S^2.25] is finite (every Black-Scholes market, every QuantLib case), the grid doubled at the same spacing until two successive grids agree within 5e-5 of the spot at every strike, QuantLib's prices where its own grid agrees with the first doubling and the finer grid's where a later one agrees, up to 2^22, past which a refusal: QuantLib's period λn aliases the damped call's tail once σ√T passes about 1.2, an at-the-money call pricing −298.9 against 66.80 at σ√T 2; the same refusal where the damped tail's growth, ln E[S^2.25] − 2.25 ln E[S] (α(α + 1)σ²T/2 under Black-Scholes), passes 18, σ√T 3.58, where the recovered prices carry a rounding error no grid changes, so two grids agree while both are off; otherwise half the strip's upper bound with the grid doubled until α·nλ/2 ≥ 20, while the grid stays within 2^22 points; past that the put side, α + 1 = max(u_lo/2, −0.25) inside the strip's lower part, the grid doubled from QuantLib's until two successive grids agree within 1e-8 of each strike's larger of call and put, up to 2^22, the calls by QuantLib's parity; past that a refusal. api/NanoQL.Experimental.FireflyAlgorithm.title: Class FireflyAlgorithm | nanoql
api/NanoQL.Experimental.FireflyAlgorithm.summary: Class FireflyAlgorithm Namespace NanoQL.Experimental Assembly NanoQL.dll The firefly algorithm, with a differential evolution subpopulation: QuantLib's FireflyAlgorithm. [Experimental("NQL0001")] public sealed class FireflyAlgorithm : OptimizationMethod Inheritance object OptimizationMethod FireflyAlgorithm Inherited Members OptimizationMethod.Minimize(Problem, EndCriteria) OptimizationMethod.Minimize(ProblemState, EndCriteria) object.GetType() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks M fireflies explore the N-dimensional parameter space, each moved by its attraction to the brighter ones (the intensity) and a random walk: X_{i,j}^{k+1} = X_{i,j}^k + I(X^k)_{i,j} + RandomWalk_{i,j}^k, the intensity monotonic. The population is sorted each iteration and split: the M − M_de brightest move as fireflies, the M_de others by the differential evolution operator Y^{k+1} = X_best^k + F (X_{r1}^k − X_{r2}^k), each coordinate crossed over with probability C (one always), and accepted where it improves. With M_de = M it is a differential evolution optimizer whose base is a random member. The algorithm stops at its iterations or after its stationary iterations. Reference: A. Abdullah et al., "A New Hybrid Firefly Algorithm for Complex and Nonlinear Problem", Advances in Intelligent and Soft Computing 151, pp. 673-680, 2012. The population starts on a Sobol sequence within the bounds, its seed the algorithm's: QuantLib's is 0, the clock, read only past the 32 dimensions of Jaeckel's direction integers, so the bits are QuantLib's up to there. A problem's constraint is never empty, so QuantLib's refusal of one doesn't arise. The differential evolution's integers are std::uniform_int_distribution's on a std::mt19937, drawn as MSVC draws them, and its crossover's uniforms a Mersenne Twister's, both on the seed, which is required: QuantLib's default seeds from the clock. Immutable: each minimization copies the intensity and the walk and starts the generators from the seed, where QuantLib's continues them. Fixes (Divergences/FireflyAlgorithmTests.cs): each moved firefly's new value goes to its own place in the sorted population, where QuantLib's writes it at the place its index names, another firefly's, so the population's values and positions part after the first move; pure differential evolution takes a copy of its random base, where QuantLib's assigns through a reference and overwrites the best firefly with it; and fewer than three differential evolution members are refused, since three distinct members can't be drawn from fewer, where QuantLib's draws loop forever. The differential evolution's donors, and pure differential evolution's base, are drawn in [Mfa, M − 1] and read as fireflies' labels, the order of the Sobol start, not as places in the sorted population, as QuantLib reads them; its header doesn't say which members it means. So in a hybrid the donors are the fireflies labelled Mfa to M − 1, which may be moving as fireflies, and a target may be its own donor; in pure differential evolution the two readings agree. The three-member refusal follows the label reading. api/NanoQL.Experimental.GaussNonCentralC.summary: Class GaussNonCentralChiSquaredPolynomial Namespace NanoQL.Experimental Assembly NanoQL.dll The orthogonal polynomial of the non-central χ² distribution with ν degrees of freedom and non-centrality λ, for Gauss quadrature on that distribution: QuantLib's GaussNonCentralChiSquaredPolynomial. [Experimental("NQL0001")] public sealed class GaussNonCentralChiSquaredPolynomial : MomentBasedGaussianPolynomial Inheritance object GaussianOrthogonalPolynomial MomentBasedGaussianPolynomial GaussNonCentralChiSquaredPolynomial Inherited Members MomentBasedGaussianPolynomial.Mu_0() GaussianOrthogonalPolynomial.LogW(double) GaussianOrthogonalPolynomial.Value(int, double) GaussianOrthogonalPolynomial.WeightedValue(int, double) object.GetType() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks QuantLib sums each ordinary moment's closed form in double and runs MomentBasedGaussianPolynomial's recursion in double; the map from ordinary moments to the recurrence is ill-conditioned (Gautschi), so at QuantLib's own CLV cases its 14 nodes are 2.6e-2 and 0.61 relative off the exact ones, at λ 50 and 75 Boost refuses a negative node and at λ 100 it doesn't return. Here the moments are exact, from the cumulants 2^(j−1)(j−1)!(ν + jλ) on ν and λ as the binary fractions they are, QuantLib's recursion runs on those exact rationals, and α and β are rounded to double once: the nodes are within a few ulps of the exact ones at every λ. QuantLib's recursion is a template on its number type for this, tested on a multi-precision type; exact rationals are that precision's limit (Divergences/NonCentralChiSquaredPolynomialTests.cs). Moment(int) is the exact moment rounded once. As QuantLib's, the moments stop at the 27th, so a rule takes at most 14 nodes. The recursion's values are memoised as the base memoises its own, under a lock; a 14-node rule's numbers reach about 9,000 bits. Its parameters are α's values at its speed dates and σ's at its volatility dates, in that order, interpolated over their times from the curve's reference date (InterpolationParameter). A, B and the bond options are Hull-White's with time-dependent parameters (Gurrieri, Nakabayashi and Wong, 2009), on QuantLib's numerical integrals of α and σ, and valid only where f is the identity: at a constant α and σ they are within those integrals' error of HullWhite's closed forms (4.6e-4 relative on a bond option at α 0.1), QuantLib's design, kept. Dynamics() refuses, as QuantLib's does: the general model has no process, and HwDynamics() gives Hull-White's at α(0) and σ(0), with the analytical fitting parameter φ(t) = f(t) + ½[σ(1 − e^(−αt))/α]², f the instantaneous forward. api/NanoQL.Experimental.HaganIrregularSw.title: Class HaganIrregularSwaptionEngine | nanoql
api/NanoQL.Experimental.HaganIrregularSw.summary: Class HaganIrregularSwaptionEngine Namespace NanoQL.Experimental Assembly NanoQL.dll The engine for European irregular swaptions by super-replication with a basket of vanilla swaptions: QuantLib's HaganIrregularSwaptionEngine. [Experimental("NQL0001")] public static class HaganIrregularSwaptionEngine Inheritance object HaganIrregularSwaptionEngine Inherited Members object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks References: P.S. Hagan, "Methodology for Callable Swaps and Bermudan 'Exercise into Swaptions'"; P.J. Hunt and J.E. Kennedy, "Implied interest rate pricing models", Finance Stochast. 2, 275-293 (1998). A static class in the engines' form. The floating leg's spread moves to the fixed leg first, the fixed rates lowered by the rate whose fixed-leg value is the spread's; the swap then splits into vanilla swaps ending at each fixed payment date, whose weights solve a linear system (by SVD) and whose rates are shifted by a λ that Bisection finds in [−0.5, 0.5] to 1e-8 so that the basket's value matches the swap's; the price is the sum of the weighted vanilla swaptions, each by BachelierSwaptionEngine on a normal volatility. The basket is a working object per call. As QuantLib warns, a spread isn't handled exactly, and the swaptions assume that the exercise date is the swap's start. On a regular swap the replication is close to the Bachelier engine's price, not equal to it: within 5.1e-7 relative on a five-year swap a year forward at a flat normal 1%, QuantLib's values to 12 digits, and 7.5e-5 out of the money on a four-year swap at 0.8%. QuantLib's engine takes the discount curve as an optional handle and dereferences it, so an empty one throws; here it is required. Methods Calculate(IrregularSwaption, EvaluationContext, SwaptionVolatilityStructure, YieldTermStructure) Prices a European irregular swaption. public static InstrumentResults Calculate(IrregularSwaption swaption, EvaluationContext context, SwaptionVolatilityStructure volatilityStructure, YieldTermStructure termStructure) Parameters swaption IrregularSwaption The swaption. context EvaluationContext The evaluation context. volatilityStructure SwaptionVolatilityStructure The swaption volatility, normal. termStructure YieldTermStructure The discount curve. Returns InstrumentResults The swaption's value: the expired results when the swaption has expired. Exceptions ArgumentNullException An argument is null. NanoQLException A fixed cash flow isn't a fixed-rate coupon or a floating one an Ibor coupon, the swaption isn't European, the volatility isn't normal, λ can't be bracketed, or a leg can't be priced.

api/NanoQL.Experimental.HybridSimulatedA.summary: Class HybridSimulatedAnnealing<TSampler, TProbability, TTemperature, TReannealing> Namespace NanoQL.Experimental Assembly NanoQL.dll The hybrid simulated annealing: a sampler draws each new point, a probability accepts it, a temperature schedule cools the dimensions and a reannealing rescales their steps, with a local optimizer at each new or best point: QuantLib's HybridSimulatedAnnealing. [Experimental("NQL0001")] public class HybridSimulatedAnnealing<TSampler, TProbability, TTemperature, TReannealing> : OptimizationMethod where TSampler : IAnnealingSampler<TSampler> where TProbability : IAnnealingProbability<TProbability> where TTemperature : IAnnealingTemperature<TTemperature> where TReannealing : IAnnealingReannealing<TReannealing> Type Parameters TSampler The sampler. TProbability The probability. TTemperature The temperature schedule. TReannealing The reannealing. Inheritance object OptimizationMethod HybridSimulatedAnnealing<TSampler, TProbability, TTemperature, TReannealing> Derived GaussianSimulatedAnnealing LogNormalSimulatedAnnealing MirrorGaussianSimulatedAnnealing Inherited Members OptimizationMethod.Minimize(Problem, EndCriteria) OptimizationMethod.Minimize(ProblemState, EndCriteria) object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks The sampler provides a density, on the current point, for the parameters; the probability decides whether the new point is accepted; the temperature is a schedule T(k) over the iteration k, which the sampler and the probability read; the reannealing, a departure from Boltzmann annealing, rescales k for each dimension to improve convergence. The hybrid is the local optimizer, run at every accepted point or at every new best point. A trial whose evaluation throws is skipped, as QuantLib's catch(...) skips it. It stops at its iterations, after its stationary iterations, or when every temperature is below the end temperature, then returning None, as QuantLib's does. Immutable: it copies its functors at construction, and each minimization copies them again, so each starts from their state at construction, where QuantLib's continues from the last minimization's. api/NanoQL.Experimental.IntegralHestonVa.title: Class IntegralHestonVarianceOptionEngine | nanoql
api/NanoQL.Experimental.IntegralHestonVa.summary: Class IntegralHestonVarianceOptionEngine Namespace NanoQL.Experimental Assembly NanoQL.dll The integral engine for variance options under Heston: the realized variance's law inverted by Bailey and Swarztrauber's fractional transform (see <http://www.econ.univpm.it/recchioni/finance/w4/>). [Experimental("NQL0001")] public static class IntegralHestonVarianceOptionEngine Inheritance object IntegralHestonVarianceOptionEngine Inherited Members object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks A call has QuantLib's one-dimensional integral. The engine reads the risk-free curve on the model's clock, the earliest reference date of the process's curves on the risk-free day counter, the maturity's time from it and the rate the curve accrues to the maturity per unit of that time, where QuantLib measures the time from the evaluation date; on curves dated on the evaluation date QuantLib's numbers stand. Documented divergences (Divergences/IntegralHestonVarianceOptionTests.cs). A put is the call's integral without its forward term, the integrated variance's mean less the strike, by parity, and other payoffs are refused, where QuantLib sums any payoff but a call against the integrated variance's density on 4,096 points of spacing √(2π)/64, about one standard deviation of it: QuantLib's put case prices 0.0466796 against 0.0465915, a forward-start put 2.6% low, a cash-or-nothing put 13% to 24% low and above 1 at a strike past the distribution. The process's dividend curve isn't read, as the integrated variance's law doesn't depend on the drift, where QuantLib refuses a process whose dividend handle isn't empty. An option starting after the clock's origin is priced on the variance integrated from its start: each integrand is affine in the variance at the start, so its expectation over that variance's non-central χ² law from v₀ is the CIR transform, E[e^(Bv_s)] = (1 − 2cB)^(−d/2) exp(Bv₀e^(−κs)/(1 − 2cB)), c = σ²(1 − e^(−κs))/(4κ), d = 4κθ/σ², and the mean term takes E[v_s] = θ + (v₀ − θ)e^(−κs), where QuantLib prices every option as starting today; a seasoned option, its start before the evaluation date, is refused, as QuantLib's header says. Methods Calculate(VarianceOption, EvaluationContext, HestonProcess) Prices a variance option under Heston. public static InstrumentResults Calculate(VarianceOption option, EvaluationContext context, HestonProcess process) Parameters option VarianceOption The variance option. context EvaluationContext The evaluation context. process HestonProcess The Heston process; its dividend curve isn't read. Returns InstrumentResults The option's results: the value; the expired results when the option has expired. Exceptions ArgumentNullException An argument is null. NanoQLException The payoff isn't a plain-vanilla call or put ("this engine prices plain-vanilla calls and puts only"), the option starts before the evaluation date ("this engine does not manage seasoned variance options"), 2κθ/σ² − 1 isn't positive ("this parameter must be greater than zero"), or the integral leaves an imaginary part.

QuantLib's engine takes the basket as homogeneous, hard-coded: the recovery is read from the basket's first name for all, and its branch for unequal recoveries is never taken, so it isn't ported. A discount before the discount curve's reference date is 1, and a default probability before a default curve's 0, where QuantLib's reads refuse them ("negative time"). A realized default lowers the order the basket's probabilities read; once the realized defaults reach it, the contract is triggered. The year-on-year curve is bootstrapped linearly on year-on-year swap helpers every year from the nominal curve's reference date to the last maturity, each quoting the swap rate at its maturity, then checked to reprice them to 1e-5. Everything is computed at construction (Create(int, Period, YoYInflationIndex, CPIInterpolationType, YieldTermStructure, DayCounter, Calendar, BusinessDayConvention, IReadOnlyList<double>, IReadOnlyList<double>, IReadOnlyList<Period>, Matrix, Matrix, EvaluationContext, TInterpolator2D, TInterpolator1D)), the curve's helpers dated and priced in the context given, as QuantLib computes at construction and again on a change. Two fixes (Divergences/YoYCapFloorPriceSurfaceTests.cs): each swap rate's date is its own maturity's option date, where QuantLib's takes the date of the maturity counted among the valid ones, another maturity's once one fails the intersection (yoycapfloortermpricesurface.hpp:506-508); and the repricing check reads each helper's own maturity, where QuantLib's reads the surface's reference date plus whole years while the helpers sit on the nominal curve's. With every maturity valid and the two reference dates equal, both are QuantLib's. api/NanoQL.Experimental.InterpolatedYoYO.summary: Class InterpolatedYoYOptionletStripper<TInterpolator> Namespace NanoQL.Experimental Assembly NanoQL.dll Strips year-on-year optionlet volatilities along each strike by bootstrapping an interpolated curve on the price surface's caps or floors: QuantLib's InterpolatedYoYOptionletStripper. [Experimental("NQL0001")] public class InterpolatedYoYOptionletStripper<TInterpolator> : YoYOptionletStripper where TInterpolator : struct, IInterpolator Type Parameters TInterpolator The interpolator of each strike's curve in time. Inheritance object YoYOptionletStripper InterpolatedYoYOptionletStripper<TInterpolator> Derived InterpolatedYoYInflationOptionletStripper Inherited Members object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks Each strike is stripped on floors up to the last floor strike and on caps above it. Its first volatility is solved by Brent, between 0.001% and 8% to 1e-7, so that a linear curve from the surface's base date to a week past its first maturity, sloping by the slope in proportion to its level, prices the first maturity's quote; then a piecewise curve starting at that level less the slope's change over the first maturity's time is bootstrapped on a helper per maturity, each an integer number of years long, over a strike range of ±0.1% of the strike (at least 0.002%). The instruments read a generic year-on-year index on the surface's year-on-year curve, with the surface's lag and frequency, observed flat. QuantLib's generic index takes the empty currency, which nothing reads; nanoql's inflation indexes take a currency, so it takes the surface's index's. QuantLib binds each helper to a constant volatility at the first level before the bootstrap, which only sets the shared engine's volatility that the bootstrap then resets; here each trial passes its own volatility, so the binding isn't made. api/NanoQL.Experimental.IsotropicRandomW.summary: Class IsotropicRandomWalk<TDistribution> Namespace NanoQL.Experimental Assembly NanoQL.dll An isotropic random walk: a step whose radius is drawn from a distribution and whose direction on the d-dimensional sphere is uniform, every direction equally likely: QuantLib's IsotropicRandomWalk. Inheritance object IsotropicRandomWalk<TDistribution> Inherited Members object.GetType() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks The radius is drawn on the given engine, the direction on the walk's own Mersenne Twister, as QuantLib's. In one dimension the sign is a fair coin and in two the angle is uniform on the circle, QuantLib's forms and bits. From three dimensions QuantLib's hyperspherical angles are each uniform in [0, π], where a uniform direction needs densities ∝ sin^(d−k−1)φ, so its draws crowd the poles; nanoql's direction is Muller's (1959), d standard normals from the walk's generator through the inverse cumulative normal, scaled to unit length, the radius and weights then QuantLib's (Divergences/IsotropicRandomWalkTests.cs). [Experimental("NQL0001")] public sealed class LognormalCmsSpreadPricer : CmsSpreadCouponPricer Inheritance object FloatingRateCouponPricer CmsSpreadCouponPricer LognormalCmsSpreadPricer Inherited Members CmsSpreadCouponPricer.WithCorrelation(double?) CmsSpreadCouponPricer.Correlation object.GetType() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks The two swap rates' convexity adjustments are the CMS pricer's, on its swaption volatility, whose type and shifts the spread model inherits by default; or the type is given, and on a lognormal model the shifts, 0 when not given. An at-the-money surface takes only the inherited type; a cube is read on the model's type and shifts through its smile sections. The correlation is clamped to ±0.9999, so that the integrand never divides by 0; at the default 16 Gauss-Hermite points its value at 0.9999 is 1.5e-3 off the 256-point value, the points the caller's choice. References: Brigo and Mercurio, Interest Rate Models - Theory and Practice, 2nd edition, Springer, 2006, chapter 13.6.2. With unequal shifts, the integrand branches on the displaced strike k + g₁s₁ + g₂s₂, and its negative branch shifts the second rate by its own shift, as QuantLib's master does after 1.44 (#2874); QuantLib 1.44 branches on the strike and shifts the second rate by the first's, which prices NaN caplets and floorlets at strikes 0.008 and 0.002 on #2874's set-up and breaks put-call parity by 2.03e-2 at others (Divergences/CmsSpreadUnequalShiftsTests.cs). Equal shifts take the same branch either way. Without a coupon discount curve, each coupon is discounted on its own first swap index's curve, its discounting curve when exogenous and its forwarding curve otherwise; QuantLib's pricer keeps the first coupon's curve for every later coupon, so one pricer serving coupons on different indexes discounts them all on the first's (Divergences/CmsSpreadCouponDiscountCurveTests.cs). A pricer is stateless here, as every nanoql pricer: what QuantLib's initialize stores is computed per call, one state serving a capped coupon's three rates. api/NanoQL.Experimental.MCDoubleBarrierE.summary: Class MCDoubleBarrierEngine Namespace NanoQL.Experimental Assembly NanoQL.dll The Monte Carlo pricing engine for double barrier options, the barriers checked at the path's points (DoubleBarrierPathPricer). [Experimental("NQL0001")] public static class MCDoubleBarrierEngine Inheritance object MCDoubleBarrierEngine Inherited Members object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks A static class over a private simulation deriving McSimulation<TPath, TStats> directly, as QuantLib's engine derives McSimulation: Calculate builds the simulation with QuantLib's checks and returns the NPV and, where the random-number traits allow one, the error estimate. The seed is explicit. Documented divergences. The paths and the discounts run on the engine's clock, Clock(GeneralizedBlackScholesProcess, FdmQuantoHelper?), from the earliest reference date of the structures, where QuantLib's run on the risk-free curve's (Divergences/McDoubleBarrierTests.cs). And a non-European exercise is refused, as MCBarrierEngine refuses it, where QuantLib prices any exercise to its last date. The number of samples, or null. requiredTolerance double? The absolute tolerance, or null; it takes precedence. maxSamples int? The most samples for a tolerance, or null for no limit. seed long The seed, in [1, 4294967295]. Returns OneAssetOptionResults The option's results, the NPV and the error estimate; the expired results when it has expired. Type Parameters TRng The random-number traits. TStats The statistics accumulator. Exceptions ArgumentNullException The option, the context or the process is null. ArgumentException The time steps are given neither or both ways, or aren't positive. ArgumentOutOfRangeException A number of samples is negative, or the seed is outside its range. NanoQLException The exercise isn't European, the spot isn't positive or lies on or beyond a barrier ("barrier touched"), the payoff isn't plain vanilla, the type is a KIKO or a KOKI, neither a tolerance nor a number of samples is given, or the samples can't reach the tolerance.

QuantLib's assigns each product where it should add it (distribution.cpp:309) and spreads its n₁ + n₂ − 1 buckets over [0, xmax₁ + xmax₂], one bucket wider, so its result's mass isn't 1 (an unused class; Divergences/DistributionMembersTests.cs). api/NanoQL.Experimental.MidPointCDOEngin.summary: Class MidPointCDOEngine Namespace NanoQL.Experimental Assembly NanoQL.dll The mid-point engine for synthetic CDOs: each premium period's loss taken at its midpoint, the premium paid on the tranche's notional less the expected loss at the period's end. It reads the statistics through the CDO's basket, which must be of the engine's evaluation date. Premium accrual on default isn't paid, as in QuantLib's. The legs and the upfront are levered by the CDO's leverage factor, and the fair premium and fair upfront are the unlevered rates: QuantLib's levers the premium leg alone, so a tranche at twice its notional reads half its fair premium, 0.02268 for 0.04535; and its additional "fairPremium" is −(protection + upfront)·rate/premium, −0.04535 where the instrument's is 0.04535 (Divergences/CdoLeverageTests.cs). The fair upfront is the side-invariant rate that zeroes the value, over the first accrual's discount: QuantLib's reads −0.2000 for a buyer where the seller's is 0.2000, and a forward start's value at it −0.22. A basket with realized defaults is priced on the tranche's outstanding notional, its inception notional less the realized tranche loss and the amortized recovery: the premium leg pays on it less the live names' expected loss, the upfront is due on it, and a paid first coupon starts the losses from the realized tranche loss. A discount before the discount curve's reference date is 1, and a default probability before a default curve's 0, where QuantLib's reads refuse a seasoned CDO and curves dated T+2 ("negative time"). api/NanoQL.Experimental.MtMCrossCurrency.summary: Class MtMCrossCurrencyBasisSwap Namespace NanoQL.Experimental Assembly NanoQL.dll A mark-to-market cross-currency basis swap. [Experimental("NQL0001")] public sealed class MtMCrossCurrencyBasisSwap : CrossCurrencySwap Inheritance object Instrument Swap CrossCurrencySwap MtMCrossCurrencyBasisSwap Inherited Members CrossCurrencySwap.LegCurrency(int) CrossCurrencySwap.Validate() CrossCurrencySwap.Currencies Swap.IsExpired(EvaluationContext) Swap.StartDate() Swap.MaturityDate() Swap.Leg(int) Swap.Payer(int) Swap.NumberOfLegs Swap.Legs object.GetType() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks A float-vs-float cross-currency basis swap in which the notional of one leg (the resettable leg) is reset for each coupon period to track the prevailing FX rate, while the other leg keeps a constant notional that is exchanged at inception and maturity. Each reset has a fixing date, on which the FX rate is observed, and a value date at the start of the accrual period. Following the convention of MtMCrossCurrencyBasisSwapRateHelper, the two legs are identified by their role in the FX pair: the base-currency leg (the first) and the quote-currency leg (the second), and isFxBaseCurrencyLegResettable selects which of them carries the resetting notional. The trade's type controls whether the base-currency leg is paid or received. Resetting the notional removes most of the FX exposure of the principal and is the market-standard convention for many currency pairs. The resettable leg is built from FX-linked cash flows: FxResetCoupon instances, whose notional is the constant-leg notional converted at the period's FX-reset observation, and FxResetNotionalExchange instances paying the netted notional differences (the first notional at inception, the reset difference at each period boundary, and the last notional at maturity). During pricing, DiscountingMtMCrossCurrencyBasisSwapEngine gives copies of the FX-linked cash flows an FxResetPricer built from its market data, leaving the swap's own cash flows unchanged; querying them independently needs a pricer set through SetFxResetPricer<T>(T, int, FxResetPricer?). A future reset is projected as the forward FX implied by its pricer's discount curves. If a reset fixing date precedes the evaluation date, the realized exchange rate must be available from the context's ExchangeRates on that fixing date; direct, inverse and derived exchange rates are supported. The constructor builds the legs, as QuantLib's does: an Ibor leg reads the context's at-par switch, so it takes the context. api/NanoQL.Experimental.NoArbSabrModel.h.title: Class NoArbSabrModel | nanoql
api/NanoQL.Experimental.NoArbSabrModel.h.summary: Class NoArbSabrModel Namespace NanoQL.Experimental Assembly NanoQL.dll Doust's no-arbitrage SABR model (Paul Doust, "No-arbitrage SABR", The Journal of Computational Finance, 2012): the SABR density with the absorption at zero read off a simulated table, its option and digital prices the density's integrals, the forward adjusted so the density reprices it. [Experimental("NQL0001")] public sealed class NoArbSabrModel Inheritance object NoArbSabrModel Inherited Members object.GetType() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks Immutable: QuantLib's forward solve, which changes its forward and normalization as it searches, runs over a working state at construction, the found forward and normalization stored. The model's domain is QuantLib's: an expiry in (0, 30], β in [0.01, 0.99], σ_I = αF^(β − 1) in [0.05, 1], ν in [0.01, 0.8], ρ in [−0.99, 0.99]. As QuantLib's header says, the forward adjustment can fail at extreme parameters, which Forward against NumericalForward shows: at an expiry of 30, ρ 0.9, ν 0.8 the adjustment is 0.0157 off and the call flat in strike; at β 0.9, ν 0.8, |ρ| 0.7 the density beyond QuantLib's integration domain carries a strike-independent call value, 4.0e-6 at an expiry of 1 (σ_I 0.3) and 3.5e-4 at 4 (σ_I 0.05). Out-of-the-money prices below the integrator's 1e-7 carry no relative accuracy, so implied volatilities read there are unreliable. Documented divergence (Divergences/NoArbSabrShortExpiryTests.cs): where σ_I√T is below 0.1, each of the model's integrals (the normalization and the price inside the forward solve, the price, the digital) is split at the density's peak, the current forward ± 8w with w = Fσ_I√T, where QuantLib's single interval misses the spike: out of the money from T 0.005, at the money from 0.003, the forward adjustment failing at 0.001; at and above 0.1 QuantLib's single interval and bits stand. api/NanoQL.Experimental.NormalCLVModel.h.summary: Class NormalCLVModel Namespace NanoQL.Experimental Assembly NanoQL.dll The collocating local volatility (CLV) model with a normally distributed kernel process, an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process, collocated to a Black-Scholes process's distribution at given maturities: QuantLib's NormalCLVModel. [Experimental("NQL0001")] public sealed class NormalCLVModel Inheritance object NormalCLVModel Inherited Members object.GetType() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks References: A. Grzelak, N. Thijs, 2016, "The CLV Framework — A Fresh Look at Efficient Pricing with Smile", http://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2747541. Immutable, its mapping function computed once, on the first call of G(), as QuantLib's lazy object computes it, so that a model read only through Cdf(Date, double) and InvCDF(Date, double) takes no maturities and no kernel process, as QuantLib's own cases build one. The collocation points are √2 times the Gauss-Hermite nodes of the Lagrange order, scaled by σ so that the outer one meets the pMax quantile, or else the pMin one, or 1. The mapping interpolates each collocation value linearly in time, extrapolated past the maturities, then by Lagrange interpolation at the kernel's standardized value; at t = 0 the kernel's deviation is 0 and QuantLib's standardized value σ(x − E)/0 is NaN at x₀ and infinite elsewhere, so the mapping refuses a time that isn't positive (Conventions/CLVModelTests.cs). QuantLib's mapping shares one buffer for its interpolated values among its calls; here each call has its own. The variables Yᵢ = a·M + √(1 − a²)·Zᵢ, M and Zᵢ independent of zero mean and unit variance, their correlation a² the copula's; a name's default by t is Yᵢ below F_Y⁻¹(Qᵢ(t)), so that, given M = m, it defaults with probability F_Z((F_Y⁻¹(p) − a·m)/√(1 − a²)). The densities of M and Z are the derived models'; F_Y is tabulated by them unless it is analytic, and the integrals over M are Euler sums on a midpoint grid. api/NanoQL.Experimental.OvernightIborBas.summary: Class OvernightIborBasisSwapRateHelper Namespace NanoQL.Experimental Assembly NanoQL.dll A rate helper for bootstrapping over overnight-IBOR basis swaps. [Experimental("NQL0001")] public sealed class OvernightIborBasisSwapRateHelper : RelativeDateRateHelper, IBootstrapHelper Inheritance object BootstrapHelper<YieldTermStructure> RateHelper RelativeDateRateHelper OvernightIborBasisSwapRateHelper Implements IBootstrapHelper Inherited Members BootstrapHelper<YieldTermStructure>.QuoteError(EvaluationContext) BootstrapHelper<YieldTermStructure>.Quote BootstrapHelper<YieldTermStructure>.EarliestDate BootstrapHelper<YieldTermStructure>.MaturityDate BootstrapHelper<YieldTermStructure>.LatestRelevantDate BootstrapHelper<YieldTermStructure>.PillarDate BootstrapHelper<YieldTermStructure>.LatestDate object.GetType() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Extension Methods BootstrapHelperExtensions.SetTermStructure<T>(T, YieldTermStructure) Remarks The swap is assumed to pay overnight plus the basis and receive IBOR. As a default, the helper is used to bootstrap the forecast curve for the IBOR index; the overnight index will need an existing forecast curve. If bootstrapBaseCurve is set to true, instead, the helper will be used to bootstrap the forecast curve for the overnight index; in this case, the IBOR index will need to be given a forecast curve. An exogenous discount curve can be passed; if not, the curve being bootstrapped is also used for discounting. A payment lag can also be passed; it is applied to both legs. The payment frequency of the overnight leg can be overridden. It defaults to the tenor of the IBOR index. The IBOR leg always pays at the tenor of its own index. Passing NoFrequency creates a single overnight coupon spanning the full swap tenor. The averaging method and use of telescopic value dates can be configured for the overnight leg. Telescopic value dates are only applied to compounded coupons. The basis is quoted on the overnight (base) leg by default. Setting basisOnIborLeg solves for a margin quoted on the IBOR leg instead. A stub-index configuration can be passed for the IBOR leg; it is applied to that leg's irregular coupons (see StubIndexSelection). Since the candidate indexes keep their own forwarding curves, this is only allowed when bootstrapBaseCurve is true, i.e. when the IBOR index has an exogenous forecast curve; otherwise the candidates could not track the curve under construction. api/NanoQL.Experimental.ParticleSwarmOpt.title: Class ParticleSwarmOptimization | nanoql
api/NanoQL.Experimental.ParticleSwarmOpt.summary: Class ParticleSwarmOptimization Namespace NanoQL.Experimental Assembly NanoQL.dll Particle swarm optimization: QuantLib's ParticleSwarmOptimization. [Experimental("NQL0001")] public sealed class ParticleSwarmOptimization : OptimizationMethod Inheritance object OptimizationMethod ParticleSwarmOptimization Inherited Members OptimizationMethod.Minimize(Problem, EndCriteria) OptimizationMethod.Minimize(ProblemState, EndCriteria) object.GetType() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks M particles explore the N-dimensional parameter space. Each position moves by its velocity, X_{i,j}^{k+1} = X_{i,j}^k + V_{i,j}^{k+1}, the velocity V_{i,j}^{k+1} = χ(V_{i,j}^k + c₁ r_{i,j}^k (P_{i,j}^k − X_{i,j}^k) + c₂ R_{i,j}^k (G_{i,j}^k − X_{i,j}^k)), with r and R uniform in [0, 1], P the particle's personal best and G its social best, which the topology sets: the PSO with constriction factor (PSO-Co). The PSO with inertia factor (PSO-In) takes ω, ĉ₁ and ĉ₂ in place of χ, χc₁ and χc₂. χ is 2/|2 − φ − √(φ² − 4φ)| with φ = c₁ + c₂; stable convergence needs φ ≥ 4, and Clerc and Kennedy recommend c₁ = c₂ = 2.05. The inertia scales the previous velocity, a constant in the canonical PSO. The optimization stops at its iterations or after its stationary iterations; positions are clamped to the bounds, the velocity zeroed there. The swarm starts on a Sobol sequence within the bounds, its seed the optimizer's: QuantLib's is 0, the clock, read only past the 32 dimensions of Jaeckel's direction integers, so the bits are QuantLib's up to 16 parameters. The velocities' uniforms are a Mersenne Twister's on the seed, which is required: QuantLib's default seeds from the clock, and its two constructors are ambiguous for an integer literal there. A problem's constraint is never empty, so QuantLib's refusal of one doesn't arise. Immutable: each minimization copies the topology and the inertia and starts the generators from the seed, where QuantLib's continues them and appends a new swarm to the last. api/NanoQL.Experimental.PerturbativeBarr.summary: Class PerturbativeBarrierOptionEngine Namespace NanoQL.Experimental Assembly NanoQL.dll The perturbative engine for up-and-out put options on time-dependent Black-Scholes markets (Fatone, Recchioni and Zirilli): the barrier price on the market's averages, corrected to first or second order in the drift and variance's departures from them. [Experimental("NQL0001")] public static class PerturbativeBarrierOptionEngine Inheritance object PerturbativeBarrierOptionEngine Inherited Members object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks QuantLib's algorithm, its midpoint rules in the time variables (npoint outer and npoint2 inner points) and its local distribution helpers: Hart's normal (algorithm 5666 by Recchioni), and Genz's bivariate normal (Drezner and Wesolowsky's method) and trivariate normal (Plackett's formula by adaptive Kronrod integration), as QuantLib's port of Genz's TVPACK has them. QuantLib's warning: the engine was reported to fail tests on Mac OS X 10.8.4. Documented divergences (Divergences/PerturbativeBarrierEngineTests.cs), each leaving QuantLib's bits where it doesn't apply, order 0's among them. Three lines of QuantLib's TVPACK port are Genz's: Plackett's integrand squares BA − R·BB where QuantLib 1.44 takes its square root (upstream's own fix after v1.44, #2935); its Student branch belongs to the degrees-of-freedom test, where QuantLib's attaches it to the normal integrand's cut, so a normal integrand past the cut returns 0, not QuantLib's 0.5 or NaN; and the bivariate normal's |ρ| ≥ 0.925 branch takes √(1 − x²), where QuantLib's takes (1 − x²)². QuantLib's first 12-point weight, short of Genz's in the last digits, stands. The second-order term's derivative helpers are their functions' derivatives in a, term by term from the identity ∂Φ₂(h, k; ρ)/∂h = φ(h) Φ((k − ρh)/√(1 − ρ²)) their own terms apply: the F helper's factor at tt − s, its function's, where QuantLib's reads tt − p; and the E helper's limits √(τ(p − s)/(2ps)) and √(τ(p − s)/(2(τ − p)(τ − s))) with the sign of its derivative through the first limit, where QuantLib's are mistranscribed. The rate, carry and variance integrals run on the engine's clock, Clock(GeneralizedBlackScholesProcess, FdmQuantoHelper?), each structure read at the instants its times denote on its own clock; where every structure shares the risk-free curve's times, QuantLib's. Methods Calculate(BarrierOption, EvaluationContext, GeneralizedBlackScholesProcess, int, bool, int, int) Prices an up-and-out put option. public static OneAssetOptionResults Calculate(BarrierOption option, EvaluationContext context, GeneralizedBlackScholesProcess process, int order = 1, bool zeroGamma = false, int npoint = 1000, int npoint2 = 100) Parameters option BarrierOption The option: up-and-out, no rebate, a plain-vanilla put. context EvaluationContext The evaluation context. process GeneralizedBlackScholesProcess The Black-Scholes process. order int The approximation's order: 0, 1 or 2. zeroGamma bool Whether the approximation's γ is 0, where it is the market's average carry over half its average variance by default. npoint int The number of points of the outer time integrals, positive. npoint2 int The number of points of the second-order term's inner time integral, positive. Returns OneAssetOptionResults The option's value; the expired results when it has expired. Exceptions ArgumentNullException An argument is null. ArgumentOutOfRangeException order is negative. ArgumentException The order is above 2, or a number of points isn't positive. NanoQLException The option isn't an up-and-out ("this engine only manages up-and-out options"), has a rebate, or isn't a plain-vanilla put.

api/NanoQL.Experimental.PolarStudentTFac.summary: Class PolarStudentTFactorSampler<TUrng> Namespace NanoQL.Experimental Assembly NanoQL.dll A Student t latent model's factor sampler by polar Student t draws, bypassing the copula: one generator per systemic factor, and one for every idiosyncratic factor. QuantLib's LatentModel::FactorSampler specialized on RandomSequenceGenerator<PolarStudentTRng>. [Experimental("NQL0001")] [WorkingType] public sealed class PolarStudentTFactorSampler<TUrng> : IRsg where TUrng : class, IRng Type Parameters TUrng The uniform generator. Its seed constructor is Create<TUrng>(TCopulaPolicy, long), a seed in [1, 4294967295] with no default, where QuantLib's defaults to 0, the clock; a generator given instead is copied. One uniform stream feeds the t generators in turn, and each draw is scaled by its factor's variance factor √((ν − 2)/ν), so that the factors are independent and of unit variance, as the policy's are. api/NanoQL.Experimental.Pool.html.summary: Class Pool Namespace NanoQL.Experimental Assembly NanoQL.dll A pool of issuers by name, each with the default key it enters with and a time. [Experimental("NQL0001")] public sealed class Pool Inheritance object Pool Inherited Members object.GetType() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks Immutable: QuantLib's add, clear and setTime return new pools. DefaultKeys lists each name's key in the pool's order, the order of Names, which every basket and model read pairs it with. QuantLib's lists them in name order, iterating a map keyed by name (pool.cpp:77-82), so a pool not added in name order reads each name's probability on another name's key: names C and A entering with keys KA and KB read C's probability on KB's curve. And QuantLib's clear keeps the cleared names' keys (pool.cpp:34-38), which a name added later then reads; Clear() returns an empty pool. A documented divergence (Divergences/PoolKeyOrderTests.cs); on a pool added in name order, QuantLib's. api/NanoQL.Experimental.Quantity.html.summary: Struct Quantity Namespace NanoQL.Experimental Assembly NanoQL.dll An amount of a commodity, in a unit of measure. [Experimental("NQL0001")] public readonly struct Quantity : IEquatable<Quantity> Implements IEquatable<Quantity> Inherited Members object.GetType() object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) Remarks A value: its zero value, default(Quantity), is QuantLib's Quantity(), 0.0 of no commodity type in no unit, both null. The operators combine quantities in one unit as QuantLib's do, and never convert: QuantLib's operators read the static Quantity::conversionType, and these see no context, so they behave as under its NoConversion. On a unit mismatch every operator but == and != throws QuantLib's "unitOfMeasure mismatch and no conversion specified"; == returns false and != true, where QuantLib's throw, as Money's do. The conversion modes are methods that take the context, which holds the settings (QuantitySettings) and the conversions (UnitOfMeasureConversions): Add(Quantity, EvaluationContext), Subtract(Quantity, EvaluationContext), Divide(Quantity, EvaluationContext), Equals(Quantity, EvaluationContext), LessThan(Quantity, EvaluationContext), LessThanOrEqual(Quantity, EvaluationContext), GreaterThan(Quantity, EvaluationContext), GreaterThanOrEqual(Quantity, EvaluationContext), and QuantityFunctions' Close and CloseEnough. A converted quantity is rounded by its unit's rounding, which leaves it as it is (Rounding). Equals(Quantity) and GetHashCode() compare the commodity type, the unit and the amount, the amount by Equals(double), so that equality is reflexive. Its statistics read the stored paths. TInitTraits The policy's initialization parameters. TUsng The uniform sequence generator, which the copula inverts (QuantLib's default SobolRsg). Inheritance object DefaultLossModel RandomLM<TCopula, TInitTraits, TUsng> Implements IDefaultLossModel Derived RandomDefaultLM<TCopula, TInitTraits, TUsng> RandomLossLM<TCopula, TInitTraits, TUsng> Inherited Members DefaultLossModel.SetBasket(Basket) DefaultLossModel.ProbOverLoss(Date, double) DefaultLossModel.SplitESFLevel(Date, double) DefaultLossModel.DensityTrancheLoss(Date, double) DefaultLossModel.ExpectedRecovery(Date, int, DefaultProbKey) DefaultLossModel.ResetModel() DefaultLossModel.RestrictTo(ImmutableArray<int>, int) DefaultLossModel.Basket DefaultLossModel.BoundBasket object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks The simulation runs once, when the model is bound to a basket, on the basket's live names, and is stored in the bound copy: QuantLib's simulates lazily at its first statistic and keeps a model's paths across baskets. The path count is required and at least 1 (QuantLib's defaults to 0, "stats will crash on div by zero, FIX ME"); the seed is required, in [1, 4294967295], QuantLib's default 2863311530. A default's day counts from the evaluation date, its probability 0 before its curve's reference date: QuantLib's counts from each curve's date and reads the count from the evaluation date, so curves dated T+2 read today's statistics. Defaults count to a horizon, QuantLib's 4,050 days by default, a construction parameter here, and a statistic dated past it is refused: QuantLib's reads any later date, its expected loss stopping where the simulation does. The default correlation is the paths' Pearson correlation, refused where a name's frequency is 0 or 1 (0/0): QuantLib's divides the joint frequency by n − 1 and the single ones by n, so a name's correlation with itself is 1.0013 on 5,000 paths. The n-th event counts every default on a day, in name order: QuantLib's keys its order by day, so two names defaulting on one day count once (randomdefaultlatentmodel.hpp:270-286). The percentile and the shortfall are refused where they read past the sorted losses (the percentile at a position of n, the shortfall where ⌈p·n⌉ = n); the percentile's interval keeps its indices within the losses, so at 0 it reads QuantLib's value without its read before the start. api/NanoQL.Experimental.RecursiveLossMod.title: Class RecursiveLossModel<TCopula, TInitTraits> | nanoql
api/NanoQL.Experimental.RecursiveLossMod.summary: Class RecursiveLossModel<TCopula, TInitTraits> Namespace NanoQL.Experimental Assembly NanoQL.dll The recursive STCDO default loss model of a heterogeneous pool: names heterogeneous in their default probabilities, notionals and recoveries, their correlations given by the latent model. The recursive pricing algorithm is Andersen, Sidenius and Basu's, "All your hedges in one basket", Risk, November 2003, pages 67-72. [Experimental("NQL0001")] public class RecursiveLossModel<TCopula, TInitTraits> : DefaultLossModel, IDefaultLossModel where TCopula : struct, ICopulaPolicy<TCopula, TInitTraits> where TInitTraits : struct Type Parameters TCopula The copula policy. TInitTraits The policy's initialization parameters. Inheritance object DefaultLossModel RecursiveLossModel<TCopula, TInitTraits> Implements IDefaultLossModel Derived RecursiveGaussLossModel Inherited Members DefaultLossModel.SetBasket(Basket) DefaultLossModel.ProbOverLoss(Date, double) DefaultLossModel.SplitVaRLevel(Date, double) DefaultLossModel.SplitESFLevel(Date, double) DefaultLossModel.DensityTrancheLoss(Date, double) DefaultLossModel.ProbsBeingNthEvent(int, Date) DefaultLossModel.DefaultCorrelation(Date, int, int) DefaultLossModel.ProbAtLeastNEvents(int, Date) DefaultLossModel.ExpectedRecovery(Date, int, DefaultProbKey) DefaultLossModel.RestrictTo(ImmutableArray<int>, int) DefaultLossModel.Basket DefaultLossModel.BoundBasket object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks With copulas other than the Gaussian it is only an approximation (see the remark on p. 68). The expected tranche loss inverts the sum and the integral (the first, unnumbered, equation on p. 70): EL(t) = ∫ q(ω) dω Σ_k l_k P(l_k; t | ω), the conditional expected loss integrated over the factor. The losses are counted in a loss unit, the smallest nonzero loss given default over the number of buckets, each name's loss given default rounded to a whole number of units, so the distribution's attainable losses are the sums of the names' weights. To be done, as in QuantLib: a loss unit from some small fraction of the portfolio's loss weights (fine for pricing, not for risk metrics; O'Kane 18.3.2), and integrands reading the inverted probabilities throughout. The loss distribution labels each point by its attainable loss, and the percentile at 0 and 1 is the tranche's loss at the first and last, as its interior's are tranche losses: QuantLib's labels the i-th attainable loss i times the loss unit, wrong where the weights aren't 0, 1, 2, …, and its percentile returns the distribution's probability at both ends (1.0000000003 and 0.717; Divergences/RecursiveLossModelTests.cs). Bound to a basket, a copy computes the weights afresh, where QuantLib's appends them to the previous basket's, and prices the live names over the restated tranche. Refused, where QuantLib's reads before or past its vectors: a basket whose losses given default are all 0, and a percentile or shortfall whose search leaves the distribution. A shortfall the distribution never reaches is refused, as the binomial model's is, where QuantLib's reads 0 with its comment "well, we are in error.... fix: FAIL" (recursivelossmodel.hpp:298). Constructors RecursiveLossModel(ConstantLossLatentModel<TCopula, TInitTraits>, int) Initializes a new instance of the RecursiveLossModel<TCopula, TInitTraits> class. public RecursiveLossModel(ConstantLossLatentModel<TCopula, TInitTraits> m, int nbuckets = 1) Parameters m ConstantLossLatentModel<TCopula, TInitTraits> The constant-loss latent model. nbuckets int The number of loss units in the smallest loss given default (nope! use the max common divisor, see O'Kane; or give both options at least). Returns double The loss. Exceptions NanoQLException The model doesn't implement it. NanoQLException The search ends before the distribution's start or past its end, where QuantLib reads there. api/NanoQL.Experimental.RiskyAssetSwap.h.title: Class RiskyAssetSwap | nanoql
api/NanoQL.Experimental.RiskyAssetSwap.h.summary: Class RiskyAssetSwap Namespace NanoQL.Experimental Assembly NanoQL.dll A risky asset swap: a risky fixed-rate bond bought at par and swapped into the floating rate plus a spread, the bond's value from the default-probability curve with its recovery integrated over the default density. [Experimental("NQL0001")] public sealed class RiskyAssetSwap : Instrument Inheritance object Instrument RiskyAssetSwap Inherited Members Instrument.Validate() Instrument.FetchResults(InstrumentResults) object.GetType() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks An instrument QuantLib prices without an engine: Calculate(EvaluationContext) computes it. Its NPV is the package's value, the risky bond's price less the fixed leg plus the floating leg and the spread, so at the fair spread it is the par nominal, QuantLib's. Without a coupon the par coupon is used on every calculation, where QuantLib's first calculation stores it in place of the coupon for later ones. The annuities: the fixed annuity runs over the fixed schedule, where QuantLib's runs over the float schedule's dates with the fixed day counter, and the fair spread's denominator is the float annuity, the leg the spread is paid on, where QuantLib's is that fixed annuity: an annual-fixed, quarterly-float swap's fair spread reads 0.0118084 in QuantLib for 0.0115616 on equal schedules, and its package 99.58 on 100 at the fair spread. Where the schedules and the day counters coincide the values are QuantLib's. The recovery value: the daily Euler sum runs to each period's end, where QuantLib's stops a day short, −2.74e-3 relative on annual periods. Reads between the evaluation date and a curve's later reference date are a discount and a survival of 1, where QuantLib's refuses them; before the evaluation date, a seasoned swap's past periods, they are QuantLib's, which refuses a date before the curve's (Divergences/RiskyAssetSwapTests.cs). It keeps the context it was built with, which the index's fixings and forecasts read and on which each smile section is dated; each section is fitted per query, uncached. Quotes are values. QuantLib's updateSabrGuesses, private and never called, isn't ported (it writes past its guesses); its guess search is kept, every guess equal. QuantLib's acyclic visitor isn't ported. Documented divergence (Divergences/SabrVolSurfaceFixingTests.cs): the section at time t reads the index's fixing on the date ⌊365t⌋ days after the reference date adjusted on the index's fixing calendar by Following, the adjustment QuantLib's interest-rate surface makes to its reference date, where QuantLib reads the unadjusted date, refused ("Fixing date … is not valid") two days in seven; the section keeps the unadjusted date. Rows of volatility spreads fewer than the option tenors are refused, where QuantLib reads past them. api/NanoQL.Experimental.SaddlePointLossM.summary: Class SaddlePointLossModel<TCopula, TInitTraits> Namespace NanoQL.Experimental Assembly NanoQL.dll The saddle-point portfolio credit default loss model: the saddle-point expansion's integrations of several default risk metrics, the dependence dealt with through a latent model that makes the integrals conditional on its factor, the latent variables integrated indirectly. [Experimental("NQL0001")] public class SaddlePointLossModel<TCopula, TInitTraits> : DefaultLossModel, IDefaultLossModel where TCopula : struct, ICopulaPolicy<TCopula, TInitTraits> where TInitTraits : struct Type Parameters TCopula The copula policy. TInitTraits The policy's initialization parameters. Inheritance object DefaultLossModel SaddlePointLossModel<TCopula, TInitTraits> Implements IDefaultLossModel Derived SaddlePointTailLossModel<TCopula, TInitTraits> Inherited Members DefaultLossModel.SetBasket(Basket) DefaultLossModel.SplitESFLevel(Date, double) DefaultLossModel.DensityTrancheLoss(Date, double) DefaultLossModel.ProbsBeingNthEvent(int, Date) DefaultLossModel.DefaultCorrelation(Date, int, int) DefaultLossModel.ProbAtLeastNEvents(int, Date) DefaultLossModel.ExpectedRecovery(Date, int, DefaultProbKey) DefaultLossModel.RestrictTo(ImmutableArray<int>, int) DefaultLossModel.Basket DefaultLossModel.BoundBasket object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks See R. Martin, K. Thompson and C. Browne, "Taking to the saddle", Risk, June 2001, p. 91; R. Martin, "The saddlepoint method and portfolio optionalities", Risk, December 2006; R. Martin, K. Thompson and C. Browne, "VAR: who contributes and how much?", Risk, August 2001; R. J. Martin, "Shortfall: Who contributes and how much?", Credit Suisse, 3 January 2007; J. Annaert, C. Garcia Joao Batista, J. Lamoot and G. Lanine, "Don't Fall from the Saddle: the Importance of Higher Moments of Credit Loss Distributions", Gent University, February 2006; A. Antonov, S. Mechkov and T. Misirpashaev, "Analytical techniques for synthetic CDOs and credit default risk measures", NumeriX, 23 May 2005; X. Huang, C. W. Oosterlee and M. Mesters, "Computation of VaR and VaR contribution in the Vasicek portfolio credit loss model: a comparative study", Journal of Credit Risk 3(3), Fall 2007, and "Higher-order saddlepoint approximations in the Vasicek portfolio credit loss model", Journal of Computational Finance 11(1), Fall 2007. A high order expansion is used, more expensive; see Antonov et al. for the terms retained. A. Owen, A. McLeod and K. Thompson's hybrid saddlepoint method fixes the error at low loss levels (Risk, August 2009), not implemented here; for the general theory, R. W. Butler, "Saddlepoint approximations with applications", Cambridge, 2007. To be done, as in QuantLib: some portfolios' instabilities in the high order terms; calls avoiding the copula inversions; the saddle point search's convergence in extreme cases (very high factors, factors not ordered from high to low). Random recoveries would have to be passed to the conditional methods as the probabilities are. Kept, QuantLib's method: the expected tranche loss is the tranche of the conditional expected loss, a large-pool reading, not a saddle-point expansion; at correlation 0 on 100 names its four tranches read 292.78, 0, 0, 0 where the recursive model on the same latent model reads 245.40, 46.48, 0.89, 0.0022. SaddlePointTailLossModel<TCopula, TInitTraits> reads it from the model's own tail instead. The tail's degenerate nodes and domain (Divergences/SaddlePointLossModelTests.cs). QuantLib's saddle search brackets on the name of the largest loss, taking the logarithm of a ratio of its conditional probability p and 1 − p, so a node where that name is at 0 or 1 throws ("invalid range"): at the evaluation date every probability is 0, and on ten names every correlation from 0.9 throws. Here the bracket's name is the largest among those strictly between 0 and 1, the certain ones carried by the cumulants (a name at 1 a linear term, one at 0 nothing), and a node where every name is at 0 or 1 reads its exact conditional loss: its tail 1 or 0, its density 0, its split and shortfall exact. Where QuantLib's throws (100 names, hazard 0.03, recovery 0.4), the tail at 10% of the pool reads the exact (recursive) model's within 1.2% through correlation 0.9 and within 5% at 0.95, below it (5.0% at three months), the expansion's own accuracy on near-comonotonic pools, where QuantLib's runs reading it within 1% at 0.7 and 0.75. Refused, naming the saddle-point expansion: a tail outside [0, 1] (beyond the quadrature's rounding, 1e-12), and a largest relative loss at or below the bracket's 1e-5, whose logarithm QuantLib takes of a negative number. The factor nodes' tails are QuantLib's, inside [0, 1] or not: at low losses single nodes read up to 6.31 or slightly below 0 where the integrated tail and the percentile are right (on 100 names, hazard 0.03, the percentile at 50%, 90% and 99% within the exact distribution's loss unit at correlations 0.1 to 0.5 and 30 days to ten years). Kept, the method's domain: on small pools the expansion misreads the tail inside [0, 1], on ten names at correlation 0.3 P(L ≥ 1%) 0.983 for an exact 0.0223 at a month and 0.754 for 0.603 at five years, where 100 names read 0.4389 for 0.4387 at a year; outside it (26.78 a day out at correlation 0.548, 2.61 at a week on ten names) the refusal. The saddle search. QuantLib's brackets the point on the name of the largest loss and, below or above the bracket's losses, returns the bracket's end instead of solving, so on pools whose largest loss is a name unlikely to default it reads up to 40 times the exact tail (0.978 for 0.198 at 1% of 100 names a year out at correlation 0.7, 0.2008 for 0.0049 at 10% at 0.9); here the bracket widens until it holds the level and the point is solved, QuantLib's search wherever its bracket holds it. The cumulants keep QuantLib's arithmetic but for names at 0, out of the sums, names at 1, their linear terms, and where QuantLib's form overflows the logistic form, so a widened point reads no 0·∞; the split's contributions take the same treatment, where QuantLib's form reads ∞/∞. Above the largest loss a factor node reaches, its names' losses given default but those certain not to default, no point exists: the tail reads 0 there by QuantLib's own return above 1 less the average recovery, and the density and the conditional shortfall read 0 too, where at the widened end QuantLib's expressions read 0/0, so the shortfall of a tranche detaching above the pool's largest loss was NaN (QuantLib's TO DO list: "Failing when the tranche upper loss limit goes over the max attainable loss"). Divergences/SaddlePointLossModelTests.cs. ProbOverLoss(Date, double) reads 0 above the whole tranche, where QuantLib's compares the fraction with the detachment amount; ExpectedShortfall(Date, double) is the tranche loss's, at most the tranche's remaining notional, where QuantLib's integrates the whole portfolio's tail above the tranche's percentile and caps it at the tranche notional times the remaining ratio (9 for a 300 tranche; "ESF <- tranched????!!" in its TO DO list). Bound to a basket with realized defaults, the model prices its live names over the restated tranche. object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks For a tranche [A, D] with A above 0 the expected loss is ∫_A^D P(L > y) dy, by 24-node Gauss-Legendre over the tranche. For the equity tranche it is E[L] − ∫_D^N P(L > y) dy: E[L] the live portfolio's conditional expected loss integrated over the factor, and the upper tail over [D, D + 5%], [D + 5%, D + 20%] and [D + 20%, 100%] of the live notional N. So the equity tranche never reads the tail near zero loss, where the pool's loss is a lattice of single-name losses the expansion follows coarsely and its tail exceeds 1 at high correlation; a tranche attaching close above zero does, its integral starting below the pool's smallest single-name loss. The attachment that counts is the live one, which a seasoned tranche's realized losses write down (Basket's restated tranche). Every other member is the base's. The check is the recursive model on the same latent model. On 100 names (notional 100, hazard 1%, recovery 40%), at one and five years, the variant is within 2% of it on the tranches from 3% to 22% at correlations from 0.3 to 0.9, and on the equity tranche within 0.6% to 0.75. Attaching closer to zero it errs more: [2%, 5%] by up to +2.5% at a year, [1%, 3%] by up to +7.5%, [0.5%, 3%] by +13% to +21%, and [0.1%, 3%] is refused from correlation 0.6 (the base's refusal of a tail outside [0, 1]); after four defaults a 3–6% tranche of that pool attaches at 0.625% of the live notional, one default's loss. At 0.9 the equity tranche reads +9.1% at five years; and a tranche whose integral reaches the pool's largest loss meets the expansion's other weak region there, where its tail can read below 0: senior tranches err by −2.6% to −4.4% at five years, and [22%, 60%] is refused at both horizons, its nodes crowding the largest loss (the base's refusal of a tail outside [0, 1]); the equity tranche's upper pieces cross it too. At low correlation the pool's loss is a binomial lattice, which a continuous expansion follows coarsely: at 0.1 a small tranche reads +9% at a year. Both models read the latent model's quadrature, its default QuantLib's 25-node Gauss-Hermite, which itself errs by up to 30% on 3% tranches at correlation 0.9 against its trapezoid integration.
