[WorkingType] public sealed class GeneralStatistics : IEmpiricalStatistics, IStatistics, ISummaryStatistics Inheritance object GeneralStatistics Implements IEmpiricalStatistics IStatistics ISummaryStatistics Inherited Members object.GetType() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Extension Methods GaussianStatisticsExtensions.GaussianAverageShortfall<TStat>(TStat, double) GaussianStatisticsExtensions.GaussianDownsideDeviation<TStat>(TStat) GaussianStatisticsExtensions.GaussianDownsideVariance<TStat>(TStat) GaussianStatisticsExtensions.GaussianExpectedShortfall<TStat>(TStat, double) GaussianStatisticsExtensions.GaussianPercentile<TStat>(TStat, double) GaussianStatisticsExtensions.GaussianPotentialUpside<TStat>(TStat, double) GaussianStatisticsExtensions.GaussianRegret<TStat>(TStat, double) GaussianStatisticsExtensions.GaussianShortfall<TStat>(TStat, double) GaussianStatisticsExtensions.GaussianTopPercentile<TStat>(TStat, double) GaussianStatisticsExtensions.GaussianValueAtRisk<TStat>(TStat, double) RiskStatisticsExtensions.AverageShortfall<TStat>(TStat, double) RiskStatisticsExtensions.DownsideDeviation<TStat>(TStat) RiskStatisticsExtensions.DownsideVariance<TStat>(TStat) RiskStatisticsExtensions.ExpectedShortfall<TStat>(TStat, double) RiskStatisticsExtensions.PotentialUpside<TStat>(TStat, double) RiskStatisticsExtensions.Regret<TStat>(TStat, double) RiskStatisticsExtensions.SemiDeviation<TStat>(TStat) RiskStatisticsExtensions.SemiVariance<TStat>(TStat) RiskStatisticsExtensions.Shortfall<TStat>(TStat, double) RiskStatisticsExtensions.ValueAtRisk<TStat>(TStat, double) Remarks It doesn't suffer the numerical instability problem of IncrementalStatistics. The downside is that it stores all samples, thus increasing the memory requirements. A working type: Add(double, double), Reset(), Reserve(int) and the sorting members change it, where QuantLib's sorts through mutable members of a const object; it isn't thread-safe. The constructor, and Add(ReadOnlySpan<double>, double) where the first sample sets the dimension, reset this class's own state, not a derived class's, as QuantLib's call its own reset: a derived override isn't run before its class's constructor. api/NanoQL.Numerics.GumbelCopula.html.summary: Class GumbelCopula Namespace NanoQL.Numerics Assembly NanoQL.dll The Gumbel copula, C(x, y) = exp(−((−ln x)^θ + (−ln y)^θ)^(1/θ)). public sealed class GumbelCopula Inheritance object GumbelCopula Inherited Members object.GetType() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks Immutable. On the unit square's edges it returns the boundary values, C(u, 0) = C(0, v) = 0, C(u, 1) = u and C(1, v) = v, before its formula, as every copula here does. Above θ 19, where (−ln x)^θ can underflow (from θ 19.3 at the largest x below 1, so QuantLib's is 1e-8 off at θ 50 and reads C(0.9, 0.7) as 1 for 0.7 at θ 1000), the larger logarithm M is factored out, exp(−M(1 + r^θ)^(1/θ)) with r the ratio of the two; QuantLib's formula to θ 19, where no power leaves the doubles' normal range. [WorkingType] public sealed class IncrementalStatistics : IStatistics, ISummaryStatistics Inheritance object IncrementalStatistics Implements IStatistics ISummaryStatistics Inherited Members object.GetType() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Extension Methods GaussianStatisticsExtensions.GaussianAverageShortfall<TStat>(TStat, double) GaussianStatisticsExtensions.GaussianDownsideDeviation<TStat>(TStat) GaussianStatisticsExtensions.GaussianDownsideVariance<TStat>(TStat) GaussianStatisticsExtensions.GaussianExpectedShortfall<TStat>(TStat, double) GaussianStatisticsExtensions.GaussianPercentile<TStat>(TStat, double) GaussianStatisticsExtensions.GaussianPotentialUpside<TStat>(TStat, double) GaussianStatisticsExtensions.GaussianRegret<TStat>(TStat, double) GaussianStatisticsExtensions.GaussianShortfall<TStat>(TStat, double) GaussianStatisticsExtensions.GaussianTopPercentile<TStat>(TStat, double) GaussianStatisticsExtensions.GaussianValueAtRisk<TStat>(TStat, double) Remarks QuantLib's class wraps Boost.Accumulators' weighted accumulator set (count, minimum, maximum, weighted mean, variance, skewness and kurtosis, and the sum of weights) and a second set over the negative samples (count, weighted second moment, sum of weights). This port keeps each feature's running value and updates them in Boost's order, through the ported Boost arithmetic: the weighted variance's iterative recurrence on the lazy weighted mean, the moments' powers by squaring, the minimum and maximum starting from ±MaxValue. That order gives QuantLib's results bit for bit. A working type: Add(double, double) and Reset() change it; it isn't thread-safe. Skewness() and Kurtosis() refuse a set whose samples weigh 0 in all, with the text Mean() refuses it with, where QuantLib's divide 0 by 0 and return NaN: a documented divergence. The weighted variance's recurrence resets the variance to 0 at a sample whose predecessors' weights vanish in the sum (they weigh 0, or less than its rounding), where Boost's divides 0 by 0, or x by 0, and leaves Variance() NaN or infinite for good: a documented divergence, the variance then that of the samples that carry the weight, as GeneralStatistics' is. api/NanoQL.Numerics.InverseCumulativeNor.summary: Struct InverseCumulativeNormal Namespace NanoQL.Numerics Assembly NanoQL.dll The inverse cumulative normal distribution: given a probability p between zero and one, the y with F(y) = p, F the cumulative normal distribution of average μ and standard deviation σ. It uses Acklam's approximation, by Peter J. Acklam, University of Oslo, Statistics Division. public readonly struct InverseCumulativeNormal : IInverseCumulative Implements IInverseCumulative Inherited Members ValueType.Equals(object) ValueType.GetHashCode() ValueType.ToString() object.GetType() object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) Remarks It also turns a uniform distribution into a normal one; for a low-discrepancy uniform sequence it keeps the sequence's low discrepancy, which the Box–Muller approach and its variants don't. A configuration struct: its zero value (default, new InverseCumulativeNormal(), an unassigned field or array element) is QuantLib's default construction, the standard normal (μ = 0, σ = 1). QuantLib's static f_, a cumulative distribution that only its disabled Halley refinement reads, isn't ported, nor its alias InvCumulativeNormalDistribution. api/NanoQL.Numerics.LBFGSB.html.summary: Class LBFGSB Namespace NanoQL.Numerics Assembly NanoQL.dll Limited-memory BFGS for bound-constrained optimization (L-BFGS-B). public sealed class LBFGSB : OptimizationMethod Inheritance object OptimizationMethod LBFGSB Inherited Members OptimizationMethod.Minimize(Problem, EndCriteria) OptimizationMethod.Minimize(ProblemState, EndCriteria) object.GetType() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks Faithful implementation of the algorithm of Byrd, Lu, Nocedal and Zhu, "A Limited Memory Algorithm for Bound Constrained Optimization", SIAM J. Sci. Comput. 16(5):1190-1208, 1995. Coordinates whose bound is ±MaxValue are treated as unbounded, so with no active bounds the method reduces to plain limited-memory BFGS. Explicit bounds may instead be passed to the constructor, overriding the constraint. Limited memory trades accuracy of the Hessian model for cost: it stores only the last memory correction pairs, needing O(memory·n) storage and work per step instead of the O(n²) of dense BFGS, at the price of linear rather than superlinear convergence. This typically results in a modest increase in iteration count. Immutable: each minimization keeps its correction pairs and working arrays to itself. On the relative function-reduction stop the problem's gradient norm is the projected gradient's at the point returned, where QuantLib's keeps the previous iterate's (Divergences/LBFGSBTests.cs). The breakpoints of the Cauchy search are sorted stably, so equal breakpoints keep QuantLib's order up to 32 variables (MSVC's insertion sort) and their own beyond, where MSVC's introsort reorders them. Trefethen, "Barycentric Lagrange interpolation", SIAM Review 46(3), 2004): the polynomial through every point, evaluated by the barycentric formula. public sealed class LagrangeInterpolation : Interpolation Inheritance object Extrapolator Interpolation LagrangeInterpolation Inherited Members Interpolation.XValues() Interpolation.YValues() Interpolation.IsInRange(double) Interpolation.Evaluate(double, bool) Interpolation.Primitive(double, bool) Interpolation.Derivative(double, bool) Interpolation.SecondDerivative(double, bool) Interpolation.XMin Interpolation.XMax Extrapolator.AllowsExtrapolation object.GetType() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Extension Methods ExtrapolatorExtensions.DisableExtrapolation<T>(T, bool) ExtrapolatorExtensions.EnableExtrapolation<T>(T, bool) Remarks It copies its inputs, as every Interpolation does; its barycentric weights depend on the x values alone. The x values must not repeat, which QuantLib checks only under its extra safety checks. At a node the value is the node's y. QuantLib finds the node by a binary search for the first x not below x − 10ε|x| and returns its y when that x is less than 10ε|x| above (lagrangeinterpolation.hpp:114-120): at x = 0 the band is empty, so a node at zero falls through to the barycentric sum, which divides by zero, and on descending x values (QuantLib's own Chebyshev-points test gives them) the search never lands on a node, so every node's value is NaN. Here the band is closed and the nodes are scanned in order: on ascending x values the node is QuantLib's, and the value off the nodes is QuantLib's on any order. Documented divergences (Divergences/LagrangeZeroNodeTests.cs). api/NanoQL.Numerics.LevenbergMarquardt.h.summary: Class LevenbergMarquardt Namespace NanoQL.Numerics Assembly NanoQL.dll The Levenberg–Marquardt optimization method, minimizing the sum of the squares of the cost function's values. public sealed class LevenbergMarquardt : OptimizationMethod Inheritance object OptimizationMethod LevenbergMarquardt Inherited Members OptimizationMethod.Minimize(Problem, EndCriteria) OptimizationMethod.Minimize(ProblemState, EndCriteria) object.GetType() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks This implementation is based on MINPACK (http://www.netlib.org/minpack, http://www.netlib.org/cephes/linalg.tgz). It has a built in finite-difference scheme to compute the Jacobian, which is used by default. If useCostFunctionsJacobian is true the corresponding method in the cost function of the problem is used instead. Note that the default implementation of the Jacobian in CostFunction uses a central difference (order 2, but requiring more function evaluations) compared to the forward difference implemented here (order 1). A point that fails the constraint, or whose values aren't all finite, gets the value 1e10 for every function, so the method steers away from it; its Jacobian there is the initial point's. Immutable: the problem the MINPACK callbacks read, which QuantLib keeps in a member, is the minimization's own. Constructors LevenbergMarquardt(double, double, double, bool) Initializes a new instance of the LevenbergMarquardt class. public LevenbergMarquardt(double epsfcn = 1E-08, double xtol = 1E-08, double gtol = 1E-08, bool useCostFunctionsJacobian = false) Parameters epsfcn double The functions' relative errors, which set the forward-difference step. xtol double The relative error desired in the solution, non-negative. gtol double The orthogonality desired between the values and the Jacobian's columns, non-negative. useCostFunctionsJacobian bool Whether to use the cost function's Jacobian rather than forward differences. api/NanoQL.Numerics.LogCubic.html.title: Struct LogCubic | nanoql
api/NanoQL.Numerics.LogCubic.html.summary: Struct LogCubic Namespace NanoQL.Numerics Assembly NanoQL.dll The log-cubic interpolation factory and traits. public readonly struct LogCubic : IInterpolator Implements IInterpolator Inherited Members ValueType.Equals(object) ValueType.GetHashCode() ValueType.ToString() object.GetType() object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) Remarks A configuration struct holding QuantLib's six parameters, which it doesn't expose, as QuantLib doesn't. QuantLib's LogCubic has no default constructor, since its derivative approximation has no default, so its zero value (default, new LogCubic(), an unassigned field or array element) is refused by every member with InvalidOperationException, as ImmutableArray<T>'s default is. QuantLib's presets MonotonicLogCubic and KrugerLog are structs of their own, each converting to the LogCubic it is. Constructors LogCubic(CubicInterpolationDerivativeApprox, bool, CubicInterpolationBoundaryCondition, double, CubicInterpolationBoundaryCondition, double) Initializes a new instance of the LogCubic struct. public LogCubic(CubicInterpolationDerivativeApprox da, bool monotonic = true, CubicInterpolationBoundaryCondition leftCondition = CubicInterpolationBoundaryCondition.SecondDerivative, double leftConditionValue = 0, CubicInterpolationBoundaryCondition rightCondition = CubicInterpolationBoundaryCondition.SecondDerivative, double rightConditionValue = 0) Parameters da CubicInterpolationDerivativeApprox The first-derivative approximation of the logarithms. monotonic bool Whether to apply Hyman's monotonicity filter to the logarithms' cubic. leftCondition CubicInterpolationBoundaryCondition The left boundary condition, for the spline approximation. leftConditionValue double The left condition's value, where it takes one. rightCondition CubicInterpolationBoundaryCondition The right boundary condition, for the spline approximation. rightConditionValue double The right condition's value, where it takes one. Exceptions ArgumentOutOfRangeException An enum argument isn't a member of its type. Methods CheckPoints(int) Runs the checks QuantLib's interpolation makes when it is built over a number of points, before it reads their values: the fewest points its implementation takes, and the counts its configuration needs. public void CheckPoints(int points) Parameters points int The number of points. Remarks The bootstraps read it on their first pass: QuantLib builds a curve's interpolation over its first nodes before their values are solved (interpolateWithoutUpdate), and takes linear interpolation where a global interpolation refuses to be built over that many points (iterativebootstrap.hpp:295-310). Interpolate(ReadOnlySpan<double>, ReadOnlySpan<double>) runs every check, these and the ones on the values alike. The default refuses none, so a factory of one's own keeps compiling; a factory overrides it with its construction checks, so that a curve on it takes the fallback where QuantLib's would. Exceptions ArgumentException The interpolation can't be built over that many points. NanoQLException The interpolation's configuration can't be built over that many points. Interpolate(ReadOnlySpan<double>, ReadOnlySpan<double>) Builds a LogCubicInterpolation over the given points, which it copies, with this factory's parameters. public Interpolation Interpolate(ReadOnlySpan<double> x, ReadOnlySpan<double> y) Parameters x ReadOnlySpan<double> The x values, which must be sorted. y ReadOnlySpan<double> The y values, one per x value, each positive. Returns Interpolation The interpolation. Exceptions InvalidOperationException This is the zero value, which QuantLib can't construct. ArgumentException The sizes differ, there are too few points, or a y value isn't positive. NanoQLException The scheme or a condition isn't implemented, or the spline's system has a zero pivot. Explicit Interface Implementations Global Gets a value indicating whether the interpolation is global: true. static bool Global { get; } Returns bool RequiredPoints Gets the fewest points the interpolation takes: 2. static int RequiredPoints { get; } Returns int

It implements the concept of a matrix as used in linear algebra, and is not meant to be used as a container. [WorkingType] public sealed class Matrix : IEquatable<Matrix> Inheritance object Matrix Implements IEquatable<Matrix> Inherited Members object.GetType() object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) Remarks A working type: mutable, owned by one computation and not thread-safe, as an array is. The indexer sets elements, and the compound assignments (m += n, m *= x, ...) change the matrix in place, so every reference to it sees the change; the binary and unary operators return new matrices. Clone() is the deep copy, where QuantLib copies a Matrix by value. The matrices of a sum or a difference need the same size. QuantLib's iterators over the whole storage are AsSpan() and GetEnumerator(); its row iterators are Row(int), a span over a row's elements; its column iterators are Column(int), a copy of a column, and indexed loops; its reverse iterators (rbegin(), rend(), over the storage, a row or a column) are indexed loops run backwards. m[i][j] and m(i, j) are both m[i, j]. api/NanoQL.Numerics.MidPoint.html.summary: Struct MidPoint Namespace NanoQL.Numerics Assembly NanoQL.dll QuantLib's midpoint policy: each refinement splits every interval in three, adding the integrand at the outer thirds' midpoints, so it refines a midpoint estimate. public readonly struct MidPoint : ITrapezoidIntegrationPolicy Implements ITrapezoidIntegrationPolicy Inherited Members ValueType.Equals(object) ValueType.GetHashCode() ValueType.ToString() object.GetType() object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) Remarks QuantLib starts it from the trapezoid's estimate, as every policy (trapezoidintegral.hpp:58-82), which its refinement doesn't refine: the start's error then falls by a third per tripling, first order, so exp on [0, 1] at 1e-6 takes 531,442 evaluations where the midpoint start takes 2,187, and at 1e-10 it doesn't return. api/NanoQL.Numerics.MultiCubicSpline.htm.summary: Class MultiCubicSpline Namespace NanoQL.Numerics Assembly NanoQL.dll N-dimensional cubic spline interpolation between discrete points, in 1 to 15 dimensions. public sealed class MultiCubicSpline Inheritance object MultiCubicSpline Inherited Members object.GetType() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks QuantLib's recursion: at construction a natural cubic spline's second derivatives along the last dimension, for every line of it; at each evaluation the splines of the lower dimensions through the values the higher ones interpolate, the first dimension last, each step's arithmetic and order QuantLib's, so the values are QuantLib's. Immutable and safe to share across threads: the grid and the values are copied, and each evaluation computes QuantLib's coefficients in scratch of its own, where QuantLib's spline holds references to its inputs and evaluates through mutable members. The dimension is the grid's, read at construction, where QuantLib's is a template parameter. The last grid point of a dimension is interpolated on its last interval, where QuantLib refuses it as extrapolation (its documented bug, "cannot interpolate at the grid points on the boundary surface"), and with extrapolation allowed a point beyond it reads the last value, where QuantLib's flat value reads one value past the data; an argument that isn't a number is refused, where QuantLib's search reads past the grid (Divergences/MultiCubicSplineBoundaryTests.cs). api/NanoQL.Numerics.NonCentralCumulative.title: Class NonCentralCumulativeChiSquareDistribution | nanoql
api/NanoQL.Numerics.NonCentralCumulative.summary: Class NonCentralCumulativeChiSquareDistribution Namespace NanoQL.Numerics Assembly NanoQL.dll The cumulative non-central chi-squared distribution with df degrees of freedom and non-centrality ncp, by the series of Poisson-weighted central terms (Ding's algorithm, as R's pnchisq sums it). public sealed class NonCentralCumulativeChiSquareDistribution Inheritance object NonCentralCumulativeChiSquareDistribution Inherited Members object.GetType() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks QuantLib 1.44's series returns values past its range (chisquaredistribution.cpp:33-91): where its first term or its Poisson weight exp(−ncp/2) falls below the normal range of doubles, it runs on subnormal numbers, then zeros (at df 10 and x 1,547 it reads 1.81 where the answer is 1; from ncp 1,490.3 every term is 0 and the sum 0); and where its loop ends at 10,000 iterations with its bound's denominator never positive, the negative bound passes as converged. Here the series is QuantLib's master's, upstream's #2908 (b76016ff5): it skips the underflowing weights and terms by their logarithms, returns 1 where a Chernoff bound puts the upper tail below 1e-12, runs to 1,000,000 iterations, and refuses a loop that ends before its bound can be computed ("didn't converge"). A documented divergence from 1.44 (Divergences/ChiSquaredSeriesRefusalTests.cs), checked by upstream's case against Boost's distribution (DistributionsTests.TestNonCentralChiSquareLargeArguments); every value inside 1.44's range is QuantLib's bit for bit. QuantLib's large-df branch tests |x/2 − df/2| without assigning it and starts from t = 0 (:48-52), as #2908 keeps it; above df 1.1e15 and within 1.5e-8 of df its bound then never falls to 1e-12 within the iterations, so it is refused, and its missing assignment needs no fix of its own. api/NanoQL.Numerics.PlackettCopula.html.summary: Class PlackettCopula Namespace NanoQL.Numerics Assembly NanoQL.dll The Plackett copula, C(x, y) = (s − √(s² − 4xyθ(θ − 1)))/(2(θ − 1)), s = 1 + (θ − 1)(x + y). public sealed class PlackettCopula Inheritance object PlackettCopula Inherited Members object.GetType() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks Immutable. On the unit square's edges it returns the boundary values, C(u, 0) = C(0, v) = 0, C(u, 1) = u and C(1, v) = v, before its formula, as every copula here does. QuantLib's formula cancels wherever the root nears s: near the edges at every θ (1e-7 relative at θ 0.5 and 2 on points 1e-8 from them) and everywhere as θ nears 1 (9.5e-5). nanoql takes the stable root, 2xyθ/(s + √…) where s is positive, QuantLib's form elsewhere, and above θ 1 the radicand as 1 + 2(θ − 1)(x(1 − y) + y(1 − x)) + ((θ − 1)(x − y))², whose terms are all non-negative, where QuantLib's cancels as θ grows (1e-8 at θ 1e8): within 4e-16 relative of a high-precision evaluation of QuantLib's formula on points within 1e-12 of the edges, from θ 0.1 to 1e12; toward θ 0 the copula nears max(x + y − 1, 0), whose cancellation near x + y = 1 no form avoids. The result equals QuantLib's root at the rank that keeps the non-negative eigenvalues, with zero columns appended. api/NanoQL.Numerics.Ranlux64UniformRng.h.summary: Class Ranlux64UniformRng Namespace NanoQL.Numerics Assembly NanoQL.dll M. Luescher's "luxury" uniform random-number generator, at the luxury level its derived class sets: Ranlux3UniformRng (any theoretically possible correlations have a very small chance of being observed) or Ranlux4UniformRng (the highest possible luxury). [WorkingType] public abstract class Ranlux64UniformRng : IRng Inheritance object Ranlux64UniformRng Implements IRng Derived Ranlux3UniformRng Ranlux4UniformRng Inherited Members object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks QuantLib's implementation is a proxy for the standard library's generator: a 48-bit subtract-with-carry engine (std::subtract_with_carry_engine<std::uint_fast64_t, 48, 10, 24>) under a discard-block engine that keeps r of every p draws, QuantLib's template parameters, here the protected constructor's. Its numbers are those of MSVC's standard library, which built the Python wheel and the harness. For more detail see M. Luescher, A portable high-quality random number generator for lattice field theory simulations, Comp. Phys. Comm. 79 (1994) 100. A mutable working type: each draw changes the generator, and it is not thread-safe. Its seed is explicit, in [1, 4294967295], with no default, where QuantLib's defaults to 19780503: the standard's seeding takes 0 as that default, and reduces a seed modulo 2147483563 through its linear congruential seed sequence, so seeds that differ by that modulus draw one sequence, and a multiple of it draws the sequence of seed 1, in QuantLib as here. api/NanoQL.Numerics.RoundingType.html.title: Enum RoundingType | nanoql
api/NanoQL.Numerics.RoundingType.html.summary: Enum RoundingType Namespace NanoQL.Numerics Assembly NanoQL.dll The rounding methods of Rounding: QuantLib's Rounding::Type, with its values. public enum RoundingType Fields Ceiling = 5 Positive numbers are rounded down and negative numbers rounded up, using the OMG round-up and round-down rules. Closest = 3 The first decimal place past the precision is rounded up if greater than or equal to the rounding digit; this corresponds to the OMG round-up rule. When the rounding digit is 5, the result is the one closest to the original number, hence the name. Down = 2 All decimal places past the precision are truncated. Floor = 4 Positive numbers are rounded up and negative numbers rounded down, using the OMG round-up and round-down rules. None = 0 Do not round: return the number unmodified. Up = 1 The first decimal place past the precision is rounded up. This differs from the OMG rule, which rounds up only if the decimal to be rounded is greater than or equal to the rounding digit. Remarks The methods follow the OMG specification available at http://www.omg.org/cgi-bin/doc?formal/00-06-29.pdf. The names of Floor and Ceiling might be misleading: check the reference.

api/NanoQL.Numerics.SABRInterpolation.ht.summary: Class SABRInterpolation Namespace NanoQL.Numerics Assembly NanoQL.dll The SABR smile fitted to discrete volatilities: SABR's four parameters fitted to the volatilities at the strikes, interpolated by the SABR volatility at the fitted parameters. public sealed class SABRInterpolation : Interpolation, IXabrInterpolation Inheritance object Extrapolator Interpolation SABRInterpolation Implements IXabrInterpolation Inherited Members Interpolation.XValues() Interpolation.YValues() Interpolation.IsInRange(double) Interpolation.Evaluate(double, bool) Interpolation.Primitive(double, bool) Interpolation.Derivative(double, bool) Interpolation.SecondDerivative(double, bool) Interpolation.XMin Interpolation.XMax Extrapolator.AllowsExtrapolation object.GetType() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Extension Methods ExtrapolatorExtensions.DisableExtrapolation<T>(T, bool) ExtrapolatorExtensions.EnableExtrapolation<T>(T, bool) Remarks The fit runs when the interpolation is built: QuantLib's construction followed by its update(), which every QuantLib user calls at once. A new fit is a new interpolation, so update() isn't ported. The fit minimizes the (vega-weighted, by default) squared errors from the given guesses, then, while the error stays above errorAccept, from up to maxGuesses − 1 more guesses drawn from a Halton sequence seeded with QuantLib's 42, keeping the best; its results are QuantLib's at every step. As QuantLib's, a restart is kept by the error the cost function's last evaluation gives: the result's under LevenbergMarquardt, the default, which evaluates its result last, but a later trial's under Simplex, which returns its best vertex without evaluating it again. Fixed parameters go through the parameter transforms at every evaluation, as QuantLib's do, so a fixed β of 0.5 is reported as 0.5000000000000001. A fixed or guessed ρ beyond ±0.9999, or α or ν below 1e-7, is taken as the nearest value the transform reaches, where QuantLib's transform flips ρ's sign or fails; and a smile of zero volatilities with vega weights is refused, where QuantLib fits on NaN weights. Immutable and thread-safe once built: it copies its inputs, and nothing writes the fit after it. api/NanoQL.Numerics.SVD.html.summary: Class SVD Namespace NanoQL.Numerics Assembly NanoQL.dll The singular value decomposition of a real matrix, M = U·S·Vᵀ. public sealed class SVD Inheritance object SVD Inherited Members object.GetType() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks Refer to Golub and Van Loan, "Matrix computation", The Johns Hopkins University Press. QuantLib's implementation is adapted from the TNT project (JAMA), developed at the National Institute of Standards and Technology and in the public domain. It requires at least as many rows as columns; a matrix with fewer rows is decomposed transposed, and its U and V swapped, since M = (U·S·Vᵀ)ᵀ = V·S·Uᵀ. The decomposition is computed in the constructor; U(), V(), SingularValues() and S() return copies. A matrix with a NaN or infinite entry is refused on entry, where QuantLib's main loop, which has no test for too many iterations, never ends; and so is a finite matrix whose decomposition leaves the range of doubles, a singular value beyond it (entries near 1e307), refused at the main loop's first non-finite singular value or superdiagonal entry, where QuantLib's loop never ends either. Documented divergences (Divergences/SvdNonFiniteRefusalTests.cs). Every matrix QuantLib decomposes keeps its arithmetic. api/NanoQL.Numerics.Simplex.html.title: Class Simplex | nanoql
api/NanoQL.Numerics.Simplex.html.summary: Class Simplex Namespace NanoQL.Numerics Assembly NanoQL.dll The multi-dimensional downhill simplex method of Nelder and Mead. public sealed class Simplex : OptimizationMethod Inheritance object OptimizationMethod Simplex Inherited Members OptimizationMethod.Minimize(Problem, EndCriteria) OptimizationMethod.Minimize(ProblemState, EndCriteria) object.GetType() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks This method is rather raw and requires quite a lot of computing resources, but it has the advantage that it does not need any evaluation of the cost function's gradient, and that it is quite easily implemented. First, we choose N+1 starting points, given here by a starting point P₀ and N points such that Pᵢ = P₀ + λeᵢ, where λ is the problem's characteristic length scale. These points will form a geometrical form called simplex. The principle of the downhill simplex method is, at each iteration, to move the worst point (highest cost function value) through the opposite face to a better point. When the simplex seems to be constrained in a valley, it will be contracted downhill, keeping the best point unchanged. The minimization ends when the simplex's size, the mean distance of its vertices from their centre, falls below the end criteria's root epsilon, or at the maximum number of iterations. Immutable: the vertices, which QuantLib keeps in mutable members, live inside each minimization. api/NanoQL.Numerics.SobolRsg.html.summary: Class SobolRsg Namespace NanoQL.Numerics Assembly NanoQL.dll The Sobol low-discrepancy sequence generator. A Gray code counter and bitwise operations are used for very fast sequence generation. [WorkingType] public sealed class SobolRsg : ISeedableRsg<SobolRsg>, IRsg Inheritance object SobolRsg Implements ISeedableRsg<SobolRsg> IRsg Inherited Members object.GetType() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks The implementation relies on primitive polynomials modulo two from the book "Monte Carlo Methods in Finance" by Peter Jäckel; 21 200 of them are provided, so the dimensionality is at most 21,200. The choice of initialization numbers (also known as free direction integers) is crucial for the homogeneity properties of the sequence (SobolRsgDirectionIntegers). For more info on Sobol' sequences see also "Monte Carlo Methods in Financial Engineering," by P. Glasserman, 2004, Springer, section 5.2.3. A mutable working type: each draw changes the generator, and it is not thread-safe. A draw returns a view of the generator's buffer, valid until its next draw. The seed, in [1, 4294967295], only affects the direction integers beyond those tabulated for the chosen set, so lower dimensionalities give the same sequence for any seed; QuantLib's seed 0, which there draws a seed from the clock, is refused. With the Gray code, the counter stops one short of QuantLib's period: SkipTo(long) refuses 4294967295, and the draw that would take the counter there throws "period exceeded", where QuantLib's behaviour is undefined. Remarks The so called generating integer is chosen to be γ(n) = n if useGrayCode is false and γ(n) = G(n), where G(n) is the Gray code of n, otherwise. The Sobol integers are then constructed using formula 8.20 resp. 8.23, see "Monte Carlo Methods in Finance" by Peter Jäckel. The default is to use the Gray code since this allows a faster sequence generation. api/NanoQL.Numerics.SobolRsgDirectionInt.title: Enum SobolRsgDirectionIntegers | nanoql
api/NanoQL.Numerics.SobolRsgDirectionInt.summary: Enum SobolRsgDirectionIntegers Namespace NanoQL.Numerics Assembly NanoQL.dll The initialization numbers (free direction integers) of a SobolRsg (QuantLib's SobolRsg::DirectionIntegers). Their choice is crucial for the homogeneity properties of the sequence: Sobol defines two, Property A and Property A'. public enum SobolRsgDirectionIntegers Fields Jaeckel = 1 Jäckel's, in his book (section 8.3), up to dimension 32. Coefficients for d ≤ 8 are the same as in Bratley and Fox, so Property A' holds for d ≤ 6 but Property A holds for d ≤ 32. JoeKuoD5 = 4 A set of the Joe–Kuo numbers, due to Stephen Joe and Frances Kuo (S. Joe and F. Y. Kuo, Constructing Sobol sequences with better two-dimensional projections, preprint Nov 22 2007; see http://web.maths.unsw.edu.au/~fkuo/sobol/), tabulated up to dimension 2,000. JoeKuoD6 = 5 A set of the Joe–Kuo numbers, tabulated up to dimension 21,200, every dimension the generator takes. JoeKuoD7 = 6 A set of the Joe–Kuo numbers, tabulated up to dimension 1,900. Kuo = 7 The Kuo numbers, due to Stephen Joe and Frances Kuo, tabulated up to dimension 4,926. They were generated to work with a different ordering of primitive polynomials for the first 40 or so dimensions, which is why they use the alternative primitive polynomials. Kuo2 = 8 A second set of the Kuo numbers, tabulated up to dimension 3,947, with the alternative primitive polynomials. Kuo3 = 9 A third set of the Kuo numbers, tabulated up to dimension 4,587, with the alternative primitive polynomials. SobolLevitan = 2 Bratley and Fox's coefficients up to dimension 40, crediting unpublished work of Sobol' and Levitan (Bratley, P., Fox, B.L. (1988) "Algorithm 659: Implementing Sobol's quasirandom sequence generator," ACM Transactions on Mathematical Software 14:88-100). They satisfy Property A for d ≤ 20 and d = 23, 31, 33, 34, 37; Property A' holds for d ≤ 6. SobolLevitanLemieux = 3 The coefficients of Lemieux, Cieslak, and Luttmer's implementation up to dimension 360: those for d ≤ 40 are the same as in Bratley and Fox, and for 40 < d ≤ 360 they have been calculated as optimal values based on the "resolution" criterion ("RandQMC user's guide - A package for randomized quasi-Monte Carlo methods in C," by C. Lemieux, M. Cieslak, and K. Luttmer, version January 13 2004). Unit = 0 The unit initialization numbers suggested in "Numerical Recipes in C", 2nd edition, by Press, Teukolsky, Vetterling, and Flannery (section 7.7), which fail the test for Property A even for low dimensions.

api/NanoQL.Numerics.SparseILUPreconditio.summary: Class SparseILUPreconditioner Namespace NanoQL.Numerics Assembly NanoQL.dll A preconditioner by the incomplete LU factorisation ILU(k) of a sparse matrix (Saad 1996, Iterative Methods for Sparse Linear Systems): A ≈ L·U, the fill kept to the given level, applied by a forward and a backward solve. public sealed class SparseILUPreconditioner Inheritance object SparseILUPreconditioner Inherited Members object.GetType() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks Immutable: the factors are computed at construction; L() and U() return copies, and Apply(Vector) returns a new vector, the form of the Krylov solvers' preconditioner. QuantLib records each new entry's fill level from the levels' nonzero entries by the entries' rank among the row's nonzero values, which a value that cancels to 0 shifts, so a later row reads another entry's level; here each entry's level is its own (a documented divergence; QuantLib's factors wherever no entry cancels). QuantLib's reads of U also insert zero elements where none is stored, past its last column too, which changes U's structure but not its values; here they insert nothing. A row that keeps no entry on or right of its diagonal, where QuantLib's elimination loop never ends, is refused, and Apply(Vector) refuses a vector not of the matrix's size, which QuantLib reads unchecked. api/NanoQL.Numerics.TqrEigenDecompositio.title: Class TqrEigenDecomposition | nanoql
api/NanoQL.Numerics.TqrEigenDecompositio.summary: Class TqrEigenDecomposition Namespace NanoQL.Numerics Assembly NanoQL.dll The eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a symmetric tridiagonal matrix by QR steps with an explicit shift (Wilkinson): J.H. Wilkinson and C. Reinsch, Linear Algebra, vol. II of Handbook for Automatic Computation (Springer, 1971); "Numerical Recipes in C", 2nd edition, Press, Teukolsky, Vetterling, Flannery. public sealed class TqrEigenDecomposition Inheritance object TqrEigenDecomposition Inherited Members object.GetType() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks The eigenvalues are sorted in decreasing order, each eigenvector with its first component non-negative. The decomposition is computed in the constructor; Eigenvalues() and Eigenvectors() return copies. QuantLib's iteration has no bound, and on some inputs it never returns: eigenvalues in pairs of opposite sign under NoShift, and, under any strategy, a NaN, an infinite off-diagonal element or entries whose squares overflow. While one eigenvalue converges, the next step is a function of the diagonal and off-diagonal alone, so a state repeated bit for bit proves the iteration endless: Brent's cycle test on that state refuses there, and every input QuantLib answers keeps QuantLib's result (Divergences/TqrEigenDecompositionCycleTests.cs). The test catches the inputs whose state repeats, as a zero diagonal's does, but not every pair: under NoShift a pair whose magnitudes differ slightly converges at their ratio without repeating a state, about 18.7/ε iterations for [[ε, 1], [1, ε]], and a pair equal only to rounding may never repeat one either. Such an input runs as long as QuantLib's, without end once the ratio rounds to 1: a QuantLib defect kept, since no bound on the iterations would separate these inputs from slow ones QuantLib answers. The shifted strategies, the default among them, converge on them. Inheritance object Integrator TrapezoidIntegral<TIntegrationPolicy> Derived SimpsonIntegral Inherited Members Integrator.SetAbsoluteAccuracy(double) Integrator.SetMaxEvaluations(int) Integrator.Integrate(Func<double, double>, double, double) Integrator.IntegrateWithStatistics(Func<double, double>, double, double) Integrator.IntegrationSuccess(IntegrationResult) Integrator.AbsoluteAccuracy Integrator.MaxEvaluations object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks Given a target accuracy ε, the integral of f between a and b is calculated by means of the trapezoid formula ∫ f dx = ½f(x₀) + f(x₁) + … + f(x_{N−1}) + ½f(x_N), where x₀ = a, x_N = b and xᵢ = a + iΔx with Δx = (b − a)/N. api/NanoQL.Numerics.Vector.html.summary: Class Vector Namespace NanoQL.Numerics Assembly NanoQL.dll A 1-D array used in linear algebra: QuantLib's Array, renamed. It implements the concept of a vector as used in linear algebra, and is not meant to be used as a container. Inheritance object Extrapolator Interpolation ZabrInterpolation<TEvaluation> Implements IXabrInterpolation Inherited Members Interpolation.XValues() Interpolation.YValues() Interpolation.IsInRange(double) Interpolation.Evaluate(double, bool) Interpolation.Primitive(double, bool) Interpolation.Derivative(double, bool) Interpolation.SecondDerivative(double, bool) Interpolation.XMin Interpolation.XMax Extrapolator.AllowsExtrapolation object.GetType() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Extension Methods ExtrapolatorExtensions.DisableExtrapolation<T>(T, bool) ExtrapolatorExtensions.EnableExtrapolation<T>(T, bool) Remarks The fit is SABRInterpolation's, XABR's, over ZABR's parameters: it runs when the interpolation is built, from the guesses and then, while the error stays above errorAccept, from up to maxGuesses − 1 Halton guesses seeded with QuantLib's 42, keeping the best; its values are QuantLib's at every step. ν is fitted in [0, 5] and γ in [0, 1.9], the ranges QuantLib's transform maps them into. The model the interpolation prices with is a section built from a copy of the parameters, as QuantLib's is. QuantLib doesn't rebuild it after writing the best restart's parameters back, so where the restarts run out without an accepted fit, or the last trial wasn't the best one, its values and errors are its last trial's while its parameters are the best restart's. Here the section is rebuilt from the best parameters, so the values, the errors and the parameters agree. A fixed or guessed ν above 5, or γ above 1.9, is taken as 5 or 1.9, where QuantLib's transform wraps it to another value inside the range; ρ and α as SABRInterpolation takes them. Immutable and thread-safe once built: it copies its inputs, and nothing writes the fit after it.
