api/NanoQL.PricingEngines.AnalyticGJRGAR.title: Class AnalyticGJRGARCHEngine | nanoql
api/NanoQL.PricingEngines.AnalyticGJRGAR.summary: Class AnalyticGJRGARCHEngine Namespace NanoQL.PricingEngines Assembly NanoQL.dll The analytic GJR-GARCH(1,1) engine for European options: Duan, Gauthier, Simonato and Sasseville's Edgeworth approximation, from the first four moments of the log return over the option's days. public sealed class AnalyticGJRGARCHEngine Inheritance object AnalyticGJRGARCHEngine Inherited Members object.GetType() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks An immutable object over its GJRGARCHModel. It keeps the moments of each maturity it prices in a memo keyed by the day count and the rate they read, each entry QuantLib's arithmetic on the engine's model, whose parameters and curves are fixed with it, so a price is a fresh engine's bit for bit whatever the engine priced before and on whichever thread; QuantLib's engine keeps one maturity's moments and its key leaves out the rate, so a model relinked to another curve can price on the old rate. QuantLib's prices are corrected where they're wrong: the model's time runs from the earliest curve date, as GJRGARCHProcess's; a maturity of no day prices the forward's discounted intrinsic value, where QuantLib's moments are 0/0; with a dividend yield the call is D_q times QuantLib's approximation and the put D_q·C + K·D_r − S·D_q, where QuantLib returns the price over D_q; and a payoff that isn't a plain vanilla is refused, where QuantLib returns the call's or put's value by its option type. Two of QuantLib's defects are kept, its prices returned. Its fourth moment is wrong in the variance's own terms: where the variance is deterministic (α = γ = 0) the log return is normal, but the engine's kurtosis is about 3 − Σh, Σh the total variance, so at a daily variance of 2e-4 a year's calls at 0.9, 1 and 1.1 of the spot price 0.12%, 0.23% and 0.29% above Black-Scholes at the same variance. And its Edgeworth expansion is a density only for moderate skewness and kurtosis: against a Monte Carlo of the discrete model it approximates, the day's shock moving the log return and then the next day's variance (QuantLib's gjrgarchmodel test model from its stationary variance, spot 50, a flat 4% curve, calls at 45, 50 and 55, 180 days and a year; 2,560,000 paths on QuantLib's Mersenne twister), it errs from −3.2% to +0.3% at λ 0, down to −8.8% at λ 0.1 and from −8.3% to −32% at λ 0.2 and 180 days, and at λ 0.2 and a year its calls are negative, −0.63 to −6.60 where the model's are 10.67 to 5.55 (QuantLib's own Monte Carlo engine, daily steps of its continuous-time process, gives the model's prices within 1.3%). Where the variance's second or third moment grows without bound its prices run off: −41,067 at two years on that model at λ 0.2 (m₂ 1.0022, m₃ 1.0257), and −3.4e19 at two years at 252 days a year with α 0.05, β 0.85, γ 0.1 and λ 0.3 (m₂ 1.0135, m₃ 1.1208). CalculateWithinBounds(VanillaOption, EvaluationContext), experimental, returns the same price but refuses one outside the no-arbitrage bounds beyond rounding (Conventions/AnalyticGJRGARCHBoundsTests.cs): on that model it refuses both wings at every λ, the low strikes at every maturity and the high strikes from two years, where the expansion's expected spot misses the forward (at λ 0 a deep in-the-money call falls below its bound by 4.7e-7 at two days and by 0.0194 at two years), and the runaway prices from λ 0.15; a price it returns keeps the expansion's error. Where two of the variance's growth factors m₁, m₂ and m₃, or one of them and 1, are equal (α = β = γ = 0; an integrated GARCH), QuantLib's divided differences of their powers are 0/0 and its price NaN; here each is taken at its limit, the same polynomial in the factors, the limit of QuantLib's prices as the factors meet. QuantLib's own prices, kept bit for bit off the meeting point, lose their accuracy within about 1e-7 of all three factors meeting at 1 (α = γ = 0, β near 1), where its nested difference quotients cancel: a year's call there moves by as much as 12%. Reference: Jin-Chuan Duan, Genevieve Gauthier, Jean-Guy Simonato, Caroline Sasseville, 2006. Approximating the GJR-GARCH and EGARCH option pricing models analytically. Journal of Computational Finance, Volume 9, Number 3, Spring 2006. QuantLib's values are corrected where they're wrong: Where the fit has no decaying exponential, the ratio (Λ − a)/b that gives c at or below 0, or b = 0, c is the limit c = +∞, the b terms dropped, and at or above 1 the limit c = 0, its b terms b·T and −b(1 − e^{−λT})/λ; QuantLib's c is NaN there, and so is its price, at ρ_Sr = 0 too, or the fit grows exponentially. In between, QuantLib's fit and bits. I₄'s last term is b·e^{−cT}·(−expm1((c − λ)T))/(c − λ), with its limit −b·T·e^{−cT} at c = λ, where QuantLib's b/(c − λ) is 0/0, and below λT = 2e-2, where I₄'s terms cancel to order λ and QuantLib's double departs from the expression's exact value by more than 1e-12 relative, I₄ is evaluated in double-double, below 1e-10 in quad-double and below 1e-12 by the cubic through four quad-double values, the cut and floors measured against the expression in 120 digits. api/NanoQL.PricingEngines.AnalyticHeston.summary: Class AnalyticHestonEngine Namespace NanoQL.PricingEngines Assembly NanoQL.dll The analytic Heston engine: European plain-vanilla options under the Heston model, by the Fourier transform of the model's characteristic function, integrated by a FourierIntegration. public class AnalyticHestonEngine Inheritance object AnalyticHestonEngine Derived AnalyticHestonHullWhiteEngine BatesDoubleExpEngine BatesEngine Inherited Members object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks Two algebraically equivalent formulations of the characteristic function's complex logarithm exist. Gatheral's (also Duffie, Pan and Singleton's, and Schoutens, Simons and Tistaert's) has no discontinuities and works with adaptive integrations; Heston's original needs a branch correction, which refuses them. The control-variate forms, Andersen and Piterbarg's, the asymptotic expansion's and the angled contour's, integrate the difference from a value they price in closed form. Immutable: it holds the model and the integration settings. Each price returns its number of evaluations with it (PriceVanillaPayoffWithStatistics(PlainVanillaPayoff, Date), and the results' additional result "numberOfEvaluations"), where QuantLib keeps the last call's count on the engine. The static Calculate overloads build an engine with the given settings and price through it. An extension point, as in QuantLib: jump-diffusion engines such as Bates's derive from it and add their term to the characteristic function through AddOnTerm(double, double, int). A price at a maturity date runs the model's time on the risk-free curve's day counter from the earliest reference date of the model's curves, each accruing nothing before its own, so the variance accrues from the evaluation date beside a risk-free curve settling later, as QuantLib's engine on the market restated from that date prices it; QuantLib's time runs from the risk-free curve's date, so its reads throw before that date and its integrations read 0/0 on it. An option expiring at the model's time 0, on or before every curve's date, is priced at the forward's intrinsic value. Where the dividend curve isn't dated before the risk-free curve, the time is QuantLib's. A documented divergence (Divergences/ExerciseBeforeReferenceDateTests.cs, Divergences/HestonMismatchedTimesTests.cs). api/NanoQL.PricingEngines.AnalyticHolder.summary: Class AnalyticHolderExtensibleOptionEngine Namespace NanoQL.PricingEngines Assembly NanoQL.dll The analytic engine for a holder-extensible option: Longstaff's formula, the vanilla to the first maturity and bivariate terms over the region where the holder extends, between two critical prices. public static class AnalyticHolderExtensibleOptionEngine Inheritance object AnalyticHolderExtensibleOptionEngine Inherited Members object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks Stateless. QuantLib's fixes after v1.44 (#2892) are taken: the put's correlation sign, the Newton seeds at the strike, the put's derivative, the empty extension region and the call's with dividends (Divergences/HolderExtensibleCriticalPricesTests.cs). QuantLib evaluates the formula on one zero rate, dividend yield and volatility, read at the first maturity, for both periods, so it is exact only on flat markets; here each term reads the variances to each maturity at the first strike, the correlation from their ratio and the discounts by date, and the critical prices solve the forward Black values from the first maturity (Divergences/HolderExtensibleTermStructureTests.cs, against the exact integral at the first maturity within the critical prices' accuracy). The bivariate normal is West's, QuantLib's default, where its engine reads Drezner's; an infinite critical price meets its limit there. QuantLib's Newton iterations and stopping rule are kept, capped at 1,000 iterations. Every structure is read by date, accruing nothing before its own date (Divergences/ExoticMismatchedTimesTests.cs); a date before the process's clock keeps QuantLib's "negative time" refusal. api/NanoQL.PricingEngines.AnalyticPDFHes.summary: Class AnalyticPDFHestonEngine Namespace NanoQL.PricingEngines Assembly NanoQL.dll The Heston engine for European options on any payoff: the payoff integrated against HestonRNDCalculator's density of the log spot at expiry. public sealed class AnalyticPDFHestonEngine Inheritance object AnalyticPDFHestonEngine Inherited Members object.GetType() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks An immutable object over its HestonModel and the integrations' accuracy and limit; the static Calculate builds one. The model's time runs from the earliest curve date, each curve read at the instant a time denotes; at the model's time 0 the price is the forward's discounted payoff, where QuantLib's window is zero-wide. The window is centred on the log forward, x₀ + ln(D_q/D_r), where QuantLib centres it on x₀ + ln(D_r/D_q), the forward's mirror, and misses the density at high carry and long expiry; its half-width 8√(θt + (v₀ − θ)(1 − e^{−κt})/κ) takes 1 − e^{−κt} by −expm1(−κt) below κt = 1e-2, where QuantLib's loses the (v₀ − θ) term. The window misses the density's mass beyond it: on QuantLib's own markets, a half-year put at half the forward 3% to 53% low, and at a vol of variance of 1 and correlation −0.9 puts up to 18% low. nanoql adds the tails' values where they're worth more than the integrations' accuracy, QuantLib's price where they aren't: the payoff a line between its strikes, each piece's value is exact from the spot's distribution under the risk-neutral measure and under the share measure, a Heston distribution again, at the window's edges and the strikes; a payoff not linear on a tail with mass beyond the accuracy is refused. The value added is the additional result tailsValue (Divergences/AnalyticPdfHestonTailsTests.cs). A tail is left out where both its probabilities, under the two measures, are within the accuracy, the distribution's own noise there; such a tail can be worth up to (K + F) times the accuracy, so the tails' accuracy scales with the payoff, as the window's does. Reference: A. Dragulescu, V. Yakovenko, Probability distribution of returns in the Heston model with stochastic volatility, 2002, http://arxiv.org/pdf/cond-mat/0203046.pdf. api/NanoQL.PricingEngines.AnalyticPartia.title: Class AnalyticPartialTimeBarrierOptionEngine | nanoql
api/NanoQL.PricingEngines.AnalyticPartia.summary: Class AnalyticPartialTimeBarrierOptionEngine Namespace NanoQL.PricingEngines Assembly NanoQL.dll The analytic engine for partial-time barrier options: Haug's formulas ("Option Pricing Formulas"), a put priced by the put-call symmetry from the call. public static class AnalyticPartialTimeBarrierOptionEngine Inheritance object AnalyticPartialTimeBarrierOptionEngine Inherited Members object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks The value alone, as QuantLib's. The bivariate normal is QuantLib's default, BivariateCumulativeNormalDistributionWe04DP, where QuantLib's engine reads Drezner's 1978 algorithm, to six decimal places; on QuantLib's 40 cases the values move by at most 3.3e-5, within QuantLib's tolerance. The put's symmetric call runs on a process whose curves QuantLib's constructor call binds in each other's places, the standard put-call symmetry P(S, K, r, q) = (K/S)·C(S, S²/K, q, r), and prices a start-window knock-in's European on that call's payoff and process, upstream's fix after v1.44 (#2876, Divergences/BarrierUpstreamFixesTests.cs). Documented divergences. Each rate is read on the volatility's clock, the curve's zero rate times its own time over the volatility's, and each time is the volatility's, as AnalyticBarrierEngine reads them, where QuantLib reads every structure at the risk-free curve's times (Divergences/BarrierClosedFormMismatchedTimesTests.cs). A start-window knock-out's rebate, paid at the hit before the cover event, is priced as the analytic barrier engine prices a knock-out's rebate to the cover event, where QuantLib's engine ignores the rebate; no formula covers the end windows' or the knock-ins' rebates, which are refused. A cover event on the evaluation date takes the formulas' limit: the start window's, the vanilla for a knock-out and 0 for a knock-in; the end windows', the standard barrier option through the analytic barrier engine, where QuantLib's formulas take infinite arguments. A start-window option whose spot lies beyond the barrier is refused ("barrier touched"), as the family's other engines refuse it, where QuantLib's prices it. The end-window knock-ins, which QuantLib refuses, are priced by in-out parity on QuantLib's European and end-window knock-out, the parity QuantLib applies to the start window's. And a non-European exercise is refused, as the family's European engines refuse it, where QuantLib prices it to its last date and its start-window knock-in crashes (Divergences/PartialTimeExerciseTests.cs). The formulas are first-passage closed forms in equivalent-constant rates and volatilities: no exact closed form exists under general deterministic term structures, and on shaped markets they miss an independent Monte Carlo by up to +3.9%. They are exact only where σ and r − q are flat, r and q themselves free: the engine reads the volatility at the cover date and at expiry and splits the variance at the cover date in calendar time, so a time change doesn't carry it, and where the volatility steps at the cover date under a constant (r − q)/σ² it misses by −72% to +31% (Conventions/ClosedFormExactnessTests.cs). A start-window knock-out's rebate, paid at the hit, is exact where r and q are also flat to the cover date, as the analytic barrier engine's rebate to it is. No engine in the library prices a partial-time barrier under term structures. api/NanoQL.PricingEngines.AnalyticRoughH.summary: Class AnalyticRoughHestonEngine Namespace NanoQL.PricingEngines Assembly NanoQL.dll The analytic engine for European plain-vanilla options under RoughHestonModel: the characteristic function's fractional Riccati equation solved by the Adams scheme, the Padé approximation or the lifted approximation, and the price by Andersen and Piterbarg's Fourier integral with a Black-Scholes control variate. public sealed class AnalyticRoughHestonEngine Inheritance object AnalyticRoughHestonEngine Inherited Members object.GetType() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks An immutable object over its model and settings; the static Calculate builds one. It keeps QuantLib's caches inside itself: the characteristic function by (z, t) and the lifted grid by t, keyed by their arguments' bits, and the two Riemann-Liouville weight sets, built once; each entry is computed from the engine's immutable model and settings, by QuantLib's arithmetic, and filled thread-safely, so every answer is what a fresh engine returns, whatever the engine priced before and on whichever thread. A model with other parameters is a new model and so a new engine, where QuantLib's update() drops the caches. Each price returns its integration's evaluations as the additional result "numberOfEvaluations", where QuantLib's engine keeps the count in a mutable member. The model's time runs from the earliest curve date (HestonProcess's model time), the date form reading the curves by date and the time form at the instants its time denotes on that clock, where QuantLib's time form reads both curves at the risk-free curve's times; a market whose curves share the risk-free curve's dates and day counter keeps QuantLib's times. At the model's time 0 the engine refuses, as QuantLib's does ("maturity must be positive"). The Adams scheme is the reference route, O(N²) in the time steps; the Padé approximation is a closed form matching the Riccati solution's short- and long-time asymptotics, most precise at the strongly negative correlation of equity indices; the lifted approximation replaces the power-law kernel by a sum of n exponentials, an n-dimensional classical Riccati equation solved in O(nN). api/NanoQL.PricingEngines.AnalyticSoftBa.summary: Class AnalyticSoftBarrierEngine Namespace NanoQL.PricingEngines Assembly NanoQL.dll The analytic engine for European soft barrier options: Haug's closed form ("The Complete Guide to Option Pricing Formulas", 2nd ed., after Hart and Ross, 1994), and the soft barrier's definition, the average of the single-barrier options with barriers in [L, U], where that form doesn't hold. public static class AnalyticSoftBarrierEngine Inheritance object AnalyticSoftBarrierEngine Inherited Members object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks The value alone, as QuantLib's. A soft barrier option is the average of the single-barrier options with barriers in [L, U], as upstream's own test states it (#2883's testSoftBarrierDirection); its knock-in is computed here as that average of AnalyticBarrierEngine's standard knock-ins, (1/(U − L))∫ DI(H) dH, the barriers on the spot's far side counted as knocked in, by the adaptive Gauss-Kronrod rule split at the strike, the spot and the forward and at one to thirty transition widths either side of the last two, at the tolerance's measure on the average, and its knock-out as the vanilla less it. Haug's form integrates the standard knock-in's branch for a barrier at or below the strike, so it is the average only for a down barrier on a call with U ≤ K, or an up barrier on a put with L ≥ K, the spot outside the band; it is taken there, with QuantLib's bits, where it is finite, its carry b = r − q is 2e-3 or more from 0 and from −σ², where its terms cancel, and the band's relative width (U − L)/U is 3e-3 or more, below which its difference quotient cancels. Elsewhere the average is taken (documented divergences; Divergences/SoftBarrier*Tests.cs): QuantLib's nudge of the rate at r ≈ q, its rebuild of flat Act/360 curves for a band narrower than 1e-4 in price, the NaN of its overflowing powers at small volatility, and its values outside the form's domain are superseded. Upstream's refusal of the directions the form doesn't cover (#2883) isn't taken: they are priced by the average (Divergences/BarrierUpstreamFixesTests.cs). A band of zero width is the analytic barrier engine's single barrier. QuantLib's limits on the rates, which no formula needs, aren't ported. Each rate is read on the volatility's clock and each time is the volatility's, as the analytic barrier engine reads them. The exercise must be European, as the option's documentation states and the average's engine requires; QuantLib's engine doesn't check it and prices any exercise to its last date (Divergences/SoftBarrierExerciseTests.cs). Haug's form and the average are first-passage closed forms in equivalent-constant rates and a volatility, the variance and discounts to expiry: no exact closed form exists for a first passage under general deterministic term structures, and on shaped markets they miss the average of FdBlackScholesBarrierEngine's single-barrier knock-ins by -0.8% to +1.5%; that average is the term-structure-exact route. Both are exact where (r − q)/σ² is constant over the option's life and the volatility depends on time alone, the price then a time change of a constant market's (Conventions/ClosedFormExactnessTests.cs). Methods Calculate(SoftBarrierOption, EvaluationContext, GeneralizedBlackScholesProcess) Prices a soft barrier option. public static OneAssetOptionResults Calculate(SoftBarrierOption option, EvaluationContext context, GeneralizedBlackScholesProcess process) Parameters option SoftBarrierOption The option. context EvaluationContext The evaluation context. process GeneralizedBlackScholesProcess The Black-Scholes process. Returns OneAssetOptionResults The option's results: the value; the expired results when the option has expired. Exceptions ArgumentNullException An argument is null. NanoQLException The payoff isn't plain vanilla, the exercise isn't European, or QuantLib's checks of its inputs refuse them (a non-positive spot, strike, time or volatility; barriers not positive, or the upper below the lower).

api/NanoQL.PricingEngines.AnalyticTwoAss.summary: Class AnalyticTwoAssetBarrierEngine Namespace NanoQL.PricingEngines Assembly NanoQL.dll The analytic engine for a barrier option on two assets: the first asset's payoff, knocked in or out by the second asset at the barrier (Haug, "The Complete Guide to Option Pricing Formulas", 2nd ed.). public static class AnalyticTwoAssetBarrierEngine Inheritance object AnalyticTwoAssetBarrierEngine Inherited Members object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks The value alone, as QuantLib's. The bivariate normal is QuantLib's default, BivariateCumulativeNormalDistributionWe04DP, where QuantLib's engine reads Drezner's 1978 algorithm, to six decimal places; on QuantLib's cases the values move by at most 6.7e-6, within QuantLib's tolerance. Five documented divergences. Each asset's carry reads its own process's curves and the payoff is discounted on the first process's risk-free curve, where QuantLib takes the second asset's carry from the first process's rate (Divergences/TwoAssetBarrierTwoCurvesTests.cs). The knock-in's vanilla carries the first asset's dividends, S₁e^((b₁−r)T)N(d₁), where QuantLib's drops them, so in-out parity holds (Divergences/TwoAssetBarrierDividendTests.cs). The second asset's volatility is read at the barrier, its own price level, where QuantLib reads it at the first asset's strike (Divergences/TwoAssetBarrierSmileTests.cs). And every rate and volatility is read over the time to expiry on the clock across both processes (NanoQL.Methods.FdmBlackScholesOp.ClockAcross(System.Collections.Generic.IReadOnlyList{NanoQL.Processes.GeneralizedBlackScholesProcess})), each structure at the instants that time denotes, accruing nothing before its date, where QuantLib reads everything at the first process's time; a structure sharing the clock's times is read as QuantLib reads it (Divergences/BarrierClosedFormMismatchedTimesTests.cs). And a non-European exercise is refused, as the family's European engines refuse it, where QuantLib prices it to its last date (Divergences/TwoAssetBarrierExerciseTests.cs). The formula is a first-passage closed form in equivalent-constant rates and volatilities, the variance and discounts to expiry: no exact closed form exists for a first passage under general deterministic term structures, and its single correlation term, ρσ₁σ₂, can't carry a first volatility that moves over the option's life. On shaped markets (1.5 years; forward rates 1%, 3%, 6%, dividends 0%, 1%, 3% and volatilities 15%, 25%, 35%, rising or falling; ρ 0.5) it misses an independent Monte Carlo by −24% to +21%, and by 3% to 7% with the first volatility flat, where on a flat market it agrees. It is exact where one clock serves both assets: each asset's (r − qᵢ)/σᵢ² constant, σ₁/σ₂ constant and the correlation constant (Conventions/ClosedFormExactnessTests.cs). No engine in the library prices it under term structures; a Monte Carlo on the two processes would, monitoring the barrier at its grid's dates. api/NanoQL.PricingEngines.BachelierCalcu.summary: Class BachelierCalculator Namespace NanoQL.PricingEngines Assembly NanoQL.dll The Bachelier calculator: the value and sensitivities of a striked payoff on a forward with a normal distribution of a given standard deviation (in price units), discounted. It supports plain vanilla, cash-or-nothing, asset-or-nothing and gap payoffs. public sealed class BachelierCalculator Inheritance object BachelierCalculator Inherited Members object.GetType() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks Three of QuantLib's results are fixed, documented divergences: QuantLib tells a call from a put by alpha >= 0 (bacheliercalculator.cpp:102-114, :183-188), which a put's N(d) − 1 meets where N(d) rounds to 1, so a put far out of the money prices as the call; here the payoff's type decides (Divergences/BachelierPutBranchTests.cs). QuantLib's visitor sets alpha, beta and x for cash-or-nothing, asset-or-nothing and gap payoffs, which its value and Greeks never read, so each prices as the plain vanilla; here the value is D·(F·α + x·β + σ·∂α/∂d) and the Greeks its derivatives, Bachelier's closed forms for each payoff (Divergences/BachelierPayoffTests.cs). The plain vanilla's are QuantLib's expressions. QuantLib's theta reads the spot gamma where the time decay reads the forward gamma, missing (S/F)²; its vanna, the sensitivity of the vega to the spot by its documentation, misses D·F/S; its volga divides by σ√T where the derivative in σ divides by σ, missing √T. Each is here the derivative, the vanna taking the spot as Vanna(double, double) does (Divergences/BachelierGreeksTests.cs). Immutable. At a standard deviation within QL_EPSILON the density terms are 0, as QuantLib's: the value is the discounted payoff at the forward, the gammas, vega, vanna and volga 0. api/NanoQL.PricingEngines.BachelierCapFl.summary: Class BachelierCapFloorEngine Namespace NanoQL.PricingEngines Assembly NanoQL.dll The Bachelier-Black-formula cap/floor engine: normal volatilities. public static class BachelierCapFloorEngine Inheritance object BachelierCapFloorEngine Inherited Members object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks A static class: Calculate runs QuantLib's four steps (playbook §2.1) and returns the instrument's results, with BlackCapFloorEngine's additional results under the same keys, from the Bachelier formulas, which take no displacement and accept negative strikes and forwards. A collar's results hold no optionletsStdDev, as QuantLib's don't, and a caplet the engine prices whose coupon is paid before the evaluation date has no forward, refused where QuantLib prices on its Null<Rate>() sentinel, a documented divergence. QuantLib's constructors on a volatility value and on a quote coincide once a quote is a double: the overload on a double builds, at each call, the constant volatility QuantLib's builds, on no calendar, with its reference date the context's evaluation date and QuantLib's default type, shifted lognormal, which the engine reads as a normal volatility. Its day counter defaults to QuantLib's, Actual365Fixed, for null. api/NanoQL.PricingEngines.BaroneAdesiWha.title: Class BaroneAdesiWhaleyApproximationEngine | nanoql
api/NanoQL.PricingEngines.BaroneAdesiWha.summary: Class BaroneAdesiWhaleyApproximationEngine Namespace NanoQL.PricingEngines Assembly NanoQL.dll The Barone-Adesi and Whaley pricing engine for American options (1987). public static class BaroneAdesiWhaleyApproximationEngine Inheritance object BaroneAdesiWhaleyApproximationEngine Inherited Members object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks The correctness of the returned value is tested by reproducing results available in literature. Where early exercise is never optimal the engine reports the European value and every Greek; otherwise the value alone. The critical price's Newton step can leave (0, K) for a put, or (K, ∞) for a call, and the next Black formula then throws (baroneadesiwhaleyengine.cpp:83-130); so does a call's seed where h > 0 takes it below zero (:59-64, then the Black formula of :93). Here the critical price is then the root of QuantLib's own equation over that range, by Brent's method. Every case where Newton stays in range keeps QuantLib's bits (Divergences/BaroneAdesiWhaleyCriticalPriceTests.cs). Each structure is read at the exercise date by date, nothing accrued before its own reference date; where early exercise is never optimal the theta's terms run over each structure's own time, as the analytic European engine's, where QuantLib's run over the volatility's (Divergences/ApproximationThetaMismatchedTimesTests.cs). An exercise window opening after the reference date is priced by NanoQL.PricingEngines.ApproximationWindow, where QuantLib reads the last date alone (Divergences/ApproximationWindowTests.cs). Returns OneAssetOptionResults The option's results; the expired results when it has expired. Exceptions ArgumentNullException An argument is null. api/NanoQL.PricingEngines.BasketGenerati.summary: Class BasketGeneratingEngine Namespace NanoQL.PricingEngines Assembly NanoQL.dll The base of the pricing engines that generate a calibration basket: per live exercise date, a standard swaption matching the underlying's value, delta and gamma in the model's state, or the at-the-money coterminal one. public abstract class BasketGeneratingEngine Inheritance object BasketGeneratingEngine Derived Gaussian1dFloatFloatSwaptionEngine Gaussian1dNonstandardSwaptionEngine Inherited Members object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks The generated calibrating swaptions have a strike floored at 0.1bp (minus the lognormal shift, if applicable); this is not true for at-the-money swaptions, whose strike the swaption helper generates. The standard swap base index should have forwarding and discounting curves, which the helpers' market prices read, so the model's prices in a calibration must read the same curves; the volatility structure should be consistent with them, and the engine's discount curve should be the index's discounting curve. Immutable; the derived engines (Gaussian1dNonstandardSwaptionEngine and the float-float one) bind the underlying an instrument gives, where QuantLib's read the arguments they hold. A flipped match, a negative nominal read as the other swap type, gives its helper the nominal's size, where QuantLib floors the signed nominal at 1e-6 first and so gives 1e-6 (basketgeneratingengine.cpp:213-214, :230). api/NanoQL.PricingEngines.BatesDetJumpEn.summary: Class BatesDetJumpEngine Namespace NanoQL.PricingEngines Assembly NanoQL.dll The analytic Bates engine with a deterministic jump intensity: the log-normal jumps' term at the intensity's average over the maturity, which mean-reverts at κ_λ from λ to θ_λ. public sealed class BatesDetJumpEngine : BatesEngine Inheritance object AnalyticHestonEngine BatesEngine BatesDetJumpEngine Inherited Members BatesEngine.Calculate(VanillaOption, EvaluationContext, BatesModel, int) BatesEngine.Calculate(VanillaOption, EvaluationContext, BatesModel, double, int) AnalyticHestonEngine.Calculate(VanillaOption, EvaluationContext, HestonModel, int) AnalyticHestonEngine.Calculate(VanillaOption, EvaluationContext, HestonModel, double, int) AnalyticHestonEngine.Calculate(VanillaOption, EvaluationContext, HestonModel, AnalyticHestonEngineComplexLogFormula, FourierIntegration, double, double) AnalyticHestonEngine.OptimalControlVariate(double, double, double, double, double, double) AnalyticHestonEngine.Calculate(VanillaOption, EvaluationContext) AnalyticHestonEngine.ChF(Complex, double) AnalyticHestonEngine.LnChF(Complex, double) AnalyticHestonEngine.PriceVanillaPayoff(PlainVanillaPayoff, Date) AnalyticHestonEngine.PriceVanillaPayoff(PlainVanillaPayoff, double) AnalyticHestonEngine.PriceVanillaPayoffWithStatistics(PlainVanillaPayoff, Date) AnalyticHestonEngine.PriceVanillaPayoffWithStatistics(PlainVanillaPayoff, double) object.GetType() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks A BatesEngine, as QuantLib's derives from it, over its BatesDetJumpModel. The intensity's average weights the constant-intensity term by (x − 1 + e^{−x})/x and (1 − e^{−x})/x, x = κ_λt, which QuantLib writes as differences that cancel as x falls: 1.2e-6 off the constant-intensity price at κ_λ = 1e-12 (batesengine.cpp:80, :140). Here, below x = 1e-2, the first is x·φ₂(−x), φ₂(u) = (eᵘ − 1 − u)/u² by its series, and the second −expm1(−x)/x; QuantLib's expressions and bits at and above it (Divergences/BatesDetJumpSmallReversionTests.cs). For Cox-Ross-Rubinstein trees the number of steps is raised to Boyle and Lau's optimum ("Bumping up against the barrier with the binomial method", Journal of Derivatives, 1/1994). public static class BinomialBarrierEngine Inheritance object BinomialBarrierEngine Inherited Members object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks QuantLib's template on the tree and the discretized asset: Calculate<TTree, TAsset>(BarrierOption, EvaluationContext, GeneralizedBlackScholesProcess, int, int) takes both as type arguments, the tree built through Create(StochasticProcess1D, double, int, double) and the asset through Create(BarrierOption, StochasticProcess, TimeGrid?), DiscretizedBarrierOption or DiscretizedDermanKaniBarrierOption or a user's own. The delta and gamma come from the lattice's first two steps, the gamma and delta null where the nodes don't separate, and the theta from the second step's middle node, as QuantLib's. Documented divergences. The tree runs on the risk-free curve's day counter from the earliest reference date of the structures, each structure on another day counter or reference date flattened on it from its discount or variance at the maturity date, as BinomialVanillaEngine's tree, where QuantLib flattens each curve from the risk-free curve's date on its own day counter (Divergences/BinomialBarrierMismatchedTimesTests.cs); where every structure shares the risk-free curve's day counter and reference date, the tree is QuantLib's. The time grid and the lattice take their step count from the tree, its columns less one, where QuantLib's take the count given; Boyle and Lau's optimum reads the flattened volatility. api/NanoQL.PricingEngines.BinomialConver.summary: Class BinomialConvertibleEngine Namespace NanoQL.PricingEngines Assembly NanoQL.dll The binomial Tsiveriotis-Fernandes engine for convertible bonds: the bond rolled back on a Tsiveriotis-Fernandes lattice over a binomial tree, built on the process's curves and volatility flattened at the last exercise date, the dividends' present values taken from the spot. public static class BinomialConvertibleEngine Inheritance object BinomialConvertibleEngine Inherited Members object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks QuantLib's template on the tree: Calculate<TTree>(ConvertibleBond, EvaluationContext, GeneralizedBlackScholesProcess, int, double, ImmutableArray<Dividend>) takes the tree as its type argument; the seven named engines, as QuantLib-Python names them, fix it. The credit spread is a number, where QuantLib observes a quote. Its clock: the tree runs from the bond's settlement date over the risk-free curve's year fraction to the last exercise date, and the NPV is the bond's value there, the settlement value equal to it, as QuantLib's are: a named departure from the playbook's lattice clock, since the engine prices the bond at its settlement date and QuantLib's convertible cases assert that definition. The structures are flattened at the last exercise date, dated at the risk-free curve's reference date, as QuantLib's are; where the dividend curve or the volatility has another day counter or reference date than the risk-free curve, its rate or volatility is the one that gives its discount or variance from the risk-free curve's reference date to that date, counted on the risk-free day counter, each structure accruing nothing before its own date, where QuantLib reads it on its own day counter and the tree reads it as the risk-free curve's (Divergences/ConvertibleClockTests.cs). Where every structure shares the risk-free curve's day counter and reference date, the tree is QuantLib's. The tree's stock starts at the settlement date's forward, the spot less the dividends' present values divided by the risk-free discount to the settlement date, as QuantLib's master starts it after 1.44 (#2752, issue #2701), where QuantLib 1.44 starts it at the evaluation date's spot, so a bond with a settlement lag converts on a spot short of the carry over the lag (Divergences/ConvertibleUpstreamFixesTests.cs). The time grid and the lattice take their step count from the tree, its columns less one, where QuantLib's take the count given: the Leisen-Reimer and Joshi trees build an even count on the next odd one, as the binomial vanilla engine handles them. Every odd count and every other tree is QuantLib's. api/NanoQL.PricingEngines.BinomialVanill.summary: Class BinomialVanillaEngine Namespace NanoQL.PricingEngines Assembly NanoQL.dll The binomial pricing engine for vanilla options: the option rolled back on a Black-Scholes lattice over a binomial tree, built on the process's curves and volatility flattened at the option's maturity. public static class BinomialVanillaEngine Inheritance object BinomialVanillaEngine Inherited Members object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks QuantLib's template on the tree: Calculate<TTree>(VanillaOption, EvaluationContext, GeneralizedBlackScholesProcess, int) takes the tree as its type argument, which the engine builds through Create(StochasticProcess1D, double, int, double); the seven named engines, as QuantLib-Python names them, fix it. The delta and gamma come from the lattice's first two steps, the theta from the Black-Scholes relation, as QuantLib's do. The time grid and the lattice take their step count from the tree, its columns less one, where QuantLib's take the count given (binomialengine.hpp:111-116): the Leisen-Reimer and Joshi trees build an even count on the next odd one, so QuantLib rolls back a tree built for n + 1 steps over n, which at 250 steps errs by 4.7e-2 against the analytic engine. Every odd count and every other tree is QuantLib's. A documented divergence. QuantLib's tree runs on the risk-free curve's time to maturity, and QuantLib flattens the dividend curve and the volatility on their own day counters and reads them over that time, so where either has another day counter or reference date it integrates the wrong dividend or variance. Here the tree runs on the risk-free curve's day counter from the earliest reference date of the structures, as the finite-difference engine's grid does, and a structure on another day counter or reference date is flattened on it, its rate or volatility the one whose discount or variance at the maturity date is the structure's own; where every structure shares the risk-free curve's day counter and reference date, the tree is QuantLib's (Divergences/BinomialMismatchedTimesTests.cs). A structure accrues nothing before its own date, so an option expiring before a later risk-free curve's is priced, where QuantLib's read throws, and the theta reads no rate or volatility of a structure dated on or after the exercise, where QuantLib reads each at the structure's own time 0 (Divergences/ExerciseBeforeReferenceDateTests.cs). Methods Calculate<TTree>(VanillaOption, EvaluationContext, GeneralizedBlackScholesProcess, int) Prices a vanilla option on a binomial tree. public static OneAssetOptionResults Calculate<TTree>(VanillaOption option, EvaluationContext context, GeneralizedBlackScholesProcess process, int timeSteps) where TTree : Tree, IBinomialTree<TTree> Parameters option VanillaOption The option, with a plain-vanilla payoff. context EvaluationContext The evaluation context. process GeneralizedBlackScholesProcess The Black-Scholes process. timeSteps int The number of time steps, at least 2. Returns OneAssetOptionResults The value, delta, gamma and theta; the delta, the gamma and the theta are null where the tree's first nodes don't separate, as QuantLib's Null<Real>(). Type Parameters TTree The binomial tree. Exceptions ArgumentNullException An argument is null. ArgumentException timeSteps is below 2. NanoQLException The option's payoff isn't plain vanilla, the underlying isn't positive, or the tree can't be built.

api/NanoQL.PricingEngines.BjerksundStens.summary: Class BjerksundStenslandApproximationEngine Namespace NanoQL.PricingEngines Assembly NanoQL.dll The Bjerksund and Stensland approximation engine for American options (1993), puts by the put-call symmetry. public static class BjerksundStenslandApproximationEngine Inheritance object BjerksundStenslandApproximationEngine Inherited Members object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks The correctness of the returned value is tested by reproducing results available in literature. The engine reports the value, the delta, gamma, theta (and per day), vega, rho, dividend rho and strike sensitivity, and the additional results "strikeGamma" and "exerciseType" (European, American or Immediate); no forward delta, elasticity or in-the-money probability, which QuantLib's engine leaves uninitialized (its results are built in a local it never resets; Divergences/BjerksundStenslandUnsetGreeksTests.cs). The Greeks call the C runtime's erfc, which nanoql reads through Boost's, so their last bits can differ from QuantLib's. Documented divergences, each leaving QuantLib's arithmetic where it doesn't apply: Below a variance of ε the value is the European one floored at the exercise value, as QuantLib's master does since the pin (#2854). Where the trigger price falls below its lower bound B₀, or isn't finite (bjerksundstenslandengine.cpp:196-206, the trigger's exponent positive), the trigger is the perpetual boundary B∞, in the same closed form and Greeks, its derivatives B∞'s: a flat boundary at or above B₀ is a feasible exercise rule, whose value bounds the option's from below (Bjerksund and Stensland 2002, §3). QuantLib prices there with an infeasible trigger and returns its European floor, up to 3.4 below its own finite-difference engine. Where the perpetual boundary is infinite the European value stands (Divergences/BjerksundStenslandTriggerTests.cs). The value jumps at the region's edge, between QuantLib's trigger and B∞, two of the method's lower bounds. QuantLib's shortcut to the European value where the trigger lies 12.5 standard deviations above the forward (:212-216) isn't taken at B∞: in the region the forward falls far below the spot while B∞ stays just above it, so the path reaches B∞ early or not at all. Where a power (I/S)^κ overflows against an underflowing normal tail, QuantLib's product is NaN or 0 (:37-112); there the product is taken through logarithms, log N's asymptotic tail beyond −30, as one exponent with the Gaussian densities it divides; QuantLib's arithmetic elsewhere (Divergences/BjerksundStenslandOverflowTests.cs). The American Greeks' times run from each structure's own reference date, where QuantLib's run from the risk-free curve's (Divergences/BjerksundStenslandMismatchedTimesTests.cs); each structure is read at the exercise date by date, nothing accrued before its own reference date; and an exercise window opening after the reference date is priced by NanoQL.PricingEngines.ApproximationWindow. Here they are the nonzero branch's formulas with the derivative terms zero, from alpha and beta, so the theta, the theta per day, the elasticity, the rho and the dividend rho that read them are fixed too. The engine assumes that the exercise date lies before the start date of the passed swap, and fully supports an overnight-indexed underlying. QuantLib's constructors on a volatility value and on a quote coincide once a quote is a double: the overload on a double builds, at each call, the constant volatility QuantLib's builds, on no calendar and with its reference date the context's evaluation date. Its day counter defaults to QuantLib's, Actual365Fixed, for null; QuantLib's empty day counter, which fails at the volatility's first conversion of a date to a time, has no spelling. Every function takes the context: the settlement date reads the evaluation date, and whether a cash flow on the settlement date has occurred reads the context's IncludeTodaysCashFlows when that date is the evaluation date, despite the false passed. The bond's Notional(EvaluationContext, Date?) and AccruedAmount(EvaluationContext, Date?) are called virtually, as QuantLib's are, so a derived bond's own accrued amount reaches these functions. A price or yield function refuses a settlement date at which the bond isn't tradable, its notional being 0, with QuantLib's text ("non tradable at …", with " settlement date" in the curve-based dirty price's alone); the accrued amount is 0 there instead, and the cash-flow and coupon-rate inspectors don't check. The yield is solved for by NewtonSafe, QuantLib's default, or by the NewtonSafe or Brent solver given, the two solvers nanoql has of those QuantLib's template takes. api/NanoQL.PricingEngines.CEVCalculator..summary: Class CEVCalculator Namespace NanoQL.PricingEngines Assembly NanoQL.dll The undiscounted value of a European option on the constant elasticity of variance (CEV) process df = α·f^β·dW with an absorbing boundary at f = 0, by the non-central chi-squared distribution (D. R. Brecher and A. E. Lindsay, "Results on the CEV Process, Past and Present"). public sealed class CEVCalculator Inheritance object CEVCalculator Inherited Members object.GetType() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks Near β = 1 the formula fails: δ = (1 − 2β)/(1 − β) divides by zero at β = 1, and around it Boost's non-central chi-squared refuses or runs for seconds. For |β − 1| < 1e-3 the value is Black's formula at Hagan's CEV-equivalent volatility, the SABR volatility at ν = 0 (UnsafeSabrLogNormalVolatility(double, double, double, double, double, double, double)), which is α at β = 1 and within 4.6e-7 of the CEV formula at the band's edge, where QuantLib throws or hangs. A documented divergence (Divergences/CevNearOneTests.cs). Where a tail QuantLib takes as 1 − cdf (or Γ-ratio − cdf, analyticcevengine.cpp:50-80) is below 1e-3, the difference loses most of its digits: a 36-day call at a strike of 150 comes out about 20% low. There the tail is Boost's complement cdf (and gamma_q); QuantLib's arithmetic and bits elsewhere. A documented divergence (Divergences/CevTailTests.cs). At a time of 0 the formula's non-centrality x₀/t is infinite, which Boost refuses; the value there is the payoff at f0, the limit QuantLib's own values approach as the time shrinks. A documented divergence (a run find, Divergences/CevAtExpiryTests.cs). api/NanoQL.PricingEngines.COSHestonEngin.summary: Class COSHestonEngine Namespace NanoQL.PricingEngines Assembly NanoQL.dll The COS-method Heston engine, on efficient Fourier-cosine series expansions. public sealed class COSHestonEngine Inheritance object COSHestonEngine Inherited Members object.GetType() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks An immutable object over its HestonModel, the truncation range's width and the series' length; the static Calculate(VanillaOption, EvaluationContext, HestonModel, double, int) builds one and prices through it. The model's time runs from the earliest curve date and the forward and discount are read by date (AnalyticHestonEngine's reads); at the model's time 0 the price is QuantLib's bound, the forward's discounted intrinsic value, before any cumulant. The cumulants are QuantLib's expressions, evaluated where κt calls for it in another arithmetic: QuantLib's double, and so its bits, from each cumulant's cut to its upper cut; double-double below the cut, quad-double below double-double's floor and, below quad-double's, each cumulant's cubic in κ through four quad-double values; past the upper cut, where e^{nκt} overflows, an extended-range double, each cut measured at the run against QuantLib's expressions in 50 to 250 digits. At a term of 0 the cumulants, the skew and the kurtosis are their limits, 0. Below σ = NanoQL.PricingEngines.COSHestonEngine.SigmaCut, where the classic form's division by σ² cancels, the characteristic function is ChF(Complex, double)'s, the same function in Andersen and Lake's form. The series' length has to grow with the vol of variance and the term: at QuantLib's defaults, a range of 16 and 200 terms, a vol of variance of 1 prices a five-year call at twice the forward at −7.8 times its value and a twenty-year one 39% low, where 2,000 terms bring them within 0.6% and 0.02%; QuantLib's own large-σ case takes a range of 25 and 600 terms. References: F. Fang, C.W. Oosterlee, A Novel Pricing Method for European Options based on Fourier-Cosine Series Expansions; F. Le Floc'h, Fourier Integration and Stochastic Volatility Calibration. api/NanoQL.PricingEngines.CashDividendEu.summary: Class CashDividendEuropeanEngine Namespace NanoQL.PricingEngines Assembly NanoQL.dll The (semi-)analytic engine for European options on an underlying paying cash dividends: J. Healy, "The Pricing of Vanilla Options with Cash Dividends as a Classic Vanilla Basket Option Problem" (2021), https://arxiv.org/pdf/2106.12971. public static class CashDividendEuropeanEngine Inheritance object CashDividendEuropeanEngine Inherited Members object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks Under the spot model the option is a basket of the dividends and the strike against the spot, priced by ChoiBasketEngine with QuantLib's arguments (λ 10, 2,000 steps, the control variate); a single dividend on the risk-free curve's date, or the escrowed model, is priced by AnalyticDividendEuropeanEngine, and no dividend by AnalyticEuropeanEngine. The value alone, as QuantLib's. Stateless: the dividends' processes are built per call, as QuantLib builds them. The settlement and the time to maturity are the process's clock's (Clock(GeneralizedBlackScholesProcess, FdmQuantoHelper?)), from its earliest structure date, and the curves and the volatility are read by date, accruing nothing before their dates, where QuantLib's settlement and time are the risk-free curve's, so a dividend before that curve's date is dropped, and its reads throw for an expiry before it (Divergences/TwoAssetMismatchedTimesTests.cs). Each dividend's flat volatility is dated and counted on the clock, so its variance to expiry is the one read by date, where QuantLib's is dated and counted on the volatility's own clock and sized on the risk-free curve's, its variance scaled by the ratio of the two times. On structures dated and counted alike the clock is the risk-free curve and the reads are QuantLib's. The dividends are ordered by date by a stable sort, where QuantLib's sort leaves dividends of one date in no set order. api/NanoQL.PricingEngines.ChoiAsianEngin.title: Class ChoiAsianEngine | nanoql
api/NanoQL.PricingEngines.ChoiAsianEngin.summary: Class ChoiAsianEngine Namespace NanoQL.PricingEngines Assembly NanoQL.dll Choi's engine for discrete arithmetic average-price Asian options: the average replicated by a basket of the future fixings, priced by Choi's basket engine ("Sum of all Black-Scholes-Merton Models: An efficient Pricing Method for Spread, Basket and Asian Options", 2018). public static class ChoiAsianEngine Inheritance object ChoiAsianEngine Inherited Members object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks The value alone, as QuantLib's. The basket's processes are QuantLib's: each fixing's forward as the spot, zero rates, and a constant volatility scaled to the last fixing's time; the basket priced by ChoiBasketEngine with QuantLib's λ and integration steps. Documented divergences. A seasoned option reads its correlations and volatilities at the future average's own strike, K_f = (K − A/m)·m/f for f of m fixings to come, so it prices as (f/m) times the unseasoned option at K_f, where QuantLib reads its correlations at K − A/m and its volatilities at K, −2.6% to +306% off on a smile varying with maturity (Divergences/SeasonedAsianSmileTests.cs). An effective strike below zero is the certain exercise, priced as Turnbull and Wakeman's engine prices it, its value alone, where QuantLib refuses it (Divergences/ChoiCertainExerciseTests.cs). Its times run on the engine's clock, Clock(GeneralizedBlackScholesProcess, FdmQuantoHelper?), where QuantLib takes them from the process. A fixing dated from the evaluation date to the latest structure's date, where the structures settle after the evaluation date, is taken there, the spot with no variance and no discount accrued, so as a past fixing at the spot (Divergences/AsianLateSettlementTests.cs), where QuantLib refuses it as past. Returns OneAssetOptionResults The option's results: the value; the expired results when the option has expired. Exceptions ArgumentNullException An argument is null. api/NanoQL.PricingEngines.ChoiBasketEngi.summary: Class ChoiBasketEngine Namespace NanoQL.PricingEngines Assembly NanoQL.dll The engine for European basket and spread options on several assets by Choi's method: the basket's projection on one factor priced in closed form, integrated over the others by Gauss-Hermite quadrature. public static class ChoiBasketEngine Inheritance object ChoiBasketEngine Inherited Members object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks J. Choi, "Sum of all Black-Scholes-Merton Models: An efficient Pricing Method for Spread, Basket and Asian Options", 2018, https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2913048; the author's Python implementation is at https://github.com/PyFE/PyFENG. With calcFwdDelta (or the control variate) the forward deltas are returned among the additional results as "forwardDelta k", as QuantLib's. Each node is priced by the single-factor engine's formula on the node's forwards and signed deviations, where QuantLib builds quotes, processes and an option priced by that engine; the arithmetic is the same. Where every volatility is 0 a node's value is the intrinsic one and its root's d the limit, ±∞ by the side of the strike the forward basket is on, where QuantLib's node sets no d and its read fails (Divergences/BasketZeroVolatilitiesTests.cs). The structures are read by date, accruing nothing before their dates, where QuantLib's reads throw for an option expiring before a later structure's date (Divergences/BasketExpiryBeforeReferenceDateTests.cs). The processes must discount alike: QuantLib's check that every risk-free discount is close enough to the first's. The correctness of the returned value is tested by reproducing results available in literature. The largest number of integration nodes, the scale reduced until the orders fit; null (QuantLib's largest Size) for no limit. calcFwdDelta bool Whether to compute the forward deltas. controlVariate bool Whether to correct the value by the forward deltas' control variate. Returns MultiAssetOptionResults The value, and the forward deltas among the additional results where asked for. Exceptions ArgumentNullException An argument is null. api/NanoQL.PricingEngines.ContinuousArit.summary: Class ContinuousArithmeticAsianLevyEngine Namespace NanoQL.PricingEngines Assembly NanoQL.dll Levy's engine for continuous arithmetic average-price Asian options: the average matched to a log-normal by its first two moments (Haug, "Option Pricing Formulas"). public static class ContinuousArithmeticAsianLevyEngine Inheritance object ContinuousArithmeticAsianLevyEngine Inherited Members object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks The value alone, as QuantLib's. The averaging's start date is the option's (QuantLib's deprecated constructor taking it isn't ported); a seasoned option takes the current average, a value where QuantLib takes a quote. Documented divergences. The two moments are integrated under deterministic term structures, each at 1e-12 relative: E[A] from the forwards on NanoQL's adaptive Kronrod rule, as spot·t₂ plus the integral of F/spot − 1, exact at zero carry (QuantLib's master's #2926 cases), and the average's covariance, on a first 15-point estimate, (2/T²)∫∫F(s)F(t)(e^{V(min(s, t))} − 1) on QuantLib's adaptive Gauss-Lobatto rule, the log-variance ln(E[A²]/E[A]²) its log1p over E[A]², so nothing cancels, where QuantLib reads one volatility and the zero rates at maturity, +38.5% and −17.2% off a Monte Carlo on shaped markets, and its closed form cancels near the carries b = 0, −σ²/2 and −σ², up to 75% off and NaN, and at small volatility, NaN (Divergences/LevyTermStructureTests.cs). The covariance's integrands have kinks where the structures have nodes, where the Kronrod rule accepts panels whose two estimates agree while both are off: 9e-9 off the exact value on shaped markets, in tens of millions of evaluations, where the Gauss-Lobatto rule is within 7e-13 of Levy's formula on the moments in 30 digits, in under 100,000. At zero variance the average is its forward. An effective strike at or below zero is the certain exercise, the call Se − X·e^{−rT₂} and the put 0, the formula's limit, where QuantLib takes log(X) and prices NaN (Divergences/LevyEffectiveStrikeTests.cs). An averaging started from the evaluation date to the clock's origin, where the structures settle after the evaluation date, reads the span before the origin at the spot (Divergences/AsianLateSettlementTests.cs), where QuantLib takes it as seasoned and asks for a current average. api/NanoQL.PricingEngines.CounterpartyAd.summary: Class CounterpartyAdjSwapEngine Namespace NanoQL.PricingEngines Assembly NanoQL.dll The bilateral counterparty-risk adjusted swap engine: the swap's NPV less the counterparty's expected loss on its exposure, plus the investor's, each exposure a sequence of swaptions at the swap's fixed rate, one per fixed period, weighted by the party's default probability over the period. public static class CounterpartyAdjSwapEngine Inheritance object CounterpartyAdjSwapEngine Inherited Members object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks Collateral is not considered, nor wrong-way risk: rates and default are uncorrelated (Sorensen and Bollier, "Pricing swap default risk", Financial Analysts Journal, 1994; Brigo and Masetti, 2004 and 2005). The fair rate is QuantLib's approximation, not an iteration. QuantLib's three constructors are the overloads of Calculate(FixedVsFloatingSwap, EvaluationContext, YieldTermStructure, Func<Swaption, EvaluationContext, InstrumentResults>, DefaultProbabilityTermStructure, double, DefaultProbabilityTermStructure?, double), its volatility quote and constant volatility one overload; with no investor curve, QuantLib's default-free one, a flat hazard rate of 1e-12 on the counterparty curve's day counter, is built per call under the context. QuantLib's loop over the fixed payment dates skips those before the counterparty curve's reference date with no end check (cvaswapengine.cpp:128), reading past the dates when every one is before it; here it stops at the end, and the swap is then worth its NPV. QuantLib strikes every swaptionlet and its reverse at the swap's risk-free fair rate (cvaswapengine.cpp:147, :170, :179), so its adjustment is the same whatever the swap's fixed rate: a swap away from par takes the at-the-money swap's CVA and DVA. Here the NPV's are struck at the swap's fixed rate, the exposure of the contract itself, which is QuantLib's within a few ulps where the fixed rate is the fair rate. The fair rate keeps QuantLib's: its first-order root of the adjusted NPV, taken on swaptionlets struck at the risk-free fair rate, the market's, so the same whatever the fixed rate; on the contract's strikes it would move with the fixed rate, away from the root off par. api/NanoQL.PricingEngines.DengLiZhouBask.summary: Class DengLiZhouBasketEngine Namespace NanoQL.PricingEngines Assembly NanoQL.dll Deng, Li and Zhou's engine for a European basket or spread option on several assets: S. Deng, M. Li and J. Zhou, "Multi-asset Spread Option Pricing and Hedging" (2008), https://mpra.ub.uni-muenchen.de/8259/1/MPRA_paper_8259.pdf, with the typo in formula (37) for J² corrected. public static class DengLiZhouBasketEngine Inheritance object DengLiZhouBasketEngine Inherited Members object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks The formula prices exactly one positive weight; several positive weights are lumped into one lognormal asset by C. A negative strike enters as a zero-volatility asset of weight 1. Every process must discount alike, as in QuantLib. Stateless. api/NanoQL.PricingEngines.DiscountingFxF.summary: Class DiscountingFxForwardEngine Namespace NanoQL.PricingEngines Assembly NanoQL.dll The discounting engine for FxForward: each leg discounted on its currency's curve from the settlement date to maturity, the target leg converted at the spot rate, and the result discounted to each curve's reference date. public static class DiscountingFxForwardEngine Inheritance object DiscountingFxForwardEngine Inherited Members object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks In the source currency, the NPV is (±N_source·D_source(τ,T) ∓ N_target·D_target(τ,T) / S)·D_source(τ), the signs by the side paid, where D(τ,T) is a curve's discount factor from the settlement date τ to the maturity T and S the spot rate, units of the target per unit of the source; the fair forward rate is S·D_source(τ,T) / D_target(τ,T). api/NanoQL.PricingEngines.DiscountingPer.summary: Class DiscountingPerpetualFuturesEngine Namespace NanoQL.PricingEngines Assembly NanoQL.dll The discounting engine for perpetual futures: the spot times the funding payments' discounted sum (a linear payoff), or over it (an inverse payoff), the funding rates and interest-rate differences interpolated in time and flat past the last, the sum to a horizon on a grid and its tail in closed form. public static class DiscountingPerpetualFuturesEngine Inheritance object DiscountingPerpetualFuturesEngine Inherited Members object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks Stateless. The grid's times are the instrument's day counter's from the evaluation date, and each curve is read at the instants they denote, on its own clock, nothing accruing before its date (Divergences/PerpetualFuturesMismatchedTimesTests.cs), where QuantLib reads the curves at the grid's times themselves; on curves counted and dated as the grid, QuantLib's reads. The tail past the horizon converges only where the last funding rate k and the curves' last forward rates r_f and r_d give k + r_f − r_d > 0 (continuous funding) or (1 + k)·e^{Δt(r_f − r_d)} > 1 with 1 + k > 0 (discrete funding); elsewhere it is refused, where QuantLib refuses only k ≤ 0 and returns the divergent series' analytic continuation below (Divergences/PerpetualFuturesDivergentTailTests.cs). A non-positive last funding rate on a convergent tail is priced. A caplet still to be fixed is added in the pre-adjustment at its fixing time, as the option to pay (1 + Kτ) at its payment time for 1 at its start, the two discount bonds rolled back there: (1 + Kτ)·max(P(start)/(1 + Kτ) − P(end), 0) times its nominal and gearing, a floorlet likewise; one fixed after its start, in arrears, at its fixing time too, on its index's own period from the fixing date, three bonds rolled back there: τ·P(pay)·max(L − K, 0), L = (P(s)/P(e) − 1)/τᵢ over the period (s, e) and its index's year fraction τᵢ, times its nominal and gearing; one fixed on its start at its start time, as QuantLib adds every caplet, (1 + Kτ)·max(1/(1 + Kτ) − P, 0). A caplet fixed on or before the reference date, as the analytic engine knows it (its fixing time at most 0), is added in the post-adjustment at its payment time, as its known amount, max(F − K, 0)·τ times its nominal and gearing; one paid on the reference date counts only when the context includes today's cash flows, as the discretized swap's known coupon does. The times are the given day counter's year fractions from the reference date. The fixing time: QuantLib exercises every caplet still to be fixed at its start (discretizedcapfloor.cpp:53-55), where the instrument fixes its rate and QuantLib's Monte Carlo engine reads it at the fixing date, so a caplet with a fixing lag is priced on the variance to its start; a divergence (Divergences/CapletFixingExpiryTests.cs). On a caplet fixed on its start, the fixing time is the start time and the value QuantLib's, bit for bit. A rollback must reach the earliest fixing time a caplet is valued at, which precedes the first start QuantLib's engine rolls back to (NanoQL.PricingEngines.DiscretizedCapFloor.EarliestFixingTime). An in-arrears caplet: QuantLib values it as the caplet in advance, at its start on its accrual period, reading neither its later fixing nor its index's period; a divergence (Divergences/CapletInArrearsTests.cs) with no QuantLib check, checked on Hull-White against each caplet's Gaussian integral at its fixing. Its fixing time and its index period's start and end are mandatory times, the end past the cap's last payment. A seasoned cap (widened): its mandatory times are its non-negative start and payment times, as the discretized swap's are, then the fixing times of the caplets valued there, and a caplet is known by its fixing date: a divergence, QuantLib's keeping the started caplets' negative times, so its engine refuses "negative times not allowed", and knowing a caplet by its start, so between its fixing and its start it values the caplet as an option, ignoring its fixing (discretizedcapfloor.cpp:55, :91; Divergences/TreeCapFloorSeasonedTests.cs, Divergences/TreeKnownCouponTests.cs). A caplet still to be fixed whose start is before the reference date can only be in arrears, and is valued at its fixing as any other, its start unread, where QuantLib's grid refuses its negative start time ("negative times not allowed"). Its discount bonds. As DiscretizedSwap's: one bond to the payment, one to the start (or the index period's start) and one to the index period's end, re-initialized for each optionlet, their buffers reserved by Reset(int) at the widest step of the grid, so no optionlet's bonds allocate. Each coupon is added at its reset time, in the pre-adjustment or, as its adjustment says, the post-adjustment: a fixed coupon as its amount times a discount bond from its payment time, a floating one as the nominal times one less that bond, plus the nominal times its accrual time and spread times the bond. A coupon whose reset time is before the reference date and whose payment isn't (or is on it, when the context's IncludeTodaysCashFlows is true) is added in the post-adjustment at its payment time instead, as its known amount; a floating one whose amount can't be computed is refused there. The coupons' times are the given day counter's year fractions from the reference date. A floating coupon known by its fixing date: the public constructor, a swap's own value as the tree swap engine prices it, knows a floating coupon whose fixing date is on or before the reference date, adding its amount at its payment time, where QuantLib knows it by its accrual start (its reset date, vanillaswap.cpp:67; discretizedswap.cpp:84-87), so between its fixing and its start the tree forecasts a coupon whose fixing the discounting engine reads (Divergences/TreeKnownCouponTests.cs). The internal constructor, which the discretized swaption calls, keeps QuantLib's rule, so a swaption exercised in that window takes its floating leg at par, QuantLib's convention. A floating coupon paid after its accrual end: QuantLib values a floating coupon as a par floater to its payment date, the nominal times one less the bond from its payment time (discretizedswap.cpp:199-218), which overprices one paid on a lag or an adjusted date after its accrual end. Here such a coupon takes its forward over its own accrual period and is paid on its payment date: the nominal times the bond from its payment time over the bond from its accrual end, less the bond from its payment time, plus its spread; its accrual end is a mandatory time only there. With QuantLib's check, the finite-difference engine on a lagged swap (Divergences/TreeSwaptionSnappingTests.cs); a coupon paid on its accrual end keeps QuantLib's value. Its discount bonds. QuantLib's swap builds a discount bond for each coupon it adds, initializes it at the payment time and rolls it back to the swap's time. This swap keeps one bond, re-initialized for each coupon (a discount bond has no adjustments, so the adjustment times its memo keeps skip nothing), and a second for the accrual ends, whose buffers its Reset(int) reserves at the widest step of the swap's own rollback, from its initial step down to the grid's start: every coupon's bond starts at or before the swap's initial time and rolls back to the swap's time, so no coupon's bond allocates. Here the CIR generator's coefficients, and the rate grid uniform on [0, max(upper, r₀, θ, E[r_T])], upper the last point of QuantLib's grid, where at r = 0 the equation is its own boundary condition. api/NanoQL.PricingEngines.FdHestonHullWh.summary: Class FdHestonHullWhiteVanillaEngine Namespace NanoQL.PricingEngines Assembly NanoQL.dll The finite-difference Heston-Hull-White pricing engine for vanilla options, European, American or Bermudan, with cash dividends optional: FdmHestonHullWhiteSolver on the log spot, the variance and the Hull-White short rate's state, with a control variate, the analytic Heston engine's price less the finite-difference Heston engine's, optional. public static class FdHestonHullWhiteVanillaEngine Inheritance object FdHestonHullWhiteVanillaEngine Inherited Members object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks The engine reports the value, delta, gamma and theta, the theta null when the problem's first stopping time is time 0; the delta and gamma are central differences at a shift of 1% of the spot. Of the Hull-White process it reads the reversion and the volatility only, its short rate's curve the Heston process's risk-free curve. Its finite-difference working types are built inside each calculation and dropped after it. Its times run on Clock(HestonProcess, FdmQuantoHelper?, LocalVolTermStructure?), from the earliest reference date of the Heston process's structures, each accruing nothing before its own date, where QuantLib's run from the risk-free curve's; where none is dated before the risk-free curve, they are QuantLib's (Divergences/HestonHullWhiteMismatchedTimesTests.cs). QuantLib sizes the equity mesher on a helper process whose curves its call binds in each other's places, as the finite-difference Heston engine's does (FdHestonVanillaEngine), so where the carry is large against the volatility its grid falls short of the distribution: a five-year call at 1.25 times the forward, volatility 0.1, priced −6.32 at carry −0.30 where the analytic Heston-Hull-White engine gives 0.392 and 0 at carry 0.30 for 1.760, and a year's put at 0.7 of the forward, carry −0.2, priced 0 for 0.0068. Here the mesher is QuantLib's wherever its range holds the true forwards' band and the strike's, at half this engine's scale factor of 1.5, and widened to the bands where it doesn't, and the multi-strike solve solves each strike alone where its grid doesn't hold the forwards' band at the points it is read at (Divergences/FdHestonHullWhiteHighCarryTests.cs). QuantLib's enableMultipleStrikesCaching serves later options at its strikes from one solve, each V(S·d)/d with d = K/Kᵢ, the strike a later call is served depending on which option solved first, which a cache may not do here: a value doesn't depend on what was computed before it. Here CalculateStrikes(VanillaOption, IEnumerable<double>, EvaluationContext, HestonModel, HullWhiteProcess, double, int, int, int, int, int, bool, FdmSchemeDesc?) returns every strike's results from one solve on the given option, each QuantLib's cached value bit for bit; after a reference whose payoff isn't a plain vanilla, whose scaled values aren't the strikes' prices, each strike's plain vanilla is solved alone, QuantLib's engine priced for that strike (Divergences/FdHestonHullWhiteStrikesReferenceTests.cs). api/NanoQL.PricingEngines.FdHestonVanill.summary: Class FdHestonVanillaEngine Namespace NanoQL.PricingEngines Assembly NanoQL.dll The finite-difference Heston pricing engine for vanilla options, European, American or Bermudan, with cash dividends, a quanto adjustment and a leverage function optional: FdmHestonSolver on FdmBlackScholesMesher's grid of the log spot, sized by the variance mesher's volatility estimate, by FdmHestonLocalVolatilityVarianceMesher's grid of the variance. public static class FdHestonVanillaEngine Inheritance object FdHestonVanillaEngine Inherited Members object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks The engine reports the value, delta, gamma and theta, the theta null when the problem's first stopping time is time 0. Its finite-difference working types are built inside each calculation and dropped after it. Its times run on Clock(HestonProcess, FdmQuantoHelper?, LocalVolTermStructure?), from the earliest reference date of the structures it reads, each accruing nothing before its own date, where QuantLib's run from the risk-free curve's; where none is dated before the risk-free curve, they are QuantLib's (Divergences/FdHestonMismatchedTimesTests.cs). The variance mesher's skew factor is bounded and its fallbacks are master's. QuantLib sizes the equity mesher on a helper process whose curves its call binds in each other's places, so the mesher walks the forward's mirror about the spot; where the carry is large against the volatility the grid's far edge falls inside the distribution and the price stops converging (a five-year call at 1.25 times the forward, carry 0.30 and volatility 0.1, priced 0 where the analytic engine gives 1.5732), and where cash dividends take the mirrored walk below zero its bound isn't a number and the engine refuses. Here the mesher is QuantLib's wherever its range holds the true forwards' band, the walk's ends on the helper's curves in place widened by the volatility's quantile, half the mesher's own margin, and the strike widened by the same half margin, and QuantLib's mesher widened to the band through its own constraints where it doesn't, a bound that isn't a number falling short. The multi-strike solve, whose mesher takes no constraints, solves each strike alone where its grid doesn't hold the band at the points the solve is read at, S·K/Kᵢ, their forwards quanto-adjusted where a quanto helper is given; the two paths run on different grids, so a strike's value steps where the switch moves, by up to about 0.4% at carry 0.06 (Divergences/FdHestonHighCarryTests.cs). QuantLib's enableMultipleStrikesCaching solves once on a mesher spanning several strikes and serves later options at those strikes from the solve, each V(S·d)/d with d = K/Kᵢ; the strike a later call is served depends on which option solved first, which a cache may not do here: a value doesn't depend on what was computed before it. Here CalculateStrikes(VanillaOption, IEnumerable<double>, EvaluationContext, HestonModel, int, int, int, int, FdmSchemeDesc?, LocalVolTermStructure?, double) returns every strike's results from one solve on the given option, each QuantLib's cached value bit for bit. Where the scaling doesn't hold, QuantLib's cache serves values far from the strike's own price: with a leverage function, which a spot-dependent leverage breaks (at 125, 0.830 cached where the direct price is 0.433), and after a reference whose payoff isn't a plain vanilla (6.819 served for a plain call at 80 after a cash-or-nothing reference, its direct price 22.945); there each strike's plain vanilla is solved alone, QuantLib's engine priced for that strike (Divergences/FdHestonMultipleStrikesLeverageTests.cs, Divergences/FdHestonStrikesReferenceTests.cs). The variances and the European discount, read by date, accrue nothing before their structures' dates, where QuantLib's reads throw for an option expiring before a later structure's date (Divergences/BasketExpiryBeforeReferenceDateTests.cs).
