InterpolatedZeroInflationCurve<TInterpolator> An inflation term structure interpolating zero-coupon inflation rates. KahaleSmileSection An arbitrage-free smile section by Kahale's C¹ interpolation and extrapolation of a source section's call prices (Kahale, "An arbitrage-free interpolation of volatilities", Risk, May 2004). KerkhofSeasonality Kerkhof's seasonality: twelve monthly factors, the correction between two months the product of the factors of the months between them. KrugerLogDiscountCurve A yield term structure based on log-cubic interpolation of discount factors with Kruger's derivatives. LinearForwardCurve A yield term structure based on linear interpolation of instantaneous forward rates. LinearInterpolatedSmileSection QuantLib-Python's LinearInterpolatedSmileSection: an InterpolatedSmileSection<TInterpolator> with linear interpolation. PiecewiseYieldCurve<TTraits, TInterpolator, TBootstrap> A yield term structure bootstrapped on rate helpers: each helper's pillar marks the end of an interpolated segment, solved so that the helper reprices its quote. PiecewiseYoYInflation A year-on-year inflation term structure bootstrapped on inflation helpers, on linearly interpolated year-on-year inflation rates. PiecewiseYoYInflationCurve<TInterpolator, TBootstrap, TTraits> A year-on-year inflation term structure bootstrapped on inflation helpers: each helper's pillar marks the end of an interpolated segment of year-on-year inflation rates, solved so that the helper reprices its quote. PiecewiseZeroInflation A zero-inflation term structure bootstrapped on inflation helpers, on linearly interpolated zero-coupon inflation rates. PiecewiseZeroInflationCurve<TInterpolator, TBootstrap, TTraits> A zero-inflation term structure bootstrapped on inflation helpers: each helper's pillar marks the end of an interpolated segment of zero-coupon inflation rates, solved so that the helper reprices its quote. PiecewiseZeroSpreadedTermStructure A yield curve with spreads added to another curve's zero rates, interpolated linearly between their dates. QuantoTermStructure The quanto-adjusted dividend curve of an underlying in a foreign currency, for quanto option pricing: the zero yield q + r − r_f + ρ σ_S σ_X, from the underlying's dividend curve, the domestic and foreign risk-free curves, the underlying's and the exchange rate's Black volatilities and their correlation. RateHelper The base of the helpers a yield curve is bootstrapped on: QuantLib's RateHelper, a typedef of BootstrapHelper<YieldTermStructure>. RelativeDateBootstrapHelper<TTermStructure> The base of a bootstrap helper whose dates follow the evaluation date: QuantLib's RelativeDateBootstrapHelper. RelativeDateRateHelper The base of a yield helper whose dates follow the evaluation date: QuantLib's RelativeDateRateHelper, a typedef of RelativeDateBootstrapHelper<YieldTermStructure>. SabrFunctions The SABR functions: Hagan's lognormal and normal expansions of the SABR volatility, Le Floc'h and Kennedy's expansion, the parameters' validation and Le Floc'h and Kennedy's initial guess for a calibration. SabrInterpolatedSmileSection A shifted lognormal smile section whose volatilities are a SABR fit to market volatilities at given strikes. SabrSmileSection A SABR smile section: the shifted SABR volatility at given parameters. SabrSwaptionVolatilityCube The SABR swaption volatility cube: QuantLib's SabrSwaptionVolatilityCube, the XABR cube on the SABR model, whose smiles are SABRInterpolation fits and whose sections are SabrSmileSections. Seasonality A seasonality: a correction of an inflation term structure's zero and year-on-year rates for seasonal effects in the price index. SimplePolynomialFitting The simple polynomial fitting method: a discount function d(t) = Σ_{i=0}^{degree} c_i t^i, a simple and crude, but fast and robust, means of fitting a yield curve. SimpleQuoteVariables Additional bootstrap variables that are plain values, each with an initial guess and an optional lower bound: QuantLib's SimpleQuoteVariables. SimpleZeroCurve A yield term structure based on linear interpolation of simply compounded zero rates. SmileSection An interest-rate volatility smile section: the volatilities of options on one exercise date. SmileSectionUtils A smile section's grid of strikes and call prices and its arbitrage-free region: the widest range of the grid, around the at-the-money point, on which the call prices decrease and are convex in the strike. SofrFutureRateHelper A rate helper on a CME SOFR future: overnight SOFR rates from the reference month's third Wednesday, inclusive, to the third Wednesday a quarter later, exclusive, compounded; or over the reference month, averaged. SplineCubicInterpolatedSmileSection QuantLib-Python's SplineCubicInterpolatedSmileSection: an InterpolatedSmileSection<TInterpolator> with QuantLib-Python's SplineCubic, Cubic with the spline's derivatives and no monotonicity filter. SpreadCdsHelper A bootstrap helper on a credit default swap quoted as a running spread: its implied quote is the swap's fair spread. SpreadDiscountCurve A spread yield curve based on log-linear interpolation of spread discount factors, which gives piecewise-constant spreads. SpreadFittingMethod The spread fitting method: a spread curve fitted on top of a discounting curve, by an underlying parametric method, so that the fitted discount is the method's times the discounting curve's. SpreadedBackwardFlatZeroInterpolatedTermStructure A yield curve with spreads added to another curve's zero rates, backward-flat between their dates. SpreadedCubicZeroInterpolatedTermStructure A yield curve with spreads added to another curve's zero rates, interpolated cubically between their dates. SpreadedOptionletVolatility An optionlet volatility structure that adds a constant spread to another's volatilities. SpreadedSmileSection A smile section shifted by a volatility spread: another section's volatilities plus the spread. SpreadedSwaptionVolatility A swaption volatility structure that adds a constant spread to another's volatilities. StrippedOptionlet A matrix of optionlet (caplet and floorlet) volatilities, also called forward-forward volatilities, calculated elsewhere, as a StrippedOptionletBase. StrippedOptionletAdapter An optionlet volatility structure on a StrippedOptionletBase: linear in strike at each fixing date, then linear in time. StrippedOptionletBase The base class of a vector, indexed by time, of optionlet (caplet and floorlet) volatilities indexed by strike. SurvivalProbabilityCurve The survival-probability curve with linear interpolation: QuantLib-Python's SurvivalProbabilityCurve, QuantLib's InterpolatedSurvivalProbabilityCurve<Linear>. SurvivalProbabilityStructure The survival-probability term structure: an adapter that lets a derived curve implement the survival probability, from which the default densities and hazard rates follow. SvenssonFitting The Svensson fitting method: a discount function d(t) = e^(−r t), the zero rate r = c_0 + (c_1 + c_2)(1 − e^(−κt))/(κt) − c_2 e^(−κt) + c_3((1 − e^(−κ_1 t))/(κ_1 t) − e^(−κ_1 t)). SwapRateHelper A rate helper for bootstrapping over swap rates: the fixed rate of the vanilla swap, built at construction, that the curve prices at par. SwaptionVolatilityCube The base class of swaption volatility cubes: an at-the-money swaption volatility structure, and the smile around it given by volatility spreads at strike spreads from the at-the-money strike, on a grid of option and swap tenors. SwaptionVolatilityDiscrete The base class of swaption volatility structures given on a grid of option dates and swap tenors: the grid's dates, times and lengths, and the interpolation from an option time to its date. SwaptionVolatilityMatrix The at-the-money swaption-volatility matrix: the volatility of a swaption, bilinearly interpolated in the swap length and the option time between the market volatilities of a grid of option dates and swap tenors. SwaptionVolatilityStructure The base class of swaption volatility structures: volatilities by option date and swap tenor. UltimateForwardTermStructure The Dutch regulatory term structure for pension funds: another curve, the original, up to a first smoothing point, and past it a forward rate extrapolated from the last liquid forward rate towards an ultimate forward rate, for discounting long-dated liabilities. UpfrontCdsHelper A bootstrap helper on a credit default swap quoted as an upfront, in fractional units, with a running spread: its implied quote is the swap's fair upfront. VolatilityTermStructure The base class of volatility term structures. XabrSwaptionVolatilityCube<TModel> The swaption volatility cube that fits a smile model per option and swap tenor: the fit-early, interpolate-later cube, generic over its model. YearOnYearInflationSwapHelper A bootstrap helper for year-on-year inflation term structures, on a year-on-year inflation swap's quoted fixed rate. YieldTermStructure The interest-rate term structure: the base of the curves that give discount factors, zero rates and forward rates. YoYInflationCurve A year-on-year inflation curve interpolating its rates linearly: QuantLib's typedef InterpolatedYoYInflationCurve<Linear>, named as QuantLib-Python names it. YoYInflationHelperExtensions QuantLib's setTermStructure for year-on-year inflation helpers, as a copy of the helper's own static type. YoYInflationTermStructure The base class of year-on-year inflation term structures. YoYOptionletVolatilitySurface The base class of year-on-year inflation optionlet volatility structures, which give total variances and observe an index with a lag. ZabrFullFdInterpolatedSmileSection QuantLib-Python's ZabrFullFdInterpolatedSmileSection: a ZabrInterpolatedSmileSection<TEvaluation> with the full finite-difference kernel. ZabrFullFdSmileSection QuantLib-Python's ZabrFullFdSmileSection: a ZabrSmileSection<TEvaluation> with the full finite-difference kernel. ZabrInterpolatedSmileSection<TEvaluation> A smile section whose volatilities are a ZABR fit to market volatilities at given strikes, by the kernel TEvaluation names. ZabrLocalVolatilityInterpolatedSmileSection QuantLib-Python's ZabrLocalVolatilityInterpolatedSmileSection: a ZabrInterpolatedSmileSection<TEvaluation> with the local-volatility kernel. ZabrLocalVolatilitySmileSection QuantLib-Python's ZabrLocalVolatilitySmileSection: a ZabrSmileSection<TEvaluation> with the local-volatility kernel. ZabrModel The ZABR model (J. Andreasen and B. Huge, "ZABR - Expansions for the masses", 2011): SABR with the volatility's own volatility scaled by a power γ of the volatility. Its short-maturity lognormal and normal volatilities, and its local volatility, and call prices by finite differences: on the Dupire equation in the strike under that local volatility, and on the model's full two-dimensional equation in the forward and the volatility. ZabrShortMaturityLognormalInterpolatedSmileSection QuantLib-Python's ZabrShortMaturityLognormalInterpolatedSmileSection: a ZabrInterpolatedSmileSection<TEvaluation> with the short-maturity lognormal kernel. ZabrShortMaturityLognormalSmileSection QuantLib-Python's ZabrShortMaturityLognormalSmileSection: a ZabrSmileSection<TEvaluation> with the short-maturity lognormal kernel. ZabrShortMaturityNormalInterpolatedSmileSection QuantLib-Python's ZabrShortMaturityNormalInterpolatedSmileSection: a ZabrInterpolatedSmileSection<TEvaluation> with the short-maturity normal kernel. ZabrShortMaturityNormalSmileSection QuantLib-Python's ZabrShortMaturityNormalSmileSection: a ZabrSmileSection<TEvaluation> with the short-maturity normal kernel. ZabrSmileSection<TEvaluation> A ZABR smile section: the volatilities and option prices of the ZABR model at given parameters, by the kernel TEvaluation names. ZabrSwaptionVolatilityCube The ZABR swaption volatility cube: QuantLib's ZabrSwaptionVolatilityCube, the XABR cube on the ZABR model with its default kernel, whose smiles are ZabrInterpolation<TEvaluation> fits and whose sections are ZabrSmileSection<TEvaluation>s, on the short-maturity lognormal kernel. ZeroCouponInflationSwapHelper A bootstrap helper for zero-inflation term structures, on a zero-coupon inflation swap's quoted fixed rate. ZeroCurve A yield term structure based on linear interpolation of zero rates. ZeroInflationCurve A zero-inflation curve interpolating its rates linearly: QuantLib's typedef InterpolatedZeroInflationCurve<Linear>, named as QuantLib-Python names it. ZeroInflationHelperExtensions QuantLib's setTermStructure for zero-inflation helpers, as a copy of the helper's own static type. ZeroInflationTermStructure The base class of zero-inflation term structures, which give zero-coupon inflation rates. ZeroSpreadedTermStructure A term structure with a spread added to the zero yield rate of another curve, the original. ZeroYieldStructure A zero-yield term structure: an adapter to YieldTermStructure that lets a derived class implement only ZeroYieldImpl(double); discount factors and forward rates are calculated from the zero yields, which are continuously compounded with an annual time unit. Structs AndreasenHugeCalibrationError AndreasenHugeVolatilityInterpl's calibration error in volatility units, QuantLib's calibrationError() tuple: each calibrated option's price error divided by its vega. DefaultDensity The default-density curve traits: the bootstrap of default densities, and the formulas of InterpolatedDefaultDensityCurve<TInterpolator>. Discount The discount-curve traits: the curve's data are discount factors, interpolated as an InterpolatedDiscountCurve<TInterpolator>'s are. ForwardRate The forward-curve traits: the curve's data are instantaneous forward rates, interpolated as an interpolated forward curve's are. GlobalBootstrap The global bootstrapper, with additional restrictions: the curve's nodes are solved together, by an optimizer that minimizes the helpers' quote errors and any additional penalties. HazardRate The hazard-rate curve traits: the bootstrap of hazard rates, and the formulas of InterpolatedHazardRateCurve<TInterpolator>. IterativeBootstrap The universal piecewise-term-structure bootstrapper: each node is solved in turn so that the helper whose pillar it is reprices its quote, and the passes repeat until the nodes stop moving when the interpolation is global or a pillar comes before its helper's latest relevant date. LocalBootstrap The localised bootstrapper: QuantLib's LocalBootstrap, which solves each section of a curve on a non-local interpolation from the few helpers around it, so that each helper's risk stays local. SimpleZeroYield The simple zero-curve traits: the curve's data are simply compounded zero rates, interpolated as an interpolated simple zero curve's are. SurvivalProbability The survival-probability curve traits: the bootstrap of survival probabilities, and the formulas of InterpolatedSurvivalProbabilityCurve<TInterpolator>. SwaptionVolCubeSabrModel The SABR model of a swaption volatility cube: QuantLib's SwaptionVolCubeSabrModel on the primary XabrModelTraits, its smiles fitted by SABRInterpolation and its sections SabrSmileSections. SwaptionVolCubeZabrModel<TEvaluation> The ZABR model of a swaption volatility cube: QuantLib's SwaptionVolCubeZabrModel<Kernel> with its XabrModelTraits specialization, its smiles fitted by ZabrInterpolation<TEvaluation> and its sections ZabrSmileSection<TEvaluation>s, five parameters α, β, ν, ρ and γ. YoYInflationTraits The year-on-year inflation curve's bootstrap traits: the curve's data are year-on-year rates, from the base date, starting at the curve's base rate. ZabrFullFd QuantLib's full finite-difference kernel for ZabrSmileSection<TEvaluation>: calls priced at the section's strike grid, each by finite differences on the model's two-dimensional equation (FullFdPrice(double)), interpolated by a spline, and the volatility implied from those prices. ZabrLocalVolatility QuantLib's local-volatility kernel for ZabrSmileSection<TEvaluation>: calls priced at the section's strike grid by finite differences on the Dupire equation under the model's local volatility (FdPrice(ReadOnlySpan<double>)), interpolated by a spline, and the volatility implied from those prices. ZabrShortMaturityLognormal QuantLib's short-maturity lognormal kernel for ZabrSmileSection<TEvaluation>: the volatility is the model's lognormal volatility at the strike, floored at 1e-6, and the option prices are SmileSection's, Black's on that volatility. ZabrShortMaturityNormal QuantLib's short-maturity normal kernel for ZabrSmileSection<TEvaluation>: the option prices are Bachelier's on the model's normal volatility at the strike, and the volatility is the lognormal one implied from the out-of-the-money price, 0 where it can't be implied. ZeroInflationTraits The zero-inflation curve's bootstrap traits: the curve's data are zero-coupon inflation rates, from the base date. ZeroYield The zero-curve traits: the curve's data are continuously compounded zero rates, interpolated as an interpolated zero curve's are. Interfaces IBootstrap A bootstrap: QuantLib's Bootstrap template parameter (IterativeBootstrap, GlobalBootstrap), as a configuration struct whose Calculate<TTermStructure, TTraits, TInterpolator>(BootstrapState<TTermStructure>, TInterpolator, EvaluationContext) fills a curve's working state. IBootstrapHelper A bootstrap helper seen without its term structure's type: what a global bootstrap's penalties and initial-guess function read of the helpers they are given (IBootstrapState). IBootstrapState The working state of a curve under construction, seen without its term structure's type: what a global bootstrap's penalties and initial-guess function read (BootstrapState<TTermStructure> implements it). IBootstrapTraits<TTermStructure> A bootstrap's traits: what the bootstraps ask of a curve kind (QuantLib's Discount, ZeroYield and the other traits structs), as static members. IDefaultProbabilityTraits A default-probability curve's bootstrap traits, which also carry the curve kind they bootstrap: its survival probability, default density and hazard rate, and its maximum-date rule. IInterpolatedCurve<TTraits, TInterpolator> An interpolated curve of the kind its traits name, over the given interpolator: QuantLib's Traits::curve<Interpolator>::type, which a piecewise curve on those traits derives from. ILocalInterpolator An interpolation factory that builds a curve a section at a time: the interpolator LocalBootstrap needs, QuantLib's localInterpolate and dataSizeAdjustment (of its interpolators, only ConvexMonotone has them). IXabrCubeModel The smile model of an XABR swaption volatility cube, QuantLib's XabrModelTraits<Model> with its model's Interpolation and SmileSection types: the model's parameter count, the fit of a smile, the fitted fifth parameter of a five-parameter model, and the smile section at given parameters. IYieldTraits A yield curve's bootstrap traits, which also carry the curve kind they bootstrap: its discount formula and its maximum-date rule. IYoYInflationTraits A year-on-year inflation curve's bootstrap traits, which also carry the curve kind they bootstrap: its rate formula and its maximum-date rule. IZabrEvaluation QuantLib's ZABR evaluation tags: the kernel a ZabrSmileSection<TEvaluation> prices with. Its static members answer the section's members that QuantLib dispatches on the tag. IZeroInflationTraits A zero inflation curve's bootstrap traits, which also carry the curve kind they bootstrap: its rate formula and its maximum-date rule. Enums AndreasenHugeVolatilityInterplCalibrationType Which options AndreasenHugeVolatilityInterpl calibrates to: QuantLib's AndreasenHugeVolatilityInterpl::CalibrationType, its values QuantLib's. AndreasenHugeVolatilityInterplInterpolationType How AndreasenHugeVolatilityInterpl interpolates its calibrated volatilities between the calibration strikes: QuantLib's AndreasenHugeVolatilityInterpl::InterpolationType. BlackVarianceSurfaceExtrapolation How a BlackVarianceSurface extrapolates beyond its strikes: QuantLib's BlackVarianceSurface::Extrapolation. BlackVolTimeExtrapolationType How a Black volatility structure extrapolates beyond its last time: QuantLib's BlackVolTimeExtrapolation::Type. BlackVolatilitySurfaceDeltaSmileInterpolationMethod How BlackVolatilitySurfaceDelta interpolates its smile sections in strike: QuantLib's BlackVolatilitySurfaceDelta::SmileInterpolationMethod. CmsMarketCalibrationCalibrationType What a CMS market calibration fits: QuantLib's CmsMarketCalibration::CalibrationType. FixedLocalVolSurfaceExtrapolation How a FixedLocalVolSurface extrapolates beyond a time's strikes: QuantLib's FixedLocalVolSurface::Extrapolation. PillarChoice The alternative ways of determining a bootstrap helper's pillar date: QuantLib's Pillar::Choice. VolatilityType The type of a volatility: shifted lognormal (Black) or normal (Bachelier).

api/NanoQL.Time.Business252.html.summary: Class Business252 Namespace NanoQL.Time Assembly NanoQL.dll Business/252 day count convention. public sealed class Business252 : DayCounter, IEquatable<DayCounter> Inheritance object DayCounter Business252 Implements IEquatable<DayCounter> Inherited Members DayCounter.Equals(object) DayCounter.ToString() object.GetType() object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) Remarks The day count is the number of business days between two dates on the calendar, by QuantLib's walk over months and years. QuantLib keeps each month's count in a cache keyed by the calendar's name and shared by the whole process, filled once and never invalidated, so a count goes stale after a holiday edit and two calendars of one name share their counts (business252.cpp:31-68). Here the constructor counts each month of 1901 to 2199 once, on its own calendar, into a table no other object shares; the counts are QuantLib's wherever its cache isn't stale, a documented divergence where it is. A month the calendar refuses (a calendar with no data for a year) is left out of the table, with the rest of its year, and counted when a count reads it, as QuantLib's walk counts it, so the calendar's refusal comes where QuantLib's does. Two Business/252 day counters are equal when their calendars are (by type, name, and added and removed holidays), where QuantLib compares their names alone. api/NanoQL.Time.ECB.html.summary: Class ECB Namespace NanoQL.Time Assembly NanoQL.dll European Central Bank reserve maintenance dates. public sealed class ECB : IEquatable<ECB> Inheritance object ECB Implements IEquatable<ECB> Inherited Members object.GetType() object.ToString() object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) Remarks The known dates are a value: Default holds QuantLib's, from January 2005 to December 2024, and AddDate(Date) and RemoveDate(Date) return a new value, so two calculations can use different sets and neither changes the other's. In QuantLib they are one static set that addDate and removeDate change for the whole process. Two values are equal when their known dates are. QuantLib's functions whose date defaults to Date(), read as the global evaluation date, take the context after QuantLib's parameters without a default, and the date as a nullable after it: the context's evaluation date is read only when the date is null. At the start of Date's range QuantLib steps one day before the month's first day, or before the date, and so throws on 1 January 1901 (ecb.hpp:42, :81-84; ecb.cpp:200): here a month's date is the first known date on or after its first day, and IsECBdate(Date) is membership in the known dates up to the last one, QuantLib's answers everywhere else; a documented divergence. A method of this class is named Date, which hides the type inside it, so the class writes the type NanoQL.Time.Date. Holiday dates compiled from the gazetted Malaysian public holiday lists published at https://www.officeholidays.com/countries/malaysia, cross-checked for 2021-2026 against Google's public Malaysia holiday calendar. api/NanoQL.Time.Philippines.html.summary: Class Philippines Namespace NanoQL.Time Assembly NanoQL.dll The Philippine calendar. public sealed class Philippines : Calendar, IEquatable<Calendar> Inheritance object Calendar Philippines Implements IEquatable<Calendar> Inherited Members Calendar.IsBusinessDay(Date) Calendar.IsHoliday(Date) Calendar.IsStartOfMonth(Date) Calendar.StartOfMonth(Date) Calendar.IsEndOfMonth(Date) Calendar.EndOfMonth(Date) Calendar.AddHoliday(Date) Calendar.RemoveHoliday(Date) Calendar.ResetAddedAndRemovedHolidays() Calendar.HolidayList(Date, Date, bool) Calendar.BusinessDayList(Date, Date) Calendar.Adjust(Date, BusinessDayConvention) Calendar.Advance(Date, int, TimeUnit, BusinessDayConvention, bool) Calendar.Advance(Date, Period, BusinessDayConvention, bool) Calendar.BusinessDaysBetween(Date, Date, bool, bool) Calendar.Equals(object) Calendar.Equals(Calendar) Calendar.GetHashCode() Calendar.ToString() Calendar.AddedHolidays Calendar.RemovedHolidays object.GetType() object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) Remarks Holidays for the Philippine Stock Exchange. The exchange is closed on both classes of holiday defined by the Labor Code, the regular holidays and the special (non-working) days, which are also the days on which banks supervised by the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas are closed. The list additionally contains a few dates on which the exchange alone suspended trading, so it is not a banking calendar. Holidays with a fixed date or a computable rule: Saturdays Sundays New Year's Day, January 1st Maundy Thursday Good Friday Araw ng Kagitingan (Day of Valor), April 9th Labor Day, May 1st Independence Day, June 12th Ninoy Aquino Day, August 21st (a special non-working day since RA 9256 of 2004) National Heroes Day, the last Monday of August All Saints' Day, November 1st Bonifacio Day, November 30th Feast of the Immaculate Conception, December 8th (a special non-working day since RA 10966 of 2017) Christmas Day, December 25th Rizal Day, December 30th Last Day of the Year, December 31st Black Saturday is proclaimed a special (non-working) day every year, but by construction it always falls on a Saturday and so is already covered by the weekend rule. Holidays with no fixed rule, tabulated for 2020 to 2027: Eid'l Fitr Eid'l Adha Chinese New Year (a special non-working day since 2012) All Souls' Day and Christmas Eve, which are proclaimed in most but not all years EDSA People Power Revolution Anniversary, a special non-working day up to 2023 and a special working day from 2025 Election days One-off additional special non-working days, and the two days on which the exchange was closed by the COVID-19 trading suspension of March 2020 A handful of the rule-based holidays above were transferred to another date by proclamation (Bonifacio Day in 2023, Ninoy Aquino Day in 2024) or downgraded to a special working day (the Last Day of the Year in 2021); those years are handled as explicit exceptions. The Islamic festivals, Chinese New Year and the additional special days are set each year by presidential proclamation rather than by rule, so they are tabulated from the published proclamations rather than computed. Outside the tabulated range only the rule-based holidays above are returned. The 2027 proclamation had not been issued when this calendar was written, so the 2027 entries cover only the festivals whose dates can be predicted (Chinese New Year and the two Islamic festivals, the latter still subject to moon sighting); any additional special (non-working) day declared for that year is missing. The rules also predate the "holiday economics" transfers of RA 9492, so years before 2011 are not reliable. Holiday dates compiled from the presidential proclamations published by the Official Gazette and the Presidential Communications Office (Proclamations 845 s.2019, 986 and 1107 s.2021, 1236 s.2021, 1357 s.2022, 42 and 90 s.2022, 167 and 425 s.2023, 368 and 665 s.2024, 727 s.2024 and 1006 s.2025), cross-checked against https://www.officeholidays.com/countries/philippines. They should be verified against the trading calendar published by the Philippine Stock Exchange at https://www.pse.com.ph/ before being relied upon. api/NanoQL.Time.Thirty360.html.title: Class Thirty360 | nanoql
api/NanoQL.Time.Thirty360.html.summary: Class Thirty360 Namespace NanoQL.Time Assembly NanoQL.dll 30/360 day count convention: the 30/360 day count can be calculated according to a number of conventions. public sealed class Thirty360 : DayCounter, IEquatable<DayCounter> Inheritance object DayCounter Thirty360 Implements IEquatable<DayCounter> Inherited Members DayCounter.Equals(object) DayCounter.ToString() object.GetType() object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) Remarks US convention: if the starting date is the 31st of a month or the last day of February, it becomes equal to the 30th of the same month. If the ending date is the 31st of a month and the starting date is the 30th or 31st of a month, the ending date becomes equal to the 30th. If the ending date is the last of February and the starting date is also the last of February, the ending date becomes equal to the 30th. Also known as "30/360" or "360/360". Bond Basis convention: if the starting date is the 31st of a month, it becomes equal to the 30th of the same month. If the ending date is the 31st of a month and the starting date is the 30th or 31st of a month, the ending date also becomes equal to the 30th of the month. Also known as "US (ISMA)". European convention: starting dates or ending dates that occur on the 31st of a month become equal to the 30th of the same month. Also known as "30E/360", or "Eurobond Basis". Italian convention: starting dates or ending dates that occur on February and are greater than 27 become equal to 30 for computational sake. ISDA convention: starting or ending dates on the 31st of the month become equal to 30; starting dates or ending dates that occur on the last day of February also become equal to 30, except for the termination date. Also known as "30E/360 ISDA", "30/360 ISDA", or "30/360 German". NASD convention: if the starting date is the 31st of a month, it becomes equal to the 30th of the same month. If the ending date is the 31st of a month and the starting date is earlier than the 30th of a month, the ending date becomes equal to the 1st of the next month, otherwise the ending date becomes equal to the 30th of the same month. With the ISDA and German conventions, two day counters are equal only when their termination dates are, where QuantLib compares their names alone: the termination date changes the counts. api/NanoQL.TimeGrid.html.summary: Class TimeGrid Namespace NanoQL Assembly NanoQL.dll A discrete time grid: increasing times from 0, which contain the mandatory times it was built with. public sealed class TimeGrid Inheritance object TimeGrid Inherited Members object.GetType() object.ToString() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() Remarks Immutable. The grid starts at 0 and refuses negative times; QuantLib's own note asks whether negative times could be allowed, and keeps the restriction for the time being. GetEnumerator() is QuantLib's begin() and end(). Its reverse iterators, rbegin() and rend(), are an indexed loop run backwards: for (int i = grid.Size - 1; i >= 0; i--). Constructors TimeGrid() Initializes a new instance of the TimeGrid class with no times. public TimeGrid() TimeGrid(double, int) Initializes a new instance of the TimeGrid class, regularly spaced from 0 to an end. public TimeGrid(double end, int steps) Parameters end double The last time, positive. steps int The number of steps. Remarks With no steps the grid holds one time, 0 times the infinite step: NaN, as QuantLib's does. The mandatory time is end. Exceptions ArgumentOutOfRangeException end isn't positive, or steps is negative. TimeGrid(ReadOnlySpan<double>) Initializes a new instance of the TimeGrid class with mandatory time points, which it copies: the grid holds them, and 0 before them, and no other point. public TimeGrid(ReadOnlySpan<double> times) Parameters times ReadOnlySpan<double> The mandatory times, in any order; times close enough to one another count once. Exceptions ArgumentException times is empty or holds a negative time. ArgumentOutOfRangeException times holds a NaN, which QuantLib's sort leaves undefined. TimeGrid(ReadOnlySpan<double>, int) Initializes a new instance of the TimeGrid class with mandatory time points, which it copies, and further points regularly spaced between each pair of them to reach about the given number of steps. public TimeGrid(ReadOnlySpan<double> times, int steps) Parameters times ReadOnlySpan<double> The mandatory times, in any order; times close enough to one another count once. steps int The number of steps over the whole grid, from which the longest step is the last mandatory time divided by it; with 0, the longest step is the shortest distance between the mandatory times, 0 aside. Exceptions ArgumentException times is empty or holds a negative time, or, with no steps, holds no time but 0. ArgumentOutOfRangeException steps is negative; or times holds a NaN, or gives a period whose number of steps isn't a finite int (an infinite time, or no steps and a shortest distance too small), which QuantLib leaves undefined. docs/bindings.html.title: The bindings | nanoql
docs/bindings.html.summary:
The bindings nanoql crosses to other languages through one C ABI: its assemblies compiled with Native AOT into one shared library (nanoql.dll, libnanoql.so, libnanoql.dylib) that exports a C function per member, described by a generated header, nanoql.h. Every other language's layer is generated over it: Python (ctypes), C++ (a header with RAII) and Java (the FFM API). A release ships the C archive, which carries the C++ layer and its CMake package, and the Python wheel; the C archive serves any language that calls C, and the Java layer is built and tested in the repository and not released. This page gives the C ABI's rules, the tool that generates and builds it, and how it is checked; the language pages follow. The tool: nanoql-bind nanoql-bind (the .NET tool NanoQL.Bind, src/NanoQL.Bind/) reads built assemblies' metadata without running them, selects what crosses, and writes the outputs. In the repository, dotnet run --project src/NanoQL.Bind -c Release -- runs it; outside it, the tool installed from NuGet runs as nanoql-bind (Outside the repository, below): Command What it does update regenerates bindings/c/include/nanoql.h, bindings/surface.json and bindings/coverage.md check regenerates them into memory and compares their bytes with bindings/'s; a difference fails freeze writes a release's shipped files, bindings/surface.shipped.json and bindings/excel/functions.shipped.json, from the checked-in surface; it refuses, writing nothing, unless check and excel check are green build --rid --out [--test-exports] generates the export shims, publishes the native host (src/NanoQL.Native/) with Native AOT, and writes include/ and lib/ shims --out writes the C# export shims the native host compiles (its build runs this) python --out [--test-exports] writes the Python package's generated modules into its folder (Python, below) cpp --out [--test-exports] writes the C++ headers: nanoql.hpp, and a user assembly's own (C and C++, below) java --out [--prefix ]... [--test-exports] writes the Java layer's sources over jextract's, a directory per package: every prefix's, or the named ones alone (Java, below) headers --out [--test-exports] writes the C headers alone, without a native build: nanoql.h, and a user assembly's own twins --out , replay-c --out , replay-cpp --out , replay-java --out write the vector suite's recording twins and the C, C++ and Java replayers' dispatches report prints the surface's counts Each takes --assembly = for every assembly to cross (nanoql's two by default), --roles for a roles table (the repository's bindings/roles.json by default) and --shipped for the last release's surface (bindings/surface.shipped.json when it exists). The Native AOT build needs the platform's C toolchain: on Windows, Visual Studio's C++ tools with the Visual Studio Installer's folder on PATH. Checked in: nanoql.h, surface.json and coverage.md, so any change to the C surface shows in a commit's diff. After a change to nanoql's public API, nanoql-bind update regenerates them and the commit carries the difference. The shims, the language layers and the native library are generated at build. Assemblies built on nanoql: one native library per process holds every assembly it prices with, nanoql's and a user's, since two Native AOT libraries can't share an object. nanoql-bind build --assembly nql=NanoQL.dll --assembly nql=NanoQL.Extensions.dll --assembly acme=Acme.dll builds one: the user's functions take its own prefix (acme_...) and its own header (acme.h, which includes nanoql.h), and a user's roles table sits beside nanoql's. Outside the repository: the tool installed from NuGet (dotnet tool install --global NanoQL.Bind) carries beside it nanoql's two assemblies and, under defaults/, the roles table, the released names and the native host's project and sources, so a user builds a library of their own in any folder. nanoql-bind build writes the host into its output and publishes it there, against the nanoql assemblies the generation reads: the two given with --assembly nql=, from one folder (a build output holding both), or the tool's own copies when none is given, so the library's nanoql is the one the user's assembly was built on; include/ holds the C and C++ headers (nanoql.h and acme.h, nanoql.hpp and acme.hpp); nanoql-bind cpp writes the C++ headers alone, nanoql-bind python the user's Python package, and nanoql-bind excel build their add-in (excel.md). The commands that work on the repository's own files refuse there (update, check, freeze, --test-exports, excel update, excel check and excel package), and so do replay-cpp, which writes the C++ replayer's dispatch, the repository's own test, and those writing the Java layer, which the repository builds and tests but doesn't release (java and replay-java). The C ABI Names nql__: the type's nanoql name and the member's: new for a constructor, get_

for a getter, set_

for a static setter, with_

for a record's init-only property, op_ for an operator (.NET's metadata name, op_Addition). A type whose simple name another type of the same prefix shares takes its namespace's last segment in front. Statics cross under their declaring type alone: a type carries the static and extension members it declares, and a named class (a sealed class naming a closed generic, QuantLib-Python's %template name for it) also those of the closing it names. A base's factory stays with its base, which crosses for it: nql_LatentModel_GaussianCopulaPolicy_ GaussianCopulaPolicyInitTraits_FromCorrelation builds the latent model, and no named latent model carries a copy. Each language reaches a base's static through its own inheritance. A type's own members: a type surfaces the members it declares and, for a closing's name, those of its closed generic bases. A member a type declares with new hides its base's of the same C signature, as C#'s lookup binds it (a named class's own Create returns the named class); an override doesn't, since C# call sites name the virtual's declaration. Overloads: two underscores and the shortest run of the parameters' type names that tells the overload from the others: nql_Calendar_Advance__Date_int beside __Date_Period. Type names: double, int, long, bool, string, Date, OptDate for Date?, doubleArray for a collection of doubles, ValueTuple and its elements' names for a tuple (ValueTupleOptdoubleOptdouble), a nanoql type's name. Overloads whose C signatures are the same cross once: the one a type declares with new, else the one taking a ReadOnlySpan, else an ImmutableArray, else the first. Generics: a generic method crosses closed: per named factory where its type argument is a trait's, and at its constraint where each type parameter has one class or interface constraint, no constructor or value-type one (nql_CalibratedModelExtensions_Calibrate takes any calibrated model); any other generic method doesn't cross. A closed generic type a crossing function takes or returns crosses as a type of its own, its members too, named by its definition and its arguments: nql_CalibrationResults_Gsr_get_Model. An engine's calculations generic in their traits and statistics cross through its named classes, each a static class of them closed: MCPREngine and MCLDEngine at PseudoRandom or LowDiscrepancy and GeneralStatistics, QuantLib's default statistics, for the 19 engines QuantLib-Python names and the six it doesn't, named as their siblings are; and BinomialBarrierEngine and BinomialDoubleBarrierEngine for the seven trees on Derman and Kani's assets, the wheel's closings (nql_MCPREuropeanEngine_Calculate, nql_BinomialCRRBarrierEngine_Bind). A curve, surface or generator QuantLib-Python names with a %template crosses as its named class, a sealed subclass of the closed generic (ForwardFlatForwardCurve, PiecewiseLogCubicSpreadDiscount, YoYInflationCapFloorTermPriceSurface, InvCumulativeBurley2020SobolGaussianRsg); the four the wheel deprecates (LogLinearZeroCurve, LogCubicZeroCurve, NaturalCubicDiscountCurve, PiecewiseSplineCubicDiscount) are deprecated in every layer, their messages the wheel's reasons with nanoql's replacements. Released names never move: each release writes its surface to bindings/surface.shipped.json (nanoql-bind freeze), and the generator keeps every released function's name, by the type it crosses under and its member, and every released type's. A type is read by its name without its assemblies' version, culture and public key token, which a closed generic's arguments carry and a release or a runtime moves. A released name the surface no longer holds, a removed function's, one whose parameters changed or a removed type's, stays in the file under "retired", and no later function or type takes it. A name is held within its prefix: nanoql's released nql_Calendar leaves a user's Calendar its own name. Only a new member is named against the names in use: a member that gains its first overload keeps its short name and the newcomer takes the suffix. Parameters keep their C# names; one a C or C++ keyword takes, or self, result or has_value, gets a trailing underscore. A tuple's elements take the parameter's name and their own in snake case, C#'s tuple element names (calibrationSet_option), or item1... where C# names none; a returned tuple's elements their own (first). In a collection's tuple an element named count or has_value gets a trailing underscore, those being the collection's own. An optional parameter of a type that doesn't cross, null by default (a TimeProvider, a line search, the caller's functions), is left out of the C function and takes its default: nql_BFGS_new(&optimizer) builds QuantLib's default line search, and nql_Date_TodaysDate(&today) reads the computer's clock. Any other parameter that doesn't cross withholds its member, listed in coverage.md with why. Handles One handle type, nql_handle, for every object. The header names each parameter's expected type in its name and in the comment above the function. Ownership: every handle a function returns is the caller's, released once with nql_release; nql_retain gives a second owner, a new handle to the same object. NULL is the null reference. Refusals: a handle is a slot, a generation and the library's tag drawn when it loads, so a released, stale, never-issued or another library's handle is refused with NQL_ERROR_HANDLE, never followed. A handle of the wrong type is refused with NQL_ERROR_TYPE. A slot whose generation would wrap is retired. Threads: every object behind a handle is immutable, so any thread may use any handle at the same time, with no lock. Releasing a handle while another thread uses it is the caller's error. Working types never cross as handles. nanoql's working types (playbook §2.5: mutable, owned by one computation, each marked [WorkingType]) take other forms: Matrix and Vector as arrays, by rows; a generator as an immutable snapshot drawn in batches; a loss model's Distribution as its values. The stepping parts (finite-difference operators and schemes, lattices' discretized assets, market-model curve states and evolvers, optimizer states) stay inside nanoql, with the members that take or return them; an engine built from them is written in C# on nanoql and bound into the same library. A user's type that derives from a marked class, or implements a marked interface, is a working type too. Results records cross as objects: a getter per field. nql_type_name gives an object's .NET type, so a layer wraps a base-typed result as its own class. A nanoql struct's implicit parameterless constructor, default(T), crosses as its new (nql_BackwardFlat_new, or nql_IterativeBootstrap_new__void beside its other constructors). Errors Every function returns an nql_status: 0 for success, a positive code per refusal kind. Results come back through the last parameters. Code Name Refusal 0 NQL_OK none 1 NQL_ERROR NanoQLException: QuantLib's own checks 2 NQL_ERROR_ARGUMENT ArgumentException 3 NQL_ERROR_ARGUMENT_NULL ArgumentNullException; a NULL self 4 NQL_ERROR_ARGUMENT_RANGE ArgumentOutOfRangeException 5 NQL_ERROR_INVALID_OPERATION InvalidOperationException 6 NQL_ERROR_INVALID_CAST InvalidCastException 7 NQL_ERROR_NOT_SUPPORTED NotSupportedException 8 NQL_ERROR_KEY_NOT_FOUND KeyNotFoundException 9 NQL_ERROR_HANDLE a released, stale, foreign or never-issued handle 10 NQL_ERROR_TYPE a handle of the wrong type; a bound engine that can't serve the member 11 NQL_ERROR_OUT_OF_MEMORY OutOfMemoryException 12 NQL_ERROR_IO IOException and its kinds, UnauthorizedAccessException: a file not read or written 13 NQL_ERROR_FORMAT malformed input: XmlException, XmlSchemaValidationException, FormatException 99 NQL_ERROR_INTERNAL anything else: a defect, to report A kind outside the table maps by the member's own documentation: a documented IndexOutOfRangeException is NQL_ERROR_ARGUMENT_RANGE, an undocumented one NQL_ERROR_INTERNAL. The calling thread's last refusal is nql_last_error_code, _message, _param (the parameter as .NET names it) and _type (the .NET exception), valid until the thread's next nanoql call. Values C# C, in C, out double, int, long, bool double, int32_t, int64_t, bool a pointer to it string const char*, UTF-8, NUL-terminated, NULL for null char**, freed with nql_free Date, Date? nql_date: QuantLib's serial (Excel's), 0 for no date nql_date* Period nql_period {length, units} by value nql_period* an enum int32_t, with NQL__ int32_t* T? for a value T const T*, NULL for none T* and bool* has_value Complex nql_complex {re, im} nql_complex* an object, a nanoql struct nql_handle; NULL for an optional struct is its default, default(T), what C# passes for the omitted argument nql_handle*, the caller's a collection a pointer and an int32_t count; a ReadOnlySpan of numbers is read in place a pointer and a count, freed with nql_free (an array of handles: each released first) Span, Span a pointer and a count, written in place a collection of nullables values and has_value flags the same a jagged array its values flat by rows, their count, the rows' lengths and the rows' count the same a dictionary, key–value pairs keys, values, count the same a tuple one parameter per element, _, each in its element's form; C#'s default is each element's zero value, NULL for a nullable one one out-parameter per element, by its name a collection of tuples one array per element, _, a nullable element with its _has_value flags, and _count; NULL first array for null, arrays of no rows for empty one array per element, by its name, then has_value flags for a collection of nullable tuples, then count, each freed with nql_free (each handle released first) Matrix, Vector values by rows with the rows and columns; values and their count; one the member writes into (coverage.md's list) by double*, written back after the call the same, freed with nql_free a generator its snapshot's handle; for a closed generator construction (RandomSequenceGenerator), the snapshot of a class deriving it, checked at the call nql__Draws: draws and weights, the next snapshot a loss Distribution its normalized buckets' edges, widths, densities, cumulative and excess probabilities and averages A tuple's or a collection's elements are scalars, dates, enums, strings, nullable doubles, integers and dates, and objects. A returned collection of tuples with a nullable element, a collection of nullable tuples in, and a tuple holding a collection or a tuple don't cross, each listed in coverage.md. An optional parameter's default is in the header's comment and in surface.json; C passes every parameter, and each language layer applies the defaults. Generators A generator's constructor returns an immutable snapshot holding a private copy of the generator as built. nql__Draws(snapshot, count, &values, &weights, &next) copies it, draws count values (for a sequence generator, count points of its dimension, by rows, the dimension out too) with their weights, and returns the copy as the next snapshot. The same snapshot always gives the same draws, a stream continues from next with nothing recomputed, and threads may draw from one snapshot at once. A member that takes a generator copies the snapshot's. A parameter of a closed generator construction takes the snapshot of a class deriving it (the Gaussian sequence generators over MersenneTwisterUniformRsg, KnuthUniformRsg and the rest), refused with NQL_ERROR_TYPE for another generator's; a member taking a construction no generator class derives doesn't cross. The context and the conventions The context is a handle: nql_EvaluationContext_new(evaluationDate), then nql_EvaluationContext_with_ for each other field, each returning a new context. Conventions by name: the coded presets' constructors (TARGET, Actual365Fixed, Euribor6M, ...) don't cross; a convention set gives each by its name: nql_ConventionSet_Calendar(set, "TARGET", &calendar), nql_ConventionSet_IborIndex__string_Period(set, "Euribor", tenor, curve, &index). A preset that takes arguments has a lookup taking them after its name, as QuantLib-Python's constructor takes them: the daily-tenor LIBORs' settlement days (nql_ConventionSet_IborIndex__string_int(set, "DailyTenorUSDLibor", 2, curve, &index)), AUCPI's frequency and revised flag and GenericCPI's with its lag and currency, and their year-on-year twins; the BMA index, no Ibor index, by nql_ConventionSet_InterestRateIndex, which gives the BMA index, or any Ibor or overnight index, by name or alias; the index lookups follow the set's aliases. A set comes from nql_ConventionSet_get_QuantLib, or from XML: nql_ConventionsXml_Read__string(path, &snapshot) then nql_ConventionSet_With. A NULL set is the current provider read as a set: QuantLib's set where the default provider is the core's, refused where it is a user's provider. nql_ConventionProvider_set_Default sets the default; scopes (ConventionProvider.Use) don't cross. Bound engines A member that takes one of nanoql's engines as a delegate (an instrument builder's pricer, a calibration helper's engine) takes a bound engine: an immutable handle naming an engine with its inputs filled in. nql__Bind takes the inputs the engine's calculations take after the instrument and the context, one function per set of them, each input optional: NULL leaves it open (a value goes by pointer, a collection of tuples by its first element's array). nql__BindOn takes the instrument too, for a member that takes the context alone (a composite instrument). The member supplies its own arguments, always the instrument and the context, and for some members more (a calibration helper's trial model, the quanto engine's process, YoY optionlet stripping's trial surface, the callable bond's OAS spread). Each goes into the engine's parameter of its role: an object into the one parameter of its type; a value, or an object two parameters can take, into the parameter bindings/roles.json names; a calibration helper's trial model always by its entry's names, cast to that parameter's type at each call (a model the engine can't take fails with NQL_ERROR_INVALID_CAST). The bound inputs fill the rest, and a parameter open on both sides keeps its default; a nullable value with no default is null, C#'s value for it (a Monte Carlo engine's timeStepsPerYear beside its bound timeSteps). The calculation: the member takes its engine's calculation for the input set Bind named, for the most derived instrument type its own is. Refused with NQL_ERROR_TYPE when the member takes the engine: an input both bound and supplied, a required one neither bound nor supplied (a non-nullable one with no default), an engine with no calculation for the member, an engine with no parameter for a role (the Black callable engines on the OAS members, where QuantLib's engine reads no spread). The generator stops on a value a member supplies with no entry in the roles table, an object two parameters take that the table names neither of, and two calculations tied for one member. coverage.md lists every pair, where its arguments go, and each calculation that forms none, with why. Experimental functions nanoql's experimental API (NQL0001) crosses, each declaration compiled only under #ifdef NANOQL_EXPERIMENTAL, C's form of C#'s opt-in. A member of a stable type whose signature names an experimental type is experimental too, and so is an experimental member of a stable type, beside the type's stable functions: AnalyticGJRGARCHEngine's CalculateWithinBounds is nql_AnalyticGJRGARCHEngine_CalculateWithinBounds__VanillaOption_EvaluationContext, and its static form, both under NANOQL_EXPERIMENTAL. Versions The first release is 2.0. A version is major and minor, with a third part only for a fix (2.1.1). nanoql.h defines NQL_VERSION_MAJOR, NQL_VERSION_MINOR, NQL_VERSION_PATCH, NQL_VERSION ("2.0") and NQL_ABI_VERSION, the major times 1,000 plus the minor (2000), which a fix keeps; the library answers nql_version() and nql_abi_version(). A 2.y header works with the 2.y library alone; a program linking a separately installed library checks assert(nql_abi_version() == NQL_ABI_VERSION). A 2.y release may remove or change the stable API only where it was deprecated at least two releases and at least a year before. A member nanoql marks [Obsolete] is declared NQL_DEPRECATED("...") in the header and deprecated in every layer. The experimental API (NQL0001, NANOQL_EXPERIMENTAL, the Excel add-in's experimental build) may change or go in any release, outside that window. Its released names still never move and are never reused: a removed function's name is retired. nanoql's assemblies carry the major version alone, 2.0.0.0, for every 2.y release, since surface.json names closed generic types by assembly-qualified names that carry it. Fixed functions nql_release, nql_retain, nql_type_name, nql_equals, nql_hash, nql_to_string, nql_free, nql_last_error_code, nql_last_error_message, nql_last_error_param, nql_last_error_type, nql_version, nql_abi_version, and nql_live_handles, the handles issued and not released, for diagnostics. surface.json The surface's language-neutral description, which every language back end reads and which another generator may read too. Schema 1, its "schema" field raised on any change of meaning; one row a line. assemblies: each input's prefix and name. types: name, prefix, cname, base (the nearest base that crosses: a public class of the inputs that isn't generic, or a closed construction), interfaces, shape (class, sealed, abstract, static, struct, interface), form (how it crosses: handle, value for Date and Period, boxed for another struct, static, and for the working types matrix, vector, snapshot, distribution or withheld), experimental. enums: name, prefix, cname, experimental, flags, members as [name, value]. functions: name (the C name), kind (new, method, static, get, set, with, field, indexer, operator, draws, bind, bindon), type, member, key (the member's metadata key: declaring type, name and parameter types), static, experimental, deprecated (its message, when there is one), overloaded, set (a bind's engine input set), params (each name, kind, type, and optional with its default), returns (its kind and type), and c, the C parameters as [type, name]. A kind is a scalar (double, int32, int64, bool, string, date, period, enum, complex), a nullable value (double? and the like), an object (handle, boxed, snapshot, engine), a working type's form (matrix, vector, distribution), or a collection: array:, span:, jagged:double, map::, tuple:,..., array:tuple:,... for a collection of tuples, and as a result array:tuple?:,... for one of nullable tuples; vector& and matrix& for one the member writes into. A tuple's or a collection of tuples' C# element names are its items. A reader meeting a kind it doesn't know refuses it. presets: each withheld preset constructor: its dictionary, name, member, the convention set's lookup function, and its args, each a constant, the lookup's parameter or computed. engines: each engine input set: its id, engine, inputs and calculations. Checking the bindings The surface: nanoql-bind check keeps the checked-in outputs in step with the code. The tool's own tests, bindings/NanoQL.Bind.Tests, check its rules on nanoql's assemblies and on fixtures it binds as a user's assembly. The test build: nanoql-bind build --test-exports adds the assembly bindings/NanoQL.Bind.TestTypes under the prefix nqlt (an echo per kind, each refusal kind, a deprecated member, a user's generator, a member that sleeps, members that read past an array or an index under one widened value each, with their checked twins, and the bound-engine cases' markets with their C# routes) and narrows handles' generations to 8 bits; the packages ship without it. Each language's conformance suite runs on it: bindings/c/tests/ for C, bindings/cpp/tests/ for C++, bindings/python/tests/ for Python, bindings/java/src/test/ (JUnit 5) for Java, the test types' Java layer compiled with its tests, as a user's package beside nanoql's. The vector suite through each binding: the recorder (tools/replay/) compiles nanoql-bind twins with its runtime, rewrites the test assembly's call sites into nanoql to call them, and runs the vector classes with their own checks against QuantLib's vectors; a red stops it unless --keep-reds keeps the trace, which CI passes except on Windows x64, the reference platform: elsewhere a vector red is reported, and the replays compare each layer with C#'s results on the same machine. Each twin writes its call as its C function's: arguments and result in the C forms above, objects by ids (a struct by its value), doubles by their bits, a preset's constructor, called or reached by reflection, as its set's lookup, a record built by an object initializer as new and its with_ calls, a struct made by default or new T() as its implicit constructor's call, a generator's draws as Draws calls along its snapshots. A call made from inside nanoql (a callback into the test code) isn't written. Each language's replayer then calls its own layer for every line and compares every result with C#'s, bit for bit (off Windows x64, a double within NANOQL_REPLAY_TOLERANCE relatively, or else within NANOQL_REPLAY_ABS_TOLERANCE absolutely, is a match, tallied; CI sets 1e-12 and 1e-13), NaN as NaN, a new object by its class's name (a file-local class's without its compiler prefix, F__, whose hash is of its source file's path, so a trace replays against a library built from another checkout); hash and equality calls aren't recorded (the conformance suites check them); a fact replays up to its first call that needs something the trace couldn't write (a delegate, an object a call that doesn't cross made, a generator a call that doesn't cross moved, or one a crossing call took, which C# shares where the C ABI copies; a call that writes into a Matrix or Vector argument crossing in only, which the C call doesn't give back). The C replayer is bindings/c/replay/, its dispatch generated by nanoql-bind replay-c; C++'s is bindings/cpp/replay/, its dispatch generated by nanoql-bind replay-cpp, which calls each C function through its C++ member with arguments of the member's own parameter types; Python's is bindings/python/tests/replay.py, which calls each C function through the Python member the generated map names, an overload through its group's dispatch; where the dispatch, reading the arguments' own classes, takes another form than C#'s static choice, it counts the call and calls the recorded form; Java's is bindings/java/src/test/java/org/nanoql/replay/, its dispatch generated by nanoql-bind replay-java, which calls each C function through its Java member, a fact stopping where Java's types can't hold an input (an enum value no constant has, which only a refusal's test passes, or a matrix of no rows and some columns), each such stop counted by its reason. A record's generated equality pair, which no class declares, goes through the language's own == or equals (nql_equals) in the C++, Python and Java replayers, its C function called by the C replayer alone. Given bindings/replay-floor.json, the C and Java replayers also fail below the floor: at least as many facts replayed whole, each with calls, as the floor lists (the facts that reach only crossing members), at least its calls replayed, refusals matched, and the facts it names whole. Every function called, its arrays and indexes widened: the Python replayer's --sweep , after its replay of the whole suite and before its objects are released, calls each function of the layer's table, those the trace doesn't call first, then those it calls: through its Python member, or, for a record's equality pair the layer leaves to ==, through its C function, its answer checked against == and !=. Its standing arguments are the replay's objects by class, at most 40 of each, each taken at its first sight in the facts' name order, so that the recording's order of facts doesn't move them (but for a fact whose replay stops before it reaches an object another fact made), and values by kind and parameter name, the names from bindings/surface.json (--surface names another; a run with neither stops), up to three choices; the objects an uncalled function returns join them, in passes until one reaches nothing new. Then, on the choice that returned (each one tried, when none did), its widened attempts change one thing each, their objects joining nothing: an array-like argument empty, of one element or of twelve, and every one at once where there are two or more (zero:, one: and many:, with the parameter's name or *); and an index-like integer, by its name (i, index, iName and the like) at 1,000 and at -1 (past: and neg:). An orthogonal polynomial's order takes no index probe, and a map no array probe, each exemption with its reason. The calls run in a fresh temporary folder, removed after a clean sweep and kept after a red, each under a limit (--limit, 30 s), past which faulthandler ends the process, the call and its probe named on standard error. It fails on a Python-layer error, code 99 or code 9 in any attempt, standing or widened, and on an exclusion that names no function of the layer; the outcomes file gives each function's line: returned, refused with its code, unreached with the class it lacked, or excluded, a red's probe beside its kind, the trace's functions marked trace, and the widened attempts' outcomes last. EXCLUDED in replay.py lists the functions it skips, in both stages, each with its reason and its time. --prefix sweeps a user's package, nqlt for the test build, through its own members, importing it and its experimental module first, so a trace of its calls replays too. CI's Python step runs it on Windows x64; a replay of a subset doesn't sweep, as its objects aren't the whole suite's. Parity with QuantLib-Python: tools/bindings/wheelparity.py reads the wheel's QuantLib.py (the release tools/vectors/requirements.txt pins), surface.json and bindings/wheel-routes.json, and puts every class the wheel constructs, and every module function that constructs one, in one group: it crosses with a maker (a constructor, a factory, a preset lookup, an engine's calculation or Bind); a route the table names, with its reason, to a type the surface makes, an enum it carries, a C function it has or a language form; an exclusion with its reason (handles, observers and settings, SWIG's containers, the stepping parts, the caller's own functions); or a gap. --fail-on-gap exits 1 on a gap, and CI's bindings job runs it on Windows x64; --report writes the parity table. The table's notes keep the differences a crossing class still has (GlobalBootstrap's initial guess). Debugging into nanoql Windows: the native library's PDB holds line records for nanoql's C# code, so a debugger attached to a C, C++, Python or Java program steps from its call into nanoql's source, the generated export the frame above. tools/replay/stepin.py shows it from a C program: python -I tools/replay/stepin.py nanoql.dll "*FlatForward___ctor*" stops in FlatForward's constructor and prints the stack's source lines. Visual Studio's mixed-mode debugging does the same from Python. A release's library, built in release mode, maps nanoql's sources to its commit on GitHub (Source Link), so the debugger fetches them; a library built from a checkout reads the checkout. Linux and macOS: the build strips the DWARF line records into libnanoql.so.dbg and libnanoql.dylib.dSYM; point gdb at a checkout with set substitute-path , or lldb with settings set target.source-map . Symbols ship apart from the packages, as an archive per platform on the release, nanoql---symbols beside the C archive: nanoql.pdb, libnanoql.so.dbg or libnanoql.dylib.dSYM (tools/release/symbols.py). Platforms The library is built natively on each of five platforms: win-x64, win-arm64, linux-x64, linux-arm64 and osx-arm64; Linux in a manylinux_2_28 container, so it runs on glibc 2.28 and later; Intel Macs aren't among them (nanoql's C# library runs there; nanoql builds and tests no bindings for them). It loads no ICU (invariant globalization), so its messages read the same in every locale and it runs where libicu is absent. Windows x64 is the validated platform; on the others, a result's last bits may differ where the C runtime's maths functions do. A release ships the platforms release.yml names in RIDS: Windows x64 and Linux x64, with Windows Arm64, Linux Arm64 and macOS on Apple silicon in later releases. C and C++ Install: an archive per platform on the release, nanoql---c-api.zip on Windows and .tar.xz elsewhere: include/ (nanoql.h and nanoql.hpp), lib/ (nanoql.dll with its import library nanoql.lib, libnanoql.so or libnanoql.dylib, and cmake/nanoql/, the CMake package) and the notices: LICENSE, NOTICE, THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md, and the .NET runtime's LICENSE.TXT and THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.TXT, which Native AOT compiles into the library. The symbols ship apart. python bindings/c/archive.py --library --out writes one. C: include nanoql.h and link the library; the C ABI above is the whole of it. C++: nanoql.hpp, C++17, over nanoql.h, its CMake target nanoql::cpp (find_package(nanoql CONFIG); cpp.md gives the install, CMake and a first program). NANOQL_EXPERIMENTAL, defined first, opts in to the experimental API. Its hand-written part is bindings/cpp/runtime.hpp; the tool writes the rest, never checked in, as nanoql-bind build does into include/. The bullets below describe it. C++ can also include nanoql.h as it is; its declarations sit in extern "C". Names: namespace nanoql; nanoql's type names; members in QuantLib's camelCase (curve.discount(5.0), swap.fixedRate(), NPV(), yoyInflationIndex()), a getter a member function; a static member or an extension method a static member of its declaring class (ConventionSet::quantLib()), a record's init-only property with(value), an operator a static op_ (a record's == and != aside, under Objects) and, for arithmetic and ordering, C++'s operator (and == for Date and Period). A name a keyword or a type takes gets a trailing underscore: Echo::double_. Objects: each class owns a handle: a copy takes a new handle to the same object, a move takes the handle, the destructor releases it. A class's bases and interfaces are virtual bases, so an object converts to each (const ICalibratedModel& m = gsr;). Nanoql's null reference is a null object, T(nullptr), which if (obj) tests; a constructor taking no arguments, where nanoql has one, makes the object (a struct's is default(T)); a constructor one argument can call is explicit, so no argument converts to an object implicitly, as in C#. object_cast(o) gives an object as another class, unchecked until a member of a class it isn't refuses. Equality, hashCode(), toString() and typeName() are nanoql's, and a record's == and != are that equality, with no op_Equality or op_Inequality of their own. Values: Date holds QuantLib's serial (Date() is no date; serial() the C form) with nanoql's members (year(), month(), dayOfMonth(), Date::todaysDate()); Period has length() and units(); enums are enum classes over int32_t; std::string (a null string comes back empty; a parameter whose default is null takes std::optional, null as std::nullopt), std::optional for nullable values, std::complex; std::vector out, and in array_view, a read-only view of a vector or a braced list, or nullptr for null, which differs from empty; a key-value collection as pairs; Matrix by rows; a std::vector& or Matrix& nanoql writes into in place; a tuple as std::tuple both ways ({} for C#'s default), a collection of tuples in as an array_view> and out as a std::vector of them, of std::optional ones for nullable tuples; a loss distribution as Distribution; a generator's draws(count) its values, weights and next snapshot. A parameter of a closed generator construction is an Object, the snapshot of a class deriving it, checked at the call. Defaults and overloads: C++ default arguments with nanoql's defaults, at each argument count the forms whose leading parameters agree offering it once, through the shortest (§2.2's rule). A form whose C++ parameters another form's are takes its C overload suffix (outerProduct_doubleArray beside outerProduct), a constructor a static create_.... A braced list fits several collections' views, as in any C++ overload set: a vector names one. Errors: nanoql::error, a std::runtime_error with code(), param() and type_name(); under it argument_error, with argument_null_error and argument_out_of_range_error under that, and handle_error for a refused handle (codes 9 and 10). Deprecation: a member nanoql marks [Obsolete] is [[deprecated]] with its message. A user's assembly: a header of its own, .hpp, its classes in namespace extending nanoql's (acme::ExponentialCurve a nanoql::YieldTermStructure), linked against the library holding nanoql's assemblies and the user's. Python Install: pip install nanoql, a py3-none- wheel holding the library for Windows x64 and Linux x64 (manylinux_2_28), with Windows Arm64, Linux Arm64 and macOS on Apple silicon (14 or later) in later releases: one wheel for every Python from 3.11, with NumPy 1.26 or later, and nothing compiled on install. Names: nanoql's type names; members in PEP 8's snake case (curve.discount(5.0), swap.fixed_rate); enum members as nanoql's (Compounding.Continuous). A constructor is the class's call, a getter a property, a static member or an extension method a static method of its declaring class (ConventionSet.quant_lib()), a record's init-only property with_(value), an operator a static op_ (a record's == and != aside, under Objects) and, for arithmetic and ordering, Python's operator. A member that would take another's name, or one of Object's, takes a suffix: close_. Constructors: every class has its own: its constructors' dispatch, or a TypeError where none crosses, never a base's, which would build the base under the class's name. A preset's names its lookup by name: USDCurrency() raises "USDCurrency is made by ConventionSet.currency". An experimental constructor added on the opt-in replaces the refusal. Values: datetime.date in and out, None for no date; nanoql.Period(length, units) or a plain tuple in, a Period out, its operators and equality nanoql's (Period(1, Years) == Period(12, Months)); enums as IntEnum; NumPy arrays out (float64 for doubles), any sequence in; a matrix a 2-D array by rows; a span nanoql writes into a writable, contiguous NumPy array; lists of objects; a dictionary for key–value results; a tuple in as a tuple (None for C#'s default) and out as a named tuple (Result(first, second)), a collection of tuples in as any sequence of them and out as a list of named tuples, None for a null tuple, its stubs typed (Sequence[tuple[VanillaOption, float]]), a tuple of the wrong length refused with a TypeError; nanoql.Distribution for a loss distribution; a generator's draws(count) returns its values, weights and next snapshot. Defaults and overloads: keyword arguments with nanoql's defaults. An overload group is one method that picks its form by the arguments' types, exact matches first, then conversions (an int for a float, a tuple for a period, an int for an enum), an object nearer the form's class first; each form is declared with typing.overload, and at each argument count the forms whose leading parameters agree offer it once, through the shortest. The package carries py.typed. Objects: each holds a handle, released when Python collects it or at once by close() or a with block; a closed object raises HandleError before the call crosses. A result is of the most derived class the package knows; equality, hashing and str() are nanoql's, and a record's == and != are that equality, with no op_equality or op_inequality of their own. Errors: NanoQLError, with code, param and type_name; ArgumentError, also a ValueError, and under it ArgumentNullError and ArgumentOutOfRangeError; HandleError for a refused handle (codes 9 and 10). The experimental API: import nanoql.experimental opts in: its classes, and the experimental members of stable classes, added on import. A member nanoql marks [Obsolete] warns with a DeprecationWarning carrying its message. The library: the package's own (nanoql/lib/); NANOQL_LIBRARY, or nanoql.use_library(path) before any object is made, loads another, such as a build holding a user's assembly; once an object exists, use_library raises RuntimeError, since objects of one library are foreign to another. The hand-written runtime is bindings/java/src/main/java/org/nanoql/.
