Objects: each NanoObject owns a handle, released by close() (a try-with-resources block) or by a cleaner once unreachable; a closed object throws NanoQLException with code 9 before the call crosses. Every member keeps the objects it reads handles from reachable until its call returns (Reference.reachabilityFence), so a temporary's handle isn't released mid-call. A result is of the most derived class the layer knows; obj.as(Cls.class) gives the object as another class, always a new object holding a new handle, for the caller to close, unchecked until a member of a class it isn't refuses with code 10. equals, hashCode, toString and typeName() are nanoql's, and a record's equality is that equals, with no opEquality or opInequality. A member C# declares new with the inherited member's parameters and result overrides it in Java, as in Python: through a VolatilityTermStructure, optionDateFromTenor on an InterestRateVolSurface is the surface's, where C# and C++ call the base's (the tool's tests list such members; that is the one). Errors: NanoQLException, a RuntimeException, and NanoQLArgumentException, an IllegalArgumentException, for codes 2 to 4; both are NanoQLError, with code(), param() and typeName(). Bound engines: an engine's bind(...) and bindOn(instrument, ...) return a BoundEngine for the members that take one. The experimental API: its classes in org.nanoql.experimental; a stable class's experimental members are statics of org.nanoql.experimental.Experimental, the object first, a constructor create. A member nanoql marks [Obsolete] is @Deprecated, its message in the javadoc. The library: the natives jar's. On Linux and macOS it is copied into a private temporary folder and deleted with it once loaded, which those systems allow; on Windows, which can't delete a library a process has loaded, it is copied once to the user's temporary folder under a name its bytes' SHA-256 keys (nanoql-/), and each later run loads that copy only when its whole SHA-256 is the jar's library's, writing a fresh one otherwise. The system property nanoql.library, or NanoQL.useLibrary(path) before any object is made, loads another, such as a build holding a user's assembly; once a library is loaded, useLibrary of another path throws IllegalStateException. NanoQL.libraryPath() gives the path it was loaded from. A user's assembly: a jar of its own beside nanoql's. nanoql-bind java --assembly ... --prefix acme writes its classes alone, in packages by its own namespaces (acme.curves.ExponentialCurve, a org.nanoql.termstructures.YieldTermStructure; its experimental ones in acme.curves.experimental), each calling its own jextract class, acme.ffi.acme_h over acme.h with its own functions alone (stage.py's jextract_user gives the flags), and registering its classes through its own acme.internal.AcmeTypes, which its classes' static initializers run, so its objects come back as its classes. It compiles against nanoql's jar, and nanoql.library names the library nanoql-bind build made of nanoql's assemblies and the user's. The test build's test types are built this way, compiled with the conformance suite against nanoql's main classes. Building: python bindings/java/stage.py --library --jextract (or --ffi , the layers jextract made, a folder per header) fills bindings/java/target/: jextract 22's layer over nanoql.h, the generated layer (nanoql-bind java --prefix nql), the notices (LICENSE, NOTICE, THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md, the .NET runtime's LICENSE.TXT and THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.TXT) and the library, and prints the natives jar's classifier; --test-exports adds the test types' two layers as test sources. Then mvn package -Dnanoql.classifier= in bindings/java writes the main, natives, sources and javadoc jars, each but the javadoc with the notices under META-INF. python bindings/java/jar_check.py bindings/java/target checks them. CI runs jextract once, checked against its SHA-256, over nanoql.h and the test build's nqlt.h, which nanoql-bind headers writes without a native build; the headers hold fixed-width types only, so the one layer serves every platform.

docs/concepts.html.title: Concepts | nanoql
docs/concepts.html.summary: Concepts nanoql's types and their names follow QuantLib's, which a QuantLib user will recognise: Date, Calendar, YieldTermStructure, Euribor6M, VanillaSwap, MakeOIS, BlackSwaptionEngine. What differs is how they fit together. This page covers that design; the stateless design shows the patterns an application builds on it. Values and functions Instruments, curves, indexes, volatility structures and models are immutable values, built once from their inputs. Engines are static functions: Calculate takes the instrument, the evaluation context and the engine's market inputs, and returns a results record. var euribor = new Euribor6M(curve); VanillaSwap spot = new MakeVanillaSwap(new Period(5, TimeUnit.Years), euribor) .WithFixedRate(0.025) .WithNominal(10e6) .ToVanillaSwap(context); VanillaSwap forward = new MakeVanillaSwap(new Period(5, TimeUnit.Years), euribor) .WithForwardStart(new Period(5, TimeUnit.Years)) .WithFixedRate(0.025) .WithNominal(10e6) .ToVanillaSwap(context); FixedVsFloatingSwapResults spotResult = DiscountingSwapEngine.Calculate(spot, context, curve); FixedVsFloatingSwapResults forwardResult = DiscountingSwapEngine.Calculate(forward, context, curve); Inputs are values. A rate helper takes its quote as a number, an index takes its forecasting curve, and an engine takes its discounting curve and its volatility. There are no quote or curve handles to relink: a new quote means a new curve, built from the new quotes. Results are records. The swap engine's record holds the NPV, the fair rate and spread, and each leg's NPV and basis-point value. A result QuantLib doesn't compute for an instrument is null. No hidden state. No object watches another. Apart from the working types, which their caller owns (arrays and matrices, random-number and path generators, a Monte Carlo simulation's state), no object changes once built, and the few that keep a cache key it by everything the answer reads. So the same inputs always give the same results, and calls run side by side on any number of threads. The evaluation context QuantLib reads its evaluation date and settings from a global. nanoql passes them in an EvaluationContext, to every function that reads them, directly or through a callee: Field What it holds Default EvaluationDate the date prices are as of required Fixings the indexes' stored past fixings none IncludeReferenceDateEvents, IncludeTodaysCashFlows, EnforcesTodaysHistoricFixings when an event on the reference date counts, as QuantLib's settings QuantLib's UseAtParCoupons whether Ibor coupons are priced as par coupons true, as QuantLib-Python ExchangeRates, MoneySettings the exchange rates, and how amounts in different currencies combine QuantLib's known rates; no conversion CommoditySettings, UnitOfMeasureConversions, QuantitySettings the energy instruments' base currency and units QuantLib's A context is a record: a variation is made with with, and two contexts holding the same values are equal. A past fixing is stored in the context, never in the index: var euribor = new Euribor6M(curve); Date yesterday = euribor.FixingCalendar.Advance(Curves.Today, -1, TimeUnit.Days); EvaluationContext context = Curves.Context with { Fixings = Curves.Context.Fixings.AddFixing(euribor, yesterday, 0.0212), }; Date[] fixingDates = [ yesterday, Curves.Today, euribor.FixingCalendar.Advance(Curves.Today, new Period(6, TimeUnit.Months)), ]; Conventions as data QuantLib keeps its market conventions in code: a calendar's holidays, an index's fixing days, a builder's defaults. nanoql keeps QuantLib's values and reads each preset's and each builder's conventions through a ConventionProvider when the object is built. With nothing configured, every object is QuantLib's. The NanoQL.Extensions package reads and writes conventions as XML records, so a desk overrides a value, or adds a convention of its own, as data (conventions.md; every shipped value in the catalogue). ConventionProvider.Default is the library's one global. It is read only when an object is built, never while it prices, so a price doesn't depend on when or where it runs. Where nanoql differs from QuantLib nanoql fixes QuantLib's defects where it finds them, and a few of its design choices give different results. Each departure is a documented divergence, with the test that asserts it: divergences.md lists them. Experimental code The types ported from QuantLib's experimental folder carry [Experimental("NQL0001")]: the compiler reports NQL0001 where code uses them, until a project opts in with <NoWarn>$(NoWarn);NQL0001</NoWarn>. Deriving your own types The public bases QuantLib's hierarchy derives from, abstract or unsealed, are the extension points: term structures, stochastic processes, volatility structures, calendars, day counters, cash flows, coupons, instruments and more. A type of your own derives from one, or implements one of the interfaces the library's types implement; the extension points page lists them all. Every other public class is sealed, so that no subclass can add mutable state or change equality behind its base's back. Compose instead, or add members through C# 14's extension members.

docs/conventions.html.title: Market conventions as data | nanoql
docs/conventions.html.summary: Market conventions as data QuantLib keeps its market conventions in code: a calendar's holidays, a currency's rounding, an index's fixing days, a swap builder's fixed leg by currency. nanoql keeps QuantLib's values and lets them be configured. The library reads each preset's and each market builder's conventions through a ConventionProvider when the object is built, QuantLib's values unless a provider configures them, and the NanoQL.Extensions package reads and writes them as XML records: using NanoQL; using NanoQL.Extensions.Conventions; // a desk's conventions over QuantLib's presets, the system's defaults from here on ConventionProvider.Default = ConventionSet.QuantLib.With(ConventionsXml.Read("desk-conventions.xml")); // built after it, so they take the desk's values var euribor6M = new Euribor6M(forwardingCurve); var swap = new MakeVanillaSwap(new Period(5, TimeUnit.Years), euribor6M).WithFixedRate(0.03).ToVanillaSwap(context); With nothing configured every object is QuantLib's. Every value nanoql ships is QuantLib's, generated from QuantLib and checked against it; the catalogue lists them all. The format A conventions file is a Conventions element in the namespace https://nanoql.org/schemas/conventions, holding records in any order. Each record is an element named after its kind, with a name attribute, an optional base attribute, and its fields as child elements, each named after nanoql's API: <Conventions xmlns="https://nanoql.org/schemas/conventions"> <!-- TARGET with an extra holiday, the preset itself replaced --> <Calendar name="TARGET" base="TARGET"> <AddedHoliday>2026-12-24</AddedHoliday> </Calendar> <!-- a family member: Euribor at two months, every other field the family's --> <IborIndex name="Euribor2M" base="Euribor"><Tenor>2M</Tenor></IborIndex> <!-- a swap convention of a desk's own --> <SwapConvention name="EUR-SWAP"> <SettlementDays>2</SettlementDays> <FixedLegTenor>1Y</FixedLegTenor> <FixedLegConvention>ModifiedFollowing</FixedLegConvention> <FixedLegDayCounter>Thirty360.BondBasis</FixedLegDayCounter> <Index>Euribor</Index> <IndexTenor>6M</IndexTenor> </SwapConvention> </Conventions> The schema, nanoql-conventions.xsd, documents every element; ConventionsXml.Read validates against it and refuses a bad file with its line and position. ConventionsXml.WriteDefaults(folder) writes the shipped files and the schema, for an editor or a diff. Other tools' content, elements and attributes in their own namespaces, is kept through a read and a write. Several files read as one snapshot: ConventionsXml.Read(paths). A set layers snapshots one on another with With, a later layer's record replacing an earlier one's of the same name. Names, bases and aliases A coded preset keeps its class's name: a calendar by its type and market (TARGET, UnitedStates.SOFR), a day counter by its type and convention (Actual360, Thirty360.BondBasis), a currency by its ISO code, an index, a region or a unit of measure by its class (Euribor6M, EURegion, BarrelUnitOfMeasure). A record under that name configures the preset, and a preset is built as its own class with the configured values. A builder's defaults are records named after it: MakeVanillaSwap.EUR, MakeVanillaSwap.GBP and the other currencies', MakeOIS and MakeOIS.Sonia by the index's class, MakeCreditDefaultSwap, MakeCapFloor, MakeSwaption, MakeCms, MakeMultipleResetsSwap, MakeYoYInflationCapFloor and FixedRateBond. Each holds only the options its builder fixes, read when the builder builds and needs one. GBP's and AUD's fixed leg tenors depend on the swap's tenor, so their records carry a threshold, compared as QuantLib compares it. Each kind has its own names: the calendars share one name space, the day counters another, the indexes another, and each instrument convention kind its own. So USD-SOFR can be both an alias of the Sofr index and an OIS convention. A base names a record of the same kind, and the record gives only the fields it changes: every other field comes from the base, down its chain, then from QuantLib's reference. A record based on its own name replaces the record of that name in the layers below. A convention takes its builder's defaults without naming them as its base. An alias names a calendar, day counter, currency, region, index or unit of measure by another name: <Alias name="bbl" base="BarrelUnitOfMeasure" />. FpML's codes nanoql ships FpML's codes from four of its lists as aliases of nanoql's names: the day-count-fraction, business-center and floating-rate-index coding schemes and the BusinessDayConventionEnum. So ACT/360 names Actual360, USGS names UnitedStates.GovernmentBond and USD-SOFR names Sofr. Only a code that maps to a nanoql name exactly is an alias: a business centre naming a city's banking days, GBLO, USNY or JPTO, is no QuantLib calendar exactly, so it ships no alias, and a desk adds its own where it treats one as a calendar it uses. The codes are FpML's, under the FpML® Public License, Version 3.0, whose text is in LICENSES/LicenseRef-FpML-Public-License-3.0.txt. The mapping of each code to a nanoql name is nanoql's own work, not part of the FpML Specifications, under the Apache License, Version 2.0. The licence's Exhibit A notice: The FpML Specifications of this document are subject to the FpML Public License (the “License”); you may not use the FpML Specifications except in compliance with the License. You may obtain a copy of the License at https://www.FpML.org. The FpML Specifications distributed under the License are distributed on an “AS IS” basis, WITHOUT WARRANTY OF ANY KIND, either express or implied. See the License for the specific language governing rights and limitations under the License. The Licensor of the FpML Specifications is the International Swaps and Derivatives Association, Inc. All Rights Reserved. The kinds Time: calendar presets and calendars based on one, with holidays added and removed; joint calendars; bespoke calendars; day counter presets, Business252 on a calendar; currencies. Indexes: regions; Ibor indexes and families, overnight indexes, swap index families, overnight-indexed swap indexes, zero and year-on-year inflation indexes. A preset that takes constructor arguments (AUCPI, GenericCPI, the daily-tenor Libors) takes them from a record based on it. Instrument conventions: schedule, swap, OIS, CDS, zero-coupon and year-on-year inflation swap, cross-currency basis and fixed-against-floating swap, FX swap and forward, cap and floor, swaption, CMS, multiple-resets swap, year-on-year inflation cap and floor, and bond. Each resolves in a set to the builders and rate helpers it feeds: set.Swap("EUR-SWAP").Builder(tenor, curve), set.Ois("USD-SOFR").RateHelper(rate, tenor, context). Commodities (experimental, as the types they configure): commodity types, units of measure, conversion factors, payment terms, commodity indexes, and the commodity and quantity settings. A set's conversions, set.UnitOfMeasureConversions(), are QuantLib's known factors with the set's records added as QuantLib adds one, a record between a known factor's units replacing it; two known factors ship the right way round (the divergences, the known unit factors). The settings' records named CommoditySettings and QuantitySettings are QuantLib's defaults; EvaluationContext keeps its own, QuantLib's. Trade and market data are no conventions: a trade's dates, rates and nominal are a builder's arguments, and curves, quotes, fixings, forward curves and exchange contracts are market objects, which no record holds. The provider and the set ConventionProvider has QuantLib, QuantLib's values; Default, the system's provider, QuantLib until set and restored by setting null; Current, the innermost scope's provider or else Default; and Use(provider), which opens a scope and returns the IDisposable that closes it. A scope flows with asynchronous calls, as a culture does. A provider of a user's own, a database's or a service's, derives from it and overrides the members it configures, each taking the preset's name and QuantLib's reference. ConventionSet is the provider the XML records answer: ConventionSet.QuantLib holds the shipped records, ConventionSet.Empty none, and With(snapshot) layers a file on a set, resolving every record, so a misspelt name, a cycle or a value the library refuses fails when the file loads. A set is immutable. Its lookups build an object in the set's scope: set.Calendar("TARGET"), set.IborIndex("Euribor6M", curve), set.UnitOfMeasure("BarrelUnitOfMeasure"). Empty is strict: an index, region, unit of measure or builder default it doesn't define is refused, so a file read onto it must define them. Calendars, day counters and currencies are code, and resolve to QuantLib's presets there too. set.Provenance() reports where each name comes from, QuantLib's records or a file's, and warns of a record that overrides no name and that nothing references, a likely misspelling (Euribor6m). ConventionRecords.Describe(name, value) turns a built object back into the records that rebuild it in a set. A field is never ignored: a route that can't take a field the record gives, such as a rate helper whose legs share one calendar given two, refuses the record, naming the route, the kind, the record and the field. What follows which provider A provider is read only when an object is built, never while it prices, so a price doesn't depend on the scope it runs in. A preset (a calendar, a currency, an index, a unit of measure) reads Current once, in its constructor, and its nested presets (an index's calendar, a currency's triangulation currency) are built in the same provider's scope. An index keeps the provider it was built with, and every clone of it keeps the same one. A market builder takes the provider of its index, reads its defaults from it when it builds, and builds in it. The CDS builder, with no index, takes the provider current when it is created. The outer object's provider wins for a builder built inside it: a swap index's underlying swap takes the swap index's provider, so a swap index built under one set on an Ibor index built under another takes the swap index's set's swap defaults and the Ibor index's set's conventions for its floating leg. Whatever is built on an index later follows the index: a swap index's underlying swap, a rate helper's swap when a bootstrap re-dates it, an engine's auxiliary swaps. An object with no index that builds after its construction keeps the provider current at its construction. QuantLib's registry defaults, ExchangeRates.Default, UnitOfMeasureConversions.Default and EvaluationContext's defaults, are QuantLib's, whatever is current when they are first read. Set Default before building indexes So setting Default reaches the objects built after it, and everything built on them. Objects built before keep their conventions, and a builder on an earlier index takes that index's set, so no object mixes two sets. Set Default once at startup, before building indexes; after a reload, rebuild the indexes to take it, as curves are rebuilt. An example: a SOFR curve tests/NanoQL.Tests/Extensions/SofrCurveExample.cs builds a SOFR curve through an illustrative OIS convention, in a file of its own, SofrCurveExample.xml: <OisConvention name="USD-SOFR"> <Index>Sofr</Index> <SettlementDays>2</SettlementDays> <PaymentLag>2</PaymentLag> <PaymentFrequency>Annual</PaymentFrequency> <PaymentCalendar>USGS</PaymentCalendar> <FixedLegDayCounter>ACT/360</FixedLegDayCounter> </OisConvention> Swaps settling two days after the trade, paid annually two business days after each period ends on the US government bond calendar, the fixed leg on Actual/360; USGS and ACT/360 are FpML's codes. The example reads the file over QuantLib's presets, makes a rate helper per quote through the convention, and bootstraps the curve: ConventionSet set = ConventionSet.QuantLib.With(ConventionsXml.Read("SofrCurveExample.xml")); var context = new EvaluationContext { EvaluationDate = new Date(15, Month.October, 2026) }; OisConvention sofr = set.Ois("USD-SOFR"); OISRateHelper[] helpers = [.. Quotes.Select(q => sofr.RateHelper(q.Rate, q.Tenor, context))]; var curve = new PiecewiseLogLinearDiscount(context.EvaluationDate, helpers, new Actual365Fixed(), context); The quotes are illustrative SOFR swap rates from one month to ten years, 4.30% to 3.70%; the curve's list of instruments is code. Every helper reprices to its quote within 1e-12. A 5-year SOFR swap paying 3.60% fixed on 10 million is then priced on the curve twice, on the example's conventions and on MakeOIS's defaults: OvernightIndexedSwap onExample = sofr.Builder(new Period(5, TimeUnit.Years), curve) .WithFixedRate(0.036).WithNominal(10e6).ToOvernightIndexedSwap(context); OvernightIndexedSwap onDefaults = new MakeOIS(new Period(5, TimeUnit.Years), set.OvernightIndex("Sofr", curve)) .WithFixedRate(0.036).WithNominal(10e6).ToOvernightIndexedSwap(context); Conventions Payment lag NPV The example's 2 days 0.0000, the 5-year quote's swap, at par MakeOIS's defaults none −3.1103 Difference 3.1103 The two swaps differ only in their payment dates, so on a curve bootstrapped with the lag a swap without it is worth 3.11 less on 10 million.

docs/cpp.html.title: C++ | nanoql
docs/cpp.html.summary: C++ nanoql's C++ layer, nanoql.hpp, is C++17 over the C interface: objects that release their handles, refusals thrown as exceptions, nanoql's type names and QuantLib's member names (curve.discount(5.0)). It ships in each platform's C archive, for Windows x64 and Linux x64, with a CMake package. The bindings guide's "C and C++" section gives its rules: names, objects, values, defaults and overloads, errors. Coming from QuantLib's C++, the migration guide pairs its code with nanoql's. Install Unpack the archive for your platform from the release, nanoql-<version>-win-x64-c-api.zip or nanoql-<version>-linux-x64-c-api.tar.xz. It holds: include/: nanoql.h, the C interface, and nanoql.hpp, the C++ layer over it; lib/: the library, nanoql.dll with its import library nanoql.lib on Windows or libnanoql.so on Linux, and cmake/nanoql/, the CMake package; the notices: LICENSE, NOTICE, THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md and the .NET runtime's two, which the library carries. CMake Give CMake the archive's folder and link nanoql::cpp: cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.21) project(app CXX) find_package(nanoql 2.1 CONFIG REQUIRED) add_executable(app main.cpp) target_link_libraries(app PRIVATE nanoql::cpp) cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=<the archive's folder> cmake --build build --config Release nanoql::cpp brings C++17 and nanoql::c, the library and include/; a C program links nanoql::c alone. A request for a version takes this release or an earlier one of its major version, as CMake's SameMajorVersion rule has it, version ranges included. Windows: a program finds nanoql.dll beside it. A copy after the build puts it there: add_custom_command(TARGET app POST_BUILD COMMAND ${CMAKE_COMMAND} -E copy_if_different $<TARGET_RUNTIME_DLLS:app> $<TARGET_FILE_DIR:app> COMMAND_EXPAND_LISTS) Linux: a program run in its build tree finds libnanoql.so by the run path CMake gives it; one installed or copied elsewhere finds it by LD_LIBRARY_PATH or its own run path ($ORIGIN). bindings/cpp/consumer/ in the repository is this project, with the program below; CI builds it through each platform's archive with MSVC on Windows, and g++ and clang on Linux. A first program #include <cstdio> #include <exception> #include "nanoql.hpp" using namespace nanoql; int main() { FlatForward curve(Date(15, Month::March, 2023), 0.03, ConventionSet::quantLib().dayCounter("Actual365Fixed")); std::printf("discount(1) = %.6f\n", curve.discount(1.0)); // 0.970446 try { curve.discount(-1.0); } catch (const std::exception& e) { std::printf("refused: %s\n", e.what()); // refused: negative time (-1) given } } Each object holds a handle to its nanoql object and releases it when it goes out of scope; liveHandles() counts the handles still held. A refusal is nanoql::error, a std::runtime_error with the C interface's code, the parameter it names and its type, and under it argument_error and handle_error. Compile time nanoql.hpp declares the whole library, about 98,600 lines. A translation unit that includes it takes about 5 s and 600 MB with g++ at -O2, so include it in few files, or precompile it: target_precompile_headers(app PRIVATE <nanoql.hpp>) Versions A release's header works with that release's library. A program that loads a library installed apart from its header checks nql_abi_version() == NQL_ABI_VERSION first. A minor release adds to the stable API and removes only what was deprecated two releases and a year before, which the header marks [[deprecated]] meanwhile; the guide's Versions gives the rule. A new overload can make a call that compiled ambiguous, as in any C++ library; naming the argument's type settles it. The experimental API Define NANOQL_EXPERIMENTAL before including the header, or with target_compile_definitions(app PRIVATE NANOQL_EXPERIMENTAL), to declare the experimental API beside the stable one. It may change in any release. A library of your own nanoql-bind builds a library holding nanoql's functions and an assembly of yours, and writes its headers beside nanoql's: acme.h and acme.hpp, whose classes extend nanoql's (acme::ExponentialCurve is a nanoql::YieldTermStructure). Its README gives the commands. Without the C++ layer C++ can include nanoql.h as it is, its declarations in extern "C", and call the C interface directly: the guide's "The C ABI" gives its handles, status codes and values.

docs/credit/cds.html.title: Credit default swaps | nanoql
docs/credit/cds.html.summary: Credit default swaps This page follows QuantLib's CDS example, its first two cases: a hazard curve bootstrapped from quoted spreads, then ISDA's standard model. Its values match that example's output. The sample, CreditDefaultSwaps.cs, carries QuantLib's notice. A hazard curve from spreads Four CDS quoted at 150 bp, from three months to two years, with a recovery of 50% and a flat 1% discount curve. A SpreadCdsHelper per quote, and a piecewise curve of flat hazard rates bootstrapped through them: Calendar calendar = new TARGET(); Date today = calendar.Adjust(new Date(15, Month.May, 2007)); var context = new EvaluationContext { EvaluationDate = today }; var discount = new FlatForward(today, 0.01, new Actual365Fixed()); int settlementDays = 1; double recoveryRate = 0.5; (Period Tenor, double Spread)[] quotes = [ (new Period(3, TimeUnit.Months), 0.0150), (new Period(6, TimeUnit.Months), 0.0150), (new Period(1, TimeUnit.Years), 0.0150), (new Period(2, TimeUnit.Years), 0.0150), ]; var helpers = new List<BootstrapHelper<DefaultProbabilityTermStructure>>(); foreach (var (tenor, spread) in quotes) { helpers.Add(new SpreadCdsHelper(spread, tenor, settlementDays, calendar, Frequency.Quarterly, BusinessDayConvention.Following, DateGenerationRule.TwentiethIMM, new Actual365Fixed(), recoveryRate, discount, context)); } var curve = new PiecewiseDefaultCurve<HazardRate, BackwardFlat, IterativeBootstrap>( today, helpers, new Actual365Fixed(), context); The curve's nodes and its survival probabilities: Node Hazard rate 2007-05-15 0.0299685 2007-09-20 0.0299685 2007-12-20 0.0299613 2008-06-20 0.0299619 2009-06-22 0.0299607 Horizon Survival probability 1Y 97.040077% 2Y 94.175796% Each quoted CDS, priced on the curve by the mid-point engine: Calendar calendar = new TARGET(); docs/divergences.html.summary: Divergences Every documented divergence from QuantLib v1.44, one entry per test class under tests/NanoQL.Tests/Divergences/ with its file, its summary and its facts, generated from those files by tools/divergences.py: regenerate it with .venv\Scripts\python -I tools/divergences.py rather than editing it by hand. AbcdCalibrationFixedATests Divergences/AbcdCalibrationFixedATests.cs The abcd calibration's fixed a: QuantLib's transformation gives a as a positive a + d less d (abcdcalibration.cpp's AbcdParametersTransformation), so with a fixed and d free it fixes a + d, and the fit moves a. On set 1 with a fixed at −0.06, QuantLib returns a = −0.11449872096226477 and d = 0.22449872096226478, a + d held at 0.11 [the harness]. nanoql keeps a at −0.06, d above max(0, −a); the fit is valid, at a minimum of the cost over b, c and d (each gradient within the end criteria's tolerance), and a restart from a second guess reaches it too. Facts: AFixedAKeepsItsGuess AbcdCalibrationGuardTests Divergences/AbcdCalibrationGuardTests.cs The abcd calibration's guard: QuantLib's transformation leaves b free, so its optimizer can step to a trial point the abcd function's validation refuses, and the fit throws. On set 6, a dip whose total variance grows, QuantLib refuses with "b (-0.374029) less than -0.267779: negative function value at stationary point 2.45429" [the harness]; nanoql's guard fits it validly, at a minimum (each parameter's gradient within the end criteria's tolerance) that a restart from a second guess reaches too. And on the sets QuantLib completes, 0, 1, 4 and 5, the guard never acts: their fits are QuantLib's bit for bit, set 1's among them although its gradient is above the tolerance. Facts: ADipQuantLibRefusesIsFittedAtAMinimum TheFitsQuantLibCompletesKeepItsBits AbcdMaximumTests Divergences/AbcdMaximumTests.cs The abcd function's maximum. Its location is QuantLib's master's (#2841, after the pin): QuantLib 1.44 returns the stationary point 1/c − a/b whatever b's sign, a minimum when b < 0. Its value is the function at that location: QuantLib returns d whenever b = 0 or a ≤ 0. QuantLib's values are the wheel's; the check is QuantLib's own operator(). Facts: ANegativeBsStationaryPointIsAMinimum TheMaximumValueIsTheFunctionAtItsLocation AbcdPrimitiveTests Divergences/AbcdPrimitiveTests.cs The abcd function's primitive at a small c: QuantLib's closed form divides by powers of c and cancels, so the covariance of a = 0.1, b = 0.2, d = 0.15 over the first year for fixings at 2 and 3 years reads, on the wheel, 0.41570091639483625 at c = 1e-4, 0.4112554826093383 at 1e-5, 0.26249003480977007 at 1e-6 and −2220.182821037571 at 1e-7, where its Gauss-Lobatto integral is 0.4157007, 0.4158201, 0.4158320 and 0.41583320. nanoql switches to a cancellation-free series where QuantLib's form cancels; the check is the integral of the covariance's integrand, AbcdSquared, by Gauss-Lobatto, the integrals cases' route, and QuantLib's bits where it doesn't cancel. Facts: ASmallCsCovarianceIsItsIntegral AbcdTermStructures Divergences/AbcdTermStructures.cs The term structures of Black volatilities the abcd facts fit, sets 0 to 6 over 0.5 to 20 years (tools/vectors/gen/cxx/termstructures/volatility/abcdcalibration.py's): falling (0), rising (1), two whose total variance shrinks (2, 3), two dips whose total variance grows (4, 5), and a dip QuantLib refuses (6); and the cost's gradient a fit is checked by. AdaptiveRungeKuttaSizeTests Divergences/AdaptiveRungeKuttaSizeTests.cs An ordinary differential equation whose function returns a vector of another length than its argument's. QuantLib's AdaptiveRungeKutta reads the function's value at every index of the solution vector (adaptiverungekutta.hpp:111-113, 219-247), past the end of a shorter one, and ignores the extra values of a longer one; the wheel's RungeKutta refuses both with its own wrapper's check, "Python function did not return a list of correct size" (ode.i:79-81), which QuantLib doesn't make. nanoql refuses both with NanoQLException, "the ODE function returned n values for m". Facts: AFunctionOfAnotherLengthIsRefused AffineDiscountBondFactorsTests Divergences/AffineDiscountBondFactorsTests.cs An affine model's discount bond given an empty vector of factors. QuantLib's OneFactorAffineModel::discountBond(now, maturity, Array factors) reads factors[0] (onefactormodel.hpp:132-134), past the end of an empty array, which crashes the wheel with an access violation. nanoql refuses it with ArgumentException, "no factors given", naming factors; given a factor, it prices as QuantLib's, on the vector's first element. Facts: AnEmptyFactorVectorIsRefused AffineHazardRateTests Divergences/AffineHazardRateTests.cs The affine hazard-rate curve's initial intensity: the model's dynamics' short rate at the process's x0, where QuantLib squares x0. On nodes today and one, three and five years out (Actual/365 Fixed), with the Cox-Ingersoll-Ross model r0 0.02, θ 0.03, k 0.5, σ 0.05, QuantLib's curve of zero hazard rates reads S(5) 0.90893263808262059, P(0, 5, r0²), where its own base structure on the same model reads 0.87690828065332527, P(0, 5, r0); on hazard rates 0.01 to 0.04 its S(5) is 0.79418153056948726, and its conditional survival from one to three years at an intensity of 0.025 is 0.90156675873632208, which reads no x0. On Vasicek r0 0.02, a 0.1, b 0.03, σ 0.01, whose x0 is r0 − b, its curve reads 0.96957583433..., its base 0.89655379153.... Facts: TheCurveOfZeroHazardRatesIsTheBaseStructure TheCurvesSurvivalIsQuantLibsOnTheModelsOwnIntensity AlphaFinderTests Divergences/AlphaFinderTests.cs AlphaFinder's fixes, QuantLib's master's finder after the pin (#2910, dbe958954), and its b where a final part fails. QuantLib's master fixes (a) and (b) on the same quantities, returns from its bisection at an exact root and where its point stops moving, and returns the final part's success; its cases are below. alphafinder.cpp:335-346, :405-415: where the turning point's value at α₀ is at most the target, QuantLib 1.44 returns α₀ without checking finalPart's result, which fails where the variance left is negative, and its search returns its α unchecked too. nanoql returns false there, as QuantLib's master does, its α QuantLib's and its b NaN; the alpha calibration refuses the step, as the master's does (Divergences/CTSMMCapletAlphaFormCalibrationTests.cs). (a) :372-373: the downward search's loop tests topValue, which it never changes; on the hyperbolic inputs QuantLib's solve returns false where the acceptable α lie strictly below α₀, and nanoql's loop, testing bottomValue, finds α −0.3111 at the target; on a second set of inputs, QuantLib's returns false and nanoql's α 0.41286, whose final part fails. (b) :117, :145: Minimize calls the feasibility test on the objective's value, not on the trial α, so where that value isn't an acceptable α it stops at its first trial: on the hyperbolic inputs QuantLib returns α −0.48497 with homogeneity failure 3.3880, where the acceptable α run from −0.7519 to −0.3112 and the least failure is 3.3628 at −0.7519 (nanoql with QuantLib's test restored reproduces QuantLib's alpha-form calibration at maximum homogeneity bit for bit); on a third set of inputs, QuantLib's α 0.5168373510089983 fails by 0.12497903935064759 and nanoql's 0.4467697074628475 by 0.12229674463151122, and where the small α QuantLib's test reads are acceptable both return 1.2307430953608208e-08. (c) :30-111: the bisections and Minimize loop on the bracket's width alone, so at tolerance 0 QuantLib's search never ends (killed after 20 s); nanoql's also stops when the bracket no longer moves. (d) Where a final part fails QuantLib leaves b at its caller's value; nanoql's is NaN. The master's minimization tests the trial α before it reads the objective there, as nanoql's does; the alpha calibration's fallback keeps 1.44's order, the objective's value read first and tested. Checks: QuantLib's arithmetic restated at an α (the turning point's value, the final part, the homogeneity failure), and the alpha-form calibration's QuantLib case at tolerance 0 against 1e-15. Facts: AHalfSolvedInitialAlphaIsRefused TheDownwardSearchOnRoundOnesInput MaximumHomogeneityOnRoundOnesInputs TheDownwardSearchFindsTheAcceptableAlphaBelowAlphaZero MaximumHomogeneityFindsTheAcceptableMinimum ToleranceZeroEnds TestAlphaFinderExactBisectionRoot TestAlphaFinderBisectionStagnation TestAlphaFinderMaximumHomogeneity TestAlphaFinderDownwardInteriorSearch TestAlphaFinderInteriorSearch TestAlphaFinderRejectsNegativeRemainingVariance TestAlphaFinderNoRealSolution TestMaximumHomogeneityCalibration AmericanBasketStrikeScalingTests Divergences/AmericanBasketStrikeScalingTests.cs The Longstaff-Schwartz basket engine's state scaled by the strike. QuantLib scales the assets' prices by 1/K (mcamericanbasketengine.cpp:48-50, :67-73): at a zero strike, an exchange of the basket for nothing, the scale is infinite and the price NaN, and at a negative strike the scale's sign swaps the minimum and the maximum (an American maximum call 101.16 on the test's market where the European is 116.67). nanoql scales by 1/|K|, and by 1 at a zero strike; a positive scale leaves the regression's polynomial span unchanged: QuantLib's N-dimensional finite-difference engine at K ≤ 0, and QuantLib's bits at K > 0, are the checks. Facts: AZeroStrikeMeetsTheFiniteDifferenceEngine ANegativeStrikeKeepsTheMaximumAndMeetsTheFiniteDifferenceEngine APositiveStrikeKeepsQuantLibsBits AmericanBoundsOnTimeTests Divergences/AmericanBoundsOnTimeTests.cs The American window's bounds on the tree (upstream's fix after v1.44, #2878: 51c6263b7, merged as eaeac5651): TimeGrid(T, N) builds its last time as (T/N)·N, an ulp off T, the discretized assets snap their exercise times to the grid but start at the unsnapped maturity, and QuantLib 1.44's American branch compares the two with plain <= and >=; so where the last time rounds below T the exercise is never applied at expiry, and where it rounds above, a window ending at maturity is rejected. Upstream compares both bounds with isOnTime, as the European branch does, in DiscretizedVanillaOption and DiscretizedConvertible. On the wheel, at the upstream cases' market (21 September 2026, 91 days to expiry on Actual/365 (Fixed), spot 100, r = 5%, q = 0, σ = 15%), where the last time rounds below T at 51 steps and above it at 101: the CRR call struck at 85 at 51 steps, American 16.05280871761558 against European 16.074532566935556; exercisable only at maturity at 101 steps, American 0.0 against European 16.075288548193498; and the zero-coupon convertible (conversion ratio 2, redemption 100, no credit spread) at 51 steps, American at maturity 98.76131265936051 against European 200.00004055297964. nanoql takes upstream's fix; its cases are upstream's (europeanoption.cpp's testBinomialAmericanExerciseAtMaturity and testBinomialAmericanExerciseOnlyAtMaturity, convertiblebonds.cpp's testBinomialConversionAtMaturity), until the pin moves to a release that carries the fix. Facts: TheAmericanExerciseAtMaturityIsApplied AnExerciseOnlyAtMaturityIsTheEuropean TheConvertibleConvertsAtMaturity AmericanExerciseAtTheRootTests Divergences/AmericanExerciseAtTheRootTests.cs American options worth exercising on the reference date, after QuantLib's master's #2879 and #2914, which upstream's cases check (AmericanOptionTests). QuantLib 1.44's binomial engine reports the Black-Scholes theta from the tree's value and Greeks where the option is exercised at the root, where the intrinsic value is time-independent and the equation doesn't hold: 5.7500000000149 for a put at 115 on 100 and 9.149999999935266 for a call at 85, 91 days, on 201 Cox-Ross-Rubinstein steps; and its finite-difference engine's interpolant undershoots the exercise value between nodes, 9.999997372915146 for a call at 100 on 110 over 90 days (q 2%, σ 10%) on its default grid, below its intrinsic 10, which its implied volatility then can't reach ("root not bracketed: f[0.0001,4] -> [2.627085e-06,6.603111e+01]") (QuantLib-Python 1.44). nanoql's binomial theta is 0 at the root; its finite-difference value is floored at the exercise value where the holder can exercise on the clock's reference date, and the implied volatility returns its lower bound where the price error there is within rounding; elsewhere QuantLib's bits. Facts: TheBinomialThetaAtTheRootIsZero TheFiniteDifferenceValueIsTheExerciseValueAndItsVolatilityTheLowerBound AmericanPayoffAtExpiryKnockedOutTests Divergences/AmericanPayoffAtExpiryKnockedOutTests.cs The knock-out at expiry with the strike on the spot, under QuantLib's master's low-volatility fix (#2855, taken as a fix). With the strike on the spot, the knock-out is already knocked out, and QuantLib sets both probabilities to 0 (americanpayoffatexpiry.cpp:126-160); #2855 then reads N(D₂) = 0 as an underflow and replaces it by e^(2μ ln(H/S))·N(D₂) = N(D₂) with a power of 1, so the knock-out prices −D·K·N(D₂): a call paying 10, S = H = 100, r 5%, vol 20%, one year, −4.19, where QuantLib 1.44 prices 0 (QuantLib-Python 1.44, and by hand: D₂ = −μσ = −0.15). nanoql takes #2855's form only where N(D₂) is the formula's. QuantLib's check: its own 1.44 value, 0, a knocked-out option's. Facts: AKnockOutWithTheStrikeOnTheSpotIsWorthNothing AmericanPayoffAtHitNegativeRateTests Divergences/AmericanPayoffAtHitNegativeRateTests.cs The American payoff at the hit under negative rates. QuantLib's closed form takes λ = √(μ² − 2 ln D / σ²T) (americanpayoffathit.cpp:75, :90), the square root of a negative number where r < 0 and μ² < −2r/σ², so the value is NaN: at r −1%, q −1.5% and 20%, and at r −0.75%, q −0.4% and 8%, a down-and-in put at 90 and an up-and-in call at 110 paying 5 (QuantLib-Python 1.44). nanoql's value there is the payoff's present value at the hit integrated over the first-passage density, which is QuantLib's closed form where λ is real; its Greeks are that integral's derivatives. QuantLib's checks: its closed form, the same quantity where it works (the integral here computed by the test); and its finite-difference barrier engine (400 × 800) where it doesn't: the cash at the hit is a knock-out's rebate on a payoff that pays nothing, within that engine's grid error. Near the spot, where the Greeks' integrals grow as 1/b and 1/b², the value and Greeks are checked against the integrals computed to 40 digits, independently of the quadrature. Facts: WhereLambdaIsRealTheFirstPassageIntegralIsQuantLibsClosedForm WhereLambdaIsNotRealTheValueIsQuantLibsFiniteDifferenceRebate NearTheSpotTheValueAndGreeksAreTheFirstPassageIntegralsToTheirPrecision AmericanPayoffZeroVarianceTests Divergences/AmericanPayoffZeroVarianceTests.cs The American digital payoffs below a variance of ε. QuantLib divides by the variance there: the at-hit value is NaN out of the money (americanpayoffathit.cpp:87-102), and the at-expiry one takes the spot's side of the strike where the limit takes the forward's (americanpayoffatexpiry.cpp:112-121). On a cash of 10, S 100, q 0, r 5% and one year, QuantLib gives at σ = 0: at the hit at 102, NaN; at expiry at 102, 0; the knock-out at expiry at 102 (or 103), 9.512294245007139; and its own formula at σ = 1e-6 gives 9.80392156862745, 9.512294245007139 and 0 (QuantLib-Python 1.44). nanoql's underlying follows its forward: paid at the hit when the forward path reaches the strike, at expiry if it did (knock-in) or didn't (knock-out). QuantLib's check: its own formula at σ = 1e-6, which nanoql's engine there computes. Facts: AtTheHitTheForwardPathIsPaidWhenItReachesTheStrike AtExpiryTheForwardsSideOfTheStrikeCounts TheKnockOutIsPaidWhereTheForwardNeverReachesTheStrike TheGreeksAtTheHitAreTheLimitsDerivatives AnalyticDigitalAmericanMismatchedTimesTests Divergences/AnalyticDigitalAmericanMismatchedTimesTests.cs The analytic digital American engine on structures dated differently. QuantLib's engine reads the dividend curve and the volatility at the exercise date through their own clocks (analyticdigitalamericanengine.cpp:53-58), so an expiry before a structure's reference date throws. nanoql reads each structure by date, nothing accrued before its own reference date. QuantLib's check: its engine on the market restated from the earliest date, every structure accruing from today exactly what the original accrues from its own date (QuantLib-Python 1.44). Facts: LaterDatedStructuresAreReadFromTheirOwnDates AnExpiryBeforeTheStructuresDatesAccruesNothingFromThem AnalyticEuropeanVolatilityResultTests Divergences/AnalyticEuropeanVolatilityResultTests.cs AnalyticEuropeanEngine's "volatility" additional result for an option expiring on the evaluation date, priced when the reference date's events are included. QuantLib reports √(variance / time to expiry) (analyticeuropeanengine.cpp:113), 0/0 there, NaN. nanoql reports the Black volatility at the exercise date and strike, QuantLib's own value for that date; every other result is QuantLib's. Facts: TheVolatilityAtExpiryIsTheStructures AnalyticGjrGarchDividendTests Divergences/AnalyticGjrGarchDividendTests.cs The analytic GJR-GARCH engine with a dividend yield. QuantLib's engine prices on the rate r − q and discounts the call's payoff at r − q too (analyticgjrgarchengine.cpp), so its price at (r, q) is its price at (r − q, 0): a 180-day call at the money on the gjrgarchmodel test's model, r 5% and q 3%, is 3.49762, where the forward's measure gives D_q times that, 3.44608. nanoql's call is D_q times QuantLib's engine at (r − q, 0), and its put follows by parity, C − P = D_q·S − D_r·K. QuantLib's check: its engine at q = 0, where nanoql's is QuantLib's bit for bit (the engine's vectors), and parity. Facts: ThePriceIsTheDividendDiscountTimesTheZeroYieldPrice PutAndCallKeepParity AnalyticGjrGarchMomentTests Divergences/AnalyticGjrGarchMomentTests.cs AnalyticGJRGARCHEngine's moments. Where two of the variance's growth factors m₁, m₂ and m₃, or one of them and 1, are equal, QuantLib's divided differences of their powers are 0/0 and its price NaN: at α = β = γ = 0, all three 0, and in the integrated GARCH β 0.9, α 0.1, γ 0, λ 0, where m₁ is 1. nanoql takes each divided difference at its limit, a polynomial in the factors, continuous with QuantLib's prices with the factors 1e-8 and 1e-10 apart (QuantLib-SWIG 1.44); elsewhere QuantLib's arithmetic. Two of QuantLib's defects are kept, documented on the engine: its fourth moment, whose kurtosis at the deterministic limit (α = γ = 0) is about 3 − Σh where the log return is normal, so a call prices above Black-Scholes at the same total variance; and its Edgeworth price, which leaves the no-arbitrage bounds where the skewness and kurtosis are large, as on QuantLib's own model at λ 0.2 and a year. Both are QuantLib's prices, here bit for bit or within the engine's last bits (the C runtime's pow apart). QuantLib's engine reads the payoff as a StrikedTypePayoff and prices the plain vanilla on its strike and type (analyticgjrgarchengine.cpp), so a cash-or-nothing or an asset-or-nothing option is priced as the call it isn't. nanoql refuses them, as QuantLib's Monte Carlo GJR-GARCH engine does ("non-plain payoff given"). Facts: ANonPlainPayoffIsRefused AnalyticH1HWBandTests Divergences/AnalyticH1HWBandTests.cs H1HW where its fit has no decaying exponential. The engine fits E[√v_t] ≈ a + b·e^(−ct), b = √v₀ − a, c = −log((Λ(1) − a)/b) (analytich1hwengine.cpp:103-134): where the ratio isn't positive c is NaN and so is the price, at ρ_Sr = 0 too, where H1HW is the analytic Heston-Hull-White engine; where it exceeds 1, c < 0 and the fit grows exponentially, on QuantLib's own ten-year parameters at v₀/θ 0.15 a call 1.70 below its FD Heston-Hull-White engine (QuantLib 1.44). nanoql takes the fit's limits there: at or below 0, and where b = 0, c = +∞, the b terms dropped; at or above 1, c = 0; QuantLib's fit and bits in between. Facts: AtNoEquityRateCorrelationH1HWIsTheAnalyticHestonHullWhiteEngine ThePriceIsContinuousAcrossTheBandsEdges OnQuantLibsTenYearParametersH1HWHoldsTheFiniteDifferenceEngine AnalyticH1HWSmallReversionTests Divergences/AnalyticH1HWSmallReversionTests.cs H1HW's I₄ at small reversion and at c = λ. QuantLib's I₄ = −1/λ (b/c (1 − e^(−cT)) + aT + a/λ (e^(−λT) − 1) + b/(c − λ) e^(−cT)(1 − e^(−T(λ − c)))) (analytich1hwengine.cpp:126-130) cancels as λT falls to order λ, its relative error about 2ε/(λT)², 1e-12 at λT 1e-2, and its last term is 0/0 at c = λ, a NaN price. nanoql evaluates the expression in double-double below λT = 2e-2, in quad-double below 1e-10 and by the cubic below 1e-12, QuantLib's double above, and writes the last term b·e^(−cT)·(−expm1((c − λ)T))/(c − λ), exact everywhere, −b·T·e^(−cT) at c = λ. Checked against the expression in 50 digits at a 0.2, b 0.03, c 0.4 and T 10. QuantLib's m = σ²/(2a²)(t + 2/a e^(−at) − 1/(2a) e^(−2at) − 3/(2a)) (analytichestonhullwhiteengine.cpp:57-67) cancels to order (a·t)³, its relative error about ε/(a·t)³; nanoql takes the Black-Scholes-Merton Hull-White engine's series below a·t = 1e-2, QuantLib's closed form and bits above.
