Facts: TheFairRateZeroesTheSwap ZeroCouponSwapFairPaymentDelayTests Divergences/ZeroCouponSwapFairPaymentDelayTests.cs The zero-coupon swap's fair payment with a payment delay: QuantLib's fairFixedPayment divides the floating leg's NPV by its fixed leg's end discount (zerocouponswap.cpp:147-153), read at CashFlows::maturityDate of that leg (discountingswapengine.cpp:97-99), the accrual end for the fixed-rate constructor's coupon, paid a payment delay later (cashflows.cpp:52-64), so that swap's fair rate fed back leaves a non-zero NPV: on the wheel, on the vectors' 5-year receiver on 1e8 from 17 January 2025 at 3.2% on Actual/365 (Fixed), −1,013.7182254604995, −14,173.113207207993, −42,397.21247311309 and −131,035.65942218527 at delays of 1, 10, 30 and 90 days, where the fixed-payment constructor's fair payment, 16,776,091.202675004 at every delay, fed back gives 0. nanoql discounts at the fixed flow's payment date. QuantLib's check: its fixed-payment constructor on the same swap, its fair payment and rate. At an NPV date: the floating leg's NPV is given at the engine's NPV date (cashflows.cpp:498) and its end discount from the curve's reference date (discountingswapengine.cpp:97-101), so QuantLib's fair payment is high by the NPV date's discount's reciprocal: on the same swap without a delay, 17,200,779.97339953 at an NPV date of 15 January 2026 and 18,085,160.07066775 at 17 January 2028, fed back through the fixed-payment constructor at those dates 384,195.3384123612 and 1,245,139.539481705. nanoql takes the NPV back by the NPV date's discount, as QuantLib's asset swap does (assetswap.cpp:273, :294). QuantLib's check: its fair payment with no NPV date, and the fed-back NPV. Facts: TheFairPaymentIsTheFixedPaymentConstructors TheFairRateFedBackIsAtPar AtAnNpvDateTheFairPaymentIsTheReferenceDates ZeroGearingWithoutDayCounterTests Divergences/ZeroGearingWithoutDayCounterTests.cs A floating leg whose period has a zero gearing becomes a fixed-rate coupon on the leg's payment day counter (cashflowvectors.hpp:134-136; for an overnight leg, overnightindexedcoupon.cpp's OvernightLeg). Without one, QuantLib builds that coupon on an empty day counter and fails only when it is priced, "no day counter implementation provided" (daycounter.hpp:118); nanoql's FixedRateCoupon needs a day counter, so the leg is refused once it is built, after every refusal QuantLib raises while building it, with QuantLib's text: a builder's stored setting with NanoQLException, and the function form's argument with ArgumentException. Facts: AZeroGearingPeriodWithoutAPaymentDayCounterIsRefusedAtBuild AnOvernightLegsZeroGearingPeriodWithoutAPaymentDayCounterIsRefusedAtBuild ZeroSpreadedCompoundingTests Divergences/ZeroSpreadedCompoundingTests.cs The zero-spreaded curve's compounding and frequency are checked when it is built (the playbook's enum row): a value outside its enum is refused with ArgumentOutOfRangeException naming the parameter, "unknown compounding convention" or "unknown frequency (99)". QuantLib stores both and computes with them at every query (zerospreadedtermstructure.hpp:90-98): an unknown compounding builds and each query that reads a zero rate fails, "null interest rate", since impliedRate leaves its rate null for it (interestrate.cpp:111-132) and the rate's compound factor refuses that (:47); an unknown frequency builds and computes, a compounded spread as one compounded 99 times a year (a discount factor of 0.9607928351209212 at one year on a flat 3% Actual/365 (Fixed) curve with a 1% spread), a continuous one as if it had none. Facts: AnUnknownCompoundingOrFrequencyIsRefusedWhenTheCurveIsBuilt QLNet 1.13.2 Every documented divergence from QLNet 1.13.2, the oracle of the extensions' ports of QLNet, one entry per test class under tests/NanoQL.Tests/Divergences/QLNet/, each recording QLNet's value beside nanoql's. AmortizedCostBonds Divergences/QLNet/AmortizedCostBonds.cs The bonds the amortised-cost divergence facts build: QLNet's AB1 and AB2 (testAmortizingBond1, testAmortizingBond2) and their variants, on NullCalendar. AmortizedCostEntriesTests Divergences/QLNet/AmortizedCostEntriesTests.cs AmortizingBond's amortisations. Each pays the leg's own coupon, day-counted, where QLNet's pays the face amount times the rate over the frequency (AmortizingBond.cs:58), so that on Actual/365 (Fixed) QLNet's carrying amount misses the face amount at maturity, 1,000,367.33 on a million; nanoql's is the remaining flows' value at the effective rate at each coupon date. Each is signed, the interest less the coupon, where QLNet's sign is the bond's being at a premium (:118-124): a premium given a rate above its coupon accretes, where QLNet's amortises it, 42,875.52 on AB1 at 8% after a period where nanoql's is 43,948.48. A given rate of 0 is taken, where QLNet solves instead (:60; −0.0238 on AB1). The last closes to the face amount, where QLNet's cents leave AB2 at 500,000.02. The bond's cash flows are its coupons and redemption, its calendar the one given, where QLNet's hold 41 accounting entries and coupons with overridden amounts among its 83, on TARGET (:43, :127-128). Facts: ACouponDatesCarryingAmountIsTheRemainingFlowsValueOnAnyDayCounter AnAmortisationsSignIsItsInterestLessItsCoupon AGivenRateOfZeroIsTaken TheLastAmortisationClosesToTheFaceAmount TheCashFlowsAreTheBondsLeg AmortizedCostPartialPeriodTests Divergences/QLNet/AmortizedCostPartialPeriodTests.cs Between coupon dates, AmortizingBond.AmortizationValue accrues on the carrying amount at the period's start, over the coupon's own period: QLNet accrues every period on the cost, with no reference period (AmortizingBond.cs:163-172), so its carrying amount jumps at each coupon date, by 28.28 on a quarterly discount bond (96,952.32 the day before 15 June 2016, 96,980.60 on it) and by 68.96 before 15 December 2019. The check is QLNet's own AmortizationValue at the period's start and its FixedRateCoupon amounts on that carrying amount since then (the vectors' between-dates cases). Facts: TheCarryingAmountIsContinuousAtACouponDate AmortizedCostTradeDateTests Divergences/QLNet/AmortizedCostTradeDateTests.cs AmortizingBond solves its effective rate on the trade date, at initial recognition, as IFRS 9's and ASC 310-20's interest method require: the price paid, the cost plus the accrued interest purchased, against the remaining flows. QLNet takes the cost as the carrying amount on the coupon date on or before the trade, and solves there (AmortizingBond.cs:205-207); its first period then runs from that coupon date while its AmortizationValue accrues from the trade, so on AB2 its carrying amount jumps 96.34 at the first coupon date (471,724.66 the day before, 471,821.00 on it), and with no coupon before the trade it solves at its global evaluation date, a trade on 1 May 2010 of a bond issued 15 March 2010 yielding 0.0546 evaluated at the issue date, 0.0620 evaluated on 1 January 2012, and throwing evaluated after maturity. On a purchase on a coupon date the two methods agree, which the vectors check. The checks here: the rate is QuantLib's own CashFlows.Yield on the price paid at the trade date; the carrying amount is the cost on the trade date, continuous at the coupon dates, and the face amount at maturity; and each coupon date's is the remaining flows' value at the effective rate. Facts: TheRateIsTheYieldOfThePricePaidAtTheTradeDate TheCarryingAmountIsContinuousFromTheCost EachCouponDatesCarryingAmountIsTheRemainingFlowsValue ATradeInTheFirstPeriodDoesntReadTheEvaluationDate MbsFlowOrderTests Divergences/QLNet/MbsFlowOrderTests.cs MBSFixedRateBond's flows on a date are its coupon, then its scheduled principal, then its prepayment, as a bond's redemptions follow its coupons on a date (QuantLib's bond.cpp:325-328). QLNet's are the prepayment, the scheduled principal and the coupon (MBSFixedRateBond.cs:70-72). The amounts and dates are QLNet's bit for bit (the vectors); a sum over a date's flows, as PVDifference takes, adds them in this order. Facts: ADatesCouponComesFirst MbsFrequencyTests Divergences/QLNet/MbsFrequencyTests.cs A pool of a frequency other than monthly prepays at its model's rate: a period survives the product of its months' survival, each month's SMM at its own start, and a period counted in weeks or days its start's monthly survival to the power of the months it spans, each calendar month's share of it. QLNet applies one month's SMM a period (MBSFixedRateBond.cs:61-62), so a CPR of 8% prepays at 2.74% a year quarterly and 1.38% semi-annually, and its yields refuse such a pool ("root not bracketed", its bracket and formula being monthly). The checks: QLNet's own MBS fed the period's SMM (the vectors' quarterly and semi-annual cases); the constant-CPR closed form, a span's balance (1 − CPR)^(T/12) of the level-payment schedule's, T its months by an independent count; and the yields' closed form at par, the pass-through rate per period compounded to a month and to a half year. Facts: AConstantCprPrepaysAtItsRate AShortPeriodsPoolFollowsTheClosedForm TheYieldsAtParAreThePassThroughRatesEquivalents MbsPayOffTests Divergences/QLNet/MbsPayOffTests.cs A pool's pay-off. Under SIFMA's cap (PsaCapAndFloorTests), a 2,000% PSA pool prepays its whole balance at the 25th period, where its CPR reaches 100%, and its flows after are 0 but for one period's residue of rounding, 7.45e-9; QLNet's CPR passes 1 there and its flows from the 26th prepayment and 27th coupon are NaN, 335 of them. After a pay-off MBSFixedRateBond.MonthlyYield, MBSFixedRateBond.BondEquivalentYield, Yield and Price refuse the pool, its balance 0, as BondFunctions refuses a bond not tradable at its settlement: QLNet's yields throw too, on its stale notional (376,325,238.28 on a pool at CPR 1 settled 1 June 2007), where a solve on the pool's balance would return 0, QLNet's PVDifference being exactly 0 at both ends of its bracket. QLNet's 25th prepayment stands within six decimal places: GitHub's windows-2022 runner's C runtime and processor give it one ulp more, 59878137.771088034 (CI run 41543305018). Facts: A2000PercentPsaPoolsFlowsAfterThePayOffAreZero ThePaidOffPoolsYieldsAreRefused MbsPaymentDatesTests Divergences/QLNet/MbsPaymentDatesTests.cs MBSFixedRateBond's flows pay on each period's end adjusted by its payment convention on its calendar. QLNet's MBS takes the convention and ignores it (MBSFixedRateBond.cs:67-69): on TARGET with Following, its default, the Fabozzi pool's second payment is 1 April 2007, a Sunday, and 148 of its 358 payment dates aren't business days. The check is QLNet's level-payment base bond on the same calendar and convention, whose dates the vectors' TARGET case reads; the amounts don't move. Facts: FlowsPayOnTheAdjustedPeriodEnds TheAmountsAndTheYieldDontMove MbsPoolBalanceTests Divergences/QLNet/MbsPoolBalanceTests.cs MBSFixedRateBond's notional schedule and redemptions are the pool's expected ones, so its yields price the pool's balance at the settlement. QLNet's MBS keeps its level-payment base bond's notionals (MBSFixedRateBond.cs:39, :96), the balance with no prepayment: on the Fabozzi pool settled 1 February 2012, QLNet's notional is 371,882,785.38 against the pool's 291,474,567.29, and its monthly yield 0.0017466, where a pool priced at its own balance yields its pass-through rate, 0.055/12 a month. The check is QLNet's own PVDifference and Brent on the pool's balance (the vectors' seasoned cases); here, that yield. The yields also count the settlement date's flows as paid whatever the context's settings, as the balance does, where QLNet's include them under either setting that does: on that payment date its monthly yield moves to 0.0018220. Facts: TheNotionalIsThePoolsBalance ASeasonedPoolAtItsBalanceYieldsItsPassThroughRate TheYieldsPriceTheSettlementDatesFlowsAsPaid MbsPoolMonthsTests Divergences/QLNet/MbsPoolMonthsTests.cs MBSFixedRateBond reads its prepayment model at its start's anniversaries: period i's month at the start plus the pool's age plus i months, so a pool on the PSA curve takes SF-6's MONTH in every period (PsaMonthCountTests). QLNet reads a schedule date plus the age (MBSFixedRateBond.cs:61, :84), the same date from a start before the 29th, and on its Bond Basis month: from a start on 31 January 2007 its pool takes MONTH 1's CPR in its second period and MONTH 13's in its 14th (0.2% and 2.6% at 100% PSA), skipping MONTHs 2 and 14. The check is SIFMA's formula, each period's CPR SF-6's at its MONTH; QLNet's bits hold from a start before the 29th (the vectors). Facts: APoolFromAMonthEndTakesSf6sMonthInEveryPeriod ThePublicSmmIsTheModelAtADatePlusTheAge MbsPools Divergences/QLNet/MbsPools.cs The pools the MBS divergence facts build: QLNet's Fabozzi pool (testMBSFixedBondCached) and its variants, 400 million from 1 February 2007, 30/360 Bond Basis. MbsYieldBracketTests Divergences/QLNet/MbsYieldBracketTests.cs MBSFixedRateBond.MonthlyYield solves in QLNet's bracket of [0, 1]% a month where it holds the root, and otherwise by Brent's step search from QLNet's guess, above −100% a month. QLNet's solve refuses a yield outside its bracket (MBSFixedRateBond.cs:97): a 13% pass-through priced at par throws "root not bracketed: f[0,1]". The checks: the PV difference at the root, and the closed form at par, the pass-through rate over 12. Facts: AYieldAboveQLNetsBracketIsSolved AYieldBelowQLNetsBracketIsSolved MbsYoungPoolTests Divergences/QLNet/MbsYoungPoolTests.cs A pool whose original length is shorter than its remaining term, so that its age is negative, prepays at MONTH 1 until its loans' first month, as SIFMA's PSA model prices it (Chapter SF, SF-6, "MONTH equals 1 for all prior months"; its same-month pools are Reference/SifmaPassThroughTests'). QLNet's PSA falls to 0 and below there (PSACurve.cs:38), so an original length of 300 on a 358-month term gives 57 negative prepayments, the first −3,611,165.28. The check is SIFMA's formula, and QLNet's bits wherever the age is 0 or more (the vectors). Facts: NoPrepaymentIsNegative TheMonthsBeforeTheLoansFirstPrepayAtMonthOne PrepayRateRangeTests Divergences/QLNet/PrepayRateRangeTests.cs A prepayment rate outside SIFMA's range is refused at construction (Chapter SF: an SMM is "the percentage of the mortgage loans outstanding at the beginning of a month assumed to terminate during the month", SF-5, and SF-6 caps the CPR at 100), where QLNet takes it: ConstantCPR(1.01) gives an SMM of NaN, ConstantCPR(-0.01) a negative SMM, and a negative PSA multiplier negative rates (ConstantCPR.cs:25-36, PSACurve.cs:29-46). ConstantCPR refuses a CPR outside [0, 1] and PSACurve a negative or non-finite multiplier, with ArgumentOutOfRangeException. QLNet's values are QLNet 1.13.2's. Facts: AConstantCprOutsideZeroToOneIsRefused ANegativePsaMultiplierIsRefused PsaCapAndFloorTests Divergences/QLNet/PsaCapAndFloorTests.cs PSACurve follows SIFMA's PSA formula at its two ends (Chapter SF, SF-6), where QLNet's PSACurve.getCPR (PSACurve.cs:35-41) has neither bound. Above 1,666⅔% PSA, QLNet's CPR passes 1 and its SMM is NaN, so an MBS's flows are NaN; nanoql caps the CPR at 100%, its SMM 1. Before the curve's start, QLNet's month falls to 0 and below, its CPR 0 and then negative; nanoql counts every prior month as the first, as SIFMA's "MONTH equals 1 for all prior months". QLNet's values are QLNet 1.13.2's; elsewhere the two agree bit for bit (the vectors). Facts: ACprAboveOneIsCappedAtOne BelowTheCapTheRatesAreQLNets AMonthBeforeTheStartCountsAsTheFirst PsaMonthCountTests Divergences/QLNet/PsaMonthCountTests.cs PSACurve's MONTH is SF-6's, "the accrual period during which the age of the mortgage loans increases from MONTH – 1 to MONTH": the whole calendar months from the curve's start, plus one. QLNet counts the 30/360 Bond Basis days from the start over 30, plus one (PSACurve.cs:37-38). From a start on the 29th to the 31st, February's anniversary is under 30 such days after January's, so QLNet repeats the month there and skips the next (from 31 January 2007, MONTH 1 on 28 February and 3 on 31 March; MONTH 13 on 29 February 2008); from a start on the 1st it counts a 31st a month ahead (MONTH 2 on 31 March 2007 from 1 March), and from a 31st the 30th of a 31-day month (MONTH 3 on 30 March 2007). The check is SIFMA's formula (Reference/SifmaPrepaymentTests); QLNet's bits hold wherever the two counts agree (the vectors, which leave out the dates where they don't). QLNet's values are QLNet 1.13.2's. Facts: TheMonthIsTheCalendarMonthsFromTheStart WhereTheCountsAgreeTheRatesAreQLNets

docs/equity/options.html.title: Equity options | nanoql
docs/equity/options.html.summary: Equity options This page follows QuantLib's EquityOption example: one put, valued with European, Bermudan and American exercise by each engine family. Its values match that example's output, but for the one marked †. The sample, EquityOptions.cs, carries QuantLib's notice. The option and its market A put struck at 40 on a stock at 36, with a 6% rate, no dividends and 20% volatility, expiring a year after its settlement; the Bermudan one can be exercised every three months. The curves and the volatility are values, and the process holds them: var settlement = new Date(17, Month.May, 1998); var maturity = new Date(17, Month.May, 1999); double underlying = 36, strike = 40, dividendYield = 0.0, riskFreeRate = 0.06, volatility = 0.20; DayCounter dayCounter = new Actual365Fixed(); var riskFree = new FlatForward(settlement, riskFreeRate, dayCounter); var dividend = new FlatForward(settlement, dividendYield, dayCounter); var process = new BlackScholesMertonProcess(underlying, dividend, riskFree, new BlackConstantVol(settlement, new TARGET(), volatility, dayCounter)); var payoff = new PlainVanillaPayoff(OptionType.Put, strike); var european = new VanillaOption(payoff, new EuropeanExercise(maturity)); var american = new VanillaOption(payoff, new AmericanExercise(settlement, maturity)); Date[] exerciseDates = [.. Enumerable.Range(1, 4).Select(i => settlement + new Period(3 * i, TimeUnit.Months))]; var bermudan = new VanillaOption(payoff, new BermudanExercise(exerciseDates)); The engines Closed forms and approximations: Black-Scholes, Black-Scholes with Vasicek rates, the Heston and Bates models with their parameters set to the same volatility, the American approximations of Barone-Adesi and Whaley, Bjerksund and Stensland and the QD+ fixed point, and the integral of the payoff: rows.Add(("Black-Scholes", AnalyticEuropeanEngine.Calculate(european, context, process).NPV, null, null)); rows.Add(("Black-Vasicek", AnalyticBlackVasicekEngine.Calculate( european, context, process, new Vasicek(riskFreeRate, 0.3, 0.3, 0.15, 0.0), 0.5).NPV, null, null)); var heston = new HestonModel(new HestonProcess( riskFree, dividend, underlying, volatility * volatility, 1.0, volatility * volatility, 0.001, 0.0)); rows.Add(("Heston, semi-analytic", AnalyticHestonEngine.Calculate(european, context, heston).NPV, null, null)); var bates = new BatesModel(new BatesProcess( riskFree, dividend, underlying, volatility * volatility, 1.0, volatility * volatility, 0.001, 0.0, 1e-14, 1e-14, 1e-14)); rows.Add(("Bates, semi-analytic", BatesEngine.Calculate(european, context, bates).NPV, null, null)); rows.Add(("Barone-Adesi-Whaley", null, null, BaroneAdesiWhaleyApproximationEngine.Calculate(american, context, process).NPV)); rows.Add(("Bjerksund-Stensland", null, null, BjerksundStenslandApproximationEngine.Calculate(american, context, process).NPV)); rows.Add(("QD+ fixed point, fast", null, null, QdFpAmericanEngine.Calculate(american, context, process, QdFpAmericanEngine.FastScheme()).NPV)); rows.Add(("QD+ fixed point, accurate", null, null, QdFpAmericanEngine.Calculate(american, context, process, QdFpAmericanEngine.AccurateScheme()).NPV)); rows.Add(("QD+ fixed point, high precision", null, null, QdFpAmericanEngine.Calculate(american, context, process, QdFpAmericanEngine.HighPrecisionScheme()).NPV)); rows.Add(("Integral", IntegralEngine.Calculate(european, context, process).NPV, null, null)); Finite differences and seven binomial trees, each on 801 time steps, for all three exercises: int timeSteps = 801; rows.Add(("Finite differences", FdBlackScholesVanillaEngine.Calculate(european, context, process, tGrid: timeSteps, xGrid: timeSteps - 1).NPV, FdBlackScholesVanillaEngine.Calculate(bermudan, context, process, tGrid: timeSteps, xGrid: timeSteps - 1).NPV, FdBlackScholesVanillaEngine.Calculate(american, context, process, tGrid: timeSteps, xGrid: timeSteps - 1).NPV)); (string, double?, double?, double?) Tree<TTree>(string name) where TTree : Tree, IBinomialTree<TTree> => (name, BinomialVanillaEngine.Calculate<TTree>(european, context, process, timeSteps).NPV, BinomialVanillaEngine.Calculate<TTree>(bermudan, context, process, timeSteps).NPV, BinomialVanillaEngine.Calculate<TTree>(american, context, process, timeSteps).NPV); rows.Add(Tree<JarrowRudd>("Binomial, Jarrow-Rudd")); rows.Add(Tree<CoxRossRubinstein>("Binomial, Cox-Ross-Rubinstein")); rows.Add(Tree<AdditiveEQPBinomialTree>("Binomial, additive equiprobabilities")); rows.Add(Tree<Trigeorgis>("Binomial, Trigeorgis")); rows.Add(Tree<Tian>("Binomial, Tian")); rows.Add(Tree<LeisenReimer>("Binomial, Leisen-Reimer")); rows.Add(Tree<Joshi4>("Binomial, Joshi")); Monte Carlo: crude paths to an absolute tolerance, a Sobol sequence, and Longstaff and Schwartz's regression for early exercise: int seed = 42; rows.Add(("Monte Carlo, crude", new MakeMCEuropeanEngine<PseudoRandom, GeneralStatistics>(process, seed) .WithSteps(1).WithAbsoluteTolerance(0.02).ToEngine()(european, context).NPV, null, null)); // QuantLib's example gives the Sobol engine no seed; a one-dimensional Sobol sequence reads none, and nanoql's // seeds are explicit. rows.Add(("Quasi-Monte Carlo, Sobol", new MakeMCEuropeanEngine<LowDiscrepancy, GeneralStatistics>(process, seed) .WithSteps(1).WithSamples(32768).ToEngine()(european, context).NPV, null, null)); rows.Add((LongstaffSchwartz, null, null, new MakeMCAmericanEngine<PseudoRandom, GeneralStatistics, PseudoRandom>(process, seed) .WithSteps(100).WithAntitheticVariate().WithCalibrationSamples(4096).WithAbsoluteTolerance(0.02) .ToEngine()(american, context).NPV)); The values Method European Bermudan American Black-Scholes 3.844308 Black-Vasicek 3.818577 Heston, semi-analytic 3.844306 Bates, semi-analytic 3.844306 Barone-Adesi-Whaley 4.459628 Bjerksund-Stensland 4.453064 QD+ fixed point, fast 4.486617 QD+ fixed point, accurate 4.486669 QD+ fixed point, high precision 4.486674 Integral 3.844309 Finite differences 3.844330 4.360765 4.486113 Binomial, Jarrow-Rudd 3.844132 4.361174 4.486552 Binomial, Cox-Ross-Rubinstein 3.843504 4.360861 4.486415 Binomial, additive equiprobabilities 3.836911 4.354455 4.480097 Binomial, Trigeorgis 3.843557 4.360909 4.486461 Binomial, Tian 3.844171 4.361176 4.486413 Binomial, Leisen-Reimer 3.844308 4.360713 4.486076 Binomial, Joshi 3.844308 4.360713 4.486076 Monte Carlo, crude 3.834522 Quasi-Monte Carlo, Sobol 3.844613 Monte Carlo, Longstaff-Schwartz † 4.454440 † Longstaff and Schwartz's engine draws its calibration paths from the seed QuantLib documents, the pricing seed plus an offset, where QuantLib's code takes its null. QuantLib's example given that seed prints this value (the divergence). Each engine is a static function of the option, the context and the process, and the Monte Carlo engines take their seeds as arguments, so the table is the same on every run.

docs/equity/volatility-and-heston.html.title: A volatility surface and Heston's calibration | nanoql
docs/equity/volatility-and-heston.html.summary: A volatility surface and Heston's calibration The DAX options market of 5 July 2002, thirteen strikes by eight expiries, as QuantLib's tests calibrate Heston's model to it (from A. Sepp's "Pricing European-Style Options under Jump Diffusion Processes with Stochastic Volatility"). The calibrated parameters match QuantLib's on the same data. The sample, VolatilityAndHeston.cs, carries QuantLib's notice. The surface The quoted Black volatilities as a surface by expiry and strike, BlackVarianceSurface, which interpolates in variance: Date today = Context.EvaluationDate; Date[] expiries = [.. Days.Select(d => today + d)]; var vols = new Matrix(Strikes.Count, Days.Count); for (int s = 0; s < Strikes.Count; ++s) { for (int m = 0; m < Days.Count; ++m) { vols[s, m] = Vols[s, m]; } } var surface = new BlackVarianceSurface(today, new TARGET(), expiries, Strikes, vols, new Actual365Fixed()); Read back at three of its strikes, it gives the quotes: Expiry, days Vol at 4,000 Vol at 4,400 Vol at 5,000 13 45.41% 37.26% 33.43% 41 38.69% 33.96% 29.59% 75 34.92% 31.08% 27.05% 165 31.49% 27.81% 25.40% 256 29.63% 27.88% 25.04% 345 29.26% 27.22% 24.64% 524 28.19% 26.61% 24.48% 703 28.00% 26.86% 24.62% Between the nodes it interpolates in variance, bilinearly by default. Heston's calibration A HestonModelHelper per quote, each priced by the semi-analytic engine, and Levenberg-Marquardt minimizing the vols' errors: Date today = Context.EvaluationDate; DayCounter dayCounter = new Actual365Fixed(); var dates = new List<Date> { today }; var rates = new List<double> { 0.0357 }; double[] zeroRates = [0.0357, 0.0349, 0.0341, 0.0355, 0.0359, 0.0368, 0.0386, 0.0401]; for (int i = 0; i < Days.Count; ++i) { dates.Add(today + Days[i]); rates.Add(zeroRates[i]); } var riskFree = new ZeroCurve(dates, rates, dayCounter); var dividend = new FlatForward(today, 0.0, dayCounter); var helpers = new List<HestonModelHelper>(); for (int s = 0; s < Strikes.Count; ++s) { for (int m = 0; m < Days.Count; ++m) { var maturity = new Period((int)((Days[m] + 3) / 7.0), TimeUnit.Weeks); // to the nearest week helpers.Add(new HestonModelHelper(maturity, new TARGET(), Spot, Strikes[s], Vols[s, m], riskFree, dividend, Context, BlackCalibrationHelperCalibrationErrorType.ImpliedVolError) .SetPricingEngine<HestonModel>((option, context, model) => AnalyticHestonEngine.Calculate(option, context, model, 64))); } } var start = new HestonModel(new HestonProcess(riskFree, dividend, Spot, 0.1, 1.0, 0.1, 0.5, -0.5)); HestonModel calibrated = start.Calibrate(helpers, new LevenbergMarquardt(1e-8, 1e-8, 1e-8), new EndCriteria(400, 40, 1.0e-8, 1.0e-8, 1.0e-8), Context).Model; The calibrated model: Parameter Calibrated θ, the long-run variance 0.0745912 κ, the mean reversion 15.6627 σ, the volatility of variance 3.36192 ρ, the correlation -0.511492 v₀, the initial variance 0.195662 Sum of squared vol errors, in vol points² 177.233 Calibrate returns a new model with its record (the criterion that ended the optimization, the problem's values, the function evaluations), and leaves the starting model as it was.

docs/excel.html.title: Excel | nanoql
docs/excel.html.summary: Excel nanoql's Excel add-in puts the library in worksheet formulas: =nqlFlatForward(A1, 0.03, "Actual365Fixed") builds a curve, and =nqlYieldTermStructureDiscount(A2, DATE(2030,1,1)) reads it. It is an Excel-DNA 1.9 add-in on .NET 10 (net10.0-windows), for 64-bit Excel for Microsoft 365, whose dynamic arrays it spills into. It comes in two builds: nanoql64.xll, the stable API; nanoql-experimental64.xll, the stable API and the experimental one (bindings.md's opt-in: loading it is the consent). Both carry the same names, so a workbook built on the stable build opens unchanged in the experimental one. Load one of them per Excel process. The add-in is generated by nanoql-bind from the surface the bindings cross (bindings.md), for the types a desk's tasks need, listed by task. This page gives its rules, and how to install, build, debug and check it. Installing A release's nanoql-excel-<version>-win-x64.zip holds the two add-ins, nanoql's LICENSE, NOTICE and THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md (with Excel-DNA's and .NET's notices, whose code each .xll carries), a README, and the example workbooks with their conventions file under examples/ (Example workbooks, below). What it needs: 64-bit Excel for Microsoft 365 on Windows x64, and the .NET 10 Desktop Runtime, x64. Without the runtime, the add-in says so when it loads. Unblocking: Excel blocks an add-in downloaded from the internet, signed or not. Tick Unblock in the .xll's Properties, or put its folder in one of Excel's trusted locations (Trust Center > Trusted Locations). Loading: File > Options > Add-ins, Manage: Excel Add-ins, Go, Browse to the .xll; Excel then loads it at each start. Opening the .xll loads it for the session alone. Unsigned add-ins: the add-ins are unsigned. Excel set to "Require Application Add-ins to be signed by Trusted Publisher", which group policy often sets, disables an unsigned .xll without a prompt; a firm that enforces it signs the .xll with its own code-signing certificate. Example workbooks Five workbooks in bindings/excel/examples/, and in the release's zip under examples/, show the add-in at work, each on one sheet, its inputs in cells and its results named: curve.xlsx: a Euribor 6M curve bootstrapped from deposits and swaps, read as discounts, zero rates and forwards; swap.xlsx: Euribor and €STR swaps on that curve; bond.xlsx: a five-year fixed-rate bond's NPV, prices and yield; option.xlsx: a European call and put by Black-Scholes, with their Greeks; sofr.xlsx: the USD SOFR swaps of the SOFR example, at QuantLib's MakeOIS defaults and at the market's convention, which its cells spell out on OISRateHelper and MakeOIS, New York's calendar read from the conventions file market.xml beside it. They call the stable add-in's functions alone. The curve, the swaps and the SOFR trades are the docs' own examples, and give their numbers. Load the add-in, open a workbook and recalculate it (Ctrl+Alt+F9). sofr.xlsx reads market.xml from its own folder, so open it from a folder holding both: one opened straight from a zip is a copy with nothing beside it. Other .NET add-ins Excel holds one .NET runtime per process, and the add-ins run on .NET 10, so an add-in on another .NET version fails silently in the same Excel, its functions or nanoql's #NAME?: Loaded first Then Result nanoql an add-in on .NET 8 the other add-in's functions #NAME? an add-in on .NET 8 nanoql nanoql's functions #NAME? nanoql an add-in on .NET 10 both work nanoql an add-in compiled to native code (Native AOT) both work The tool: nanoql-bind excel In the repository, dotnet run --project src/NanoQL.Bind -c Release -- excel <command> runs it; outside it, the tool installed from NuGet runs generate and build from the defaults it carries, and refuses update, check, package and --test-exports, which work on the repository's own files (bindings.md, the tool): Command What it does update writes bindings/excel/functions.json, the experimental build's surface: each function's Excel name, C name, arguments and their kinds, result, category, experimental mark and loop mask; the add-in's own functions; and the functions the completeness check withholds check regenerates the surface into memory and compares its bytes with the checked-in file; checks its names are distinct regardless of case, none a cell reference, none the add-in's own, none over 255 characters generate --out <folder> writes a build's generated C#, its surface and its repro templates alone build --out <folder> generates a build into an Excel-DNA project in <folder>, builds it and packs its .xll there package --out <folder> builds nanoql's two add-ins and writes the release's zip, nanoql-excel-<version>-win-x64.zip, with the example workbooks, and its symbols zip there The others take: --experimental: the experimental API beside the stable; --assembly <prefix>=<path>: nanoql's two assemblies under nql by default; see Users' assemblies below; --list <prefix>=<file>|none: see The list below; --roles and --shipped, as the tool's other commands do. build also takes: --runtime-source <folder>: a local feed holding the runtime package, which a user's build otherwise restores from NuGet; --no-pack: compile only, with no .xll made. package takes --runtime-source alone: it packs nanoql's release. In the repository the runtime comes from its own pack: dotnet pack src/NanoQL.Excel -c Release -o <feed> dotnet run --project src/NanoQL.Bind -c Release -- excel build --runtime-source <feed> --out <folder> [--experimental] The build's folder then holds the add-in, nanoql64.xll or nanoql-experimental64.xll, and the notices. The project the tool writes, NanoQL.Excel.Functions, holds only the generated functions and references the runtime package, NanoQL.Excel, at the tool's version. Its .dna lists both assemblies, so the runtime's own functions register beside the generated ones, and the .xll packs nanoql's assemblies inside it. Names The prefix and the words: nql, then the words run together, QuantLibXL's form: a constructor is the type's name: nqlFlatForward; any other member is the type's and the member's: nqlYieldTermStructureDiscount, nqlInstrumentResultsNPV; a getter drops its get_, an init-only property's with_ is With (nqlEvaluationContextWithFixings), and an operator drops its op_ (nqlDateAddition); a static or extension member goes under its declaring type, a <Header>Functions class keeping its name (nqlBlackFormulaFunctionsBlackFormula). Overloads and collisions: names that meet regardless of case form a group, numbered in a stated order: the first plain, the rest 2, 3, and on. nqlCalendarAdvance is Advance(Date, int, TimeUnit, …), and nqlCalendarAdvance2 is Advance(Date, Period, …). Within a group the order is: the function's own type, by full name; its own members before inherited ones; the declaring type's full name, then the member's metadata token (QuantLib's declaration order, which the port keeps); binds by their engine input set, after the members; draws last. A numbered name doesn't say which overload it is: the Function Wizard's argument names and descriptions tell them apart, and functions.json gives each one's arguments. One numbering for every build: names are numbered over the whole surface, the experimental API included, before the stable build and the list apply. A function has one name in both builds and in any user's build, and a type added to the list renumbers nothing. Case: Excel matches names without regard to case and shows the registered case. Optional arguments: trailing optional arguments may be left out (see Values). Categories and help: a function's category is nanoql.<namespace>. Its description and each argument's come from nanoql's XML documentation, with the argument's form ("The calendar (a Calendar handle or its name)"), each cut at a word to 253 characters. IntelliSense in cells isn't packaged; Excel-DNA's standalone IntelliSense add-in reads the registered descriptions. Frozen from 2.0: each release writes bindings/excel/functions.shipped.json (nanoql-bind freeze), every released name, the experimental build's included, with its C name or its family's key. The tool keeps each released name. A new function takes its group's lowest unused number, so adding an overload never renumbers a released one. A removed function's name stays in the file, retired, and is never given to another function, so a workbook calling it gets #NAME?, never another function's result. A released stable name changes only through deprecation (two releases and a year); an experimental function may change or go in any release, its name retired. Before 2.0 nothing is frozen. The add-in's own functions take a prefix of their own, nqlxl; the tool refuses a generated name equal to one of them, regardless of case: Function What it gives nqlxlError(cell) the message of the error a cell's call returned, while the cell shows the error (Errors, below) nqlxlRepro(cell, format) the calls behind a cell: a vector, or the C# or the Python that makes them (Repro export, below) nqlxlRecipe(handle) the call that made a handle: its worksheet function and its arguments nqlxlVersion() nanoql's version and the .NET runtime the add-in runs on nqlxlDrawsValues(draws) a batch of draws' values: a column, or a draw per row for sequences nqlxlDrawsWeights(draws) a batch of draws' weights, a column nqlxlDrawsNext(draws) the generator's snapshot after the batch, from which the next batch draws The list: what Excel holds Excel holds the functions of the types on bindings/excel/list.json, each entry a type's full name and its task (a generic type by its definition, for its family). The tool carries it for nanoql's builds. It holds 309 types in 11 tasks: Task Types Some of them dates and calendars 16 Date, Period, Calendar, JointCalendar, DayCounter, MakeSchedule, IMM, ECB conventions and context 6 EvaluationContext, ConventionSet, ConventionsXml, ConventionSnapshot, Currency, IndexFixings quotes 6 ForwardSwapQuote, ImpliedStdDevQuote, LastFixingQuote indexes 9 IborIndex, OvernightIndex, SwapIndex, BMAIndex, the inflation indexes curves 30 FlatForward, DiscountCurve, PiecewiseYieldCurve, the rate helpers, the default and inflation curves cash flows 23 CashFlows, the legs and coupons, the coupon pricers instruments 84 swaps, bonds, options, caps and floors, swaptions, credit default swaps and their builders engines 53 the pricing engines, and every results record a listed function returns volatility 37 BlackConstantVol, BlackVarianceSurface, the swaption and optionlet volatilities, SABR models and calibration 19 HullWhite, G2, HestonModel, the calibration helpers, the optimizers math 26 the interpolations, the normal distribution, the sequence generators What an entry brings: the type's own functions: its constructors, members, statics, binds and draws; the instance members it inherits, each once from its nearest declaration (its own, then its base classes', an interface's only where no class declares it), constructors and statics excepted: a swap brings its legs and fixed rate, a model its parameters; the extension methods on it, such as a model's Calibrate. Excel's filter still applies inside a listed type. It drops: equality and increment operators, and a results record's constructors and with; setters, and members that return nothing but change an object other cells hold (a validation's check is kept); members writing files or reading the clock (ConventionsXml.WriteDefaults, Date.TodaysDate: Excel's own TODAY() serves); an engine's hooks, and members taking a writable span or an in-out argument. The completeness check: a listed function is withheld, to a fixpoint, when no listed function makes a required input of it, an object or an engine, and no lookup by name builds one. functions.json's "withheld" lists each, with the types it lacks. 19 on the list: the bond yields taking a solver, the short-rate models' trees, the swaps a listed engine prices but the list doesn't hold, among them. A family whole: a listed generic type keeps all its constructions. Where the check withholds one, the family's text differs from the tests' build's, and the build's tests fail naming the family and the type its construction lacks: a gap for the list to close. A type made by a lookup: where no listed function makes a type, the convention set's lookup by its record's name may: =nqlConventionSetInterestRateIndex(, "BMAIndex", curve) makes the BMA index. Asking for a type: open an issue naming the type and the task it serves. An entry added is a change that breaks no workbook. An entry removed after a release is a removed function: a stable one under deprecation (two releases and a year), an experimental one in any release, its name retired. A user's own list: --list nql=<file> widens or narrows nanoql's list for a user's build, in the same format; --list nql=none takes nanoql's whole surface, 10,228 functions with the experimental API and 8,008 without. A wider build names every function as nanoql's builds do. The budget: Excel-DNA's loader registers at most 10,000 functions, and one past them is silently missing. The tool counts a build's functions, the generated and the add-in's own, and refuses to pack one over 10,000, naming the count and the largest namespaces. The builds on the list hold 2,652 functions with the experimental API (328 experimental) and 2,324 without, leaving slots for a user's assemblies. Values Kind In a cell or an argument Out date Excel's serial number, which is QuantLib's; a time of day refused a serial number period text: "6M", "1Y6M"; days, weeks, months and years only text: "6M" enum its member's name, any case: "ModifiedFollowing", "Call" the name boolean TRUE or FALSE (1 or 0) TRUE or FALSE whole number a number with no fraction a number number, text as such as such; a non-finite number #NUM! object its handle (Handles, below); a calendar or a day counter also by name a handle results record a handle a handle, with a function per field: nqlInstrumentResultsNPV(h) array a row, a column or an array constant, read by rows a spill down a column; objects as handles matrix a 2-D range, by rows a spill by rows array of optional elements a range, its shape the array's a spill, none as #N/A map a range of two columns: keys, values two columns jagged array a range, a row per inner array a spill, short rows padded with #N/A tuple a row or a column of its items across a row array of tuples a range, a row per element and a column per item a row per element complex number Excel's complex text, "3+4i", as COMPLEX writes it the same, with round-trip digits loss distribution (not taken) six columns under a header row: x, dx, density, cumulative, excess, average generator a snapshot's handle a snapshot's handle draws (not taken) a handle, read through nqlxlDrawsValues, nqlxlDrawsWeights and nqlxlDrawsNext A 1904 workbook's serial numbers are converted at the boundary, 1,462 days, the date system read per call. An argument left out, or an empty cell, takes the parameter's default: none where the default is none, otherwise the default value. So no cell passes none where C# defaults to something else, such as the mixed interpolations' leftConditionValue = 0. A range's empty cells: trailing ones are trimmed, and an empty cell inside a range is refused, so two parallel ranges can't fall out of step. An array of optional elements is the exception: its range is the array, an empty cell none and nothing trimmed. A map's and an array of tuples' trailing empty rows are trimmed. What is refused: a map's duplicate key, and an array of tuples' range of another width, its message naming the form ("a range, a row per element: Key, Curve"); each with #VALUE!. A family's type arguments: a generic type's constructions fold into one function per family, its type arguments first, by name, in any case: =nqlPiecewiseYieldCurve("Discount", "LogLinear", "IterativeBootstrap", date, helpers, dayCounter, ctx). A nested generic's arguments join with underscores. A combination no construction has is refused, its message listing the constructions. In the stable build a family holds its stable constructions alone, and an experimental one is refused, its message naming the experimental build. What feeds back: an Excel error inside a range is refused, as an error argument passes through whole. So a returned none (#N/A), or a jagged spill's padding, fed back into another function's range refuses. A formula can't return an empty cell, so a computed range can't say none. A period in hours or minutes, which a few results carry, shows as "1h": text the period's parser, which reads days, weeks, months and years, doesn't take back. A file's path in a cell must be absolute (nqlConventionsXmlRead's). Looping over a range A range where a function takes one value is looped over: the function is called once per element, and the results spill in the range's shape, as Excel lifts its own functions. =nqlYieldTermStructureDiscount(curve, A3:A12) ten discount factors, down a column =nqlYieldTermStructureForwardRate2(curve, A3:A5, {"1M","3M","6M"}, dayCounter, "Compounded", "Annual") a 3 x 3 grid of forward rates' handles =nqlDepositRateHelper(B1:B3, "3M", 2, "TARGET", "ModifiedFollowing", FALSE, "Actual360", ctx) three deposits, one per rate Which arguments loop: every argument of a kind one cell holds: a number, a whole number, a boolean, text, a date, a period, an enum, a complex number, a handle, a snapshot, a bound engine, and their optional forms. An array, matrix, vector, jagged or map argument keeps its range. A family's type arguments don't loop, and a function whose result is itself a range doesn't loop, since Excel spills no array of arrays. A 1 × 1 range in a looped place is its value. functions.json gives each function's mask, a 1 per looping argument. Several ranges pair by Excel's rule: a single row or column repeats, and a position past a shorter range's end is #N/A. Each element is the single call, keyed as it is: three deposits from one formula are the three cells' deposits, and a curve built from them is the same curve. A failed element shows its error in its place, the others their values. Messages by cell: the formula's cell gets the first failed element's message, with its place ("row 2, column 1"), whether the looped call is the formula's value or nested in it (=SUMPRODUCT(nqlYieldTermStructureDiscount(curve, A3:A12), B3:B12)); nqlxlError on a spilled cell gives its element's message when the spill shows the looped call element by element, and nothing for an element showing a value; a spill that reorders the elements (INDEX over a reversed SEQUENCE) gives the formula's message; a cell outside the spill keeps its own call's message. Release: each looped object is held by its cell. Clearing the cell releases them all, shrinking its range releases the elements it leaves, and an element whose input changes releases its old object. Names for calendars and day counters Text where a Calendar or a DayCounter goes names it in the current convention set, as an empty set argument reads it (The context and the conventions, below): =nqlDepositRateHelper(0.03, "6M", 2, "TARGET", "ModifiedFollowing", FALSE, "Actual360", ctx) =nqlJointCalendar("TARGET", "UnitedStates.Settlement") The names: the set's own and its aliases, FpML's codes (EUTA is TARGET, ACT/360 is Actual360). A name is as the set spells it: "target" is #VALUE!. What isn't a name: a name the set doesn't know is #VALUE!, nqlxlError naming it; a handle's text stays a handle, #REF! when this session doesn't hold it; a name where another type goes stays a missing handle, #REF!. Under a desk's conventions (the settings file), a name is the desk's calendar. An array of calendars takes names too. Indexes stay handles: the set's index needs a curve: =nqlConventionSetIborIndex2(set, "Euribor", "6M", curve). Handles An object is held by the add-in and shown in its cell as a handle, <Type>#<16 hexadecimal digits>, such as FlatForward#B4D02F06C4DB1663; any cell passes the handle to another function. The key: the call itself: the function's name; each argument's value (numbers by their bits, text, booleans, a missing argument, a range's shape and cells), each handle argument by its own key; the workbook's date system; the convention provider in effect. Equal calls give one object, in any cell, sheet or workbook. The 16 digits are the key's SHA-256; an object whose 16 digits meet another's shows 32. A call that reads files (nqlConventionsXmlRead, nqlConventionsXmlRead2) keys their content beside their paths. An edited file gives a new object when its cell recalculates: F2 and Enter on the cell, or Ctrl+Alt+F9 for the whole workbook. Neither function is volatile, so a plain recalculation doesn't reread the file. One content read from two paths is two objects, each reporting its own path. Lifetime: an object lives while some cell holds its handle, through Excel's RTD topics, and is released when the last one goes. An object inside a returned array (a leg's coupons) is keyed by its parent call and its position, and goes with its parent's cell. Saving and reopening: a saved workbook's handle cells recalculate when it opens. Its handles are rebuilt, the same texts as saved, and every later edit finds them. Threads: every generated function is thread-safe, objects are built once per key, and recalculation runs on all of Excel's threads. Across workbooks: a handle referenced from another workbook works while some cell holds it. Errors Excel shows When #VALUE! the arguments are refused: a wrong value or type, an unknown name, an unreadable or malformed file, a feature not supported, a bound engine refused, the add-in's conventions failing to load #NUM! QuantLib's own checks and failed calculations, anything else, and a non-finite result #REF! a handle this Excel session doesn't hold #N/A no value: a null result, an empty collection Excel's own errors pass through: an error from Excel in an argument returns as itself, as Excel's own functions pass it. The message: =nqlxlError(cell) gives the failed call's message, with the parameter it names and the exception's kind, while the cell shows the error: =nqlFlatForward(A1, 0.03, A14) #VALUE!, A14 holding a calendar =nqlxlError(B5) nqlFlatForward: ArgumentException: dayCounter: expected a DayCounter, got a … The codes: each exception takes the C interface's error code first (bindings.md), then the code its Excel error, so the add-in and the bindings classify a failure alike. The context and the conventions The evaluation context is a handle: =nqlEvaluationContext(date), and a With<Field> per field (nqlEvaluationContextWithFixings), passed to every function that takes one. There is no today default. Conventions through a set: nqlConventionSetQuantLib(), QuantLib's own; nqlConventionsXmlRead(path) and nqlConventionSetWith(set, snapshot), a conventions file's (conventions.md); the presets by name: =nqlConventionSetIborIndex2(set, "Euribor", "6M", curve). An empty set argument reads the current conventions: the add-in's default, or QuantLib's. The settings file: each build reads its own, <add-in name>.settings.json beside the .xll (nanoql64.settings.json, nanoql-experimental64.settings.json), when Excel loads the add-in: { "conventions": "desk-conventions.xml", "recordCalls": true } "conventions": a conventions file, relative to the settings file's folder, loaded as the default conventions. "recordCalls": whether each call is recorded for export, on by default. The environment variable NANOQL_CONVENTIONS overrides "conventions", a relative path resolving against the .xll's folder. No worksheet function sets the default conventions: a setting written by one cell and read by others would make a result depend on Excel's calculation order. A failed load never falls back to QuantLib's conventions: a missing or malformed conventions file, an unknown key (a key in another case included) or a value of the wrong type each refuse every lookup on the default conventions. Every function reading them returns #VALUE!, nqlxlError giving the load's error, while a function given an explicit set still works. The provider in effect enters every handle's key: QuantLib's, the loaded file's content, or the failed load. Bound engines An engine is bound in a cell with its inputs and given where a member takes one, as the bindings do (bindings.md): =nqlDiscountingSwapEngineBind(curve) a bound engine, every input optional =nqlMakeVanillaSwapWithPricingEngine(builder, B1) the builder solves its fixed rate through it The member's own arguments are placed by role, and the bound inputs fill the rest. An engine of the wrong shape, an input both bound and supplied, or an engine without the member's calculation is refused, #VALUE!. Functions of the caller's own (solvers, integrators, quotes computed by a formula) stay out of 2.0, as in every binding. Users' assemblies A user's own assembly built on nanoql gets its worksheet functions in the same add-in as nanoql's, so its objects and nanoql's meet: nanoql-bind excel build --assembly nql=NanoQL.dll --assembly nql=NanoQL.Extensions.dll --assembly acme=Acme.dll --out x Names: each assembly's functions take its prefix: =acmeExponentialCurve(A1, 0.03, 0.001, A3) builds the user's curve, and nanoql's =nqlYieldTermStructureDiscount2(A4, 5) prices it. The same naming, freezing and budget rules apply as for nanoql's own. The build: the stable API and the user's assemblies, unless --experimental is given. nanoql's list applies to nanoql's assemblies; a user's assembly is generated whole unless --list <prefix>=<file> gives it a list. What the check withholds: a user's function whose required input only a type off nanoql's list makes is withheld as nanoql's are. The tool prints each one with the types it lacks and the remedy: --list nql=<file>, with the type added. The runtime package: a user's build restores the runtime, NanoQL.Excel, from NuGet at the tool's version. One add-in per Excel process: each Excel-DNA add-in loads its assemblies into a context of its own, so two add-ins' objects are different types and can't meet. A desk's add-in holds every assembly its workbooks price with. Repro export =nqlxlRepro(cell, format) gives the nanoql calls behind a cell, a line per row: "vector", the default: a test vector in the vector suite's envelope. It holds each call's worksheet function and the Excel values it was given: a range with its shape and its empty cells, a handle as a reference to the call that made it, an object inside a returned array as its parent call's item. Beside them: the provider, the calls' date system, and the conventions file and every file a call read, embedded. The expected outcome is the cell's own: a spill's whole value, a handle's text (its type alone where a file was read), throws for a failed call, null for no value, a non-finite number's #NUM!. "csharp": a C# program making the same calls through nanoql alone. Compiled against NanoQL.dll and NanoQL.Extensions.dll, it prints the cell's outcome as a grid of cells. "python": the same over nanoql's Python package and NumPy. A looped call's C# and Python loop over its ranges, each element guarded as Excel shows a failed element; a name where a calendar or a day counter goes is the convention set's lookup. The date system is the calls' own: a 1904 workbook's cell exported from a 1900 workbook gives a 1904 vector. The export refuses, #VALUE! with nqlxlError giving why: a cell whose value isn't its call's outcome: a scaled cell, or a cell edited to a constant; a call given an Excel error: export the cell that gave it; an object inside a returned map or tuple; calls made in workbooks of both date systems; a call reporting a read file's path (nqlConventionSnapshotSources, nqlConventionSetProvenance), which a replay reading the file from a temporary path can't reproduce. With "recordCalls": false in the settings, a value cell can't export; a handle cell still does, from its handle's recipe. The replayer runs a folder of vectors through a tests' build, each on its own (a fresh store, the vector's conventions, date system and files), every number within the vector suite's tolerance: dotnet run --project bindings/excel/replay -c Release -- vectors <folder> <the experimental tests' build> [--reverse] An export as a test: commit the vector as bindings/excel/tests/repro/<name>.json and the workbook it was exported from as bindings/excel/tests/repro/workbooks/<name>.xlsx, its read files under workbooks/files/. A workbook holds each call in a cell of its sheet Calls and the export in its sheet Repro; a read file's path is built from the workbook's own folder (its name Here), so it reads its files wherever the checkout is. The read files are kept as written, their line endings included (-text in .gitattributes), since the vector embeds their bytes. CI replays every committed vector; the Excel tests make each one's calls again and export them, and render it as C# and run it; the suite inside Excel exports it again from its workbook. Each comparison leaves out the generator's version and the checkout's own path. Debugging nanoql's symbols ship apart from the add-ins, in nanoql-excel-<version>-win-x64-symbols.zip: NanoQL.pdb and NanoQL.Extensions.pdb, with nanoql's source embedded. To stop in nanoql's source from a cell in Visual Studio: Give it the symbols' folder once: Tools > Options > Debugging > Symbols. Turn on Suppress JIT optimization on module load and turn off Enable Just My Code (Tools > Options > Debugging > General). The release build's code is optimized: without the first, a breakpoint may bind and never stop. Attach to Excel before the add-in loads (Debug > Attach to Process, Managed (.NET Core) code), or start Excel from Visual Studio with the .xll as its argument. In the repository, python -I bindings/excel/xltests/stepin.py [--netcoredbg <netcoredbg.exe>] checks the way in on nanoql's Debug build: it builds an add-in over it, nanoql's PDB left apart, attaches netcoredbg 3.2.0 to an Excel of its own, and stops in FlatForward's discount from a cell's call, the generated worksheet function a frame above. Checking the add-in Check Command Where The surface dotnet run --project src/NanoQL.Bind -c Release -- excel check CI The back end dotnet test --project bindings/NanoQL.Bind.Tests -c Release: names, the list, the fold, the forms' code, the builds CI The runtime dotnet test --project bindings/excel/NanoQL.Excel.Tests -c Release: the conversions and forms, keys, errors, settings, looping and messages, through a test host standing in for Excel, on the tests' builds; and the example workbooks' formulas, every function they call listed and stable CI The replay dotnet run --project bindings/excel/replay -c Release -- <trace> <build folder> --floor bindings/excel/replay-floor.json CI The repro vectors dotnet run --project bindings/excel/replay -c Release -- vectors bindings/excel/tests/repro <build folder>, then with --reverse CI The package dotnet run --project src/NanoQL.Bind -c Release -- excel package --runtime-source <feed> --out <folder> CI Inside Excel python -I bindings/excel/xltests/run.py [--python <interpreter>] a machine with Excel Stepping into nanoql python -I bindings/excel/xltests/stepin.py [--netcoredbg <netcoredbg.exe>] a machine with Excel The tests' builds hold nanoql's whole surface with the list off, compiled with no .xll: --list nql=none --no-pack, with --experimental for one of them. Every listed function is generated in them byte for byte, so what they pass the shipped builds pass, and the kinds the list doesn't reach today stay tested. The replay: the vector suite's recorded trace (bindings.md) through the experimental tests' build's worksheet functions, outside Excel, each result against C#'s, bit for bit. A fact stops at an input no cell gives: NaN, a whole number past 2^53, none where the default isn't none, a period in hours, an empty matrix, an enum value no member has. The suite inside Excel (bindings/excel/xltests/, ExcelDna.Testing on xUnit 2, with its own global.json) runs on the shipped builds, a test build and a user's build, in Excel instances of its own that load the add-ins for their session alone. It checks: loading, each build's registered functions its surface's; a desk's tasks to their bits; bound engines in cells; handles across saving and reopening, and in both date systems; edited conventions files and the settings' failed loads; errors and their messages; 2,000 curves on all of Excel's threads; the forms in real ranges; a user's assembly; looping and its messages by cell, names for calendars and day counters, and objects released with their cells; repro export: a desk's swap exported in each format, the vector replayed, the C# compiled and run, the Python run (with --python, an interpreter with nanoql's Python package and NumPy), each to the cell's bits; every committed vector the build holds exported again from its workbook; the export's refusals; the package's stable add-in, from its zip, priced; the example workbooks, each opened on the stable add-in and recalculated whole, its named results C#'s bits. Its wrapper builds the add-ins first. It checks that the run leaves the machine's other Excel processes and Excel's settings as it found them; it puts back Excel's window position, which Excel rewrites when a test closes a second workbook, and says so.

docs/getting-started.html.title: Getting started | nanoql
docs/getting-started.html.summary: Getting started nanoql is a .NET 10 library. Add its package to a project: dotnet add package NanoQL The conventions' XML format and QLNet's additions are in a second package, NanoQL.Extensions (conventions.md); a first price needs only the first. A first swap Price a five-year SOFR swap on a flat curve. The evaluation date goes in an EvaluationContext, the curve and the swap are values, and the engine is a static function of them: var today = new Date(15, Month.October, 2026); var context = new EvaluationContext { EvaluationDate = today }; var curve = new FlatForward(today, 0.036, new Actual365Fixed()); OvernightIndexedSwap swap = new MakeOIS(new Period(5, TimeUnit.Years), new Sofr(curve)) .WithFixedRate(0.036) .WithNominal(10e6) .ToOvernightIndexedSwap(context); OvernightIndexedSwapResults result = DiscountingSwapEngine.Calculate(swap, context, curve); The results: NPV Fair rate 7,041.24 3.6154% MakeOIS takes QuantLib's defaults for every option it isn't given: here, SOFR's own calendar and day count, annual payments, and two settlement days. DiscountingSwapEngine.Calculate returns a results record, whose NPV, FairRate and each leg's LegNPV and LegBPS are read like any other property. The same inputs give the same results, on any thread. In Python The same swap, a bootstrapped SOFR curve, €STR and Euribor curves with their swaps, a SABR smile, an American put and a CDS run in Python in a notebook you can open in Google Colab, with nothing to install; locally, pip install nanoql jupyter matplotlib runs it. The bindings guide gives the Python layer's rules. Next Concepts: values and functions, the evaluation context, conventions as data, and what is experimental. The rates guides: dates and calendars, curves, indexes and fixings, swaps, caps and floors and swaptions. Pricing a USD SOFR swap to match the market: the conventions that move a price, set in XML. The stateless design: rebuilding, memoizing and pricing scenarios in parallel. Coming from QuantLib's C++, QuantLib-Python or QLNet: from QuantLib's C++, from QuantLib-Python, from QLNet. Beyond C#: the bindings for Python and for C, which any language that calls C can use, the C++ layer over it (C++), and the Excel add-in.

docs/migration/from-qlnet.html.title: Migrating from QLNet | nanoql
docs/migration/from-qlnet.html.summary: Migrating from QLNet QLNet and nanoql are both C# libraries whose types follow QuantLib's, so most QLNet code maps class by class: the same Date, Euribor6M, MakeVanillaSwap or BlackSwaptionEngine. What changes is how they are connected, and the names' casing: nanoql's members are .NET's PascalCase, where QLNet keeps QuantLib's camelCase. This guide pairs QLNet code with nanoql's for the rates products, each pair building the same trade on the same quotes. The parity table lists the QuantLib classes nanoql ports, each with QLNet's class where it has one. The platform nanoql runs on .NET 10 alone. It uses static abstract interface members, which .NET Framework can't run, so code that QLNet serves on .NET Framework through netstandard2.0 moves to .NET 10 first. The concepts QLNet nanoql Settings.setEvaluationDate(today), held per thread new EvaluationContext { EvaluationDate = today }, passed to each call that reads it SimpleQuote, Handle<Quote> a double: a new quote means a new object, built from it Handle<YieldTermStructure>, RelinkableHandle<YieldTermStructure> the curve itself, passed where it is used instrument.setPricingEngine(engine), then instrument.NPV() Engine.Calculate(instrument, context, …), returning a results record observers and lazy recalculation the application's layer above the library: rebuild on change, or memoize by inputs (the stateless design) index.addFixing(date, value), held in a global store context.Fixings.AddFixing(index, date, value), held by the context a builder's implicit conversion, or value() .ToVanillaSwap(context), .ToCapFloor(context), … swap.fairRate(), swap.legBPS(0) the results record's FairRate, LegBPS[0] QLNet's additions: MBSFixedRateBond, PSACurve, ConstantCPR, AmortizingBond the same classes, in the NanoQL.Extensions package Curves using QLNet; var today = new Date(15, Month.October, 2026); Settings.setEvaluationDate(today); (int Years, double Rate)[] swapQuotes = [(2, 0.0225), (3, 0.0232), (5, 0.0245), (7, 0.0256), (10, 0.0270), (15, 0.0283), (20, 0.0288), (30, 0.0285)]; var helpers = new List<RateHelper> { new DepositRateHelper(new Handle<Quote>(new SimpleQuote(0.0205)), new Euribor(new Period(3, TimeUnit.Months))), new DepositRateHelper(new Handle<Quote>(new SimpleQuote(0.0210)), new Euribor6M()), }; helpers.AddRange(swapQuotes.Select(q => new SwapRateHelper(q.Rate, new EuriborSwapIsdaFixA(new Period(q.Years, TimeUnit.Years))))); var curve = new PiecewiseYieldCurve<Discount, LogLinear>(today, helpers, new Actual365Fixed()); var curveHandle = new Handle<YieldTermStructure>(curve); (int Years, double Rate)[] swapQuotes = [(2, 0.0225), (3, 0.0232), (5, 0.0245), (7, 0.0256), (10, 0.0270), (15, 0.0283), (20, 0.0288), (30, 0.0285)]; RateHelper[] helpers = [ new DepositRateHelper(0.0205 + shift, new Euribor(new Period(3, TimeUnit.Months)), context), new DepositRateHelper(0.0210 + shift, new Euribor6M(), context), .. swapQuotes.Select(q => new SwapRateHelper(q.Rate + shift, new EuriborSwapIsdaFixA(new Period(q.Years, TimeUnit.Years)), context)), ]; var curve = new PiecewiseLogLinearDiscount(today, helpers, new Actual365Fixed(), context); The helpers take their quotes as numbers and the context, and the curve is passed as itself: there is no handle. Indexes and fixings var euribor = new Euribor6M(curveHandle); Date yesterday = euribor.fixingCalendar().advance(today, -1, TimeUnit.Days); euribor.addFixing(yesterday, 0.0212); var euribor = new Euribor6M(curve); Date yesterday = euribor.FixingCalendar.Advance(Curves.Today, -1, TimeUnit.Days); EvaluationContext context = Curves.Context with { Fixings = Curves.Context.Fixings.AddFixing(euribor, yesterday, 0.0212), }; Date[] fixingDates = [ yesterday, Curves.Today, euribor.FixingCalendar.Advance(Curves.Today, new Period(6, TimeUnit.Months)), ]; QLNet's fixing goes into a global store every Euribor 6M index reads; nanoql's goes into the context. Vanilla swaps var engine = new DiscountingSwapEngine(curveHandle); VanillaSwap swap = new MakeVanillaSwap(new Period(5, TimeUnit.Years), euribor, 0.025) .withNominal(10e6) .withPricingEngine(engine); Console.WriteLine($"{swap.NPV()} {swap.fairRate()}"); var euribor = new Euribor6M(curve); VanillaSwap spot = new MakeVanillaSwap(new Period(5, TimeUnit.Years), euribor) .WithFixedRate(0.025) .WithNominal(10e6) .ToVanillaSwap(context); VanillaSwap forward = new MakeVanillaSwap(new Period(5, TimeUnit.Years), euribor) .WithForwardStart(new Period(5, TimeUnit.Years)) .WithFixedRate(0.025) .WithNominal(10e6) .ToVanillaSwap(context); FixedVsFloatingSwapResults spotResult = DiscountingSwapEngine.Calculate(spot, context, curve); FixedVsFloatingSwapResults forwardResult = DiscountingSwapEngine.Calculate(forward, context, curve); Overnight swaps var flat = new Handle<YieldTermStructure>(new FlatForward(today, 0.036, new Actual365Fixed())); OvernightIndexedSwap ois = new MakeOIS(new Period(5, TimeUnit.Years), new Sofr(flat), 0.036) .withNominal(10e6) .withPricingEngine(new DiscountingSwapEngine(flat)); Console.WriteLine($"{ois.NPV()} {ois.fairRate()}"); var today = new Date(15, Month.October, 2026); var context = new EvaluationContext { EvaluationDate = today }; var curve = new FlatForward(today, 0.036, new Actual365Fixed()); OvernightIndexedSwap swap = new MakeOIS(new Period(5, TimeUnit.Years), new Sofr(curve)) .WithFixedRate(0.036) .WithNominal(10e6) .ToOvernightIndexedSwap(context); OvernightIndexedSwapResults result = DiscountingSwapEngine.Calculate(swap, context, curve); Caps and floors CapFloor cap = new MakeCapFloor(CapFloorType.Cap, new Period(5, TimeUnit.Years), euribor, 0.025) .withNominal(10e6) .withPricingEngine(new BlackCapFloorEngine(curveHandle, 0.20)); Console.WriteLine(cap.NPV()); CapFloor capFloor = new MakeCapFloor(type, new Period(5, TimeUnit.Years), new Euribor6M(curve)) .WithStrike(strike) .WithNominal(10e6) .ToCapFloor(context); double black = BlackCapFloorEngine.Calculate(capFloor, context, curve, 0.20).NPV!.Value; double bachelier = BachelierCapFloorEngine.Calculate(capFloor, context, curve, 0.0060).NPV!.Value; Swaptions var swapIndex = new EuriborSwapIsdaFixA(new Period(5, TimeUnit.Years), curveHandle); Swaption swaption = new MakeSwaption(swapIndex, new Period(1, TimeUnit.Years), 0.025) .withNominal(10e6) .withPricingEngine(new BlackSwaptionEngine(curveHandle, 0.20)); Console.WriteLine(swaption.NPV()); var index = new EuriborSwapIsdaFixA(new Period(5, TimeUnit.Years), curve); Swaption swaption = new MakeSwaption(index, new Period(expiry, TimeUnit.Years), strike) .WithNominal(10e6) .ToSwaption(context); double black = BlackSwaptionEngine.Calculate(swaption, context, curve, 0.20).NPV!.Value; double bachelier = BachelierSwaptionEngine.Calculate(swaption, context, curve, 0.0060).NPV!.Value;

docs/migration/from-quantlib-cpp.html.title: Migrating from QuantLib's C++ | nanoql
docs/migration/from-quantlib-cpp.html.summary:
Migrating from QuantLib's C++ nanoql's C++ layer, nanoql.hpp, keeps QuantLib's class names and member names, so most QuantLib code maps class by class: the same Date, MakeVanillaSwap or DiscountingSwapEngine, and the same discount(t) or fairRate(). What changes is how they are connected, and the C++ around them: objects held by value rather than by shared pointer, no handles or quotes, and indexes and day counters taken by name from a convention set. This guide pairs QuantLib's C++ with nanoql's for the rates products, each pair building the same trade on the same quotes. The C++ page gives the install, the CMake package and a first program. Each QuantLib block below follows #include <ql/quantlib.hpp> and using namespace QuantLib;, each nanoql block #include "nanoql.hpp" and using namespace nanoql;, both with #include <cstdio> for std::printf, and each runs in main() after the blocks above it. The concepts QuantLib nanoql Settings::instance().evaluationDate() = today; EvaluationContext context(today);, passed to each call that reads it SimpleQuote, Handle<Quote> a double: a new quote means a new object, built from it Handle<YieldTermStructure>, RelinkableHandle<YieldTermStructure> the curve itself, passed where it is used ext::shared_ptr<T>, ext::make_shared<T>(…) T by value: each object holds a handle to its nanoql object, a copy takes another handle to the same object, and the destructor releases its own instrument->setPricingEngine(engine), then instrument->NPV() Engine::calculate(instrument, context, …), returning a results object whose values are std::optional<double> observers and LazyObject the application's layer above the library: rebuild on change, or memoize by inputs (the stateless design) index->addFixing(date, value), held in a global store context.fixings().addFixing(index, date, value), in a new context: context.withFixings(…) ext::make_shared<Euribor6M>(h), Actual365Fixed(), TARGET() by name from a convention set: qs.iborIndex("Euribor6M", curve), qs.dayCounter("Actual365Fixed"), qs.calendar("TARGET"), with ConventionSet qs = ConventionSet::quantLib(); (conventions as data) PiecewiseYieldCurve<Discount, LogLinear> PiecewiseLogLinearDiscount, QuantLib-Python's name for it MakeVanillaSwap(5 * Years, index, 0.025).withNominal(10e6), converted to the swap MakeVanillaSwap(Period(5, TimeUnit::Years), index), then .withFixedRate(0.025), .withNominal(10e6) and .toVanillaSwap(context) Date(15, October, 2026), 5 * Years Date(15, Month::October, 2026), Period(5, TimeUnit::Years) QuantLib::Error, from QL_REQUIRE nanoql::error, a std::runtime_error with the C interface's code and the parameter it names Curves // QuantLib Date today(15, October, 2026); Settings::instance().evaluationDate() = today; auto quote = [](Rate r) { return Handle<Quote>(ext::make_shared<SimpleQuote>(r)); }; std::vector<std::pair<Integer, Rate>> swapQuotes = { {2, 0.0225}, {3, 0.0232}, {5, 0.0245}, {7, 0.0256}, {10, 0.0270}, {15, 0.0283}, {20, 0.0288}, {30, 0.0285}}; std::vector<ext::shared_ptr<RateHelper>> helpers = { ext::make_shared<DepositRateHelper>(quote(0.0205), ext::make_shared<Euribor>(3 * Months)), ext::make_shared<DepositRateHelper>(quote(0.0210), ext::make_shared<Euribor6M>()), }; for (auto [years, rate] : swapQuotes) { auto index = ext::make_shared<EuriborSwapIsdaFixA>(years * Years); helpers.push_back(ext::make_shared<SwapRateHelper>(quote(rate), index)); } auto curve = ext::make_shared<PiecewiseYieldCurve<Discount, LogLinear>>( today, helpers, Actual365Fixed()); Handle<YieldTermStructure> curveHandle(curve); // nanoql Date today(15, Month::October, 2026); EvaluationContext context(today); ConventionSet qs = ConventionSet::quantLib(); DayCounter actual365 = qs.dayCounter("Actual365Fixed"); std::vector<std::pair<int, double>> swapQuotes = { {2, 0.0225}, {3, 0.0232}, {5, 0.0245}, {7, 0.0256}, {10, 0.0270}, {15, 0.0283}, {20, 0.0288}, {30, 0.0285}}; std::vector<BootstrapHelper_YieldTermStructure> helpers = { DepositRateHelper(0.0205, qs.iborIndex("Euribor", Period(3, TimeUnit::Months)), context), DepositRateHelper(0.0210, qs.iborIndex("Euribor6M"), context), }; for (auto [years, rate] : swapQuotes) { SwapIndex index = qs.swapIndex("EuriborSwapIsdaFixA", Period(years, TimeUnit::Years)); helpers.push_back(SwapRateHelper(rate, index, context)); } PiecewiseLogLinearDiscount curve(today, helpers, actual365, context); The helpers take their quotes as numbers and the context, the indexes come from the convention set, and the curve is passed as itself: there is no handle. The vector holds the helpers as BootstrapHelper_YieldTermStructure, the type the curve takes, which RateHelper derives from. Indexes and fixings // QuantLib auto euribor = ext::make_shared<Euribor6M>(curveHandle); Date yesterday = euribor->fixingCalendar().advance(today, -1, Days); euribor->addFixing(yesterday, 0.0212); std::printf("%.4f
", euribor->fixing(yesterday)); // 0.0212 // nanoql IborIndex euribor = qs.iborIndex("Euribor6M", curve); Date yesterday = euribor.fixingCalendar().advance(today, -1, TimeUnit::Days); context = context.withFixings(context.fixings().addFixing(euribor, yesterday, 0.0212)); std::printf("%.4f
", euribor.fixing(yesterday, context)); // 0.0212 QuantLib's fixing goes into a global store every Euribor 6M index reads; nanoql's goes into a new context, which the variable now holds and each later call takes. Vanilla swaps // QuantLib auto engine = ext::make_shared<DiscountingSwapEngine>(curveHandle); ext::shared_ptr<VanillaSwap> swap = MakeVanillaSwap(5 * Years, euribor, 0.025) .withNominal(10e6) .withPricingEngine(engine); std::printf("%.2f %.6f
", swap->NPV(), swap->fairRate()); // -23323.32 0.024500 // nanoql VanillaSwap swap = MakeVanillaSwap(Period(5, TimeUnit::Years), euribor) .withFixedRate(0.025) .withNominal(10e6) .toVanillaSwap(context); FixedVsFloatingSwapResults result = DiscountingSwapEngine::calculate(swap, context, curve); std::printf("%.2f %.6f
", *result.NPV(), *result.fairRate()); // -23323.32 0.024500 The builder ends in toVanillaSwap(context), and the engine is a function of the swap, the context and the curve. Overnight swaps // QuantLib Handle<YieldTermStructure> flat( ext::make_shared<FlatForward>(today, 0.036, Actual365Fixed())); auto sofr = ext::make_shared<Sofr>(flat); ext::shared_ptr<OvernightIndexedSwap> ois = MakeOIS(5 * Years, sofr, 0.036) .withNominal(10e6) .withPricingEngine(ext::make_shared<DiscountingSwapEngine>(flat)); std::printf("%.2f %.6f
", ois->NPV(), ois->fairRate()); // 7041.24 0.036154 // nanoql FlatForward flat(today, 0.036, actual365); OvernightIndex sofr = qs.overnightIndex("Sofr", flat); OvernightIndexedSwap ois = MakeOIS(Period(5, TimeUnit::Years), sofr) .withFixedRate(0.036) .withNominal(10e6) .toOvernightIndexedSwap(context); OvernightIndexedSwapResults oisResult = DiscountingSwapEngine::calculate(ois, context, flat); std::printf("%.2f %.6f
", *oisResult.NPV(), *oisResult.fairRate()); // 7041.24 0.036154 Caps and floors // QuantLib ext::shared_ptr<CapFloor> cap = MakeCapFloor(CapFloor::Cap, 5 * Years, euribor, 0.025) .withNominal(10e6); cap->setPricingEngine(ext::make_shared<BlackCapFloorEngine>(curveHandle, 0.20)); std::printf("%.2f
", cap->NPV()); // 117911.83 // nanoql CapFloor cap = MakeCapFloor(CapFloorType::Cap, Period(5, TimeUnit::Years), euribor) .withStrike(0.025) .withNominal(10e6) .toCapFloor(context); InstrumentResults capResult = BlackCapFloorEngine::calculate(cap, context, curve, 0.20); std::printf("%.2f
