docs/migration/from-quantlib-python.html.summary: Migrating from QuantLib-Python nanoql is a .NET library whose types follow QuantLib's, so most QuantLib-Python code maps class by class: the same Date, Euribor6M, PiecewiseLogLinearDiscount or MakeVanillaSwap, written in C#. What changes is how they are connected. This guide pairs QuantLib-Python code with nanoql's for the rates products, each pair building the same trade on the same quotes. The parity table lists every class and function QuantLib-Python constructs, with its nanoql form. nanoql's own bindings for Python (bindings.md) carry the same API to Python, over a native library. The concepts QuantLib-Python nanoql ql.Settings.instance().evaluationDate = today new EvaluationContext { EvaluationDate = today }, passed to each call that reads it ql.SimpleQuote, ql.QuoteHandle a double: a new quote means a new object, built from it ql.YieldTermStructureHandle, ql.RelinkableYieldTermStructureHandle the curve itself, passed where it is used instrument.setPricingEngine(engine), then instrument.NPV() Engine.Calculate(instrument, context, …), returning a results record observers and lazy recalculation the application's layer above the library: rebuild on change, or memoize by inputs (the stateless design) index.addFixing(date, value), held in a global store context.Fixings.AddFixing(index, date, value), held by the context ql.Settings' other flags, ql.IborCoupon.createAtParCoupons() the context's fields: IncludeReferenceDateEvents, UseAtParCoupons, … ql.MakeVanillaSwap(…, nominal=…), keyword arguments new MakeVanillaSwap(…).WithNominal(…), ending in .ToVanillaSwap(context) ql.Date(15, ql.October, 2026), ql.Period(5, ql.Years) new Date(15, Month.October, 2026), new Period(5, TimeUnit.Years) Curves import QuantLib as ql today = ql.Date(15, ql.October, 2026) ql.Settings.instance().evaluationDate = today def quote(rate): return ql.QuoteHandle(ql.SimpleQuote(rate)) swap_quotes = [(2, 0.0225), (3, 0.0232), (5, 0.0245), (7, 0.0256), (10, 0.0270), (15, 0.0283), (20, 0.0288), (30, 0.0285)] helpers = [ ql.DepositRateHelper(quote(0.0205), ql.Euribor(ql.Period(3, ql.Months))), ql.DepositRateHelper(quote(0.0210), ql.Euribor6M()), ] + [ql.SwapRateHelper(quote(rate), ql.EuriborSwapIsdaFixA(ql.Period(years, ql.Years))) for years, rate in swap_quotes] curve = ql.PiecewiseLogLinearDiscount(today, helpers, ql.Actual365Fixed()) curve_handle = ql.YieldTermStructureHandle(curve) (int Years, double Rate)[] swapQuotes = [(2, 0.0225), (3, 0.0232), (5, 0.0245), (7, 0.0256), (10, 0.0270), (15, 0.0283), (20, 0.0288), (30, 0.0285)]; RateHelper[] helpers = [ new DepositRateHelper(0.0205 + shift, new Euribor(new Period(3, TimeUnit.Months)), context), new DepositRateHelper(0.0210 + shift, new Euribor6M(), context), .. swapQuotes.Select(q => new SwapRateHelper(q.Rate + shift, new EuriborSwapIsdaFixA(new Period(q.Years, TimeUnit.Years)), context)), ]; var curve = new PiecewiseLogLinearDiscount(today, helpers, new Actual365Fixed(), context); The helpers take their quotes as numbers and the context, and the curve is passed as itself: there is no handle. Indexes and fixings euribor = ql.Euribor6M(curve_handle) yesterday = euribor.fixingCalendar().advance(today, -1, ql.Days) euribor.addFixing(yesterday, 0.0212) var euribor = new Euribor6M(curve); Date yesterday = euribor.FixingCalendar.Advance(Curves.Today, -1, TimeUnit.Days); EvaluationContext context = Curves.Context with { Fixings = Curves.Context.Fixings.AddFixing(euribor, yesterday, 0.0212), }; Date[] fixingDates = [ yesterday, Curves.Today, euribor.FixingCalendar.Advance(Curves.Today, new Period(6, TimeUnit.Months)), ]; QuantLib-Python's fixing goes into a global store every Euribor 6M index reads; nanoql's goes into the context. Vanilla swaps engine = ql.DiscountingSwapEngine(curve_handle) swap = ql.MakeVanillaSwap(ql.Period(5, ql.Years), euribor, 0.025, nominal=10e6, pricingEngine=engine) print(swap.NPV(), swap.fairRate()) var euribor = new Euribor6M(curve); VanillaSwap spot = new MakeVanillaSwap(new Period(5, TimeUnit.Years), euribor) .WithFixedRate(0.025) .WithNominal(10e6) .ToVanillaSwap(context); VanillaSwap forward = new MakeVanillaSwap(new Period(5, TimeUnit.Years), euribor) .WithForwardStart(new Period(5, TimeUnit.Years)) .WithFixedRate(0.025) .WithNominal(10e6) .ToVanillaSwap(context); FixedVsFloatingSwapResults spotResult = DiscountingSwapEngine.Calculate(spot, context, curve); FixedVsFloatingSwapResults forwardResult = DiscountingSwapEngine.Calculate(forward, context, curve); Overnight swaps flat = ql.YieldTermStructureHandle(ql.FlatForward(today, 0.036, ql.Actual365Fixed())) ois = ql.MakeOIS(ql.Period(5, ql.Years), ql.Sofr(flat), 0.036, nominal=10e6, pricingEngine=ql.DiscountingSwapEngine(flat)) print(ois.NPV(), ois.fairRate()) var today = new Date(15, Month.October, 2026); var context = new EvaluationContext { EvaluationDate = today }; var curve = new FlatForward(today, 0.036, new Actual365Fixed()); OvernightIndexedSwap swap = new MakeOIS(new Period(5, TimeUnit.Years), new Sofr(curve)) .WithFixedRate(0.036) .WithNominal(10e6) .ToOvernightIndexedSwap(context); OvernightIndexedSwapResults result = DiscountingSwapEngine.Calculate(swap, context, curve); Caps and floors cap = ql.MakeCapFloor(ql.CapFloor.Cap, ql.Period(5, ql.Years), euribor, 0.025, nominal=10e6) cap.setPricingEngine(ql.BlackCapFloorEngine(curve_handle, quote(0.20))) print(cap.NPV()) CapFloor capFloor = new MakeCapFloor(type, new Period(5, TimeUnit.Years), new Euribor6M(curve)) .WithStrike(strike) .WithNominal(10e6) .ToCapFloor(context); double black = BlackCapFloorEngine.Calculate(capFloor, context, curve, 0.20).NPV!.Value; double bachelier = BachelierCapFloorEngine.Calculate(capFloor, context, curve, 0.0060).NPV!.Value; Swaptions swap_index = ql.EuriborSwapIsdaFixA(ql.Period(5, ql.Years), curve_handle) swaption = ql.MakeSwaption(swap_index, ql.Period(1, ql.Years), 0.025, nominal=10e6) swaption.setPricingEngine(ql.BlackSwaptionEngine(curve_handle, quote(0.20))) print(swaption.NPV()) var index = new EuriborSwapIsdaFixA(new Period(5, TimeUnit.Years), curve); Swaption swaption = new MakeSwaption(index, new Period(expiry, TimeUnit.Years), strike) .WithNominal(10e6) .ToSwaption(context); double black = BlackSwaptionEngine.Calculate(swaption, context, curve, 0.20).NPV!.Value; double bachelier = BachelierSwaptionEngine.Calculate(swaption, context, curve, 0.0060).NPV!.Value; Each pair gives the same values; the rates guides show nanoql's (swaps, caps and floors, swaptions).

docs/rates/basis-and-fx.html.summary: Basis swaps and FX A basis swap between two Euribor tenors, an FX forward, and a curve implied by FX swap points, all on the stable API; then, experimental, a curve from cross-currency basis swaps. The market is flat: €STR at 2.80%, dollars at 4.00%, and EUR/USD at 1.0850. A basis swap Euribor 3M plus a spread against Euribor 6M, each forecast on its own curve and both discounted on €STR, as a FloatFloatSwap. A spread is linear in the 3M leg's coupons, so the leg's BPS gives the fair spread: var euribor3M = new Euribor3M(new FlatForward(context.EvaluationDate, 0.0295, new Actual365Fixed())); var euribor6M = new Euribor6M(new FlatForward(context.EvaluationDate, 0.0305, new Actual365Fixed())); Calendar calendar = new TARGET(); Date start = calendar.Advance(context.EvaluationDate, 2, TimeUnit.Days); Date end = calendar.Advance(start, 5, TimeUnit.Years, BusinessDayConvention.ModifiedFollowing); Schedule Quarterly() => new MakeSchedule().From(start).To(end).WithTenor(euribor3M.Tenor).WithCalendar(calendar) .WithConvention(BusinessDayConvention.ModifiedFollowing).ToSchedule(); Schedule Semiannual() => new MakeSchedule().From(start).To(end).WithTenor(euribor6M.Tenor).WithCalendar(calendar) .WithConvention(BusinessDayConvention.ModifiedFollowing).ToSchedule(); FloatFloatSwap Swap(double spread) => new(SwapType.Payer, 10e6, 10e6, Quarterly(), euribor3M, new Actual360(), Semiannual(), euribor6M, new Actual360(), context, spread1: spread); SwapResults flat = DiscountingSwapEngine.Calculate(Swap(0.0), context, EurDiscount); // A spread of one basis point on the 3M leg moves that leg's NPV by its BPS. double fairSpread = -flat.NPV!.Value / flat.LegBPS[0]!.Value * 1e-4; SwapResults atFair = DiscountingSwapEngine.Calculate(Swap(fairSpread), context, EurDiscount); 3M + spread against 6M Spread NPV Flat 0.00 bp 47,324.97 At the fair spread 10.0320 bp 0.00 An FX forward Euros sold for dollars in a year, valued from the two discount curves and spot; struck at its fair rate, it is worth nothing: Date maturity = new TARGET().Advance(context.EvaluationDate, 1, TimeUnit.Years); var probe = new FxForward(10e6, new EURCurrency(), new USDCurrency(), Spot, maturity, true); double fair = DiscountingFxForwardEngine.Calculate(probe, context, EurDiscount, UsdDiscount, Spot).FairForwardRate!.Value; var forward = new FxForward(10e6, new EURCurrency(), new USDCurrency(), fair, maturity, true); FxForwardResults result = DiscountingFxForwardEngine.Calculate(forward, context, EurDiscount, UsdDiscount, Spot); One-year EUR/USD forward Value Spot 1.0850 Fair forward rate 1.098026 NPV of €10 million sold forward at that rate, in dollars 0.00 A curve from FX swap points A euro curve, collateralized in dollars, bootstrapped from EUR/USD swap points with FxSwapRateHelper: (Period Tenor, double Points)[] quotes = [ (new Period(1, TimeUnit.Months), 0.0010), (new Period(3, TimeUnit.Months), 0.0031), (new Period(6, TimeUnit.Months), 0.0062), (new Period(1, TimeUnit.Years), 0.0125), ]; var helpers = quotes.Select(q => new FxSwapRateHelper(q.Points, Spot, q.Tenor, 2, new TARGET(), BusinessDayConvention.Following, false, false, UsdDiscount, context)).ToList(); var eurCurve = new PiecewiseYieldCurve<Discount, LogLinear, IterativeBootstrap>( context.EvaluationDate, helpers, new Actual365Fixed(), context); The curve gives back each quote: Tenor Swap points Implied by the curve 1M 10.00 10.00 3M 31.00 31.00 6M 62.00 62.00 1Y 125.00 125.00 Experimental: a curve from cross-currency basis swaps The cross-currency basis-swap helpers are experimental, as QuantLib's are: their members can change in any release. Using them needs the opt-in, NQL0001 in C# (here a #pragma in the sample's own file) and import nanoql.experimental in Python (concepts). A euro curve bootstrapped from EUR/USD basis swaps on €STR and SOFR, collateralized in dollars: var estr = new Estr(BasisAndFx.EurDiscount); var sofr = new Sofr(BasisAndFx.UsdDiscount); (int Years, double Basis)[] quotes = [(1, -0.0008), (2, -0.0010), (3, -0.0012), (5, -0.0013)]; var helpers = quotes.Select(q => new ConstNotionalCrossCurrencyBasisSwapRateHelper( q.Basis, new Period(q.Years, TimeUnit.Years), 2, new TARGET(), BusinessDayConvention.ModifiedFollowing, false, estr, sofr, BasisAndFx.UsdDiscount, isFxBaseCurrencyCollateralCurrency: false, isBasisOnFxBaseCurrencyLeg: true, context, paymentFrequency: Frequency.Quarterly)).ToList(); var eurCurve = new PiecewiseYieldCurve<Discount, LogLinear, IterativeBootstrap>( context.EvaluationDate, helpers, new Actual365Fixed(), context); Tenor Quoted basis Implied by the curve 1Y -8.00 bp -8.00 bp 2Y -10.00 bp -10.00 bp 3Y -12.00 bp -12.00 bp 5Y -13.00 bp -13.00 bp

docs/rates/caps-and-floors.html.title: Caps and floors | nanoql
docs/rates/caps-and-floors.html.summary: Caps and floors A cap is a strip of calls on an index's fixings, a floor a strip of puts. MakeCapFloor builds one from its type, a tenor and an Ibor index, as QuantLib's does: the strike, if not given, is the at-the-money rate of its floating leg. Pricing on a volatility Six five-year Euribor caps and floors on the curve of the curves guide, each priced on a 20% lognormal volatility and on a 0.60% normal one: CapFloor capFloor = new MakeCapFloor(type, new Period(5, TimeUnit.Years), new Euribor6M(curve)) .WithStrike(strike) .WithNominal(10e6) .ToCapFloor(context); double black = BlackCapFloorEngine.Calculate(capFloor, context, curve, 0.20).NPV!.Value; double bachelier = BachelierCapFloorEngine.Calculate(capFloor, context, curve, 0.0060).NPV!.Value; Instrument Strike Black, 20% Bachelier, 0.60% 5Y cap 2.00% 229,957.18 264,017.50 5Y cap 2.50% 117,911.83 143,622.77 5Y cap 3.00% 60,714.26 71,205.32 5Y floor 2.00% 44,329.30 78,389.63 5Y floor 2.50% 145,330.81 171,041.75 5Y floor 3.00% 301,180.09 311,671.15 BlackCapFloorEngine prices each caplet by Black's formula, BachelierCapFloorEngine by Bachelier's. Each takes a volatility as a number, as here, or as an optionlet volatility structure: ConstantOptionletVolatility, or one stripped from a cap volatility surface (OptionletStripper1, StrippedOptionletAdapter). A shifted lognormal volatility takes its displacement as a further argument.

docs/rates/curves.html.title: Curves | nanoql
docs/rates/curves.html.summary: Curves A yield curve gives discount factors, zero rates and forward rates from its reference date. FlatForward is the simplest; a bootstrapped curve fits the market's quotes. Bootstrapping Each quote becomes a rate helper: a deposit, a FRA, a futures contract, a swap or an overnight swap. The piecewise curve finds, pillar by pillar, the values that reprice every helper. This one bootstraps a Euribor 6M curve from two deposits and eight swaps, on illustrative quotes: (int Years, double Rate)[] swapQuotes = [(2, 0.0225), (3, 0.0232), (5, 0.0245), (7, 0.0256), (10, 0.0270), (15, 0.0283), (20, 0.0288), (30, 0.0285)]; RateHelper[] helpers = [ new DepositRateHelper(0.0205 + shift, new Euribor(new Period(3, TimeUnit.Months)), context), new DepositRateHelper(0.0210 + shift, new Euribor6M(), context), .. swapQuotes.Select(q => new SwapRateHelper(q.Rate + shift, new EuriborSwapIsdaFixA(new Period(q.Years, TimeUnit.Years)), context)), ]; var curve = new PiecewiseLogLinearDiscount(today, helpers, new Actual365Fixed(), context); A helper takes its quote as a number and the context it is dated in. The curve runs its bootstrap when it is built, and is immutable from then on: a new quote means a new curve. The curve's name gives what it interpolates and how. PiecewiseLogLinearDiscount interpolates the log of the discount factors linearly; PiecewiseLinearZero, PiecewiseCubicZero, PiecewiseFlatForward and the rest are QuantLib's other choices, and PiecewiseYieldCurve<TTraits, TInterpolator, TBootstrap> takes them as type arguments. The GlobalPiecewise curves fit every pillar at once, with QuantLib's global bootstrap. Reading it DayCounter dc = new Actual365Fixed(); foreach (int years in new[] { 1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 25 }) { Date d = Today + new Period(years, TimeUnit.Years); double discount = curve.Discount(d); double zero = curve.ZeroRate(d, dc, Compounding.Continuous).Rate; double forward = curve.ForwardRate(d, d + new Period(6, TimeUnit.Months), new Actual360(), Compounding.Simple).Rate; table.Add($"{years}Y", Table.D(d), Table.N(discount, 6), Table.Percent(zero), Table.Percent(forward)); } Tenor Date Discount Zero rate 6M forward 1Y 2027-10-15 0.978380 2.1857% 2.2388% 2Y 2028-10-15 0.956486 2.2214% 2.4126% 5Y 2031-10-15 0.885807 2.4238% 2.7943% 10Y 2036-10-15 0.764483 2.6833% 3.0842% 20Y 2046-10-15 0.562262 2.8770% 2.7046% 25Y 2051-10-15 0.490797 2.8450% 2.6977% ZeroRate and ForwardRate return an InterestRate, the rate with its day counter, compounding and frequency. Other curves Multi-curve: an €STR curve for discounting and a Euribor curve bootstrapped on it, each swap helper given the discounting curve (multi-curve bootstrapping). Interpolated curves from given nodes: InterpolatedDiscountCurve<TInterpolator>, InterpolatedZeroCurve<TInterpolator>, InterpolatedForwardCurve<TInterpolator>. Spreaded curves over another curve: ZeroSpreadedTermStructure, ForwardSpreadedTermStructure, and the piecewise spreads. Fitted bond curves, the Nelson-Siegel family and splines: FittedBondDiscountCurve with its fitting methods.

docs/rates/dates-and-calendars.html.title: Dates and calendars | nanoql
docs/rates/dates-and-calendars.html.summary: Dates and calendars Date is a day, Period a length of time in days, weeks, months or years, and a Calendar knows its market's business days. Each is an immutable value, as in QuantLib: new Date(23, Month.December, 2026), new Period(6, TimeUnit.Months). Rolling dates A calendar advances a date by business days or by a period, and adjusts a date that falls on a holiday by a business-day convention: var calendar = new TARGET(); var trade = new Date(23, Month.December, 2026); Date spot = calendar.Advance(trade, 2, TimeUnit.Days); Date oneYear = calendar.Advance(spot, new Period(1, TimeUnit.Years), BusinessDayConvention.ModifiedFollowing); Date endOfMonth = calendar.Adjust(new Date(31, Month.October, 2026), BusinessDayConvention.ModifiedFollowing); Date Weekday Business day 2026-12-23 Wednesday yes 2026-12-28 Monday yes 2027-12-28 Tuesday yes 2026-10-30 Friday yes Spot from 23 December is the 28th: TARGET closes on the 25th and 26th. The 31st of October 2026 is a Saturday, and modified following rolls it back to the Friday rather than into November. The calendars are QuantLib's, each a sealed class: TARGET, UnitedStates and UnitedKingdom with their markets, and the rest by country. JointCalendar combines several, and BespokeCalendar is one of your own. Adding a holiday returns a new calendar, and leaves the original as it was. With the NanoQL.Extensions package a calendar's holidays can be changed as data (conventions.md). Schedules and day counts MakeSchedule builds a coupon schedule as QuantLib's does, and each day counter gives a period's accrual fraction: Schedule schedule = new MakeSchedule() .From(spot) .To(calendar.Advance(spot, new Period(2, TimeUnit.Years))) .WithFrequency(Frequency.Semiannual) .WithCalendar(calendar) .WithConvention(BusinessDayConvention.ModifiedFollowing) .ToSchedule(); DayCounter[] dayCounters = [ new Actual360(), new Actual365Fixed(), new Thirty360(Thirty360Convention.BondBasis), new ActualActual(ActualActualConvention.ISDA), ]; Start End Days Actual/360 Actual/365 (Fixed) 30/360 Actual/Actual (ISDA) 2026-12-28 2027-06-28 182 0.505556 0.498630 0.500000 0.498630 2027-06-28 2027-12-28 183 0.508333 0.501370 0.500000 0.501370 2027-12-28 2028-06-28 183 0.508333 0.501370 0.500000 0.500030 2028-06-28 2028-12-28 183 0.508333 0.501370 0.500000 0.500000 Actual/Actual (ISDA) counts each day over its own year's length, so the periods in 2028, a leap year, differ from Actual/365 (Fixed).

docs/rates/indexes-and-fixings.html.title: Indexes and fixings | nanoql
docs/rates/indexes-and-fixings.html.summary: Indexes and fixings An index knows its conventions (its tenor, fixing days, calendar, day counter and currency) and holds the curve it forecasts from. The Ibor indexes (Euribor6M, USDLibor, Tibor, …) and the overnight ones (Sofr, Estr, Sonia, Tonar, Corra, …) are QuantLib's presets. Past fixings and forecasts A past fixing is stored in the evaluation context's Fixings; a fixing on a later date is forecast from the index's curve. Today's fixing is the stored one if there is one, and otherwise forecast when asked to: var euribor = new Euribor6M(curve); Date yesterday = euribor.FixingCalendar.Advance(Curves.Today, -1, TimeUnit.Days); EvaluationContext context = Curves.Context with { Fixings = Curves.Context.Fixings.AddFixing(euribor, yesterday, 0.0212), }; Date[] fixingDates = [ yesterday, Curves.Today, euribor.FixingCalendar.Advance(Curves.Today, new Period(6, TimeUnit.Months)), ]; double fixing = euribor.Fixing(d, context, forecastTodaysFixing: true); Date valueDate = euribor.ValueDate(d); Date maturity = euribor.MaturityDate(valueDate); Fixing date Value date Maturity Fixing Source 2026-10-14 2026-10-16 2027-04-16 2.1200% stored 2026-10-15 2026-10-19 2027-04-19 2.1000% forecast 2027-04-15 2027-04-19 2027-10-19 2.2388% forecast AddFixing returns a new store, so a context's fixings never change under it. A fixing the store lacks on a past date is refused, with the date and the index's name, as QuantLib refuses it. The same index on another curve An index built without a curve can still be read for its past fixings and its dates. index.Clone(curve) gives the same index forecasting from another curve, as QuantLib's clone does. Conventions The presets take QuantLib's values. With the NanoQL.Extensions package an index's conventions can be overridden, and a family member added (Euribor at two months, say), as data (conventions.md).

docs/rates/multi-curve.html.title: Multi-curve bootstrapping | nanoql
docs/rates/multi-curve.html.summary: Multi-curve bootstrapping This page follows QuantLib's MulticurveBootstrapping example: an overnight curve from OIS quotes, then a Euribor 6M curve bootstrapped from a deposit, FRAs and swaps discounted on it, the swaps priced with each curve in its role. Its values match that example's output. The example's quotes are Eonia's, here taken as €STR's, whose conventions are the same. The sample, MulticurveBootstrapping.cs, carries QuantLib's notice. The discounting curve €STR from overnight, tomorrow-next and spot-next deposits, short OIS, OIS between ECB meeting dates, and OIS out to 30 years, on 11 December 2012. Both curves interpolate the discounts' logarithms by a monotonic cubic spline, QuantLib's MonotonicLogCubic: Calendar calendar = new TARGET(); Date today = context.EvaluationDate; var estr = new Estr(); var helpers = new List<BootstrapHelper<YieldTermStructure>>(); // Overnight, tomorrow-next and spot-next deposits. foreach (int fixingDays in new[] { 0, 1, 2 }) { helpers.Add(new DepositRateHelper(0.0004, new Period(1, TimeUnit.Days), fixingDays, calendar, BusinessDayConvention.Following, false, new Actual360(), context)); } // Short OIS, then OIS between ECB meeting dates, then long OIS. foreach (var (n, unit, rate) in new[] { (1, TimeUnit.Weeks, 0.00070), (2, TimeUnit.Weeks, 0.00069), (3, TimeUnit.Weeks, 0.00078), (1, TimeUnit.Months, 0.00074), }) { helpers.Add(new OISRateHelper(2, new Period(n, unit), rate, estr, context)); } foreach (var (start, end, rate) in new[] { (new Date(16, Month.January, 2013), new Date(13, Month.February, 2013), 0.000460), (new Date(13, Month.February, 2013), new Date(13, Month.March, 2013), 0.000160), (new Date(13, Month.March, 2013), new Date(10, Month.April, 2013), -0.000070), (new Date(10, Month.April, 2013), new Date(8, Month.May, 2013), -0.000130), (new Date(8, Month.May, 2013), new Date(12, Month.June, 2013), -0.000140), }) { helpers.Add(new OISRateHelper(start, end, rate, estr, context)); } foreach (var (n, unit, rate) in new[] { (15, TimeUnit.Months, 0.00002), (18, TimeUnit.Months, 0.00008), (21, TimeUnit.Months, 0.00021), (2, TimeUnit.Years, 0.00036), (3, TimeUnit.Years, 0.00127), (4, TimeUnit.Years, 0.00274), (5, TimeUnit.Years, 0.00456), (6, TimeUnit.Years, 0.00647), (7, TimeUnit.Years, 0.00827), (8, TimeUnit.Years, 0.00996), (9, TimeUnit.Years, 0.01147), (10, TimeUnit.Years, 0.0128), (11, TimeUnit.Years, 0.01404), (12, TimeUnit.Years, 0.01516), (15, TimeUnit.Years, 0.01764), (20, TimeUnit.Years, 0.01939), (25, TimeUnit.Years, 0.02003), (30, TimeUnit.Years, 0.02038), }) { helpers.Add(new OISRateHelper(2, new Period(n, unit), rate, estr, context)); } // QuantLib's MonotonicLogCubic: a cubic spline on the discounts' logarithms, Hyman's filter keeping it monotonic. YieldTermStructure estrCurve = new PiecewiseLogCubicDiscount(today, helpers, new Actual365Fixed(), context, i: new LogCubic(CubicInterpolationDerivativeApprox.Spline, monotonic: true)).EnableExtrapolation(); The forecasting curve Euribor 6M from the 6M deposit, FRAs starting in one to eighteen months, and swaps out to 60 years. Each swap helper takes the €STR curve as its discounting curve, so the bootstrap solves for the Euribor forwards that price each swap at its quote with €STR discounting: Calendar calendar = new TARGET(); Date settlement = calendar.Advance(context.EvaluationDate, 2, TimeUnit.Days); var euribor6M = new Euribor6M(); var helpers = new List<BootstrapHelper<YieldTermStructure>> { new DepositRateHelper(0.00312, new Period(6, TimeUnit.Months), 3, calendar, BusinessDayConvention.Following, false, new Actual360(), context), }; // FRAs starting in 1 to 18 months, each on Euribor 6M. double[] fras = [ 0.002930, 0.002720, 0.002600, 0.002560, 0.002520, 0.002480, 0.002540, 0.002610, 0.002670, 0.002790, 0.002910, 0.003030, 0.003180, 0.003350, 0.003520, 0.003710, 0.003890, 0.004090, ]; for (int months = 1; months <= fras.Length; ++months) { helpers.Add(new FraRateHelper(fras[months - 1], months, euribor6M, context)); } // Swaps against Euribor 6M, annual 30/360 fixed legs, discounted on the €STR curve. foreach (var (years, rate) in new[] { (3, 0.004240), (4, 0.005760), (5, fiveYearQuote), (6, 0.009540), (7, 0.011350), (8, 0.013030), (9, 0.014520), (10, 0.015840), (12, 0.018090), (15, 0.020370), (20, 0.021870), (25, 0.022340), (30, 0.022560), (35, 0.022950), (40, 0.023480), (50, 0.024210), (60, 0.024630), }) { helpers.Add(new SwapRateHelper(rate, new Period(years, TimeUnit.Years), calendar, Frequency.Annual, BusinessDayConvention.Unadjusted, new Thirty360(Thirty360Convention.European), euribor6M, context, discountingCurve: estrCurve)); } YieldTermStructure euriborCurve = new PiecewiseLogCubicDiscount(settlement, helpers, new Actual365Fixed(), context, i: new LogCubic(CubicInterpolationDerivativeApprox.Spline, monotonic: true), bootstrap: new IterativeBootstrap(1.0e-15)); Two swaps on the two curves A five-year payer swap at 0.70%, and the same swap starting a year forward, each forecast on Euribor 6M and discounted on €STR; then both again on a Euribor curve built on a five-year quote of 0.90%: YieldTermStructure euriborCurve = Euribor6MCurve(estrCurve, fiveYearQuote); Calendar calendar = new TARGET(); Date settlement = calendar.Advance(context.EvaluationDate, 2, TimeUnit.Days); SwapValue Value(string label, Date start) { Date maturity = start + new Period(5, TimeUnit.Years); var fixedSchedule = new Schedule(start, maturity, new Period(Frequency.Annual), calendar, BusinessDayConvention.Unadjusted, BusinessDayConvention.Unadjusted, DateGenerationRule.Forward, false, context); var floatSchedule = new Schedule(start, maturity, new Period(Frequency.Semiannual), calendar, BusinessDayConvention.ModifiedFollowing, BusinessDayConvention.ModifiedFollowing, DateGenerationRule.Forward, false, context); var swap = new VanillaSwap(SwapType.Payer, 1_000_000.0, fixedSchedule, 0.007, new Thirty360(Thirty360Convention.European), floatSchedule, new Euribor6M(euriborCurve), 0.0, new Actual360(), context); // Forecast on the Euribor curve, discounted on €STR. var result = DiscountingSwapEngine.Calculate(swap, context, estrCurve); return new SwapValue(label, result.NPV!.Value, result.FairSpread!.Value, result.FairRate!.Value); } SwapValue[] values = [ Value("5-year swap paying 0.70%", settlement), Value("5-year swap a year forward, paying 0.70%", calendar.Advance(settlement, 1, TimeUnit.Years)), ]; 5Y swap quote Swap NPV Fair spread Fair fixed rate 0.76% 5-year swap paying 0.70% 3,076.04 -0.06% 0.76% 0.76% 5-year swap a year forward, paying 0.70% 19,202.54 -0.38% 1.09% 0.90% 5-year swap paying 0.70% 9,922.71 -0.20% 0.90% 0.90% 5-year swap a year forward, paying 0.70% 19,202.54 -0.38% 1.09% The spot swap's fair rate is the five-year quote, the bootstrap's condition. The forward swap's value doesn't move with that quote: its floating leg runs from one year to six, and the deposit and FRAs fix the leg to one year while the six-year quote fixes the leg to six, each on €STR discounting. A new quote is a new curve: the forecasting curve is built again from its helpers, the €STR curve unchanged.

docs/rates/sabr.html.title: A SABR smile | nanoql
docs/rates/sabr.html.summary: A SABR smile The 1Y into 10Y swaption smile of QuantLib's swaption cube tests' market data: an at-the-money vol and the market's spreads to it at four strikes about the forward, fitted by SABR with β fixed. The fit's values match QuantLib's on the same data. The sample, SabrSmile.cs, carries QuantLib's notice. The smile A flat 5% curve on 15 October 2026, the ten-year Euribor swap rate a year forward, and its quotes: 14.70% at the money, and the spreads to it at −200, −50, +50 and +200 bp: // A flat 5% curve, and the ten-year swap the option is on. YieldTermStructure curve = new FlatForward(today, 0.05, new Actual365Fixed()); var swapIndex = new EuriborSwapIsdaFixA(new Period(10, TimeUnit.Years), curve); Date optionDate = new TARGET().Advance(today, new Period(1, TimeUnit.Years), BusinessDayConvention.ModifiedFollowing); double expiry = new Actual365Fixed().YearFraction(today, optionDate); double forward = swapIndex.Fixing(optionDate, context); // The market's quotes: 14.70% at the money, and the spreads to it at four strikes about the forward. double[] strikeSpreads = [-0.020, -0.005, 0.0, 0.005, 0.020]; double[] volSpreads = [0.0729, 0.0086, 0.0, -0.0024, 0.0098]; double[] strikes = [.. strikeSpreads.Select(s => forward + s)]; double[] quotes = [.. volSpreads.Select(s => 0.1470 + s)]; The fit SABRInterpolation fits α, ν and ρ with β fixed at 0.5, minimizing the vols' errors weighted by the strikes' Black vegas, from SABR's default guesses: // β fixed at 0.5; α, ν and ρ fitted from SABR's default guesses, the errors weighted by the strikes' vegas. var sabr = new SABRInterpolation(strikes, quotes, expiry, forward, alpha: null, beta: 0.5, nu: null, rho: null, alphaIsFixed: false, betaIsFixed: true, nuIsFixed: false, rhoIsFixed: false); SABR Value Forward 5.1316% α 0.032567 β (fixed) 0.5 ν 0.522132 ρ -0.084029 Root-mean-square error 0.0491% Maximum error 0.1597% The smile section The fitted parameters as a SabrSmileSection, the smile an engine reads at any strike: // The fitted parameters as a smile section, the smile an engine or a cube reads at any strike. var section = new SabrSmileSection(expiry, forward, [sabr.Alpha, sabr.Beta, sabr.Nu, sabr.Rho]); The smile on a 50 bp grid, beside the quotes: Strike against the forward Strike Quote SABR -200 bp 3.1316% 21.99% 21.8303% -150 bp 3.6316% 19.2484% -100 bp 4.1316% 17.1568% -50 bp 4.6316% 15.56% 15.6055% 0 bp 5.1316% 14.70% 14.6913% +50 bp 5.6316% 14.46% 14.4276% +100 bp 6.1316% 14.6552% +150 bp 6.6316% 15.1568% +200 bp 7.1316% 15.68% 15.7784% Five quotes and three free parameters leave a residual: the fit misses the wing quotes by up to 0.16 vol points, and gives the smile between them.

docs/rates/short-rate-models.html.title: Short-rate models | nanoql
docs/rates/short-rate-models.html.summary: Short-rate models This page follows QuantLib's BermudanSwaption example: short-rate models calibrated to five co-terminal swaptions, then a Bermudan swaption priced on them. Its values match that example's output, but for those marked † and ‡, which two of nanoql's documented fixes of QuantLib move. The sample, ShortRateModels.cs, carries QuantLib's notice. The example's fourth model, Black-Karasinski, is left out: only the tree prices its swaptions, so nothing would check its values. The market A flat curve, Euribor 6M on it, and the swaptions 1Y into 5Y, 2Y into 4Y, … 5Y into 1Y, each with its market vol: Calendar calendar = new TARGET(); var settlement = new Date(19, Month.February, 2002); YieldTermStructure curve = new FlatForward(settlement, 0.04875825, new Actual365Fixed()); var index = new Euribor6M(curve); // The co-terminal swaptions: 1Y into 5Y, 2Y into 4Y, ... 5Y into 1Y. double[] marketVols = [0.1148, 0.1108, 0.1070, 0.1021, 0.1000]; var helpers = new List<SwaptionHelper>(); var times = new List<double>(); for (int i = 0; i < 5; ++i) { var helper = new SwaptionHelper(new Period(i + 1, TimeUnit.Years), new Period(5 - i, TimeUnit.Years), marketVols[i], index, index.Tenor, index.DayCounter, index.DayCounter, curve, context); helpers.Add(helper); times.AddRange(helper.Times(context)); } var grid = new TimeGrid([.. times], 30); Calibration G2 on its analytic formula, Hull-White on Jamshidian's, and Hull-White again on a tree, each by Levenberg-Marquardt: var optimizer = new LevenbergMarquardt(); var endCriteria = new EndCriteria(400, 100, 1.0e-8, 1.0e-8, 1.0e-8); (TModel Model, List<SwaptionHelper> Helpers) Calibrate<TModel>( TModel model, Func<Swaption, EvaluationContext, TModel, InstrumentResults> engine) where TModel : ICalibratedModel { List<SwaptionHelper> priced = [.. helpers.Select(h => h.SetPricingEngine(engine))]; return (model.Calibrate(priced.Cast<CalibrationHelper>(), optimizer, endCriteria, context).Model, priced); } var g2 = Calibrate(new G2(curve), (s, c, m) => G2SwaptionEngine.Calculate(s, c, m, 6.0, 16)); var hullWhite = Calibrate(new HullWhite(curve), (s, c, m) => JamshidianSwaptionEngine.Calculate(s, c, m)); var numerical = Calibrate(new HullWhite(curve), (s, c, m) => TreeSwaptionEngine.Calculate(s, c, m, grid)); Each swaption's value on the calibrated model, as a Black vol, beside its market vol: Model Swaption Model vol Market vol G2 † 1Y into 5Y 10.63458% 11.48000% G2 † 2Y into 4Y 10.64501% 11.08000% G2 † 3Y into 3Y 10.62873% 10.70000% G2 † 4Y into 2Y 10.63652% 10.21000% G2 † 5Y into 1Y 10.65230% 10.00000% Hull-White 1Y into 5Y 10.62037% 11.48000% Hull-White 2Y into 4Y 10.62959% 11.08000% Hull-White 3Y into 3Y 10.63414% 10.70000% Hull-White 4Y into 2Y 10.64428% 10.21000% Hull-White 5Y into 1Y 10.66131% 10.00000% Hull-White, numerical ‡ 1Y into 5Y 10.31183% 11.48000% Hull-White, numerical ‡ 2Y into 4Y 10.54617% 11.08000% Hull-White, numerical ‡ 3Y into 3Y 10.66911% 10.70000% Hull-White, numerical ‡ 4Y into 2Y 10.74017% 10.21000% Hull-White, numerical ‡ 5Y into 1Y 10.79723% 10.00000% Model Calibrated parameters G2 † a 0.046794, σ 0.0088295, b 0.046794, η 0.0088295, ρ -0.77927 Hull-White a 0.046416, σ 0.0058693 Hull-White, numerical ‡ a 0.055232, σ 0.0061063 A Bermudan swaption A payer swaption into the five-year swap, exercisable on each fixed coupon's start, at the money, out of it (the strike 1.2 times) and in it (0.8 times), on each model's tree and by finite differences: Date start = calendar.Advance(settlement, 1, TimeUnit.Years, BusinessDayConvention.ModifiedFollowing); docs/rates/swaps.html.title: Swaps | nanoql
docs/rates/swaps.html.summary: Swaps The builders make swaps as QuantLib's do: MakeVanillaSwap from a tenor and an Ibor index, MakeOIS from a tenor and an overnight index, each option not given taking the index's conventions or QuantLib's default. A builder ends in ToVanillaSwap(context) or ToOvernightIndexedSwap(context), the context giving the evaluation date its start is counted from. A vanilla swap Two five-year payer swaps on Euribor 6M at 2.50%, one spot and one starting in five years, on the curve of the curves guide, which forecasts and discounts: var euribor = new Euribor6M(curve); VanillaSwap spot = new MakeVanillaSwap(new Period(5, TimeUnit.Years), euribor) .WithFixedRate(0.025) .WithNominal(10e6) .ToVanillaSwap(context); VanillaSwap forward = new MakeVanillaSwap(new Period(5, TimeUnit.Years), euribor) .WithForwardStart(new Period(5, TimeUnit.Years)) .WithFixedRate(0.025) .WithNominal(10e6) .ToVanillaSwap(context); FixedVsFloatingSwapResults spotResult = DiscountingSwapEngine.Calculate(spot, context, curve); FixedVsFloatingSwapResults forwardResult = DiscountingSwapEngine.Calculate(forward, context, curve); An overnight swap OvernightIndexedSwap ois = new MakeOIS(new Period(5, TimeUnit.Years), new Estr(curve)) .WithFixedRate(0.025) .WithNominal(10e6) .ToOvernightIndexedSwap(context); OvernightIndexedSwapResults oisResult = DiscountingSwapEngine.Calculate(ois, context, curve); Here €STR forecasts from the Euribor curve, to keep the example short; a desk's €STR swap would take an €STR curve, bootstrapped from €STR swaps. The results Swap NPV Fair rate Fixed leg BPS 5Y payer at 2.50%, spot -23,323.32 2.4500% -4,664.66 5Y payer at 2.50%, 5Y forward 197,846.96 2.9871% -4,061.51 5Y €STR payer at 2.50% -40,175.14 2.4151% -4,732.07 DiscountingSwapEngine.Calculate returns the swap's NPV, its fair rate and fair spread, and each leg's NPV and basis-point value, the fixed leg first. A results record is a value: comparing two compares every result. Other swaps The same engine prices FloatFloatSwap, ZeroCouponSwap and a Swap of any legs, each with its own results record; the cross-currency swaps have engines of their own. A leg is built by its builder (FixedRateLeg, IborLeg, OvernightLeg and the rest), from a schedule.

docs/rates/swaptions.html.title: Swaptions | nanoql
docs/rates/swaptions.html.summary: Swaptions A European swaption is the right to enter a swap on its expiry. MakeSwaption builds one from a swap index, whose conventions give the underlying swap, an expiry and a strike, as QuantLib's does; the strike, if not given, is the underlying's fair rate. Pricing on a volatility Payer swaptions into a five-year Euribor swap, expiring in one year and in five, on the curve of the curves guide, each priced on a 20% lognormal volatility and on a 0.60% normal one: var index = new EuriborSwapIsdaFixA(new Period(5, TimeUnit.Years), curve); Swaption swaption = new MakeSwaption(index, new Period(expiry, TimeUnit.Years), strike) .WithNominal(10e6) .ToSwaption(context); double black = BlackSwaptionEngine.Calculate(swaption, context, curve, 0.20).NPV!.Value; double bachelier = BachelierSwaptionEngine.Calculate(swaption, context, curve, 0.0060).NPV!.Value; Swaption Strike Black, 20% Bachelier, 0.60% 1Y into 5Y payer 2.50% 111,256.85 127,924.14 1Y into 5Y payer 3.00% 32,834.57 38,957.46 5Y into 5Y payer 2.50% 311,110.95 330,436.01 5Y into 5Y payer 3.00% 212,463.69 214,752.13 BlackSwaptionEngine prices by Black's formula and BachelierSwaptionEngine by Bachelier's, on the annuity of the underlying's fixed leg. Each takes a volatility as a number, as here, or as a swaption volatility structure: a constant, a matrix by expiry and tenor (SwaptionVolatilityMatrix), or a cube with a smile (SabrSwaptionVolatilityCube, InterpolatedSwaptionVolatilityCube). Bermudan swaptions A swaption with several exercise dates is priced on a short-rate model: TreeSwaptionEngine on any model with a tree (Hull-White, Black-Karasinski, …), FdHullWhiteSwaptionEngine and FdG2SwaptionEngine by finite differences, and Gaussian1dSwaptionEngine on the Gaussian1d models. JamshidianSwaptionEngine prices a European one on an affine model in closed form.

docs/releasing.html.title: Releasing nanoql | nanoql
docs/releasing.html.summary: Releasing nanoql A release publishes, from one commit and its tag: On NuGet: NanoQL, NanoQL.Extensions, NanoQL.Bind and NanoQL.Excel, each with its symbol package on NuGet's symbol server. On PyPI: nanoql, a wheel per platform the release ships: win_amd64 and manylinux_2_28_x86_64, and win_arm64, manylinux_2_28_aarch64 and macosx_14_0_arm64 once those platforms ship; no source distribution, since one would need the .NET SDK and the whole repository to build. On GitHub, the release v<version>: the C archive (the C and C++ headers, the library and its CMake package) and the native symbols archive for each platform the release ships, the Excel add-in's zip and its symbols zip, SHA256SUMS over them, and the notes: CHANGELOG.md's section with the platforms' readings from the release run's own tests. The platforms it ships are release.yml's RIDS, the bindings legs its ci call runs: Windows x64 and Linux x64 (ci.yml's core). A later release adds Windows Arm64, Linux Arm64 or macOS on Apple silicon once its leg is green, by naming it in RIDS and in the set the ci call names, ci.yml's matrix gaining one where none fits; a published release's files don't grow, so a platform ships from its first release on. The site, nanoql.org, built from the tag. The notebook, docs/notebooks/first-steps.ipynb, isn't published: Colab opens it from main and its first cell installs the latest release from PyPI, so it uses released API alone. notebook.yml runs it so, weekly and on a pull request that changes it. What can't be undone Every name and file is permanent from its first upload. nuget.org deletes no package: a mistake is unlisted and deprecated, and a fix ships as the next version (2.0.1). PyPI never takes a deleted file's name again: a mistake is yanked, and a fix ships as the next version. A published GitHub Release keeps its files (immutable releases): a fix is a new release. The site redeploys from a later commit. Before the tag The release commit: the versions in step (python -I tools/release/versions.py v<version> checks the bindings tool's, the C header's, surface.json's, Directory.Build.props's, the wheel's and the Java layer's); the shipped names frozen (dotnet run --project src/NanoQL.Bind -c Release -- freeze, once check and excel check are green); the README's validation statement written from the release's gates run (tools/docs/validation-report.py --readme); CHANGELOG.md's section for the version. The checks CI can't run, on the release commit: the suite inside Excel, python -I bindings/excel/xltests/run.py on a machine with 64-bit Excel (CONTRIBUTING.md); a red stops the release; the SOFR example's trades (docs/sofr-example.md) priced again by an independent pricer, each within $0.01 on $10 million; a residual past it stops the release. The dry run: release.yml dispatched on main at the release commit. It runs ci.yml on every system and on the release's platforms, builds and inspects every package and file, writes the notes, logs in to NuGet and uploads the wheels to TestPyPI, and publishes nothing else. TestPyPI takes a filename once, as PyPI does, so a second dry run passes testpypi: false. The tag An annotated tag v<version> at the release commit, pushed, runs release.yml again from the tag: ci.yml's gates, the packages and the files built and inspected, and the GitHub Release drafted with every file. Then, each after its environment's approval: nuget pushes the four packages and their symbol packages, pypi the wheels, and release publishes the draft. Windows x64 blocks the release: a red there stops the run. Linux's and macOS's test failures are counted in the notes. A bindings leg that can't go green ships best-effort only by the maintainers' decision, named in the repository variable NANOQL_BEST_EFFORT (its runtime identifier) for the tag's run, its red checks listed in the notes; the variable is cleared once the release is out, so the next release's run starts from none. A publishing job that fails partway is not rerun: nuget.org and PyPI each take a version's file once, so the rerun fails at the first file already up, and skipping what is up (--skip-duplicate, skip-existing) would hide a retagged release's files from two commits. Either the files it didn't push go up by hand from the same run's artifact (nanoql-nuget, nanoql-python-*), with a key or token scoped to those packages and deleted once used, or the version is abandoned, unlisted on nuget.org and yanked on PyPI, and the fix ships as the next version. After it: each package installed from its registry and checked (the first swap from NuGet, pip install nanoql with bindings/python/tests/wheel_check.py, each C archive with bindings/c/tests/archive_check.py and a user's C++ project built through its CMake package, bindings/cpp/consumer/, the add-in's zip opened); then the site built from the tag and deployed. Set up once GitHub: the environments nuget, pypi, testpypi and github-release, each with a maintainer as its required reviewer; immutable releases on. NuGet: a trusted publishing policy, owned by the organization that owns the packages, naming the repository, the workflow release.yml and the environment nuget; the nuget environment's secret NUGET_USER, the nuget.org user name of a member of that organization, which NuGet/login exchanges with GitHub's token for a key that lasts an hour. No API key is stored. PyPI and TestPyPI: a trusted publisher on each, naming the repository, release.yml and the environment pypi or testpypi. No token is stored.

docs/sofr-example.html.title: Pricing a USD SOFR swap to match the market | nanoql
docs/sofr-example.html.summary: Pricing a USD SOFR swap to match the market QuantLib's MakeOIS builds an overnight swap from an index and a tenor, taking a default for every option it isn't given. For USD SOFR most of its defaults are already the market's. This example sets the market's conventions in XML, adds them one at a time, and shows what each changes in the price. The quotes are illustrative, made up for the example. The conventions are the market's, as the CFTC describes USD SOFR OIS for its trade execution requirement (Release 8745-23, 2023). The market's convention The market QuantLib's MakeOIS defaults Start spot, two New York business days after the trade two days on SOFR's fixing calendar Both legs annual, Actual/360 annual, Actual/360 Business days New York's SOFR's fixing calendar, the US government securities market's Payment two business days after each period ends at the period's end SOFR fixings on the US government securities calendar the same So the defaults already match the market's frequency, day count and spot lag. Two things differ: the payment lag, and the calendar. New York's business days are the Federal Reserve's, and the government securities calendar closes on days the Federal Reserve doesn't, Good Friday among them. The conventions file holds the market's convention, USD-SOFR, and the two steps toward it from the defaults: <!-- SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 The nanoql Authors SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0 --> <!-- USD SOFR OIS as the CFTC's 2023 trade execution table specifies it: spot (T+2), both legs annual on ACT/360, New York business days (USNY), paid two days after each period ends; SOFR fixed on the US government securities calendar. USNY maps New York's banking days to the Federal Reserve's calendar. "Lag" and "LagAndCalendars" are the steps from QuantLib's MakeOIS defaults toward the market's convention; "USD-SOFR-Dated" is the market's convention without its settlement days, for a swap given its own start date. --> <Conventions xmlns="https://nanoql.org/schemas/conventions"> <Alias name="USNY" base="UnitedStates.FederalReserve" /> <OisConvention name="USD-SOFR"> <Index>Sofr</Index> <SettlementDays>2</SettlementDays> <SettlementCalendar>USNY</SettlementCalendar> <PaymentLag>2</PaymentLag> <PaymentFrequency>Annual</PaymentFrequency> <PaymentCalendar>USNY</PaymentCalendar> <FixedLegCalendar>USNY</FixedLegCalendar> <FixedLegDayCounter>ACT/360</FixedLegDayCounter> <OvernightLegCalendar>USNY</OvernightLegCalendar> </OisConvention> <OisConvention name="Lag"> <Index>Sofr</Index> <PaymentLag>2</PaymentLag> </OisConvention> <OisConvention name="LagAndCalendars"> <Index>Sofr</Index> <SettlementCalendar>USNY</SettlementCalendar> <PaymentLag>2</PaymentLag> <PaymentCalendar>USNY</PaymentCalendar> <FixedLegCalendar>USNY</FixedLegCalendar> <OvernightLegCalendar>USNY</OvernightLegCalendar> </OisConvention> <OisConvention name="USD-SOFR-Dated"> <Index>Sofr</Index> <SettlementCalendar>USNY</SettlementCalendar> <PaymentLag>2</PaymentLag> <PaymentFrequency>Annual</PaymentFrequency> <PaymentCalendar>USNY</PaymentCalendar> <FixedLegCalendar>USNY</FixedLegCalendar> <FixedLegDayCounter>ACT/360</FixedLegDayCounter> <OvernightLegCalendar>USNY</OvernightLegCalendar> </OisConvention> </Conventions> The curve The curve is bootstrapped from nine quotes, 15 October 2026, each a SOFR swap built by the market's convention: var today = new Date(15, Month.October, 2026); var context = new EvaluationContext { EvaluationDate = today }; (Period Tenor, double Rate)[] quotes = [ (new(1, TimeUnit.Months), 0.0430), (new(3, TimeUnit.Months), 0.0428), (new(6, TimeUnit.Months), 0.0421), (new(1, TimeUnit.Years), 0.0405), (new(2, TimeUnit.Years), 0.0380), (new(3, TimeUnit.Years), 0.0368), (new(5, TimeUnit.Years), 0.0360), (new(7, TimeUnit.Years), 0.0362), (new(10, TimeUnit.Years), 0.0370), ]; ConventionSet set = ConventionSet.QuantLib.With(ConventionsXml.Read(conventionsFile)); OisConvention market = set.Ois("USD-SOFR"); OISRateHelper[] helpers = [.. quotes.Select(q => market.RateHelper(q.Rate, q.Tenor, context))]; var curve = new PiecewiseLogLinearDiscount(today, helpers, new Actual365Fixed(), context); Each convention's price Three five-year swaps on $10 million: one at the curve's par rate, one off-market at 4.25%, and one at par starting on Good Friday, 26 March 2027. Each is priced four times, from MakeOIS's defaults to the market's convention: (string Step, MakeOIS Builder)[] steps = [ ("QuantLib's MakeOIS defaults", new MakeOIS(tenor, set.OvernightIndex("Sofr", curve))), ("+ the 2-day payment lag", set.Ois("Lag").Builder(tenor, curve)), ("+ New York business days", set.Ois("LagAndCalendars").Builder(tenor, curve)), ("the market's convention", (start is null ? market : set.Ois("USD-SOFR-Dated")).Builder(tenor, curve)), ]; foreach (var (step, builder) in steps) { OvernightIndexedSwap swap = builder.WithEffectiveDate(start).WithFixedRate(rate).WithNominal(10e6) .ToOvernightIndexedSwap(context); OvernightIndexedSwapResults result = DiscountingSwapEngine.Calculate(swap, context, curve); rows.Add((trade, step, result.NPV!.Value, result.FairRate!.Value)); } Trade Step NPV Fair rate Step's difference par, spot QuantLib's MakeOIS defaults -3.11 3.6000% par, spot + the 2-day payment lag 0.00 3.6000% 3.11 par, spot + New York business days 0.00 3.6000% 0.00 par, spot the market's convention 0.00 3.6000% 0.00 off-market 4.25%, spot QuantLib's MakeOIS defaults -295,785.18 3.6000% off-market 4.25%, spot + the 2-day payment lag -295,701.82 3.6000% 83.36 off-market 4.25%, spot + New York business days -295,701.82 3.6000% 0.00 off-market 4.25%, spot the market's convention -295,701.82 3.6000% 0.00 par, from Good Friday 2027 QuantLib's MakeOIS defaults -26,181.32 3.5416% par, from Good Friday 2027 + the 2-day payment lag -26,176.39 3.5416% 4.93 par, from Good Friday 2027 + New York business days -25,782.41 3.5425% 393.98 par, from Good Friday 2027 the market's convention -25,782.41 3.5425% 0.00 The payment lag moves every trade. Paying two days late discounts each period's net payment over two more days, so its effect grows with the gap between the fixed rate and the floating leg: small at par, larger off-market. The calendars move only the Good Friday trade. Its start, 26 March 2027, and its end, 26 March 2032, are both Good Fridays: on SOFR's fixing calendar both are holidays, and the schedule rolls them to the Monday; on New York's days both stand. The market's convention adds nothing beyond the two: its frequency, day count and spot lag are the defaults'. The Good Friday trade takes USD-SOFR-Dated, the same convention without the spot lag, since a swap given its own start date can't take settlement days too. On the Good Friday trade, the first period accrues from a day SOFR isn't published. The fixing before it, Thursday's, is projected over its own value period, to the next fixing day, and accrues from the period's start, as QuantLib's overnight coupon does. Conventions checked against market prices across many more trades are Masseef's verified catalogue.

docs/stateless.html.title: The stateless design | nanoql
docs/stateless.html.summary: The stateless design Every price nanoql computes is a function of its inputs: the instrument, the evaluation context and the market data the engine takes. Nothing outside them reaches the result, and no call changes what a later one returns. So the same inputs give the same result, bit for bit, whenever and on whichever thread they are priced. Keeping a book's prices current as its market data moves is the application's part: it knows which inputs changed and what depends on them, and calls the library again. This page shows the patterns it builds that layer from. The first three price a ten-year Euribor swap on the curve of the curves guide. Rebuild on change When a quote moves, build the objects that depend on it again from the new inputs, and price on them. The old curve and the prices made on it stand as they were. // A swap is a value: its price is a function of the swap, the context and the curve. static double Price(YieldTermStructure curve, EvaluationContext context) { VanillaSwap swap = new MakeVanillaSwap(new Period(10, TimeUnit.Years), new Euribor6M(curve)) .WithFixedRate(0.027) .WithNominal(10e6) .ToVanillaSwap(context); return DiscountingSwapEngine.Calculate(swap, context, curve).NPV!.Value; } // A quote moves: build the curve again from the new quotes, and price on it. double before = Price(Curves.Build(), context); double after = Price(Curves.Build(shift: 0.0001), context); Quotes NPV as quoted 0.00 +1 bp 8,721.66 Memoize by inputs The same inputs build the same curve, so an application can keep what it has built under a key made of its inputs and share it: an immutable object is safe to read from any number of threads. // The same inputs give the same curve, so a cache keyed by the inputs can share it, across threads too. var curves = new ConcurrentDictionary<double, YieldTermStructure>(); YieldTermStructure CurveFor(double shift) => curves.GetOrAdd(shift, s => Curves.Build(s)); Price scenarios in parallel Scenarios are independent calls on immutable inputs, so they run side by side with no locks, and priced again one after another they give the same bits: double[] shifts = [-0.0050, -0.0025, -0.0010, 0.0, 0.0010, 0.0025, 0.0050]; double[] npvs = new double[shifts.Length]; Parallel.For(0, shifts.Length, i => npvs[i] = Price(CurveFor(shifts[i]), context)); // The same scenarios priced one after another give the same bits. double[] inSequence = [.. shifts.Select(shift => Price(CurveFor(shift), context))]; Shift NPV Change In sequence -50 bp -447,832.36 -447,832.36 the same bits -25 bp -221,007.55 -221,007.55 the same bits -10 bp -87,715.64 -87,715.64 the same bits 0 bp 0.00 0.00 the same bits +10 bp 86,811.36 86,811.36 the same bits +25 bp 215,355.44 215,355.44 the same bits +50 bp 425,218.79 425,218.79 the same bits Run again, in any order or on any number of threads, the scenarios give the same bits. Value as of a past date A valuation reads its date from the context and its market from its arguments, so a valuation as of another date is the same call with that day's inputs: here a swap as of its trade date, and seven months on, on that day's curve and with the fixings the index published since the trade in the context: Date start = new TARGET().Advance(tradeContext.EvaluationDate, 2, TimeUnit.Days); Date later = new TARGET().Advance(tradeContext.EvaluationDate, 7, TimeUnit.Months); static VanillaSwap Trade(YieldTermStructure curve, EvaluationContext context, Date start) => new MakeVanillaSwap(new Period(5, TimeUnit.Years), new Euribor6M(curve)) .WithEffectiveDate(start) .WithFixedRate(0.027) .WithNominal(10e6) .ToVanillaSwap(context); // As of the trade date, on that day's curve. double AtTrade() { YieldTermStructure curve = Curves.Build(); return DiscountingSwapEngine.Calculate(Trade(curve, tradeContext, start), tradeContext, curve).NPV!.Value; } // Seven months on: that day's curve, and the fixings the index published since the trade. (double Npv, int Fixings) SevenMonthsOn() { YieldTermStructure curve = new FlatForward(later, 0.0300, new Actual365Fixed()); var euribor6M = new Euribor6M(curve); IndexFixings fixings = tradeContext.Fixings; double[] published = [0.0251, 0.0262]; int k = 0; foreach (CashFlow flow in Trade(curve, tradeContext, start).FloatingLeg) { if (flow is IborCoupon coupon && coupon.FixingDate() < later) { fixings = fixings.AddFixing(euribor6M, coupon.FixingDate(), published[k++]); } } EvaluationContext context = tradeContext with { EvaluationDate = later, Fixings = fixings }; return (DiscountingSwapEngine.Calculate(Trade(curve, context, start), context, curve).NPV!.Value, k); } As of Curve Fixings NPV 2026-10-15 bootstrapped 0 -116,616.61 2027-05-17 flat 3.00% 2 -7,555.83 Neither valuation reads the other's inputs, so they run in either order, or side by side, with the same results. The one global ConventionProvider.Default, the conventions the library's presets and builders take when nothing else is given, is the one global value (conventions.md). It is read when an object is built, never while it prices: an object keeps the conventions it was built with, and a change of the default reaches the objects built after it. Set it once at start-up, or open a scope with ConventionProvider.Use for one flow's builds; a scope flows with asynchronous calls, as a culture does.

index.html.title: Quantitative finance for .NET | nanoql
index.html.summary: Quantitative finance for .NET, stateless by design. Rates, credit, equity, FX, inflation and commodities, vanilla to exotic; short-rate, market, Heston and SABR models; Monte Carlo and PDE engines. Every pricer is a plain function of its inputs, and market conventions are data you can override. Get started Migrating to nanoql GitHub A first swap Install the package: dotnet add package NanoQL Then price a five-year SOFR swap on a flat curve. The curve, the swap and the evaluation date are values, and the engine is a function of them: using NanoQL; using NanoQL.Indexes; using NanoQL.Instruments; using NanoQL.PricingEngines; using NanoQL.TermStructures; using NanoQL.Time; var today = new Date(15, Month.October, 2026); var context = new EvaluationContext { EvaluationDate = today }; var curve = new FlatForward(today, 0.036, new Actual365Fixed()); var swap = new MakeOIS(new Period(5, TimeUnit.Years), new Sofr(curve)) .WithFixedRate(0.036).WithNominal(10e6) .ToOvernightIndexedSwap(context); var result = DiscountingSwapEngine.Calculate(swap, context, curve); Console.WriteLine($"NPV {result.NPV:N2}, fair rate {result.FairRate:P4}"); It prints: NPV 7,041.24, fair rate 3.6154% Prefer Python? Run this and more in your browser: curves, SABR, options and CDS. Why nanoql Stateless Instruments, curves and models are immutable values, pricers are static functions of them, and the evaluation date is an argument, not a global setting. The same inputs always give the same outputs, and calls run side by side. Conventions as data Calendars, day counts, currencies, indexes and the instrument builders' defaults are XML records: read them, override them for a desk, and version them with your trades. Tested Checked against 3,348,122 independent reference outputs, 99.86% within a relative 1e-10, and the reference library's own tests at their tolerances; 738 departures are each documented and tested. The validation report has the figures, the divergences page each departure. C#, Python, C, C++ and Excel From C# and F#, and from Python, C and C++ through one C interface over nanoql compiled to native code: pip install nanoql needs no .NET runtime, and the C archive serves any language that calls C. In Excel on Windows, an add-in puts the library in worksheet formulas.

The vectors: 3,348,122 reference outputs in 1,169 vector files, of which four files and 39,887 outputs check QLNet's additions against QLNet 1.13.2. Each output agrees within a relative 1e-10 of the larger of the two values and the output's scale (an amount's is its notional), except 4,854 (0.14%) held to a documented looser tolerance. The tests: QuantLib's own tests, ported at QuantLib's tolerances. The types: 2,265 of the 2,266 public types with executable code are run by a QuantLib-checked test, QLNet's additions by a QLNet-checked one. The one apart, FactorReductionFunctions, every output of which is QuantLib's defect fixed, is checked by its own tests. 319 more are listed apart, 291 with no executable code and 28 own-tested (22 of them extensions, five experimental and one a term structure), and three are equality-only. 89.0% of the ported lines are covered. The divergences: 738 documented divergences, 722 from QuantLib and 16 from QLNet, each with its own test class. Measured on commit 5c8c91df48ce8c0afd6205e1d0d8139214e82cc7: 8,728 tests, every one passing, and 60,928 vector cases.
